reviews.author: Leaf_New
reviews.quote:
BEFORE YOU READ: Long exposition of the game can be skipped if you find it unnecessary. 
TLDR: Game is great and many agree for many reasons.

	Splatoon Raiders is a roguelike third-person shooter built around a variety of distinct levels with different clear conditions. The game is the first spinoff of the Splatoon series and the fourth game overall. Going into the game, I was a fan of the mainline series of the competitive 4v4 gameplay and was interested in how this spinoff had changed the core mechanics.
	Starting the game up you play as an anthropomorphic squid or octopus with the ability to switch between a human-like form and a conventional squid or octopus' form. In Splatoon Raiders, these two species are named inkling, as a squid, and octoling, as an octopus. There are no tangible gameplay differences between them. The inkling or octoling you play as is dubbed “The Mechanic” by your compatriots through the game, Deep Cut. Deep Cut is an idol group in the game series composed of an inkling, Frye, an octoling, Shiver, and a manta ray, Big Man. The three of them and the Mechanic are found on a makeshift base called the Hideout Ship after a crash-landing flying over the Spirhalite Islands, the main setting of the game. The Hideout Ship acts as a sort of base of operations for the crew where upgrades to weapons, gadgets, and the ship itself can be done. The game then revolves around joining one of the members of Deep Cut to different remote islands within the Spirhalite Islands and collecting treasure. This treasure is collected with the goal of paying off a debt back in their home city of Splatsville. To get this treasure, Deep Cut and the Mechanic must fight against the Salmonids, a varied enemy species that reside on the Spirhalite Islands.
	From there, the main gameplay loop of Raiders is starting at the Hideout Ship, picking an island to “raid,” and fighting enemy Salmonids that stand in your path. In the game, there are 6 main types of levels to explore and beat, but each individual island has a unique set of challenges to conquer. For example, one type of level will have you face to face with a Mythic Salmonid, a boss enemy far stronger than your average Lesser Salmonid. Another type will have you fight a barrage of Boss Salmonids, enemies that are much weaker than a Mythic Salmonid but a nightmare to deal with in large numbers. This variety of levels and enemies gives Splatoon Raiders significantly more replay value as the way to approach each level can vary significantly depending on what enemies you end up against.
    To even approach any of these levels though, you need some form of weapon. In the game, there are three ways of dealing with enemy salmonid. First is the most basic: your main weapon. You start with a basic shooter type of weapon and unlock new weapons as you continue through the game. These main weapons can have many different modifiers with a level system that increases weapon damage as you level higher. Your second option is your equipped gadget. To start you can only equip one but as you progress you unlock the option to equip up to three. These gadgets act as a secondary option to deal with enemies either through support, movement, or damage. Each gadget is extremely intricate with plenty of upgrades you are able to spec into. The third option is utilizing a chosen Deep Cut member’s special ability called a Showstopper. This special is only useable after filling up the Showstopper Gauge dependent on defeating a certain number of enemies. These specials are very powerful abilities that often wipe out a large number of enemies in one fell swoop. Utilizing these three methods of attack is pivotal in being successful on a per level basis.
    As you progress, each island gains a progressively higher Salmonid Level. These levels make each enemy stronger and bulkier to take down. This is offset by the Mechanic themselves gaining level ups as they make progress. This overall gives the player a lot of agency over the difficulty of the game. It’s ultimately up to the player if they want to tackle a difficult level or wait until they are properly leveled to take on a mission. That player agency is another layer of why the game is fun. I often found that the extra difficult levels made the game much more fun, but you aren’t forced into them, so it gives every player a difficulty level they’d want to play. 
    The game comes loaded with dozens of hours of gameplay in its main campaign, and plenty of post-game content to enjoy. I currently have 100 hours in the game, and I can confidently say that I enjoyed my experience. The blend of smooth controls, weapon and enemy variety, and compelling roguelike gameplay all add to an incredibly well packaged game with an endlessly satisfying postgame. Don't believe me? Look at the Universal Acclaim user reviews!

reviews.author: Filix9842
reviews.quote: Splatoon Raiders viene presentato da Nintendo come un semplice spin-off della serie, dimostrando di essere capace di fare molto di più rispetto a quello mostratoci nei trailer e video di presentazione. Il gioco, punta soprattutto su una stratificazione e ampliamento della modalità cooperativa online presente all'interno dei precedenti titoli, ovvero Salmon Run, estendendo le qualità di quest'ultima con altrettante sfide sempre differenti garantendo anche un'alta varietà di contenuti e un livello di difficoltà eccellente sia per i neofiti che per i **** gameplay seppur non si discosti tanto dalle fondamenta della sega presenta modifiche sostanziali che cambiano l'esperienza del giocatore in base al suo approccio e stile. Miriradi di congegni, serbatoi e armi secondarie garantiscono una grande complessità al gameplay, evolvendosi in modo tattico similmente a quanto accade nei metroidvania. Livelli ben stratificati e costruiti ricchi di ricompense che stringono l'occhio ai fan dei dungeon. Una storia semplice ma efficace che riesce ad espandersi in modo accurato al pari dei riscontri dei titoli precedenti, i **** inoltre sono molto più approfonditi e studiati, sia per i compagni di viaggio che per i salmonidi, la cui storia si approfondisce giocando. Vi è inoltre un alta rigiocabilità dovuta all'evoluzione di livelli già affrontati, a difficoltà estrema, soltanto dopo aver sconfitto il boss della zona garantendo un alta longevità e un aumento sostanziale delle ore di gioco che possono superare le 30 ore totali se si decide di completare inventari, congengni e storie dei ****, altrimenti il titoli si accosta tra le 12 e 15 ore di gioco solo per la storia principale, ma fidatevi se vi dico che riuscirà tranquillamente ad intrettenervi anche dopo aver raggiunto i titoli di coda. Sul piano grafico mi tocca dire di non aver notato importanti differenze rispetto ai titoli su swicht della serie e che forse l'impatto più grande lo si osserva sul piano complessivo che su quello particolare delle singole strutture, tuttavia è giusto considerare il grande lavoro svolto per il design dei salmonidi che per il **** giocabile che come sempre sono soddisfacenti e appaganti allo sguardo. La musica purtroppo risulta essere l'unica pecca effettiva poiché nessuna traccia rientra negli standard della serie, essa si presenta più come un sottofondo ambientale che un punto cardine del gioco. In sostanza Splatoon Raiders è più che un semplice da spin-off da affrontare sia in multiplayer che in singleplayer, versatile nello stile di gioco, nella costruzione del ****, nella composizione dei livelli e la varietà dei contenuti sempre alta e fresca, peccato per la musica che non raggiunge l'iconicità e l'originalità con cui la serie si è fatta conoscere e amare. Consigliato sia a chi approccia la serie e soprattutto ai fan di lunga data per scoprire come Nintendo sia nuovamente riuscita a fare la differenza coj la creatività e lo stupore.

reviews.author: KonP7
reviews.quote: When I played Splatoon 3 on the original Nintendo Switch, I had some serious problems with my internet connection, which unfortunately prevented me from really enjoying the game, even though I found its concept very interesting.Splatoon Raiders takes the core concept of Splatoon 3—inking—and reinterprets it as a single-player experience, while adding new elements such as different tanks and gadgets. The result is a beautiful game with surprising depth that is also incredibly addictive.I would 100% recommend Splatoon Raiders to every Nintendo Switch 2 owner.

reviews.author: Subby-Spaced
reviews.quote: Splatoon Raiders takes everything that the previous 3 titles' story modes, as well as the Octo Expansion and Side Order DLCs, did and improves on nearly every aspect. The gameplay is snappy and responsive, and while the visuals look near-identical to a Switch 1 title, the game makes up for it by swarming you with gigantic hordes of enemies with absolutely zero lag. It's an incredible experience.

Splatoon raiders is an action packed story based shooter. Its mechanics are amazing, the upgrade system works so well and the difficulty is on spot. reviews.author: colcaroi
reviews.quote: Didnt know what to expect for a splatoon spinoff, but apparently this was it. Starts a bit slow and may be a tad bit boring for new players, but once it picks up the pace, the train dont stop till the last station, aka the final boss. A crazy final boss i must say. Got me recreating that one famous clip in hollow knight, the "what am i gonna fight, the sun?" clip. And its amazing how chaotic it is. In the later stages, half your screen is filled with numbers and the other half is just yellow. It may be a lil bit overwhelming, but it gets the dopamine flowing through the veins. Also, theres a lotta replayability to it, you could replay the whole game but harder *T W I C E* and then some. And the amount of loot available is absolutely absurd, itll keep you busy till splatoon 4 releases. Fantastic game, youve outdone yourself, Nintendo. 11/10

reviews.author: gjviquez
reviews.quote: Splatoon Raiders is an entertaining game with fast-paced action, colorful presentation, and a fun selection of weapons that encourages you to experiment with different playstyles. The online co-op mode is one of its strongest features and makes the more chaotic missions considerably more enjoyable.However, the first one or two hours feel unnecessarily slow, and the game takes too long to show its full potential. The bigger problem comes later, when the missions and objectives become extremely repetitive. Instead of introducing enough fresh ideas, the game eventually asks you to replay previous levels at higher difficulties, which feels more like padding than meaningful new content. The enjoyable combat helps, but it cannot completely hide the lack of variety.Overall, Splatoon Raiders has a strong foundation, satisfying weapons, and a genuinely appealing co-op mode, but it does not maintain that freshness throughout the entire experience. I had fun with it, but in my opinion, it is not the masterpiece some people are making it out to be.7/10.

reviews.author: Bola_de_Bolos
reviews.quote: Mecánicas muy divertidas y super adictivo. La sensación de frenetismo que genera en la dificultad más difícil es la gracia del juego.

reviews.author: sgema
reviews.quote:
I like this game and I DON'T even like shooters!

For the amazing 40 hours I've played, this game had an addicting gameplay loop. The numerous gadgets and their swappable parts give a sense of customizability, and my build felt truly personal to me. I just prioritized speed, because that's the playstyle I enjoy. 

It feels amazing to meet up with Deep Cut again and get to know about the shenanigans they are up to. The bosses have the usual crazy Nintendo designs, and the final boss is deserving to join Splatoon's creepy roster of them.

The downsides are the Salmonid's music. I know it fits into the lore, and I exactly understand why they made it like this, but I would love more bangers in this one. The final boss OST slaps tho!

The grind was a little too boring for my taste. If you start upgrading a certain build, it's difficult to change to another one. Bottomless Buffet could definitely include more map variation.

reviews.author: RagnarX213
reviews.quote:
Let's be realistic here. This game has been getting glazed far too much. It's good but it's also incredibly overrated.

The gameplay loop is very repetitive and one dimensional. This game should be $29.99.
It feels incomplete and hollow. Every level is nearly identical and it appears they just sort of copy and pasted each arena/level and they all feel the same. There are times when this feels like a free to play Mobile game. The main game hub feels very empty and unfinished.

The levels can be fun but some are completed within 5 minutes and they are all very very similar. 

One of my biggest disappointments is in regards to the lack of creativity with the level design and platforming.

Splatoon 2's campaign feels much more creative and inspired than any of this. I expected this game to be an expanded version of splatoon 2s solo campaign but it is just a shell of that creativity and innovation.

Decent game, fun in short bursts but a 7 at best

Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 serves as an ideal sequel to an already stellar game by refining the things that matter, dropping the things that don’t, and focusing on vastly expanding the blisteringly fast-paced, brutal action.

Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 not only refines what made the first game good, it polishes out the rough edges, adds more enemies, improves boss fights, brings stronger, grander, more interactive level design, and overall, more 40K. Whether you were a fan of the first Boltgun or diving in now, you're in for a treat.

If you want something you can jump into for a quick gameplay session and have an incredible time blasting through colorful stages and fiendish foes, look no further. Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 delivers fast-paced, exhilarating action that’ll get your heart pumping and your feet stomping. This game gives you that satisfying hit of nostalgia, but with a modern twist that feels charming and unique. With slick gunplay, a brilliant soundtrack, and dozens of tight levels, this is one you won't want to miss.

Warhammer 40K: Boltgun 2 is bigger and more ambitious than the 2023 original, with a new character, more enemies, weapons and places to go in the non-linear campaign. It remains a highly effective homage to classic boomer shooters and Warhammer 40,000. However, while the battles are bigger and more chaotic, there aren’t many changes of pace and the relentless action becomes a bit repetitive if played too long. Still, it’s hard not to recommend Warhammer 40K: Boltgun 2 for fans of retro shooters or Games Workshop’s beloved franchise.

Boltgun 2 is a confident, fast-as-hell, modern boomer shooter. With plenty of different ways to purge, fans of the genre will love to embark on a purge fest as either killing machine Malum Caedo or newcomer Nyra Veyrath, Sister of Battle, who is more of a space ninja. The game’s level design and pixelated vistas are particularly impressive. Without overstaying its welcome, Boltgun 2 is a gory, pixel-styled burst of adrenaline, cut into fun, bite-sized missions.

A nurgling genocide of a sequel that directly addresses almost everything that held the first game back, while still finding time to squeeze in a generous dollop of additional creativity. The best ‘90s FPS you never played.
Warhammer 40K: Boltgun 2 is a solid sequel to a flawed original. It fixes my main issue, with smartly designed levels that help you feel like a proper badass.

Warhammer 40K: Boltgun 2 firmly establishes itself in the old-school essence of the boomer shooter genre. By introducing a branching campaign structure, heightened verticality in level design, and two playable protagonists with distinct combat styles, the sequel evolves its visceral gameplay, even as it stumbles by setting aside the narrative weight and cinematics of the original title.

Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 refines what made the first game fun by adding a greater variety of enemies and weapons, and a second, very fun playable character. If you're in the mood for an old-school-style, ultra-violent FPS (and don't mind dealing with dumb enemy AI), Boltgun 2 is for you.

Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 carries the torch of the original, amplifying its exhilarating gameplay with a compelling new character, detailed enemy and world designs, and level branches that offer a surprising touch of complexity in their objectives. Technical hiccups can lead to moments of frustration that may stunt progress or the flow of action in a few ways. However, the snappy pacing helps keep things moving and context-specific character barks inject personality to round out the gore-geous mess you make in battle. Whether you're a Warhammer die-hard, a classic shooter fan, or simply boomer shooter curious, Boltgun 2 is a genuine blast and well worth your time.

Neon Abyss 2 is a solid addition to today's indie roguelike scene. It manages to stand out thanks to its fun and frantic combat, exploration that encourages experimenting with different builds using randomly discovered items, and challenging enemy design. While its overall structure doesn't feel particularly innovative and its guidance can sometimes be unclear, it's still an experience well worth checking out.
A cracking rogue-like shooter that builds on the solid foundation of the previous game, Neon Abyss 2 offers countless hours of frantic fun.

For better or for worse, Neon Abyss 2 feels very much like more Neon Abyss. But some meaningful changes in progression and permanent upgrades, along with a whole new way to play, make this zany roguelike just as gloriously addictive as the first game ever was.

Overall, I really enjoyed my time with Neon Abyss 2. It’s fun, easy to pick up and play, has a ton of progression systems to keep you hooked, and customization to make runs as easy or hard as you want. I would’ve loved more opportunities to create proper builds rather than having mostly incremental upgrades each run, which could have added an extra layer of complexity that the best-in-class games have.

Neon Abyss 2 is a beautiful sequel, with bolder visuals, flashier weapons and more game-breaking strategies. Unfortunately, the difficulty drops fast once you find the right item combination. The flashy gameplay is fun, but finding a game-breaking strategy happens a bit too quickly. The light show it creates is a joy to behold, yet I couldn’t shake the feeling that I, not the bosses, was the overpowered god of this neon world. A future patch could balance the item drops nicely. Neon Abyss 2 is a great continuation of the franchise that would benefit greatly from some balancing updates. For now, I’ll just go ahead and kill… kill… kill… as I mow through waves of enemies in the variety of game modes on offer. And maybe shoot some hoops with friends in between.
TOEM 2 is a lovely game and a wonderful way to while away an afternoon as the beautiful visuals, hypnotic soundtrack and fun puzzles melt you into your sofa.
Through small refinements and an expansion of its central theme, Toem 2 follows 2021’s breakout with a genial photographic adventure that burrows into the soul and warms you from the inside.

TOEM 2 is a wonderful follow-up to an Indie gem that shows why the first game was so highly regarded. The charm of the world and its characters draws you in, while the puzzles feel good to solve and will require some thought. Not all of the changes stick the landing, and it’s a very short experience, but it’s a worthwhile one.
Toem 2 is another delightful photographic journey that tells us all to slow down as well as explores the power of community.

I’m jealous of newcomers who get to play TOEM 1 and 2 in quick succession. Because they’ll be getting an eight-hour experience that scratches all of the cosy and photographic itches. On its own, TOEM 2 does feel disappointingly short, but it’s also dense with some of the most delightful characters, quests and critters that gaming can find. And as a feet-up,  steamdeck-in-the-armchair experience, I don’t think there’s a game that can beat it.

Toem 2 is a charming and laid-back sequel that expands on the original with larger environments, improved traversal, new tools, and a more dimensional black-and-white world that remains a joy to photograph. Its whimsical characters and distraction-filled exploration make wandering consistently rewarding, even if forgiving progression and underdeveloped puzzle mechanics leave the adventure lacking a stronger challenge ceiling.

Toem 2 is a wonderful little game to explore. It feels like a vacation from the real world with fun gameplay, cute characters and delightful music and sound design. There’s a lot to discover in the world, with plenty of critters to find, tasks to complete and endless silly things to take photos of, so even after completing your journey to the Whirling Birch Bloom, there are still plenty of reasons to come back and add some new photos to your album.

Toem 2 is short, sweet and exceedingly lovely across its runtime. With a simplicity in its design and the overall adventure, it’s not a particularly groundbreaking sequel. But with its devotion to being good (in spirit and in experience) it’s an all-round wonderful time. Play Toem 2 and feel the whimsy wash over you. Like receiving a warm hug, you’ll feel much better afterwards.

TOEM 2 preserves the essence of the original while expanding the experience without losing its cozy charm. Photography remains the main reason to explore every corner, while new tools, smoother movement, and larger worlds make exploration more varied and enjoyable. Its lovable characters, humorous situations, and distinctive art direction remain highlights, although the new features do not radically change the established formula and may feel familiar to returning players. Even so, TOEM 2 offers a charming and competent sequel that prioritizes curiosity and creativity over challenge.

It may play it safe and is perhaps a little too similar to its predecessor, but TOEM 2 is another fantastic adventure game that has you taking photos to solve puzzles. Presented in black and white and an absolute joy to play, what TOEM 2 lacks in colour it more than makes up for in charm.

reviews.author: Mikkikon
reviews.quote:
The original TOEM is one of my favorite games in recent memory, so I was surprised and delighted to hear that a TOEM 2 was under development. I’m older and don’t have a ton of time to devote to gaming, so a bite-sized game that I can use to de-stress in the evenings is exactly what I’m looking for, and TOEM perfectly fits the bill.

The review I’m writing today is different than the review I would have written after only playing the first stage of this game. I say that because while Cropten is a perfectly serviceable “first stage” to introduce players to the game mechanics, it’s a bit on the bland side for those of us who are already familiar with how TOEM works. Thankfully, the following two stages introduce more creative quests and puzzles. That said, I think the original TOEM still has an edge over TOEM 2 when it comes to having a few more challenging, head-scratching quests.

My only major gripe about TOEM 2 is the graphical changes. While I appreciate the improved resolution of the character models, I miss the more cohesive style of the first game, where the objects and environments had the same outlined, papery look as the characters. I found the old art style less disjointed while also more unique and charming. But my strongest argument on this front is more visceral: With the first game, I never thought about the fact that it was in black and white. It just felt right. With this game, I frequently found myself aware of this fact. I think it’s because there is less contrast and more greyscale in the environments. Having said this, the graphics are more detailed this time around, and I think there’s probably a good balance that could be struck in future games if the environments restored a bit more of that contrast and the outlines were made more prominent again.

The music in TOEM introduced me to a genre of music that has come to define the Fall season for me and which I can best describe as “cozy electronic”. TOEM 2 thankfully continues this wonderful tradition, but this time pulls out all the stops! So much of what makes the TOEM games great is the depth and quality of the music and the way it complements the simplicity of the gameplay mechanics. Each of the 3 stages has 9-10 different tunes, and if it weren’t for the fact that all of them are so good, I might complain more loudly that there are too many to fully appreciate given the length of the game. If nothing else, this game has given me a slew of excellent new music from Launchable Socks and Jamal Green to brighten my days.

The new gameplay mechanics were a welcome evolution for me. The new jump feature adds a nice platforming element to the game. The new tools you can use in each stage are pretty basic and it’s always obvious when they’re needed, but they don’t detract from the rest of the experience. The new ability to fall off the map is not as welcome in my opinion—I found myself falling off the map a few times while trying to follow the arrow to the next part of the stage because I neglected to hit the A button at the right time. This seems like an oversight on the dev’s part and I can image new players getting confused and repeatedly walking off the map (since that’s what the arrow is telling them to do). Thankfully there’s no penalty for doing so!

Contrary to the opinion of one reviewer, I found the ending sequences surprisingly emotionally moving, just like the first game. A lot of that is thanks to the music and the way that the TOEM visually contrasts with the rest of the world (no spoilers), but in this case there is also a sentimental and relational element to the ending of the game that I found really charming and beautiful.

I haven’t looked forward to a video game in many years the way that I looked forward to TOEM 2. There’s something wonderfully unique and delightful about this series and I hope that there’s even more to come. If you’re looking for a cozy and relaxing way to wind down the day, you can’t go wrong with TOEM 2.

reviews.author: Mau7trap
reviews.quote:
For a sequel, I'd expect a bit more new stuff and more levels in general, but also some unique areas / biomes. Nothing really surprised me this time around. The new items were a neat gimmick, but used way to few in the game. However, this is as enjoyable as the first title! Great time. 

Maybe try out an open world and first person for TOEM 3? :)

Train Sim World 7 is leaps and bounds ahead of its competitors. Although it feels familiar and there are a few minor issues, I loved it. The traction is fantastic and I love the routes. Moreover, it is hyper realistic. A great game for lovers of trains and sim games.
An excellent new beginners control scheme, plus quality of life improvements and real-time weather effects makes Train Sim World 7 the most accessible and enjoyable entry yet.

Train Sim World 7 requires patience to push through slow tutorials, a steep learning curve, and the lack of Portuguese localization. However, it makes up for these flaws with a satisfying tactile feel in the cabs, gorgeous scenery, and a solid variety of modes. For railway enthusiasts or players seeking a relaxing change of pace, it delivers exactly what it promises.

Train Sim World 7 offers a couple of modest features to entice players of previous games. But ultimately, it will be the upcoming TSW7 exclusive DLC that will be the main draw. The DLC remains as pricey as ever, making it hard to recommend to anyone but hardcore train enthusiasts.

reviews.author: spammer3000
reviews.quote:
An amazing game. Truly brings tears to my eyes. Very nice story, and incredibly accurate physics. Fully fledged out 3rd person, and an immersing plot. Along with ChatGPT Support, this game is fully playable on super low end devices. Also being incredibly realistic, this game is truly a masterpiece. 


Spoiler: Kevin dies at the end of the game, executed by the french revolutionists.

Marsupilami 2 – Salsa Palombia does what a 2D platformer should do—entertain and engage the player and provide a fun diversion to the rest of an ordinary or boring day. Even better when you can share the diversion with a friend.

Marsupilami 2: Salsa Palombia is a platformer that understands what makes the genre such a joy to play. Making use of 3D elements and various gimmicks, the developers managed to make the experience cathartic and impressively varied. Players looking for a vibrant new title in the genre will not find fault with this one.

Even though it perhaps plays it safe, Marsupilami 2: Salsa Palombia is still an undeniably fun and competent platformer. I appreciate its impressive level variety and really enjoyed the boss battles and overall challenge. Sure, it borrows a lot from Donkey Kong Country, but it’s still a worthy adventure that any platformer fan is sure to enjoy.

Simply put, if you enjoy momentum-based platformers, you’ll want to take a closer look at Marsupilami 2: Salsa Palombia. Like other licensed games from the combination of Ocellus Studio and Microids, it’s a lot better than you might expect. It’s a little on the shorter side, and the boss battles aren’t quite up to the rest of the game, but on the whole I found this game to be a real blast.

Marsupilami 2: Salsa Palombia takes some of the best elements from classic 2.5D platformers (like Donkey Kong Country Returns and Rayman Legends) and uses them to craft a wonderful experience that's filled to the brim with colorful environments, catchy music, fast-paced gameplay, and impeccable level design. Only a criminally short duration and some occasional clunky controls are its only real shortcomings. This is a game that everybody should try, from young children who are looking to get into gaming to die-hard fans of the platforming genre.
With a pretty fresh and exciting overall platforming feel, this sequel delivers an improvement over its predecessor, but still has some rough edges.

All in all, Marsupilami 2: Salsa Palombia is a whimsical, high energy platformer that has loads of charm and a delightful soundtrack to boot. The jump in difficulty for the area bosses is a bit of a bummer, as are the forced collectathon elements, but the co-op and solo gameplay experiences are pretty solid. After having been away from the platformer genre for a little while, Marsupilami 2 certainly rekindled that passion in me, and I’m eager to show more of the game to my kids and even pick up the first game if I see it on sale. The Marsupilamis may look like skinny Chester Cheetahs with longer tails, but I’m glad I had a chance to jump and swing along to their world’s salsa beats and be reminded of all the great mascot platformers that have come before and now inspire a new generation of game makers.

Marsupilami 2: Salsa Palomba is a colorful, lighthearted platformer that builds upon the ideas of the first installment but does so in a safe, repetitive manner. While the three playable characters add variety, the level design fails to evolve alongside the mechanics, and the enemies and bosses are virtually identical. The game compensates with a friendly atmosphere, co-op play, and plenty of collectibles, yet it remains a decidedly middle-of-the-road title.
A gorgeous and cleverly designed two‑player co‑op adventure that turns retro anime nostalgia into smart, heartwarming puzzle‑driven storytelling.
Another brilliant, and incredibly varied, co-op title to enjoy with a friend, with a gobsmackingly-good and highly-memorable visual style.

I had high hopes for Orbitals after seeing that beautiful 80s anime style, but I didn’t expect the co-op to be this creative. We had a lot of fun figuring out the puzzles while messing around with all the different tools and discovering whatever strange idea the game had waiting for us next. I also love that it doesn’t really care who does what, swap tools, switch roles, and figure it out together works incredibly well, whether you play games every day or barely touch them. There really isn’t much I would change here; Orbitals is exactly the kind of co-op adventure I love to play.

Ultimately, Orbitals is a standout exclusive on the Nintendo Switch 2, one more indicative of a first-party release than a debut title from a new studio, making it an absolute must-play for owners of Nintendo’s latest hybrid console.

It feels like we’re still just scratching the surface of what co-op only games can be with the likes of A Way Out, Split Fiction, and now Orbitals. Orbitals is full to bursting with incredible ideas, more than it can properly execute on, but it remains an incredible, fun, and charming experience the whole way through.
Whether it’s due to the visuals, a puzzle’s solution, or from bumping into a screaming alien creature, Orbitals is awe-inspiring.
Orbitals is an absolute must-play for the discerning co-op sickos among us, pairing fiendishly clever puzzle design with a crisp, gorgeous retro anime aesthetic.

Orbitals is a dazzling audiovisual achievement and a brilliantly designed co-op adventure, combining the spirit of classic ’80s and ’90s anime with a constant stream of inventive ideas. Its only real flaw is that such a wonderful journey ends far too soon.

After playing it in local multiplayer on a single console, Orbitals is shaping up to be one of the most interesting co-op games coming to Nintendo Switch 2 this year. Its biggest strength is that all of its different elements seem to work together toward the same goal. The anime-inspired aesthetic isn’t separate from the gameplay, co-op doesn’t feel like an afterthought, and everything fits together seamlessly.

Orbitals is a fantastic game that uses its inspirations to the highest degree. The art design and aesthetic are a true triumph. Interlacing the cooperative video game genre with the themes of 80’s mecha anime series is executed well.

reviews.author: Tom23x
reviews.quote: Orbitals style is fantastic, probably one of my favourite looking games of the last few years. The puzzles are quite fun but unfortunately can be too easy at points. Also how forgiving the respawns are is almost laughable. There is literally no reason not to brute yourself through as you just get another shot at the thing that just killed you. The platforming was fun and how you interact with eachother is amusing and a highlight of the gameplay. The game is super short too. We finished it in 3 sittings. Its a shame as a single player game similar to this with higher difficulty could be an incredible time. Whereas currently this game, despite being gorgeous and fun at times, will probably be forgotten sooner rather than later.

reviews.author: Garoozies
reviews.quote:
6 - Good.
Artistically, I enjoy this game more than either of the Hazelight co-op releases. Genuinely perfect realization of the 80’s anime aesthetic put in smooth and snappy 3D motion. The narrative tone and character tropes from that era are also revived with great fidelity. Continuing the comparison with Hazelight, Orbitals’ decision to decouple unique mechanics from the 2 selectable player characters was a great change. My wife and I would take turns using different tools and not being restricted to playing with only one half of the games unique mechanics was very nice. I also enjoyed having a proper hub to hang around at and play mini games. Where orbitals doesn’t quite reach Hazelights pedigree is in its level and boss design. They don’t commit any grave sins, but don’t push the envelope further in any respect. The co-op traversal puzzles are a little samey - a product of using the same 4 tools from start to end. A potentially better system allowing for more puzzle diversity could’ve been to have all these tools at each characters disposal on something like an item wheel to switch between on the fly, making even the act of selecting between them a puzzle of its own. Lastly, I feel it’s important to note that evaluating this game as a product highlights one regrettable flaw - it’s an incredibly short game. Comparable in content to StarFox 64, but the latter is a lot more replayable.  Important to consider when making your purchase.

reviews.author: tom974
reviews.quote: Ce jeu m'a avant tout embarqué par son esthétique folle, nous laissant cette impression de jouer dans un anime des années 80-90, doublage et ambiance de qualité en prime, un vrai tour de force. Le gameplay coop quant à lui est bien travaillé, de la vraie coop, assez classique mais toujours plaisante. Le tout dans une histoire à mon goût un peu courte mais que l'on a pris tout de même énormément de plaisir à parcourir.

reviews.author: MongerStronger
reviews.quote:
This is a very good game and you can tell that it has been made with a lot of love. 
Visuals are stunning and It is very fun to play overall.
For me it is a bit short and it is one or two steps below the benchmark in the genre: It takes two / Split Fiction.
It comes complete on the cartridge and that's a big plus, I am supporting them for that. Got my copy for 40€ and that's a fair price.

reviews.author: Pr0methiumX
reviews.quote:
This game did not meet my expectations. To be fair, all I had heard about this game was that is was a Co-Op game akin to It Takes Two set in space and in a retro anime style, which it definitely is. But I guess I overestimated the depth of the game's systems. I found the ship navigation/combat to be woefully simple. Even when my partner and I had some difficulty, it was never for long. And there was not nearly enough of it. Outside of the visual style, the atmosphere of the space environments felt dull and further added to my boredom while playing through the ship portions. The puzzle platformer sections are more enjoyable, but for the most part very simplistic and equally linear. My partner (who is a fairly casual gamer) agreed that the puzzles were pretty easy. Why does the game tell you what items you need before starting a mission? Doesn't that remove all the trial and error that comes with a puzzle game??? We breezed through the game in about 6 hours. The final main area is when the game finally started to feel like iNarratively, the story is lackluster. Plot information is exposited and then suddenly reintroduced with great import but zero emotional weight. The characters are shallow archetypes, which definitely fits in with the retro anime style, but is frustrating when so much of the emotional arc hinges on you buying into the main characters emotional connection with the colony and it's inhabitants, and I felt none of that. How am I supposed to care about a home base when you spend absolutely zero time there? 

Overall, I got caught up in the hype, and was left wanting much more than this game could deliver. Orbitals is all flash, and very little substance.

Nearly four decades later, Flying Shark and Fire Shark still deliver taut shooting, and M2 surrounds them with an abundance of modes, assists, and informative Gadgets. Some variations feel redundant, but this remains an sky-high STG package for genre fans.
M2's superb arcade preservation shows why one of Toaplan's classics remains so playable, even if the modern UI can get in the way.

Toaplan Arcade Garage: Flying Fire Shark is another meticulously crafted M2 release that preserves two foundational STG classics with exceptional accuracy, minimal input latency, regional variants, training tools, and informative gadgets. The high asking price and separately sold console versions make the package harder to recommend to casual players, but dedicated shoot ’em up fans will find one of the best ways to experience Flying Shark and Fire Shark.

Toaplan Arcade Garage: Flying Fire Shark is mostly aimed at the hardcore players who want the absolute best takes on these games they can buy. You really only get two games here, and you’re not losing that much by playing them in Toaplan Arcade Collection Vol. 1 instead. With that said, the outstanding practice mode might prove to be the key for newcomers looking to properly get into Toaplan’s brand of shoot ’em up action. This isn’t going to be the best option for everyone, but if you don’t mind spending a little more to get the best possible experience with these games on Nintendo Switch, Flying Fire Shark is where it’s at.

ReStory is a relaxing game that combines the laid-back sense of accomplishment from repairing things with a well-designed gameplay loop that keeps you coming back for more. It’s almost hard to believe that scrubbing down metal frames and twisting screws could be such a pleasant activity, but I can’t stop doing it to unwind. If you’re in the market for a chill game that scratches your brain in a totally unique way, you cannot miss ReStory.

ReStory: Chill Electronics Repairs far surpasses all expectations, being one of the most immersive experiences in the genre. By combining extremely enjoyable gameplay, attention to atmosphere, a huge catalog of technological relics, and a narrative anchored by a humanized protagonist—even if the narrative pace can drag a little at times—the title from Mandragora Studio delivers much more than just another task simulator.

At this point in 2026 I have played a lot of video games for review, and I haven’t even begun to think about my GOTY list. But I can tell you right now, without a shadow of a doubt that ReStory: Chill Electronics Repair will make my list. I found myself just enthralled with the gameplay and its loop; earning money to get better licenses, especially for stuff I actually owned. I cannot recommend ReStory enough, its blend of great vibes, chill music and wacky customers is just what the doctor ordered for a quiet night in.

Gorgeously presented and utterly moreish, ReStory has you running your own electronics repair shop that sees you disassembling iconic tech from the early 2000s. There's a careful balance between realism and entertainment here, and developer Mandragora has absolutely nailed it.

ReStory: Chill Electronics Repairs delivers a deeply satisfying and nostalgic experience set in mid-2000s Tokyo. It blends authentic hardware restoration mechanics with a compelling, character-driven narrative. While the painting system lacks depth and long sessions reveal repetitive loops, the tactile joy of repairing retro tech makes this a standout cozy title.

ReStory: Chill Electronics Repairs is proof that you don’t really need a compelling story when taking apart old gadgets is this darn satisfying. Its Y2K nostalgia, detailed machines, and addictive restoration work make it an easy game to sink hours into, even if its characters struggle to keep up. What’s important is the work in front of you, and that’s enough to send you into a flow state of endless tinkering.
This cosy shop sim combines 2000s nostalgia, restoration mechanics and a turbulent storyline for hours of fiddly fun.

ReStory is a chill repair shoppe simulator. It’s got a fairly accurate representation of how devices are actually repaired pat down, accompanied a pleasant visual style and a strange little story that moves along as you build up your corner store. Perfect for the dood that loves making old hardware talk or someone who just wants to get through their audiobooks but has the attention span of a cat sitting near a laser pointer and a box of treats.

For a simulation title, ReStory: Chill Electronics Repairs is exceptional, giving you a great simulation of a very niche idea in an even more niche setting. That being said, the game’s main mechanic could use more complexity, and the loop can get a bit repetitive and grindy, making the game best enjoyed in short bursts.

ReStory: Chill Electronics Repairs takes a genuinely niche premise and turns it into one of the most relaxing and surprisingly fun simulators I’ve played in a long time. You don’t need to own a soldering iron or care about vintage tech to fall for this one. The narrative mystery alone will grab you. If you do care about electronics repairs, however, then I suggest you prepare yourself for your newest addiction.

HellSlave II: Judgment of the Archon, from developer Ars Goetia, is a fun turn-based RPG with a strong narrative, solid world-building, a deep backend system, and plenty of adventures throughout. It’s fun, impressive, and a lot more than I expected.
HellSlave II's combat, lovely art, and fantastic sound design make for a thoroughly absorbing dungeon crawler, that escapes a lot of the tedium inherent to the genre.
HellSlave II: Judgment of the Archon is a unique and deeply charming RPG. It's a lot of fun, but slightly held back by some unfortunate design decisions.

For a game made by a solo developer, HellSlave II: Judgment of the Archon is impressive and outright inspiring. Small problems persist, but overall the game features incredible art, a strong narrative and setting, and turn-based RPG combat that is not only incredibly fun, but also has more exciting to use and uniquely designed abilities than you’d find in a lot of games in the genre.

HellSlave II: Judgment of the Archon is a bigger, meaner sequel with a long, build-heavy campaign that makes its $19.99 price feel generous. Its time-based combat, six-class foundation, Demonic Path corruption, and hand-drawn art make it one of the most distinctive dark fantasy RPGs on PC this year, held back by a repetitive late-game loop, loot bloat, and missing quality of life features.

HellSlave II: Judgment of the Archon is a great take on role-playing mechanics for longtime fans of the genre who are looking for a hardcore experience. Variety, starting with classes and demon allegiances and progressing to skill and equipment, makes it interesting for each gamer to discover a favorite way to approach combat and then build a character that comes as close as possible to breaking the core mechanics. The narrative works off a strong premise, but dialogue isn’t great at building on that, and I suspect many players will not take the time to read collectible lore scrolls. Combat can also frustrate, sometimes through difficulty spikes and often by being slow at the worst of times. HellSlave II is an obvious labor of love that shines when the battle mechanics work just right.

Solo developer Ars Goetia has released a sequel to the dark fantasy RPG, featuring combat in the style of classic dungeon crawlers but with practical improvements. The game will be appreciated not only by fans of the original title but also by new players.

The largest strength of Lunarium is easily the bond between Ave and Lune, both narratively and gameplay-wise. In that regard, I feel this beautiful ARPG largely succeeds in what it sets out to tell. Even with the game being admittedly difficult, especially in light of my inability to effectively parry much of the time, I had genuine fun with it. I felt so much as I uncovered its various story beats and watched the two heroines grow together. For what it does well, Lunarium is a compellingly insightful action RPG with Soulslike elements, and it certainly deserves to be viewed as a shining star of the indie ARPG scene.

Lunarium is an action-rpg permeating with a wistful atmosphere that delicately embraces the best aspects of the souls-like genre while forgoing much of what can make them frustrating. While the boss battles never quite reach the heights that some other works in the souls-like genre do, the encounters prove to be regularly rewarding and enthralling throughout thanks to the tightly crafted risk and reward systems in place. With the adventure led forward by a delightful pair of protagonists who regularly outshine the rather forgettable narrative, what remains is a consistently satisfying and accessible adventure that is easy to recommend to just about anyone.

Without the technical issues, Lunarium is a solid ARPG that deserves your attention. If seeing clips or images of the game gets you at all interested, you’ll most likely enjoy what Lunarium has to offer (given the bugs are fixed). Its pleasant art style, grandiose soundtrack, and deep combat system kept me engaged, but the myriad of bugs and awkwardness in dialogue kept me from fully clicking with the whole package.

Lunarium is a quietly impressive first outing, built on genuinely phenomenal atmosphere, a story that’s simple but never dull, and a combat system that thoughtfully teaches players before it tests them. It stumbles a bit with a combat toolkit that could use more depth and a few technical issues still being smoothed out, but neither is enough to sink an experience this well put together. For players who want something serene, soulslite-adjacent, and genuinely beautiful to look at, Lunarium is well worth the trip.

Lunarium is a beautifully crafted action RPG, with an amazing atmosphere and stunning visuals. The fact that its world is fully handmade adds a lot of charm, and it makes the title way more approachable and interesting. But the true focus of the game is on combat, and for the most part, it excels at that. Lunarium is not a difficult game, instead it’s made to be approachable, yet it certainly has its challenging moments. The protagonists are great and the story is serviceable, making the romp into this world a very interesting and rather unique experience. Its soulslike roots might push some people away, but the visual style, attention to detail and incredible quality certainly pulls you in. It’s a fun one to play this summer, as its light story and immersive gameplay will help you unwind and relax.

Dodo Duckie is a pleasant surprise in the platforming game scene. By making the alternation between 2D and 3D perspectives the foundation of its level design, the title delivers ingenious puzzles and a calibrated learning curve, featuring charming art direction and a pace that entertains both newcomers and veterans.

It’s absolutely adorable and it’s got a neat gimmick, but it doesn’t just rest on those things to try to sell itself – it has gameplay that really delivers, too. It’s a neat, ambitious combination that’s a must-play for any platforming fan, regardless of how many dimensions you want the game to be in.
If you like platforming puzzlers and think that the mechanic of shifting 2D and 3D sounds interesting, you should pick this one up. It’ll be good, simple fun that you won’t regret.
A solid platformer puzzle experience that never becomes frustrating and is welcoming in its gameplay simplicity. That being said, there have been too many bugs, which bogged down my experience.

I really wanted to love Dodo Duckie, and for stretches of the game, I did. The dimensional puzzle mechanic is clever, easy to understand, and capable of producing exactly the kind of satisfying “aha” moments that puzzle platformers live or die by, but eventually I stopped wondering why more games don’t do this. I started understanding why; perspective shifting requires an enormous amount of precision from both the player and the game. When that relationship works, Dodo Duckie feels inventive. When it doesn’t, you fall off something you were convinced you were standing on. The technical problems make that harder to forgive. Being softlocked near the end of the ice level wasn’t simply an inconvenience; it undermined the trust that puzzle games depend on. There is still plenty here that I enjoyed. The presentation has charm, the concept has real potential, and some puzzles genuinely made me stop and reconsider the space around me. But Dodo Duckie feels like a game whose ambition slightly outpaces its execution. That leaves me in a strange place, mainly because I don’t regret playing it, but I still hate that I couldn’t finish it in the way I wanted to. I genuinely hope the developers keep exploring this idea, but I just hope that next time, switching dimensions feels as effortless as understanding why you’d want to.

reviews.author: vksamhith
reviews.quote:
Dodo Duckie has a clever mechanic that also is its narrative hook!

Clever puzzles that are rewarding instead of being frustrating. The pacing is well done without any extra padding. And Dodo and its cast of charming characters are clearly the highlight for me!

An easy recommendation for anyone who likes puzzle adventures or is new to platformers!

Toy Story: Retro Roundup is an incredibly well put-together compilation of some underrated classics from Disney Interactive Studios. A vast majority of the games within the collection have held up particularly well, and are given more room to shine thanks to the behind the scenes features. While not every game has stood the test of time, the abundance of new quality-of-life options means that even newcomers can enjoy the most infuriating of titles within. The work and effort put into Retro Roundup has established it as one of Digital Eclipse's best works to date, and a must-play for any Pixar/Toy Story fan.

Toy Story: Retro Roundup! is another banger of a remaster collection from the best studio doing it, but it's also an incredibly validating slice of the culture that is often overlooked or mocked – the "movie game." By paying respects to the artists making monuments out of marketing, Digital Eclipse has put together a remarkable package full of great games, and great insights.

In its careful historical preservation and attention to detail, Toy Story: Retro Roundup! is flawless. However, this unwavering fidelity to the past carries the weight of decades: without adjustments to soften the impact of the years and relying only on a few external tricks to overcome its limitations, both outdated mechanics and visuals may frustrate those seeking even a minimal contemporary experience. This will certainly test the player's patience.
Toy Story: Retro Roundup! is a great compilation, as it includes almost all the major games in the series, along with several interesting extras.

Toy Story: Retro Roundup is filled with tons of great modern-day features and extras that make it a great choice for anyone who played these games in the past and wants a burst of nostalgia. The games feel very smooth, but maybe dodge the Game Boy ports and Buzz Lightyear of Star Command.

The best parts of Alien Isolation and Resident Evil's first-person entries have merged with Silent Hill's rusty and foggy DNA to create an original nightmarish take on the series. Silent Hill: Townfall is a breath of fresh air for the genre and a must-play for horror fans.

Silent Hill: Townfall pushes the series’ modern revival to new heights with a gripping, unpredictable narrative, terrifying first-person atmosphere, inventive puzzles, and tense survival horror combat. Despite a few uneven moments in its resource balancing, Townfall confidently reimagines what a Silent Hill game can be while remaining faithful to the franchise’s psychological horror roots.

The best instalment since the opening trilogy, Silent Hill: Townfall’s shift to first-person and evocative Scottish setting make for the creepiest and most involving experience of the franchise’s reboot era. By merging the unsettling aesthetic of Silent Hill with the stealth-and-hide tension of Alien: Isolation, and placing it in the realm of retro folk horror, Screen Burn have crafted one of gaming’s most edge-of-your-seat experiences.

Silent Hill: Townfall is a stunning spin-off for the series, taking to a new setting and telling its own unique story, expanding your ideas of what exactly a Silent Hill experience can be. With a semi-open world littered with tense corners to explore, creative puzzles to unravel and heaps of analogue nostalgia – Townfall never outstays its welcome, and we are so ready to dive in again.

Silent Hill: Townfall is another brave step forward for the franchise. Moving away from the traditional third-person perspective heightens the dread and anxiety, as you tentatively avoid the many threats that linger within. Puzzles are wonderfully integrated into the world, making each task feel like a natural part of the experience. Although you’re given the tools to fight back, the peek mechanic alongside the CRTV encourages stealth, which fits with the game's oppressive atmosphere. Each aspect coalesces into a relentless experience that stands as another confident evolution of the legendary horror series.
Silent Hill: Townfall is the most atmospheric and frightening survival horror game the series has delivered in years. It feels different from any other game that I’ve ever played, in fact.

Silent Hill: Townfall is not only an amazing horror game, but it’s also a fantastic Silent Hill game. While the new focus on stealth over combat may not satisfy all fans of the franchise, those looking for a highly engrossing horror experience will find plenty to love here.

Konami's bold choices regarding Silent Hill: Townfall turn out to be anything but regrettable.  With developer Screen Burn taking at the helm, Townfall enters the Silent Hill universe as a profound first-person experience, tapping into the psychological aftermath of regret, in all its shapes and sizes. Only the obscurity of some puzzles and occasional performance issues withhold Townfall from perfection, and that's a claim I won't regret making.

Silent Hill: Townfall is yet another unique and brilliant entry in the Silent Hill series, placing more emphasis on stealth and puzzle solving. It's the story at the heart of the game that's its biggest asset, though, keeping you wondering what exactly happened in the picturesque town of St. Amelia.
Silent Hill: Townfall offers up one of the most tense and compelling survival horror experiences in recent years, as long as you're willing to meet it on its own terms.

reviews.author: balie
reviews.quote: Silent Hill Townfall is a solid entry in the series that changes the setting again to another spooky town, called St. Amelia. You play as Simon, who has washed up on the docks of the town, confused and clueless, with only one instruction - find Zoe. You pick up a CRTV radio that is used to navigate the town, find clues and detect monsters. It is used to great effect and an interesting part of the gameplay. This is a fist-person game that revolves around you sneaking from cover to cover, trying to avoid the monsters as much as you can, as combat is quite brutal. It feels a bit like Alien Isolation at times and has some very spooky, scary moments as well. The melee combat is visceral and your weapons break easily. Ammo for firearms is also scarce in the ealry sections of the game, so stealth is heavily encouraged. The town is dripping with atmosphere, with fantastic visuals that really sell the spooky, isolated feeling of being in the empty, foggy streets. Building interiors are also incredibly detailed to an almost photo-realistic level. The monster designs are also good, albeit with little variety, with some of them being genuinely terrifying. The story is as cryptic and confusing as any other Silent Hill game, but was kept things interesting and made me want to keep on playing to see how it ends. The only problem I really have with the game is some pacing issues. There are one or two sequences (one in particular at the end of the game, but I believe it got improved with a patch afterwards) that were just very frustrating and drags down the pace of the game. Other than that, I had a great time with Silent Hill Townfall - a genuinely scary, spooky, interesting game.

reviews.author: DonSmiguel13
reviews.quote:
I'm tired of all the uncs complaining about the newer Silent Hill entries. Sure, they're not perfect, but they're still very good games.

I think most fans of the original trilogy would love it if Konami just recycled the same old tropes and ideas over and over again. They don't seem to realize that more than 20 years have passed since the original trilogy, and we need to move forward and try new things. Would you really want Konami to keep putting out the same games they made 20 years ago, with the same janky controls, set in the same city and featuring the same locations? And don't get me wrong, I love the older entries, especially SH3, but I'm just tired of people whining about every new game in the series. I even saw some people somehow managing to find fault with the first-person perspective. God forbid the developers try something new. I couldn't care less whether it's a first-, second-, third-, or fourth-person perspective. It doesn't make a game good or bad; it's just a creative choice, and I think it works great for Silent Hill. Of course, I've also seen people claiming the game is woke simply because the protagonist is **** can you take these people seriously?

Sorry, but reading all that **** just makes me angry. Anyway, back to Townfall.

Positives: The story is amazing, the graphics are really good, and the town is incredibly detailed and has an amazing atmosphere. It's the scariest SH game IMO. The puzzles are the best in the series, apart from a few where the solutions were... let's just say, really out there. I also really liked how scarce ammo and healing items are, unlike in SH2 Remake, where I ended up with way too many supplies by the end, making the game too easy. The scarcity forces you to make use of stealth and think twice before wasting your ammo.

Negatives: The combat is a mixed bag for me. You die really easily, which isn't necessarily a bad thing, but the combat itself feels very janky, simplistic, and repetitive. The enemy variety is also pretty limited. Another issue is that the stealth can be a bit lackluster at times. There's a section in the game (I think they fixed this issue in a patch, but anyway) where a boss enemy stalks you and you have to sneak around an area. If he catches you, it's an instant kill. The problem is that he seems to always know which room you're in and will camp the entrance for literally minutes instead of patrolling the area properly.

Anyway, to sum it all up, it's a bit of a janky game, but for me, the atmosphere, story, and horror more than make up for its shortcomings.

Also a creature named The Weight recalls the Xenomorph. And while puzzles have always been a big part of the franchise, they are even more numerous in this entry. Personally, I think developer Screen Burn went overboard with them. Still, “Townfall” is a visually stylish horror ride with a compelling storyline. reviews.author: yourmomisaboot
reviews.quote:
A solid Silent Hill story hamstrung by truly unenjoyable gameplay. 

In terms of story and atmosphere, the game did a fairly good job of staying true to the SH formula. Aka an unreliable narrator trapped in a hellscape of their own making while dealing with the trauma and fallout from a terrible event.

The puzzles, another hallmark of SH games we're... ok. One or two good ones, one or two bad ones, but the majority was simply following literal instructions to operate machinery. Making most of them just feel like a time wasting chore in the end.

However this means very little in the end, as the combat aspects of the game are truly unforgivable. I've seen a lot of back forth regarding the stealth mechanics. People heavy criticizing it, followed by people defending it and calling the former unskilled or worse. So I'll try to lay it out a little more objectively, though you can guess my final opinion based on the context so far. Minor gameplay spoilers follow.

Your melee weapons have durability, both when attacking and blocking. Meaning that even when playing well, you'll be able to take out a few enemies at best per weapon on normal. Far below the rate at which you are provided with them by the game. "Playing well" being a very key operative here, as the enemies are relentless with their attacks. With no sort of dodge mechanic, and rather slow player speed your only option is to block attacks, which are frequent. Beyond that, they will often retaliate from your strikes nearly immediately, sometimes before you are even able to put your block back up. Alongside this, 2 of the only 4 (3.5 really) enemy types in the game have an unlockable grab attack with zero animation tell beforehand.

All that to say that melee combat is practically untenable, only to be used in dire situations and will require a trade-off in healing items. Ranged weapons do exist, but the ammo economy is equally abysmal and the noise they cause directly contradicts their focus on stealth. Therefore you are HEAVILY incentivized to stealth past the majority of enemies, utilizing the awkward handheld device to detect the enemies location.

This could be forgivable if the act of stealthing past enemies wasn't equal parts boring and frustrating. Their patrol paths are set, and placed directly where you need to go with no way to go around them. Often in the middle of areas you have to traipse back and forth through multiple times. They pause in awkward spots for awkwardly long times, forcing you to wait for them to move on. 

And sneak you must, as running is not really an option. Every enemy is faster than you, or has ranged attacks that don't miss, all while still somehow keeping pace with you. You could be willing to trade health to simply run past, but again, you are often running back and forth in the same area meaning you don't ever really have anywhere to escape past them to. This of course is not counting the special enemy in a few parts of the game, that always knows where you are, doesn't leave the room even if you hide, and can't be killed.  

So everyone saying that stealth is only a small portion of the game, or that it's not that bad, are in my eyes being disingenuous if not outright lying. 

I hate quitting games, and do enjoy Silent Hill's atmosphere so I slogged through enough for one ending. But I can honestly say, that this is one of the most unfun and frustrating games I've played in a very long time. If I could go back in time and tell my past self I would, to save the $50 I spent on this.

reviews.author: mspiz
reviews.quote:
I want to say that I specifically created an account to write a review for this game as no other game has frustrated me to this level before. Generally I can make it through  games that were designed to be frustrating but this on the other hand seems it was just never play-tested, or at least not play-tested by someone not affiliated with the development team leading to some absolutely baffling design choices and balancing issues. 

The issue in question is at one point in the game you control Simon and have to navigate a warped version of a hospital. It's at this point the game introduces a new enemy called The Weight, which is extremely fast, un-killable and can kill you from full health if it catches you. The enemy is also generally tethered to Simon's location so it will always be near you. That's all well and good however in the area you first encounter this enemy there is also another minor enemy floating around and you're in a tight hallway with only two directions you can go in and several rooms on the outer perimeter. 

You're supposed to maneuver around all this to try and proceed further so I make it into an open room and hide even though none of the enemies saw me. The Weight rushes into the room, where eventually the smaller enemy stumbles in as well. The Weight leaves first and is now camping the hallway to the right, and then the other enemy SLOWLY leaves and stumbles to the hallway on the left. You barely have any time to act as now The Weight comes rushing back in the room, even though you remain hidden, and that brings the smaller enemy back in. This cycle repeats over and over and over, like it was a purposely designed soft-lock. If you rush out of the room to the right you're bump into The Weight and immediately die. If you go to the left you'll have no choice but to deal with the smaller enemy, which can be killed, however the noise from dealing with that will bring The Weight over which is close by since it's tethered to Simon's location. 

Like what the hell is that? If it was an open space I could see this being fine but you have two enemies in tight hallways blocking your path with no way to proceed without possibly taking a death and revive (if you have the blood bag), then making you bee-line to whatever it is you have to do. If you're going to base a game around stealth gameplay you need to be able to give the player options to deal with what's around you and the solution should not be take a death and hope for the best. There's also a cheese method where if you're quick enough you can lock The Weight in a room in a floor above you but I haven't been able to pull off, but yet again, players shouldn't have to rely on cheese either in order to proceed. 

This is an issue that apparently the developer is aware of and was supposedly looking into enemy behavior, but that's something I read about around a week ago and so far no fix has been implemented. I attempted this part of the game again today and became so frustrated with it I uninstalled it. Call it a skill issue, or "git gud", I don't care. I've played some absolutely frustrating games before, which were designed to be that way, which I have pushed through and overall enjoyed myself but when playing this game you can clearly see the failure on the devs part to actually playtest their game and look at the game from the perspective of a customer that doesn't know all the nuances behind enemy behavior etc. 

Due to this I absolutely cannot recommend this game. I wanted to like it and up until this point I generally did, and thought it was mostly fair even though there were some other frustrating parts as well but those could be dealt with. As of right now this will just test your patience and further annoy you once you realize you spent $50 to rage quit.

reviews.author: My_OS
reviews.quote:

reviews.author: honayo
reviews.quote:
I genuinely regret buying this game, especially at €50.
I went into Silent Hill: Townfall with high expectations because I absolutely loved Silent Hill 2. Unfortunately, Townfall has been one of the most frustrating gaming experiences I've had in a long time.
My biggest problem isn't that the puzzles are difficult. It's that the game constantly fails to communicate what it actually wants you to do. So much of the experience consists of wandering around looking for a tiny clue, a key, a code, a specific door or some obscure interaction before you can progress.
The hospital section was where I completely lost patience. X-ray settings, medication, intubation, collecting blood bags, matching patients, valves, locked gates and an enemy chasing you while you're trying to figure out where the game even expects you to go. None of this felt scary to me. It felt exhausting.
Then I finally finished that section thinking the game might open up or improve, only to reach Clara Woods and immediately get thrown back into the same loop: find a locker code, get a key, enter a house, search for another key, find disks, leave the house again, go somewhere else to get something needed for the disks, then return to the house. It feels like excessive backtracking designed to stretch out the playtime rather than meaningful exploration.
That's the biggest disappointment: I don't feel scared, tense or intrigued. I feel annoyed. Silent Hill 2 made me want to explore because I was invested in the atmosphere, characters and mystery. Townfall regularly makes me want to look up a walkthrough simply so I can stop wandering around and continue the story.
I'm well over halfway through and at this point I'm basically forcing myself to finish it because I already spent €50 on it. I've actually turned the game off multiple times after only a few minutes because I couldn't deal with another round of searching rooms for whatever arbitrary item the game wants next.
Maybe this style of puzzle-heavy exploration works for some people, but it absolutely does not work for me. I expected psychological horror and the atmosphere that made me love Silent Hill. Instead, most of my playtime has felt like fighting the game's navigation and progression design.
€50 is way too much for an experience I've had to force myself to continue. One of my biggest gaming disappointments in a long time.

The technical state of the game only makes the frustration worse. The controls can feel weird and unresponsive at times, and I've encountered several bugs that genuinely interfere with the gameplay. I've had graphical glitches, attacks clearly connect with enemies without any damage being registered, and enemies seemingly teleport from one side of an area directly to where I'm standing. Sometimes enemies even appear to glitch straight through attacks. In a game where encounters can already be frustrating, issues like these make deaths feel cheap rather than deserved. Instead of creating tension, the game often leaves me wondering whether I actually made a mistake or whether something simply didn't work properly.
That's another reason the experience has been so exhausting. I can accept dying because I played badly. What I can't stand is dying because an enemy suddenly teleports across the room, ignores an attack that clearly connected, or because the controls don't react the way I expect them to. Combined with all the backtracking and unclear progression, these technical problems have made an already frustrating experience significantly worse.

My biggest disappointment is that this barely feels like Silent Hill. Remove the name and I wouldn't associate it with the series. The endless pipes, valves and repetitive industrial environments feel generic and lack the atmosphere I expect from Silent Hill.
The heavy focus on stealth and avoiding enemies doesn't help either. Instead of Silent Hill's mix of exploration, combat, puzzles and psychological horror, Townfall often feels like a generic stealth-horror game with the Silent Hill name attached.
At times it even gives me an asset-flip-style impression. I didn't need another Silent Hill 2 — I just wanted a game that actually feels like Silent Hill.

Gallipoli may have been a traumatic defeat for the British, in spite of ANZAC heroics, but it is a resounding success for BlackMill Games. This is the culmination of lessons and experience picked up in the previous three titles that have consistently set the bar not just for World War I shooters but large-scale warfare games as a whole. Gallipoli stands taller than the ancient ruins and towering hills it depicts, and is a strong contestant for best FPS of the year so far.
Gallipoli is an all-around improvement for the World War I series, bringing sharper visuals and better gameplay to one of the conflict’s least-explored fronts.

Gallipoli is the most beautiful game in the WW1 series yet, with excellent maps, fun new classes, and a continued focus on teamwork in order to win. The hard and dry landscapes of the Middle Eastern front are recreated with exquisite attention to detail, and the active player base of people taking it seriously enough to get the job done – but not so serious as to intimidate or scare off new players – is such a rare gem in modern gaming. It's those moments, though, when everyone is doing what needs to be done – whether it's laying down covering fire for an advance, or running from teammate to teammate healing their wounds as they dig in – that Gallipoli truly becomes a one-of-a-kind gaming experience.

WWI – Gallipoli brings more intense WWI-era multiplayer shooting, with realistic depictions of all things war. It can be grim, and certainly makes us respect those who had to do this for real even more, but it’s a good way to remember the horrors of the past whilst still having some fun with large scale matches. It’s unique rhythm might not suit all, but if you’re after a shooter that feels different to almost everything else out there, then this comes recommended.

The game offers a realistic depiction of World War I battlefields. However, some players may find the combat less dynamic and therefore less appealing. If you choose the game for its authenticity, though, it won't disappoint. However, it could offer more maps and modes.

If you can find a troop that understands this isn’t Call of Duty, and wants to work together, it’s an immensely gratifying game. Injuring someone feels as good as getting the kill in other titles. One well-placed bullet could do either, with a time-to-kill that is a haunting reminder of the history playing out. Granted, Gallipoli may prove too unforgiving for many–this is a world where you often can’t move and reload at the same time–but that’s no complaint. The back-to-basics feel is refreshing in the current market, with deliberateness in your actions replacing the need for perks and power-ups.

Gallipoli stands out by taking the WWI FPS formula to the Ottoman Fronts, delivering a slower, harsher and more tactical experience built around trench warfare, period weaponry and teamwork. Its strong historical atmosphere, satisfying gunplay and distinctive battlefields make it memorable, even if the steep learning curve, occasional rough edges and dependence on a healthy player population hold it back. It may not have Battlefield 1’s spectacle, but Gallipoli has something equally valuable: identity, character and a genuine sense of place.

Gallipoli is a meticulously crafted video game, so rich in detail that it almost feels like a documentary. It’s just a shame about its less-than-stellar technical state at launch, hampered by hit registration issues that need to be fixed as soon as possible, rough animations, and a somewhat thin initial content offering (although the game already boasts a rich roadmap). Nevertheless, it remains a diamond in the rough and a must-have for fans of hardcore tactical shooters or history buffs, destined to reach its definitive form in about a year’s time with future updates.

BlackMill Games has outdone itself with WW1: Gallipoli, clearly delivering on its promise to listen to fan feedback through additions like a medic, more dynamic maps, and improved sound. While not perfect, the game excels at capturing the chaotic and panicked atmosphere of trench warfare, with its slower pace and deliberate actions creating a constant sense of tension. Every meter feels hard-fought, and every decision could easily be your last.
The atmosphere of Gallipoli is genuinely well done, but it needs more than that to be a good game. Critical flaws in the gameplay have overshadowed what is otherwise a great idea.
