Halo: Campaign Evolved feels like it brings everything I loved about Combat Evolved into the modern era.

Halo Studios’ Unreal Engine 5-powered upgrade of the original Halo campaign elevates the original with sublime visuals, smart tweaks, and broad respect for the gameplay feel, design, and aesthetic that makes this game so beloved.

Overall, it’s been a joy to jump back into classic Halo. There’s a wonderful new sheen to this makeover but the gun game underneath is still addictive, brilliant shooter fun like it always was. And now that it is on Playstation, gamers who have always steadfastly stuck to that ecosystem will get a chance to enjoy a true great in the gaming catalogue in all its modernised glory.

The best remakes remind you why you fell in love with the original in the first place. That’s exactly what Halo: Campaign Evolved does. It preserves everything that made Combat Evolved special, but layers enough new ideas on top that even after all these years, stepping back onto Alpha Halo feels like an adventure again. For longtime fans, it’s the perfect excuse to return. For anyone discovering Halo for the first time, Halo: Campaign Evolved is the perfect place to start.

Despite the absence of competitive multiplayer, Halo: Campaign Evolved stands as a tribute to what first-person shooters meant and to Bungie’s revolution. It is a masterclass in videogame history, bringing back an immortal game and a now largely forgotten way of understanding the genre.

Halo: Campaign Evolved has brought back a true classic in style, faithfully remaking and expanding one of the best shooters of all time. With bonus missions that feel like they’ve always been there, expertly slotting into the original Halo experience, Campaign Evolved presents an incredible package of old and new that’s never looked better. Welcome back, Chief.

Halo: Campaign Evolved proves that great games never lose their shine. Rebuilt from the ground up in Unreal Engine 5, it faithfully modernizes a landmark FPS while preserving the exceptional combat, memorable storytelling, and epic scale that cemented Halo as one of gaming's most influential franchises.

This remake delivers a stunning graphical overhaul that remains faithful to the original art style while introducing fresh content. The new prequel missions provide meaningful narrative depth, yet the absence of competitive multiplayer leaves a void. Despite its familiarity for veterans, the refined gunplay and flexible Remix mode ensure a definitive, modern experience.

I thought this remake was unnecessary. After finishing it, I realized that it wasn't meant to replace a classic, but to celebrate it. It does so by honoring every memory we have of Alpha Halo while also adding enough new ideas that even those of us who know the campaign by heart have reasons to go back.
Halo Studios has done well to make Campaign Evolved feel like a respectful nod to what came before, while giving the franchise the momentum it needs to move confidently into the future.

Review: Halo Campaign Evolved
Score: 8/10 (Campaign) — but the package feels incomplete

Halo Campaign Evolved is, at its core, an incredible love letter to the original Halo. The campaign has been rebuilt with a level of care and reverence that genuinely honours Xbox’s flagship series. The graphical overhaul is stunning — not just prettier, but thoughtfully modernised in a way that preserves the soul of the classic while making it feel fresh for a new generation.

The campaign itself is a joy. Whether you’re a long‑time fan or stepping onto the ring for the first time, it’s a must‑play. And when you bring three friends along, the fun becomes limitless. Co‑op transforms the experience into chaotic, nostalgic brilliance — exactly what Halo should feel like.

But the package has one glaring flaw: the absence of multiplayer. Not even a bridge into Halo Infinite’s existing multiplayer suite. That omission leaves the whole release feeling strangely hollow. Halo has always been a two‑pillar franchise — campaign and multiplayer — and removing one of those pillars makes the experience feel incomplete, no matter how strong the campaign is.

Overall
An amazing, beautifully updated campaign that celebrates everything iconic about Halo. But without multiplayer, it’s hard not to feel like half the experience is missing.

reviews.author: Phil8707
reviews.quote:
Es ist wieder Halo in schick – wie oft habe ich diesen Klassiker schon durchgespielt? 2001 ein Meilenstein, als Anniversary eine würdige Neuauflage und in der Master Chief Collection quasi perfekt.
​Jetzt das nächste Remake. Microsoft geht das Risiko neuer Ableger aus, da der große Erfolg ausblieb. 343 Industries baute zwar einen soliden Shop, reichte aber nie an die Qualität der Trilogie und Reach heran. Nach der Umbenennung in Halo Studios hofft man nun, dass die Fans erneut zugreifen. Ohne den Game Pass hätte ich wohl gepasst, aber für eine schnelle Runde zwischendurch taugt es.
​Grafisch lässt sich streiten, doch der Look passt zum Original. Spielerisch feilt man nur an Nuancen, ohne das alte Feeling zu verfälschen. Ob KI im Spiel war? Wenn ja, fällt es nicht auf. Ganz ehrlich: Wenn KI Entwicklungen beschleunigt und Release-Zyklen verkürzt, ist das nur vernünftig – sonst warten wir auf neue Blockbuster irgendwann zehn Jahre. Kommt mal klar.

That said i hope they will make a Halo 2/3  Remaster like this and i hope that the dev team gets some more positive recognition for this fine remaster.

reviews.author: Knawty
reviews.quote:
Campaign Evolved was a huge opportunity to create the definitive edition of one of the greatest FPS games of all time, but unfortunately it doesn't seize that ****'s a fun game and a decent experience, once the strange settings such as narration, hit markers, sprint, film grain, camera shake, excessive waypoints, weapon icons, etc have been disabled.

The graphics are beautiful, and the gunplay is smooth and well executed. But it suffers from a lack of cohesive vision. Is this a remake or a remaster? The game itself doesn't seem to know.

It's too timid where it should have been brave, e.g. adding new weapons, enemies, encounters, or map redesigns. And too brave where it should have been timid, e.g. changing character faces and personalities (Johnson, Keyes), removing health packs, adding sprint.

The result is a beautiful and responsive shooter with a distinct lack of character or depth. Well worth a playthrough, but if I ever want to experience Halo CE again, the original disc is the one I'll reach for.

reviews.author: GhostX92
reviews.quote: I had a really good experience with the game; the gameplay and story were solid, the graphics were good, and the enemies were amusing with decent AI. I played on the hard difficulty setting and encountered a few minor bugs—such as the occasional loss of gunshot sounds—though these were very rare. Unfortunately, the cinematics were poor, so my final rating is 8 out of 10.

Rubinite is a confident and rewarding take on the boss rush formula, pairing expertly crafted encounters with meaningful progression, engaging characters, and a surprisingly heartfelt narrative. While a handful of bosses overstay their welcome and some story scenes lack emotional impact, its exceptional combat, inventive Focus mechanic, and memorable world make it one of the year's standout indie action RPGs.

Rubinite is a strikingly good Soulslike which slashes through the fluff and delivers a razor-sharp boss rush experience with a surprisingly potent emotional center. At its core, Rubinite’s Focus mechanic and the myriad of imposing boss fights deliver a uniquely fun and challenging take on the genre that's bolstered by the game’s beautiful 2D pixel-art style, lovable characters, and wonderful story. There are a few unfortunate issues, such as the overly cryptic narrative presentation and occasional janky hitboxes, which hold it back a bit. Still, every gemstone has a flaw or two, and Rubinite is no exception; it’s a pureblooded, crystallized gem that’s worth the adventure.

Rubinite is a challenging boss-rush action game that succeeds because defeat feel more like a lesson than a punishment. While the level of challenge is high, those who bring patience, observational skills and precision will be rewarded. Although the cautious, dodge-first combat can occasionally encourage passive play, Cup Dog Games' debut definitely impresses.

Bristling with potential, and with dynamic art direction and combat, Rubinite could have been something truly special. But with a bevy of mechanical flaws, strange decisions, and a narrative loop that defies its classification as a boss rush, Rubinite settles into being just another enjoyable Soulslike.

reviews.author: notPopcorn
reviews.quote: My goty so far, the combat is so clean and the bosses are difficult yet amazing.

reviews.author: Nyarco
reviews.quote:
I am torn between a 7 or an 8 for this game tbh, but I would generally say it's more favorable towards the green. It's a very solid Boss rush game that is quite proud of it's story. Often times I've found myself in the intermissions for much longer than the actual fights. The story is nothing revolutionary but it still pulls it off well.
Go into this game with the expectation of getting a well written story and quick fast paste fights along side it and you're most definitely not going to be disappointed.

reviews.author: huw12313212
reviews.quote: I went into Rubinite expecting a difficult boss rush game, but I didn't expect the combat to feel this satisfying.Every boss feels handcrafted. Instead of relying on random patterns or cheap tricks, each fight teaches you something new. Whenever I died, I knew exactly what mistake I made, which made every victory feel earned rather than **** Focus mechanic is easily the highlight. Charging your attack while staying dangerously close to the boss creates a constant risk-versus-reward loop, and landing a fully charged strike after a series of perfect dodges is incredibly rewarding. It gives every fight an intensity that few action games manage to **** game also respects the player's time. Instant retries mean you spend almost all of your time learning boss patterns instead of running back after every death. That keeps the challenge addictive instead of frustrating.Visually, the pixel art is beautiful without trying too hard. The animations are expressive, the bosses have memorable designs, and the sound effects make every dodge and critical hit feel impactful.Rubinite isn't a huge game, but it knows exactly what it wants to be. If you enjoy games that reward mastery, precise dodging, and learning through repetition, this is one of the most polished indie boss rush experiences I've played. Highly recommended.

reviews.author: kamadosilly
reviews.quote: For a boss rush game this is incredible the bosses are challenging but unique the focus system is very unique and with a good story it makes this game great.    not contender for game of the year but definitely a hidden gem
Nocturne is an RPG with an amazing story, beautiful visuals, and epic music. The rhythm-based fights are so fun; I looked forward to enemy encounters. You must play this game!

Nocturne manages a tight narrative in its ten-hour run, and the beat-rhythm aspect both helps to pad out the relatively small number of mobs in the game and keep things interesting. The spritework is fluid, and the animation poetic. While the concept may sound like an odd mash-up, genre-wise, Pracy Studios makes it work.

Nocturne’s RPG wrappings, strong narrative and varied difficulty settings do a lot to make what is normally a fairly impenetrable genre accessible and enjoyable. Whether or not you consider yourself a fan of rhythm games, I think that Nocturne has a lot of appeal and is worth approaching if you’re looking for an RPG with a more unique approach to combat than most.

Nocturne aims for an ambitious fusion of sci-fi storytelling and rhythm strategy, but the grindy combat and superficial RPG systems prevent it from coming together effectively, making it difficult to recommend.

reviews.author: Rolas_Racer
reviews.quote: Me es difícil ser objetivo después de la hermosa y dolorosa experiencia que viví con Nocturne. La música es espectacular, desde el menú de inicio me tenía con la piel chinita, el combate de ritmo es muy divertido y adictivo, al punto de que me pasé por el Arcade un par de veces, el pixel art es precioso, y la historia es súper emotiva. En guion es donde creo que flaquea un poco, porque hay ciertos momentos donde sentí que las cosas se resolvían muy fácil, equis personaje está convencido de algo, peleamos, le decimos que está mal, y listo, recapacita. Por eso no le pongo una calificación más alta. Pero Nocturne es de esos juegos que te recordarán porque los videojuegos son arte. En definitiva de mis juegos favoritos del año, me dejó un sabor de boca muy similar a Expedition 33 el año pasado. Lo recomiendo ampliamente.

Yet Another Zombie Survivors packs in a huge amount of content, plenty of unlockable characters and a strong permanent upgrade system, making this one of the best survivors-likes out there. If you like the idea of ripping and shooting your way through thousands of zombies, you're going to love this.

Yet Another Zombie Survivors doesn’t revolutionize the genre, but it manages to stand out thanks to its three-character squad mechanics and the numerous synergies between abilities and classes. Despite a rather conventional setting and progression that can feel predictable at times, it remains a solid, accessible, and highly entertaining “bullet heaven” game (especially when played with others).

Yet Another Zombie Survivors has a pick-up-and-play vibe, featuring a very satisfying and well put together gameplay loop while still providing an adequate enough challenge to make you want to go again. There's plenty of flexibility in game design to cater for various playstyles and squad builds, with just enough maps and game modes to try your new upgrades without the game becoming stale. Overall, Yet Another Zombie Survivors is a solid and enjoyable entry into the genre of survivors games.

Yet Another Zombie Survivors embraces every word in its name with aplomb. This is, in every way, another game that falls into top-down, wave-based combat where enemies flood the screen and players weave in and out of danger. Compelling progression keeps things fun for those who love the grind.

There are a lot of survivors games out there now, and one with zombies was due. This one has a lot of great ideas and will keep you entertained for a while, but it doesn't take long for you to have seen and done it all.
Servant of the Lake continues the wonderful ongoing saga of Rusty Lake in an extremely enjoyable new series entry, turning work to eerie fun in service of the Vanderboom family.

Servant of the Lake is a surreal and original puzzle game that retains Rusty Lake’s distinctive style and delivers unique and often gruesome puzzles. You can simply enjoy the puzzles or dive into the lore and secret achievements. The notebook is a very useful addition and helps you with tracking everything. However, a hint button would have been helpful, especially for puzzles affected by the order of actions or conversations.

With an unsettling and macabre story, and a real variety of cleverly-designed puzzles, Servant of the Lake cements itself as one of the best point-and-click games of recent years. It may only be short, but it's an absolute delight to play.

From a final stance, I loved Servant of the Lake. Yes, I know that I am a fan of the series. But it does always provide so much more than just a point-and-click puzzle game. It provides a deep, and ongoing, story that spans generations that reside around the Rusty Lake. If you have played the prior Rusty Lake titles, then Servant of the Lake is another notch to put on your shelf. If you’re new to the genre of point-and-click puzzles, or just the Rusty Lake series in general, I find that it does provide a nice jumping off point. In terms of both gameplay/puzzle difficulty, as well as the overall story of this harrowing lake.

Servant of the Lake faithfully maintains the franchise's iconic atmosphere and solid puzzle design while delivering a deeply satisfying payoff to long-standing lore mysteries. With its impeccably paced mechanics and rich content volume, it stands as a highly recommended entry for both series veterans and room-escape enthusiasts.

Servant of the Lake is unmissable stuff if you're a Rusty Lake fan already – but if that applies to you, then you probably knew that without me telling you; this series inspires a lot of loyalty among its fanbase, and enticing people back doesn't seem to be an issue for the studio. My honest recommendation for new players interested in the series is that you absolutely can start here, and if you choose to do so you're doing a good deed by supporting the developers – but if you're not sure, most of the franchise is on sale on Steam right now, and you could just as happily start with basically any of the others while they're so cheap as to be all-but-free. One thing's certain: the Lake will still be there waiting for you when you're ready to seek it out.

Beyond the still-unravelling lore, the puzzles are the key draw here. They’re clever in their many facets, and with ‘escape room’ style delivery, they allow for players to experiment freely without being too overwhelmed by choices. Between them, you’ll find more of the game’s story oozing through the cracks, leading you along the pathway to the central mystery – with trepidation in every step. A good horror makes you want to close your eyes, but to maintain focus on the action through your fingers. Servant of the Lake is a very good horror, and a great puzzle game to boot.

I wouldn’t personally recommend it to someone who dislikes difficult puzzles or gets uncomfortable with bugs and bodily grossness. For everyone else, though, I can absolutely see Servant of the Lake becoming a favourite. It’s the kind of game I’d recommend playing after dark, particularly during autumn, when you can settle in with the rain outside and let this bizarre little estate make you question everything you thought you knew about point-and-click puzzles. And yes, the cat is very cute. Even if you do have to use his spit-up as glue for a broken teacup.

Servant of the Lake is quite simply another very good Rusty Lake game. It doesn't revolutionise the series, and perhaps that's not the intention either. Instead, it takes what has worked for over a decade and packages it into a slightly more accessible adventure with clever puzzles, a wonderfully unsettling atmosphere, and just the right amount of narrative. For anyone who already loves Rusty Lake, this is practically a must-play.
If at times Servant Of The Lake feels like a puzzle to be clicked or stumbled through as much as to be solved, then, we've no desire to make it sensible. [Issue#428, p.120]

reviews.author: pashockys
reviews.quote: This is a great game and a wonderful continuation of the series. Although it has taken a slight turn toward a more mainstream audience, it still retains the core elements that define the series: the absurdity of what is happening, the occasional spookiness, the mysterious atmosphere, and that feeling of complete **** always, the puzzles are excellent. You can figure them out without too much trouble, but they still provide a satisfying challenge. The beautiful artwork, memorable characters, and now an intriguing storyline make this an outstanding entry and a major step forward for the series.I highly recommend that everyone give it a try, and I wish the studio all the best.
With a solid main story, plenty of space to explore, engaging combat, and a load of DLC to enjoy as well, this is an impressive package.

Everspace 2 shadow dropping was a really pleasant surprise, both in terms of the package on offer and the departure from the original game. Sure, there may be some pacing issues where puzzle-based missions can’t quite live up to their more action-orientated counterparts, but they do little to take away from this adventure. The RPG and looter-shooter mechanics mean every engagement holds the possibility to be faster, better, or stronger. If you’re coming to Everspace 2 expecting another roguelike experience like the original, you may be surprised by just how much has changed, but if you’re willing to embrace that change, there’s a lot to like here.

EVERSPACE 2 isn’t Mass Effect or No Man’s Sky, and after spending so much time with it, I’m glad it doesn’t try to be. I never really missed walking around planets or talking to a huge cast of companions because there was always something else pulling me back into space. Upgrading my ship, chasing another signal, or simply getting distracted on the way to a mission was often enough to keep me playing. Not everything works equally well, though. Some missions start to feel a little too similar after a while, and there are moments where the galaxy feels emptier than I would have liked. Still, I kept wanting to see what was waiting in the next system, and for a game where you never even leave your ship, that probably says enough.

Everspace 2: Galactic Edition provides a wealth of content for space combat fans on the Switch 2 and is a welcome addition to the console’s real dearth of any similar title in the genre. For fans of collecting things, exploring this vast galaxy and tweaking their ship with the vast amounts of upgrades, there are dozens and dozens of hours of fun here. While the story is just okay and nothing special, it does a decent job of putting lead character Adam in the situations where the game’s selling points really shine: the exciting combat and spacefaring. There are compromises here; the 30fps will be annoying for some and the loading screens between sectors is a considerable buzzkill. However, the framerate never diminishes the overall experience and the sense that Everspace 2 is a very welcome addition to the platform.

Everspace 2 in isolation is a bold reimagining of Everspace as a series. And in most ways it delivers on that vision. World exploration is a little clunky but combat and progression remain as fun as ever. It is a more authored experience and that benefits the story and world it presents. On the other hand, outside of image quality, the Switch 2 is a surprisingly noticeable compromise as compared to the game running on Steam Deck. Yes I get a higher resolution but that only makes the level of detail changes more blatantly obvious. I’d be curious if a lower resolution sixty frames-per-second mode could alleviate some input lag. You can certainly still fight your way through on this version, but you may find that quickly tracking small targets becomes needlessly frustrating very fast. There are other more mild issues to be addressed as well but the controls need to be a priority.

reviews.author: Torbold
reviews.quote:
Absolutely love this game! Played it through on PC/Steam a while ago and now enjoyed it for a day on Switch 2.

Holy hell, this game looks and plays incredibly smoothly on handheld mode (the only mode I play). Everything looks crystal clear, and the space battles feel amazing on the go. If you like space shooters - this game is definitely worth a while!

Truxton Extreme is not only an outstanding shmup, but it also sets a new benchmark for how to bring back cult series of the genre into the current age. Very high marks on graphical effects, sound design, and soundtrack along with spot-on gameplay makes it easy to recommend adding this one to your Switch 2 library as soon as possible. Both veteran shmup players and newcomers alike will find much to enjoy in this package. You also get an outstanding digital graphic novel to go along with your game. Toaplan’s legacy is in the good hands of Masahiro Yuge, and if this is the shape of things to come, I couldn’t be more excited for future Tatsujin projects.

Truxton Extreme is an absolute blast from the past, bringing back a decades-old franchise with an excellent new coat of paint and a killer level of challenge that will push you but isn’t unmanageable. No, this probably isn’t a great SHMUP for those who are totally new to the genre, as its unforgiving nature might put you off these games entirely, but for fans of the original or those who have enjoyed similar games in the past, this is a must-play.
With a combination of great looks and a distinctive flow of play, Truxton Extreme has a great base of classic arcade shooting that it then builds on, and throws in some story beats for good measure.
The 3D never clutters, and a wealth of game modes means there's something for everyone, but underneath it all, Truxton Extreme remains a traditional retro shooter.
Truxton Extreme is a fantastic shmup with a killer soundtrack, but it absolutely won't hesitate to blow you up over and over again.

Truxton Extreme is a celebration of all things I love about Truxton. From Masahiro Yuge’s involvement on the game’s incredible soundtrack to its modern spin on shmups, there’s much to love…assuming you’re up for a good ol’ fashioned shmup challenge.

Truxton Extreme is a very solid, classically designed shmup that impresses with responsive mechanics, a good challenge, and satisfying combat, yet disappoints with repetitive levels and the underutilized potential of its three campaigns.

Although this type of genre is more niche than others, it represents a major step forward for a franchise that managed to reach the top during the 1990s. This third entry takes everything that worked in the original games, improves upon it, and brings back the same sense of unfairness we experienced in old-school arcades. While several aspects could still be improved, the game delivers on its promises, whether in its visuals, music, atmosphere, or, most importantly, its gameplay.

“If we're going to get compared to Hotline Miami, we might as well make it count" must have been the train of thought at CIRCLEfromDOT, and boy did they ever. Even if Kusan: City of Wolves doesn't necessarily break the mold in terms of gameplay originality, it absolutely scratches that itch that Dennaton Games has been causing for many years. The only aspect that doesn't really hit the adrenalin rush spot is the Korean hiphop soundtrack, even if it isn't a bad OST in general.
Steeped in style, with excellent animations, Kusan is a stunning neon world with its own unique way of telling a gritty story through a graphic novel.

Ultimately, Kusan: City of Wolves takes a well-established concept and adds a very strong layer of identity on top of it. Fast and visceral gameplay is one of the title's highlights, alongside a sound design and aesthetic that impeccably accompany this journey of redemption. Despite occasional visual clutter amid the chaos, the game stands out as one of the most fun and memorable action experiences of the year.

"When Hotline Miami meets John Wick." Few games live up to a developer's pitch this perfectly. If you're looking for an adrenaline rush, Kusan: City of Wolves delivers. It's brutally difficult, but once it gets its hooks into you, it's hard to put down.

The story stuck with me a lot. There’s a lot of gray area that starts to justify the group and their actions; well, the people we perceived to be trying to help start to show their true colors. The motivations and actions of each party start to come into question, and we see the turmoil of Jin as he understands the group's motives but turns away to protect what matters most to him. It’s hard. It’s a great story told in a unique graphic novel-esque format that still gave the intensity I was hoping for.

Kusan: City of Wolves is a gameplay-focused game in the best sense of the word, built by four people who clearly understand exactly what 'flow' means. The story could have done with the same care as the combat, and the economy runs out of steam towards the end, but that doesn't detract from the excellent gameplay.

Kusan: City Of Wolves really takes no prisoners – you’re either the fastest or you’re dead. Though it gives you countless tries to get it right, some players may find the brutality of the one-hit-your-dead mechanic too intense to make much progress. Though it looks amazing, there are problems in Kusan that could be easily fixed, such as giving more time to explain new game mechanics and spending time making sure its narrative was accessible and easy to comprehend. Despite its shortcomings, for those who love a good-looking, brutal shooter and don’t really care much about following a narrative, you will enjoy Kusan: City of Wolves.
Despite high ambitions, it doesn't quite achieve the flow and polish of Hotline Miami, but with its "puzzle-like" combat, it is definitely one for players seeking a unique challenge.
Jacked animals jack each other up in a Hotline Miami spiritual successor with some questionable creative choices but addictive gameplay.
Set in an animal-filled cyberpunk world, Hotline Miami delivers a chaotic top-down massacre. However, it may not fully satisfy players and can be frustrating due to permadeath.

Ultimately, High Times is just a bit of fun. It’s nothing overly deep but it’s not overly taxing… you could quite easily just pick it up and play a few days of donut making then put it down again. It’s still essentially a visual novel so choices are within limits… but there’s enough variation to make a few plays worth while, there are also plenty of different characters so if you don’t like one… you should be able to find a different one that you do.

High Times delivers exactly what players are expecting based on the title. Plenty of donuts get cooked, then iced, and potentially sprinkled. Because of the mysterious mood-altering ingredients used by The Hotbox, all of them have the power to help customers have a better day or deal with a particular situation. All clients have storylines that progress as players deliver the right doughnut. Those who can be romanced get more conversations and reveal more of themselves. High Times is enjoyable and at times touching, even when it tries too hard to be funny or when its characters are weird for the sake of weirdness.

The joy in High Times comes from the story arcs and the references, even when the donut creation making becomes a bit repetitive. Sure, by day 125, I was feeling a bit over creating donuts and wished there was a way to just select the recipes and have it be automatically made. Of course, that isn’t the fault of the game, but probably some of my choices, and my marathon game play sessions that lasted for quite a few hours. High Times is enjoyed when you don’t over indulge but instead reward yourself with this sweet treat.

There is a lot to admire here. High Times swings for the fences with its ideas. A gender-neutral protagonist, meaningful romance choices, fully voiced characters, an enjoyable cooking system, and over fifty hours of content are all things I never expected to find together in one indie game. I do wish the writing reached the same level as the game’s ambition. The first couple of weeks drag, the emotional depth arrives much later than it should, and a few quality-of-life improvements would smooth over the rough edges. Even so, I kept wanting to come back. The gameplay loop is satisfying, the world is wonderfully weird, and once the relationships finally start paying off, they become genuinely engaging.

Overall, High Times is a nice, cozy game. It combines two simulator genres together. Dating sim, because you flirt and build relationships with other characters, and cooking sim because you make donuts during the late evening for these same people. The soundtrack is nice, fits the cozy environment, and the controls can be overlooked as they are non-essential for the game. The HUD is very easy to understand, nothing overdone or overexplained. The tutorials are also easy to understand, and making donuts aren’t hard either. Although the game can feel repetitive from the same gameplay loop, it is not bad by any means. The one thing that doesn’t really fit with me is the resolution issue. Not seeing the game, character and environmental details sharp is not good. It can be fixed though and hopefully will be.

Staffer Retro is the kind of game that is sure to leave an impression once the truth is finally revealed. Compared with its predecessor, it feels more mature, more polished, and more story-driven. Its pacing is also remarkably smooth, making it easy to play through in a single sitting. However, with its deduction elements taking a back seat, its case design and overall playability may represent a slight step backward from the previous game.

When viewed as a mystery-infused visual novel, Steffer Retro boasts impressive overall quality. The game’s overarching story comes together seamlessly, offering a solid narrative resolution. However, compared to its predecessor, the fun derived from the psychic deduction mechanics themselves feels a bit diminished.

When you don't even have the strength left to hold your head up, what remains by your side? It was Stepper Retro—a mystery visual novel that forces you to face your true feelings in front of the mirror of despair.

Staffer Retro: A Supernatural Mystery Quest lands as a decent sequel, one that has extensive worldbuilding, character writing, and its unique Retro deduction system. Some lost momentum, awkward localization translations, unnecessary flavor text, and a repetitive soundtrack hold it back, but the strength of its cast and presentation make it a worthwhile journey for fans of the genre nonetheless.

Valor Mortis is the kind of ambitious swing that soulslike fans have dreamed of for years. Witnessing the horrors of war through William’s eyes is one of the best stories brought to the genre in recent memory, and its dark setting of an alternate 19th century Europe carries as much weight as the narrative itself.

The perfect soulslike doesn't exist. There's no such thing, and after so many years of playing them, I'm absolutely sure of it. All of them are bound by shared metroidvania design philosophies and incapacitating issues, and no matter how hard they try, they can never truly surmount them. But Valor Mortis certainly comes dangerously close to doing so, and with gameplay so fluid and a world so fascinating, it's basically as good as they come.

Valor Mortis rarely wastes a beat, producing a surprisingly powerful tale of barbarity that portrays the brutality of war not just through its vicious combat, but through the memory of those who never stood a chance of survival.

Although there is some room for improvement when it comes to refining a few of the technical aspects of the game, Valor Mortis is still a thoroughly engaging experience that left me more than satisfied with my time going through its story and learning about its world. I’m absolutely ecstatic to see what else One More Level has in store for Valor Mortis, and I will definitely be one of the first in line to return for its promised story expansion and New Game+ mode.
Valor Mortis stands out in a saturated genre thanks to its fun combat, excellent level design, and gorgeous visuals.

Valor Mortis is a solid title that kept me hooked for a 20-hour playthrough, delivering a rollercoaster of emotions along the way. To me, that is exactly why Soulslikes have become so popular. The "all-or-nothing" gameplay, high-octane and spectacular combat, and an intriguing setting make this game a standout in the genre, offering a fresh take on a formula that had long since stagnated.

Rather than merely borrowing ideas—from Dark Souls and Dishonored to Sunset Overdrive and even Frogger—One More Level blends them with their own strengths and an original setting to create something truly unique.

Valor Mortis delivers a tense and satisfying first-person soulslike experience, combining strategic combat, rewarding exploration, and a distinctive Napoleonic horror setting. Despite a few technical issues and uneven boss encounters, its strong atmosphere and cohesive mechanics make it a memorable adventure.
Featuring buttery smooth play, fans of first-person melee filled with impactful and meaty combat shouldn't hesitate to check out Valor Mortis.
Valor Mortis is a well-realised Soulslike FPS with a 19th-century coat of paint that enthusiasts of the genre will surely enjoy.

reviews.quote:
I give Valor Mortis a 10/10 because the devs weren’t afraid to take a risk and they delivered! Finally something fresh and innovative in the soulslike genre. Sure, there could be more build variety or a few more enemy types, but I really hope this game gets popular enough to get a bigger, grander sequel. I'd love to come back to this world and find out more about the story although I haven’t even finished the game yet. I'm more than halfway through and totally hooked. And the artstyle and enemy designs are sick!

It’s an awesome gateway for newcomers to soulslikes because you can play smart. You can use the environment, guns, and magic to get by without constant parrying. You can sometimes sneak up on enemies (even some bosses) or use hit-and-run tactics, but other times the enemy placement feels like a puzzle that requires real skill to solve. The game does a great job of gradually teaching you the mechanics, and when a boss finally forces you to parry, the timing windows feel fair. At the same time, it keeps things challenging for veterans.

The whole vibe feels like BioShock meets Dishonored. The first-person view and visceral finishers make combat feel incredibly real. Fans of action games will love it, but you definitely need to be ready for a challenge. Instead of a bloated open world, you get tight, Metroidvania-style areas packed with secrets and even platforming that keeps the gameplay varied. You create shortcuts after defeating some enemies, so the progress to the next lantern gets easier. You also unlock new skills which let you come back to previous areas and unblock new secrets/bosses. Which is useful when you unblock the fast travel. 

The storytelling is great too, dropping the plot through actual voice acting and cutscenes so you don't have to sit around reading boring text notes (but there are still some notes to read if you want). There are also no long boss runbacks. 

If you want a rewarding challenge that finally tries something new, Valor Mortis is a must-play.

Maestro could have easily fallen victim to being another motion-controlled game sloppily brought over to the Nintendo Switch 2, but instead the developers have done a marvellous job translating its hand-waving experience from a platform sporting more accurate motion reading. Okay, it isn’t a perfect transition, but definitely one that deserves your attention if you’re looking for your next rhythm game fix.
One of the best rhythm games around today, featuring an outstanding soundtrack and a fantastic adaptation that makes exceptional use of the Joy-Con controllers.

A playful conducting game built around motion‑based gestures rather than traditional rhythm‑game timing, Maestro adapts surprisingly well to the Switch 2 despite its VR origins. Its great soundtrack, playful presentation and satisfying progression make it an engaging experience even with occasional tracking quirks and dated character models.

Maestro finds a very suitable home on the Switch 2, and it works—though the experience isn’t quite as polished as on the VR platforms for which it was originally designed. Its repertoire, the coordination required of both hands, and the joy of improving with each performance make up for the limited number of modes and the occasional control glitches. It’s a musical experience with personality that, perhaps, isn’t for everyone.

A great tracklist, inventive use of motion controls, and satisfying orchestral conducting effectively mask the limited content and issues with the camera and motion detection precision. It is an original experience for fans of music and rhythm games, though technical shortcomings prevent it from fully reaching its potential.

Aniimo is the next big thing. From the incredible creature designs to a world filled with life and magic, there’s just so much to enjoy. There’s a little something for everyone here, although sharing that with people can be a bit cumbersome. Aside from the usual mobile game problems and some UI issues, the game is a great experience. The monetization isn’t too bad, and there’s no gacha for the Aniimo themselves, but you can still buy plenty of things to give you a leg up in terms of consumable items. There’s a lot more coming from Aniimo, and I am very excited to see where it leads.

Aniimo takes a familiar creature-collecting formula and builds a surprisingly broad adventure around it. Idyll is a colorful world worth exploring; its creatures have plenty of uses beyond filling out a collection, and the combination of story, side activities, and progression gives the journey a satisfying sense of discovery. Some of those ideas feel more fully realized than others, but the strongest parts come together well enough to give Aniimo a character of its own. It may not reinvent the genre, but there is more than enough here to make it an engaging creature collector in its own right.

The open world stands out for bringing the distinct personalities and ecology of over 200 Aniimo to life. Capturing, Twine, and elemental interactions naturally tie collection and exploration together, though the simplistic combat and lack of polish leave something to be desired. Even so, the game remains highly accessible.

Aniimo is a gorgeous, charming creature-collecting adventure with an impressive amount to see, do, and discover. Its stunning character creator, beautiful open world, and seamless Twining system give every new creature a purpose beyond simply adding it to your collection, while its cozy gameplay makes it easy to settle in for the long haul. It can occasionally feel like it’s trying to do too much, and some quests and systems don’t quite hit the same highs, but there’s still an awful lot to love in this ambitious adventure.

Aniimo is a charmingly detailed live service game with a creature collection system, which is simple on the surface and as deep as the player wants to dive into it. With a focus on exploration, collection and housing, players who want a challenging creature battler may find it lacking, but for everyone who enjoys exploring pastel-coloured worlds along fluffy creatures, Aniimo is worth a look.

Aniimo is a mystifying blend of creature collecting and adventure that not only lets you capture these special characters, but become them too. Yes, there’s so much to do that it gives my brain an occasional case of the sads, but it also thoroughly pleases as you twine with your Aniimos rather than simply enjoying them as a bystander.

At least for the moment, Aniimo cannot even remotely be considered a "Pokémon killer," as it lacks the fundamental elements needed to truly challenge the GameFreak series—most notably the complete absence of a competitive mode worthy of the name. That said, the adventure crafted by Pawprint Studios is a joy to play and will keep you glued to the screen for hours as you hunt for every creature and its variants. Even though the story struggles to leave a lasting impression, the game succeeds in offering a fun-to-explore open world, featuring creatures with consistently impressive designs and gameplay that encourages interaction with each one. Given that the title is free-to-play, features unobtrusive microtransactions, and is available on a wide range of platforms, anyone who enjoys monster-catching games should definitely give it a try.

Aniimo is an interesting creature collector with a strong visual style, unique Twining mechanics, and an open world that gives you plenty of reasons to collect different creatures. Sanctums, sidequests, and a story that sparks curiosity add variety, although occasional animation issues and a layer of mobile-inspired systems hold the experience back. Its free-to-play model remains fairly reasonable, but players tired of energy limits, timers, currencies, events, and microtransactions may find themselves wondering why these restrictions are necessary.
Aniimo is a seriously impressive creature collecting game, with a sprawling world, so much content, and the ability to turn into monsters.

Aniimo offers an enjoyable, relaxed open-world adventure that blends creature collection with satisfying exploration. However, the experience remains held back by overly simplistic combat and a cluttered interface typical of free-to-play designs. Despite these shortcomings and occasional technical bugs, the game provides a solid foundation for casual play.

Puntuación final: 82 / 100.

Le restan un par de puntos únicamente detalles técnicos de rendimiento o menús un poco recargados que se pueden arreglar con parches, pero por todo lo que te ofrece sin pedirte nada a cambio, es una joya total.

reviews.author: ShinyGreninjaX
reviews.quote:
TLDR: There’s a really fun game here. I just hope some of the menus, controller support, tutorials, timers, and story get some additional polish as development continues.

Aniimo is a genuinely enjoyable open-world creature-collection game that clearly takes inspiration from Pokémon and Palworld while adding plenty of its own ideas. There’s a lot to do: exploring, collecting resources and Aniimo, completing activities, building up your own resource farm and oasis, and steadily improving your gear. Progression feels relatively fast, and there’s plenty of free gear and resources to keep you moving without constantly feeling like you need to grind.

My biggest issue is that the main story feels pretty bland. The world itself has a lot going on, but the story hasn’t given me much reason to feel invested in what’s happening.

There are also several areas that could use some polish: 

Menus: There are far too many menu categories, making it surprisingly difficult to find what you’re looking for, especially when you’re still learning the game. Even when there’s an indicator that you have something new to check, it can be difficult to figure out where that item actually is.

Controller support: This is probably my biggest gameplay-related frustration. For a game released on both Xbox and Steam, controller implementation feels underdeveloped. There are times when buttons aren’t clearly indicated or don’t work as expected, forcing me to grab the mouse just to interact with something.

Building timers: Waiting 45 minutes for a higher-level trailer upgrade to finish feels unnecessary. When I’m actively playing and having fun building things, being forced to stop the process for an artificial timer is frustrating.

Activities aren’t always explained well: Some activities, such as the tea party used to unlock cosmetic currency, aren’t particularly intuitive. I ended up having to watch a YouTube tutorial to figure out what I was supposed to do. An optional tutorial or explanation when entering these activities would go a long way.

Voice acting: The actors bring a lot of energy, which I appreciate, but some characters sound too similar. In particular, the two best friends can be difficult to distinguish when they’re having a conversation.

Performance: This game has earned the distinction of making my PC run hotter than anything else I’ve played. Nothing dangerous, but definitely noticeable.

One other thing that may be subjective: the title theme really isn’t for me. NBA 2K27 turns out to be a very polished installment that knows how to listen to its fans. The debut of the NBA 2K HQ app is an excellent tool for managing your MyPLAYER and your team without needing to turn on the console, despite how tricky its face scan can be. On the other hand, the integration of AI and a more refined narrative make its story mode an exciting journey, perfect to enjoy even in co-op.

NBA 2K27 keeps moving in the right direction without trying to reinvent the wheel. Instead, it focuses on polishing the core gameplay, from defensive physical contact to ProPLAY animations and player controls. When it comes to real-world fidelity, it gets pretty damn close, which is ultimately all that matters for a sports sim.

Visual Concepts and 2K Sports have pulled it off again; NBA 2K27 features targeted improvements that enhance both gameplay and realism. We know there are plenty of questionable titles vying for your money, but if you opt for this one, you’ll be getting one of the most comprehensive sports games on the market. Basketball remains well-represented in gaming, and with the 2026–2027 season just around the corner, it’s time to take control and spend months on end hitting the hardwood and the blacktop.

NBA 2K27 hits the goal it set out to reach from the beginning: giving defense back the weight it completely lacked last year, turning every possession into a genuine tactical battle where reading your opponent matters as much as building a good offensive play. Visual Concepts' work on pure gameplay convinces on almost every front, between a finally believable one-on-one battle, a more deliberate steal and shot-contest system, and an offense that now demands patience and buildup instead of a simple drive.

NBA 2K27 reaffirms the Visual Concepts-developed series as a benchmark in the sports video game landscape. The extensive selection of modes available, both online and offline, the depth of each one, the variety of options on offer, and the technical presentation are the main strengths of a title that, while not differing all that much from its predecessor, still introduces some welcome new features—most notably, the revamped defensive system. Some of the issues already present in previous installments remain, above all an overly prominent presence of microtransactions (not essential, but highly advantageous), a consequently divisive multiplayer component, and some animations that we found outdated. Nonetheless, this is a deep and rewarding game that demonstrates how the developers are able to listen to community feedback and take meaningful steps forward in the areas where players have highlighted shortcomings.

NBA 2K27 improves the on-court experience with more consistent defense, greater offensive variety, and more physical gameplay that rewards precision and player skill. MyCareer Eras is a welcome addition, while MyNBA remains one of the most complete franchise modes in the genre. However, aggressive monetization, excessive grind, and overly familiar systems continue to hold back an experience that, purely as a basketball game, ranks among the series’ best in recent years.

All in all, NBA 2K27 arrives in top form, delivering yet another rock-solid basketball simulation from Visual Concepts. The new gameplay fundamentals feel well-tuned and effectively integrated into the formula—particularly on the defensive end—while the content updates appear well-designed, despite a few missteps regarding narrative pacing. Ultimately, if you are a basketball fan looking for the best possible game to relive the exploits of legends past and present, this is the title for you.

NBA 2K27 is a resounding success when it comes to basketball simulation. The arena atmosphere, the photorealistic graphics, and—above all—the challenging defensive gameplay make the offline experience a delight.

NBA 2K27 does a great job of expanding the court-level experience, adding more realistic player interactions rather than standardized, simplified animations. A more consolidated City experience gives you the social aspect of street hoop without all the excessive running around. Finally letting men and women play together in The City is a long-awaited addition. Broadcasting and off-court presentation take up a lot of unskippable time, and the MyTeam experience lacks the same amount of immersion and story for female players as male players get. All in all, NBA 2K27 is a good entry in the long-running franchise, especially if you haven't played in a while.

NBA 2K27 delivers great on-court basketball in an excellent visual package but still has some work to do off the court. The on-court experience took a real leap… but the off-court modes need to match that energy.

reviews.author: simongrossi
reviews.quote:
Tedious, Unforgiving, and No Longer Fun: A Legacy Player’s DisappointmentI’ve been playing NBA 2K since the very first installment on the Sega Dreamcast, but over the last couple of years, the series has lost sight of what made it great: pure gameplay enjoyment. Instead, the game has become an unnecessarily punitive chore.

Finishing around the rim is completely broken: It is absurd that draining a contested three-pointer feels more reliable than making a wide-open layup. Watching NBA superstars blow uncontested bunnies right under the basket completely ruins the simulation.

Unforgiving shot timing meets terrible netcode: The strict "green-or-miss" timing window is pure agony online. European servers remain awful, with constant, unpredictable latency. It is long overdue for 2K to display opponent ping before jumping into a game instead of forcing us to guess the input delay.

Over-tuned and clunky gameplay mechanics: The shot-blocking is completely out of hand this year, turning games into unrealistic block parties. 

Paired with cheap, magnetized turnovers on routine passes and minor bumps, the flow of the game feels disjointed.

Play Now Online is entirely neglected: The standard online head-to-head mode hasn't seen a meaningful update in ages. The division tier system is stale, and there is still no way to see regional win/loss breakdowns or matchmaking statistics. 
All resources clearly go toward predatory monetization modes while the core competitive experience rots.
In attempting to turn every fundamental basketball move into a sweaty, hyper-strict e-sports mechanic, 2K forgot how to make a basketball game genuinely fun. A massive letdown for long-time fans.

Aggelos 2 is a fantastic sequel crafted by someone who truly captured the essence of the Wonder Boy franchise and created something new and modern, while still honoring its roots. Intuitive, fun, and beautiful, it is a Metroidvania that excels at encouraging exploration and rewarding the player for it, without ever feeling exhausting, repetitive, or hollow.
There’s something to be said for new-school games that somehow capture the essence of the old-school while still feeling contemporary in the right areas.

Aggelos 2 is an ambitious sequel that follows a visual style inspired by 16-bit pixel art, and which delivers a solid Metroidvania experience thanks to a balanced difficulty and a well crafted gradual introduction of the game's mechanics, showing that the genre's mantra is followed seriously. The light-darkness duality is very interesting, and the exploration keeps players engaged and eager for more elements to discover. Its plot is not as prominent as one would like, but the overall slick gameplay, visual design and performance, and quality of the exploration make Aggelos 2 a very interesting work.
Aggelos 2 feels like a Metroidvania I’d have played over and over again on my Game Boy Advance, with some great abilities and combat.

Aggelos 2 builds on its predecessor with a larger map, dual forms, and two interconnected worlds. The appealing retro visuals and rewarding movement upgrades make for an enjoyable adventure, but an unintuitive map and missing quality-of-life features make navigation more frustrating than it should be.

Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy enshrines Asobo Studio’s deep passion and expertise at delivering emotional narratives that are wrought with tension and adventure. As the pieces fall together and players have made the laborious journey along with her, Sophia does not come out unscathed. However, she emerges as one of the rawest, most emotive protagonists in memory. This harrowing spectacle full of constant surprises, daunting vistas, and moving passion is truly a thing of beauty, an unforgettable adventure.

A haunting, emotional story is paired with fantastic combat, exploration, and puzzle-solving. Resonance: A Plague Tale solidifies the franchise as one of the best franchises of the modern era and shouldn't be missed.

Although Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy doesn't tell the story of Amicia and Hugo, it manages to offer a different perspective to the player. Not only are the graphics impressive, but also the combat, setting, and puzzles which, while becoming tiresome at times, prove to be intelligent and well-developed. This is, without a doubt, one of the best titles of the year.

Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is a great game with a compelling and excellently performed story. There are still ties back to the original series for fans, and still plenty of tense stealth sections, but this is more action adventure with combat that offers a decent challenge. A new way to adapt the mythology of the Minotaur is the cherry that tops this experience.

Putting you in control of a popular character from A Plague Tale: Requiem and letting you experience an important chapter of their life, Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy exchanges rats and stealth for combat and puzzles, and is captivating from beginning to end. As long as you don't mind puzzles that involve reflecting light, anyhow.

The next step in a clear path from Innocence, through Requiem, Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy confidently switches to a full on action-adventure in the vein of Uncharted. A good combat system, simple story-serving design choices and a great story, make this a joy and to play, even as the dread mounts and you descend into the heart of darkness towards scenes every bit and terrifying and memorable as that tsunami of rats.

Between the stunning visuals, emotionally resonant storytelling that spans centuries, and satisfyingly varied gameplay loop, Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy impressed me from beginning to end. It ran well with basically no technical issues during my playthrough, and I just had a truly great time playing it. It’s a story and a gameplay experience I’ll be thinking about for quite some time, and that’s really saying something. Whether you’re a longtime Plague Tale fan or new to the franchise, Resonance is well worth picking up if you like a good action-adventure game with a strong narrative at its core.

Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy successfully fulfills the mission of expanding the franchise's universe without feeling like an expendable chapter. By swapping the Rune siblings for Sophia, Asobo Studio takes a risk with a new protagonist and a more overt approach to combat, yet retains what has always defined the series: a rich narrative, well-crafted characters, and impeccable art direction.

Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy represents one of Asobo Studio’s boldest gambles. It is not simply the third chapter in the saga. It is not Requiem 2. Above all, it does not attempt to replicate Amicia and Hugo with different characters. It is a new starting point. Sophia changes the pace of the experience, combat radically transforms the gameplay, the Greek-Mediterranean setting gives Asobo completely new material to work with, and the mythological component further expands the series’ narrative universe. The risks, however, are just as evident: some mechanics feel less original, the puzzles can disrupt the pacing, and moving away from certain iconic elements could alienate those who primarily loved the stealth-focused gameplay and distinctive atmosphere of the first two chapters. But perhaps that is precisely the point of Resonance. Asobo does not want to repeat A Plague Tale. It wants to find out how far it can push the series. We can say this having played it ourselves: the direction it has taken is surprisingly solid. Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy seems determined to prove that a series does not necessarily have to remain static in order to stay true to itself. Asobo has taken what worked, questioned what risked becoming repetitive, and built around Sophia an experience that suits her perfectly—a more vertical game, and one closer to the grand cinematic action-adventures. It may not be the Plague Tale that fans were expecting, but perhaps that is exactly why it could be the one the series needed.

Asobo Studio has delivered a fantastic adventure, leagues ahead of A Plague Tale: Requiem, and a clear demonstration of how much the team has grown. Unique, story-driven single-player experiences like this don't come around nearly as often these days, so this isn't one to skip. Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy is absolutely worth playing.

Points positifs

* L’histoire est vraiment sympa à suivre, avec de bons personnages bien écrits.

* La direction artistique est, comme toujours chez Asobo Studio, sublime, avec des décors variés.

* Les musiques sont très jolies.

* La mise en scène générale est très bonne.

* Le mythe du Minotaure est astucieusement réinventé et très sympa à découvrir.


Points négatifs

* Le système de combat manque de profondeur dans ses mécaniques et a trop peu évolué par rapport au premier opus.

* Le système RPG lite n’a aucun intérêt et n’apporte rien de nouveau au gameplay.

* Les énigmes sont sympas, mais pas assez variées et se résument, les trois quarts du temps, à jouer avec la lumière.

* Le jeu souffre également de quelques longueurs et aurait gagné à être légèrement plus court.


Pour conclure

J’ai beaucoup apprécié retourner dans l’univers d’A Plague Tale et j’ai aimé découvrir ce nouvel opus. Cependant, il manque de surprises et de nouveautés pour devenir un jeu qui me marque autant que les deux premiers opus.

reviews.author: SlLV3R
reviews.quote: Je partais avec de bonnes attentes pour Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy, et je dois dire que j’ai plutôt bien aimé l’expérience. L’histoire m’a vraiment plu, avec un scénario intéressant qui ne se dévoile pas entièrement dès les premières heures. Le jeu prend le temps de nous surprendre, et c’est un aspect que j’ai particulièrement apprécié.Visuellement, c’est une véritable réussite. Les graphismes sont magnifiques et la direction artistique est incroyable. L’ambiance, les décors et le travail artistique contribuent énormément à l’immersion. On sent qu’un soin particulier a été apporté à **** autre point qui m’a vraiment marqué, et que je tiens absolument à souligner, c’est le petit résumé de l’histoire qui s’affiche lorsqu’on reprend sa partie. Une idée toute simple, mais que j’ai trouvée extrêmement pertinente ! Ça permet de se remettre rapidement dans le contexte sans devoir se rappeler de tout ce qui s’est passé avant. J’aimerais vraiment voir cette fonctionnalité se généraliser dans les jeux vidéo à l’avenir, car elle apporte un vrai confort au joueur.J’ai également beaucoup apprécié l’adaptation de l’histoire de Thésée et du Minotaure. Je trouve que cette réinterprétation mythologique est particulièrement réussie et qu’elle s’intègre très bien à l’expérience proposée par le jeu. C’est un élément qui apporte une vraie identité au scénario.Maintenant, tout n’est pas parfait, et les principaux défauts se situent davantage sur le plan technique et au niveau du level design. Les écrans de chargement peuvent parfois casser le rythme, certaines zones mortelles ne paraissent pas forcément inatteignables au premier abord, ce qui peut être frustrant, et le level design manque parfois un peu de richesse. Il y a des passages où j’aurais aimé davantage de variété et de possibilités.Malgré ces quelques défauts, j’ai passé un bon moment sur Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy. Une histoire intéressante, une direction artistique sublime et des idées de gameplay et d’expérience très **** jeu qui possède de belles qualités et qui, je l’espère, continuera à faire évoluer ses bonnes idées dans ses prochaines aventures.

reviews.author: Adacap
reviews.quote: One of the best action games I've played recently. Exceptional gameplay and top-notch art direction. Stimulating light puzzles.

Give me a well-told story I can run through a few times as opposed to something more epic that I can barely get through once and you’ll have my heart – Frogwares certainly does. I dove into the The Sinking City 2 with a good amount of trepidation, and whilst I do hope Frogwares get the chance to revisit their earlier style at some point, in the end they made the right Call…(of Cthulhu).

The Sinking City 2 is an absolute triumph, not only due to its harrowing real-world origins, but because of how Frogwares masterfully crafted a survival horror game as their first product in the genre. Its story, world, and characters are enthralling and compelling, and by the end of my first run, I immediately began playing it again as I just wanted more of the game.

The Sinking City 2 takes another successful dive into the survival horror genre, with challenging puzzles, an engaging and heartbreaking story, and wildly fun gunplay. I just wish it were longer and a bit more replayable.
The Sinking City 2 presents itself as Frogwares' defining moment, and it should ultimately be remembered as their greatest accomplishment yet.

From its engaging puzzles to its thrilling combat, with The Sinking City 2, Ukrainian developer Frogwares has demonstrated that it is perfectly capable of creating a captivating survival horror adventure.
A deeply enriching and highly enjoyable Lovecraftian experience.

The Sinking City 2 is a survival horror that features Lovecraftian themes and creatures. Developed and published by Frogwares, this sequel aims to improve upon some of the critiques of the original by veering away from a detective game to survival horror. Combat has been polished and updated. Visuals are crisp and clean, both the world and the horrors that lurk inside. The Sinking City 2 doesn't try to change the survival horror genre and instead executes its core features well. A streamlined experience, limited resources for crafting and occasional puzzles are just to name a few. Any negative opinions I have are of my own preferences, such as a dislike for limited inventory, NG+ pandering, and a day one DLC. Overall a great game that deserves the positive score it receives. I gladly recommend this one!

The Sinking City 2 successfully transforms the series into a more focused survival-horror experience. Its oppressive Lovecraftian atmosphere, strong storytelling, rewarding exploration, improved combat and impressive DualSense support make Arkham a compelling place to get lost in. Melee combat and a few stiff cutscenes hold it back slightly, but Frogwares has delivered a confident and highly enjoyable sequel.

Not content with simply treading water, Frogwares has resurfaced with The Sinking City 2, a prequel that’s equal parts edge-of-your-seat survival horror and Lovecraftian mystery, making for a much-improved sophomore series outing.
The Sinking City 2 offers a solid survival horror experience that feels both different and similar to its predecessor.

reviews.author: Kingdim
reviews.quote:
The Sinking City 2 is a pretty good game overall, and despite its flaws, I genuinely enjoyed my time with it. I would definitely recommend it to fans of survival horror, especially those who enjoy Lovecraftian settings. 
However, I think the game has two major problems that prevent it from being as good as it could have **** first is the almost complete abandonment of the investigative aspect that made the first game so distinctive. In the original The Sinking City, talking to NPCs, gathering information and actually conducting investigations made you feel involved in the story and the world. Here, that aspect has been drastically reduced. The new Mind Palace system is supposed to provide some form of investigation, but I found it rather superficial. It never really feels like you're investigating anything. As a result, I felt much less involved in the story than I did in the first game.
The second major problem is that the game tries too hard to become a Lovecraftian version of Resident Evil or Silent Hill without having a combat system polished enough to support that direction. If you want to move away from investigation and focus much more heavily on survival horror and combat, then the combat itself needs to be extremely solid.Unfortunately, it isn't. There is no quick turn, dodging can feel unreliable, the hitboxes are sometimes questionable, and enemy attacks can deal an excessive amount of damage. There are situations where avoiding enemies seems like the sensible option, yet exploration and the need to return to dangerous areas to collect valuable resources often force you to fight them anyway.This becomes particularly noticeable when compared with games such as Resident Evil 2 Remake or the more recent Resident Evil games. The Sinking City 2 simply doesn't have the same level of precision and responsiveness in its combat mechanics. Trying to imitate that style of survival horror inevitably invites those comparisons, and the gameplay isn't polished enough to compete at that level.
On the positive side, the art direction is very good. The Lovecraftian atmosphere works well, the environments have personality, and the game can be genuinely enjoyable to explore. The story, however, feels somewhat pieced together and never becomes particularly memorable.Overall, I liked The Sinking City 2 and I would still recommend it to survival-horror fans. There is a good game here. But I think the developers sacrificed too much of what made the first game unique in an attempt to turn the sequel into a more conventional Resident Evil-style survival horror. 
The result is enjoyable, but also a missed opportunity: less investigation, less interaction with the world, and a much greater emphasis on combat without having a combat system refined enough to fully justify that change.

reviews.author: mefisto_777
reviews.quote: The development of *The Sinking City 2* by the Ukrainian studio Frogwares serves as a paradigmatic case study of operational resilience and technical efficiency in contemporary video game production. Conceived and produced amidst the highly adverse socio-political climate of the ongoing conflict in their home country, the title stands as a strong example of the "AA" category, demonstrating how budgetary constraints can be mitigated through rigorous art direction and outstanding spatial design.From an environmental design perspective, the title distinguishes itself through an architectural approach that fosters high-fidelity immersion. The layout of the environments creates an urban topography structured around a scheme of balanced linearity, cohesively organized to reinforce narrative continuity. Transitions between various locations—ranging from utility facilities to hotel complexes—serve as more than mere aesthetic backdrops; instead, they shape a dynamic ecosystem where the ludonarrative is solidified. This design is complemented by the commendable environmental and functional coherence of the adversaries, whose morphological variations directly reflect the conceptual and thematic identity of the zones they inhabit.However, the game is not without structural imbalances. A central issue lies in its scope and the handling of post-game content. Despite incorporating progression mechanics—such as skill optimization (perks) and a New Game Plus mode—the campaign's brevity (estimated at roughly 7 to 10 hours) leads to an abrupt conclusion that fails to fully capitalize on the potential of the developed combat and optimization systems. Furthermore, the protagonist’s characterization is dramatically flat; mechanically reduced to the role **** figure tasked with rescuing a threatened individual, he lacks the psychological complexity needed to drive the central conflict. Compounding this limitation is an austere sound and musical design that misses the opportunity to heighten the psychological tension inherent to the genre. Despite these shortcomings, *The Sinking City 2* succeeds as a survival horror game; its inspirations are evident, and it fully grasps the fundamental tenets of the genre's classic era. I consider the price point reasonable—$30 would be fair—though I must add that if you have the chance to support the studio, you won't regret chipping in that extra $10. It is a product made with heart, and the good intentions shine **** conclusion—and in all honesty—what Frogwares has achieved with *The Sinking City 2* strikes me as a genuine feat. Designing a survival horror game with such atmosphere, such exquisite map design, and such well-conceived spatial continuity (all set against a backdrop of a truly hostile war) demonstrates immense love and respect for the genre. Getting lost around every corner and watching how enemies adapt to the theme of each building is a real delight.Admittedly, the game has its flaws: the story cuts off too soon—just as you’re enjoying it most—the protagonist feels a bit too simple, the music leaves something to be desired, and its brevity diminishes the impact of the replayability and upgrade systems. Nevertheless, at a $40 price point, the experience was thoroughly enjoyable and stands as one of the year's most pleasant surprises. It is a "Double-A" title with huge personality, proving that the studio has tremendous potential to deliver something even more ambitious in the future. RATING: 8/10

The Sinking City 2 me ha parecido un muy buen survival horror. Frogwares ha hecho un trabajo excelente, especialmente teniendo en cuenta las circunstancias del estudio. El juego entiende y aplica muy bien los fundamentos del survival horror, algo que no es nada fácil a día de hoy, y además consigue hacerlo con un tono y una identidad propios. Sus niveles me han encantado y, aunque hay pocos, también he disfrutado mucho de los **** principal problema es la duración. 
Sé que los survival horror no suelen ser juegos especialmente largos y no espero que todos duren 30 o 40 horas, pero creo que el género ha demostrado que puede ofrecer experiencias más completas, con títulos que rondan las 18-20 horas sin necesidad de convertirse en RPGs. En mi caso, terminé la Premium Edition en un solo día y The Sinking City 2 me pareció extremadamente corto. No porque piense que un juego corto sea malo, sino porque el final llega de forma muy abrupta cuando todavía estaba disfrutando muchísimo y sentía que quedaba bastante por delante.
La rejugabilidad tampoco termina de compensarlo. Los perks, mejoras y el New Game Plus son interesantes, pero hay pocos encuentros y poco contenido para aprovechar realmente todas esas posibilidades.
Reconozco que también es algo personal: últimamente tolero bastante mal los juegos cortos. No necesito juegos de 50 o 100 horas, pero para mí unas 10 (7 si vas al grano)horas se quedan cortas, especialmente a partir de 50 €. Entiendo que para otros jugadores sea una duración perfecta, pero en mi caso me ha sabido a poco.
Un muy buen survival horror, con una excelente base, mucho potencial y un gran futuro para hacer algo realmente bueno. Ojalá Frogwares pueda aprovechar mas la próxima vez  todo lo que ha construido aquí y ofrecer una experiencia más ambiciosa en el futuro.

reviews.author: jonathaancolon
reviews.quote:
To be blunt and rip the Band-Aid off, the game plays like a Resident Evil knockoff, if the story took place in the modern era and you replaced Yog Sogoth with Nemesis, this would basically be Carlos trying to save Jill by finding an antidote and you could name this RE3 Directors cut. 

That being said, the game isn't bad, I enjoy resident evil so by proxy I enjoy this. The limited resources and puzzles, make this a survival horror game in the truest sense. But I believe this game traded all the right things for the all the wrong things. 

What made the first Sinking City fun was it's story and how immersed the you were in the game due to the story telling aspect. In the first you had plenty of Side quests, and went around solving glues and while you had enemies, the game focused more on the lore and the mysteries inside this open world. While is pretty much straight forward. Your partner got her body snatched? what? nah, can't let that slide; lets go get it, and that's Sinking City 2. 

Here's a good analogy for Sinking City 2's premise. Yog Sogoth is a Van and its sriver, Calvin Rafferty is the guy chasing the van and his partner is his wallet which is in the van. The van (Yog Sogoth aka the troll) stops in one place long enough to let Calvin get close and just to drive off when Calvin is within arms reach, then he stops again to let Calvin get close once more to repeat the process, and that's the dynamic of the game.
