I never seemed to accomplish just one thing in Doloc Town. Every upgrade naturally led to another objective, and soon after, I had spent hours optimizing my farm for efficiency instead of doing what I originally logged in to do. The story occasionally loses its momentum due to its cozy nature, and getting around the world can become a chore at times, though neither stopped me from wanting to see what I could discover next. It's why I kept coming back to Doloc Town, and why it's such an easy farming sim to lose yourself in.
Doloc Town is a genuinely fun and incredibly adorable blend of farming sim and platformer set in a post-apocalyptic world, adding a genuinely unique vibe to the genre.

For fans of farming games, Doloc Town is undoubtedly worth trying. It offers plenty of fresh mechanics, systems, and production chains that constantly give you something to work toward, whether it is building a bigger and better farm or unlocking new technologies that make life easier. However, its rather traditional gameplay loop can feel somewhat tiring by todayâ€™s standards, while some of its finer details and player guidance are not quite as polished as they could be, leaving a few small areas where it falls short of other games in the genre.

Doloc Town is mostly happy to wait while you do your own thing, although there are calendar events on specific days and job board postings that will time out. Still, if players want to take a day to go fishing, there's rarely any reason not to, and while the farm does need some attention, the bulk of it can be automated with sprinklers and, eventually, end-game devices. Exploring, plan the next upgrade, experiment with new crafting stations, hang out in town, focus on gathering a specific resource, or just chill to the soundtrack, Doloc Town is generally happy to let players plot their own course through its substantial adventure. Every new day is an opportunity to max out the farm or poke about a bit and soak up the atmosphere, or maybe a bit of both, but however one chooses to spend the time, one goal leads to another until nighttime falls. And then it's a new day, and the biggest challenge of Doloc Town is not diving straight into doing it all over again as the sun rises on an ever-more-comfortable trash pile that's been re-engineered into a home.

An impressively deep farming sim with a post-apocalyptic twist, Doloc Town offers more freedom than you can shake a pick-axe at. It'll devour hours and days of your life, but you'll love every second of it.

Doloc Town can feel slow and doesn’t always communicate its concepts to the player, but it is still a great entry into the farming sim genre, offering much-needed originality in both its setting and mechanics.

Doloc Town is another strong energy in a sub-genre that is currently in rude health, with its side-on view and pixel art style helping the game to stand out. While the gameplay systems may not ultimately deviate greatly from established formula, it nonetheless provides a charming experience with enough depth and farm customisation options to keep players engaged for a significant amount of time. Farming sim fans should find plenty to like here.

A charming post-apocalyptic farming sim with creative survival mechanics and enjoyable exploration, but repetitive dialogue, weak localisation, and shallow-feeling systems keep it from fully delivering on its strong premise.

Dragon Sword: Awakening is an open-world RPG that pushes QTEs and tag-team action to the limit. Exploration feels a bit repetitive, but the world is dense, while the outstanding combat and seamless design create a satisfying gameplay rhythm. With its classic fantasy charm and exceptional action, this is a game to watch.

I’ve always liked the premise of gacha games, but not their heavy monetization. With DragonSword: Awakening, we finally have a gacha game that’s a premium product, and I think that at $30, it’s well worth it. The high-quality visuals, excellent sound design, and extensive narrative make it a worthwhile investment, not to mention you can easily get around 30 hours out of it, maybe even more.
It doesn’t save you from the heavy grind found in this genre, and the UI takes some getting used to. But at the end of the day, it’s an amazing action RPG with beautiful visuals, creative quest design and a likeable cast of characters. And if you are willing to get past the grind and some repetitive aspects, you’ll find DragonSword: Awakening to be a true diamond in the rough.

DragonSword: Awakening is an excellent anime action RPG that takes the familiar gacha formula and strips away its core aspect, delivering a premium, complete experience without the monetisation issues that often plague the genre. Its fast-paced combat and expansive open-world exploration are its biggest strengths, and the game confidently stands alongside even the genre’s biggest names. For fans of anime RPGs, it’s a polished, player-friendly experience that is well worth your time.

DragonSword: Awakening is a gorgeous anime game that feels like they took Genshin Impact, stripped out the microtransaction garbage, and tied it together with a fun, interesting story. There’s still plenty of grinding and things to unlock, but nothing requires luck with a predatory gambling mechanic. The game has fun dungeons, solid characters, and big, flashy story moments you’ll have a good time with, all for less than half the price of a triple-A game. If you’re in the market for a fun game that’ll keep you entertained for a few dozen hours, you should definitely consider DragonSword: Awakening.

DragonSword: Awakening successfully sheds its gacha origins to become an enjoyable premium single-player RPG. Its fast, intuitive character-switching combat, rewarding exploration, and generous progression systems make it easy to get invested, even if uneven storytelling, occasionally confusing systems, and localization issues keep it from reaching greater heights.

DragonSword: Awakening is a pretty good open-world action RPG that uses the gacha formula without the genre's obvious drawbacks. While its gameplay elements and systems clash due to design flaws, its eye-catching visuals, interesting narrative, and great sound design certainly justify it as a full-fledged game. All in all, it’s a game that’s definitely worth it for the price it asks, but be sure to expect a bit of a grind in the form of gacha-like repetitive progression.

DragonSword: Awakening combines satisfying exploration, engaging team-based combat and solid PC performance, but an overcomplicated interface, slow opening hours and lingering mobile design elements keep it from becoming one of the genre's standouts.

Dragonsword: Awakening delivers well-polished, albeit familiar-feeling gameplay made popular by titles like Genshin Impact, without any of the microtransactions. While I’m not personally a fan of the title’s gameplay identity, I can see how genre fans would love Dragonsword: Awakening, which does everything the biggest games in the genre do for a fraction of the price.

DragonSword: Awakening is an excellent adventure in the spirit of Tales of, but with residual elements of the gacha world and overly slow character progression. Parallels can be drawn here with Granblue Fantasy: Relink, though the Japanese project still comes off looking better than its Korean counterpart.

reviews.author: VascoGames
reviews.quote: The "Awakening" is realizing you just wasted $30 on a mobile corpse. Score: 1 / 10 If you ever wondered what happens when a developer panics, strips the casino out of a dying mobile game, and tries to sell the remaining skeletal remains to PC gamers for thirty bucks—welcome to Dragonsword: Awakening. This isn't a video game; it’s a forensic cleanup site of a failed gacha **** Gacha Ghost Town Hound13 proudly announced they "removed the microtransactions." Sounds great on paper, right? In reality, it’s a disaster. Imagine a theme park where they removed all the rides but left the ticket booths, the endless queues, and the overpriced hot dogs. The entire game is built around mobile-game architecture. You are still collecting duplicate heroes. You are still staring at 50 different red exclamation marks on your screen. You are still logging in to claim daily digital garbage. But since there is no loot box to pull, you are forced to unlock everything through a soul-crushing, mind-numbing grind that feels less like playing a game and more like working a second shift at a data entry firm. They kept the chore, but took away the dopamine.Unreal Engine 5? More like Unreal Optimization 0The developers slap the "Unreal Engine 5" logo on the screen like a badge of honor, but the game looks like a upscaled PlayStation 3 title covered in a thick layer of **** Graphics: Textures pop in 5 seconds after you look at them. The open world is a barren wasteland of copy-pasted trees and blurry **** Performance: I am running an RTX 4080, and this game managed to turn my PC into a literal space heater. Frame rates drop to cinematic single digits inside the main city. It stutters every time you swing a sword. Optimization didn't just walk out the window; it never entered the building.Combat and Story: A Masterclass in BoredomThe combat is advertised as a high-octane action-slasher. It’s not. It is a brainless button-masher where enemies stand still and politely wait for you to cycle through your character cooldowns. There is zero weight to the hits, no tactical depth, and the boss fights have the mechanical complexity of a **** for the story? It feels like it was written by an AI that was fed a diet of generic light novels and then suffered a severe system crash. The localization is purely offensive. It is so clearly a raw, unedited machine translation that sentences frequently lose all grammatical structure. It makes Google Translate look like Shakespeare.VerdictDragonsword: Awakening is a cynical, lazy cash-grab. It is an unoptimized mobile port trying to masquerade as a premium PC RPG. Do not buy this. Do not wishlist this. If you accidentally bought it, press Alt+F4 and run to the Steam Refund button before your two hours are up.Pros:The "Exit to Desktop" button works flawlessly.Cons:Everything else.

reviews.author: metam12245
reviews.quote:
By some miracle, this **** manages to combine the worst of Genshin Impact and Dragon Nest while conveniently leaving out their best parts.

So here's Hound13, desperately firing up Unreal Engine 5, trying so hard to recapture that Genshin + Dragon Nest magic – except they cheap out on literally everything they can. They straight-up copy-paste half of Dragon Nest's assets, give us a soundtrack that's dead on arrival, characters flatter than a cardboard box, and a plot that reads like a 5-year-old's make-believe. They rip off Genshin's combat and progression system, but somehow manage to **** all the fun and nuance out of it. Then they cram in Dragon Nest's ancient dungeon designs and pad the whole thing with endless, braindead enemy spam – because apparently wasting your time is the only "content" they could afford.
And when Webzen and Korean players found out, Hound13 played the victim card. They took this steaming pile – which would've EOS'd in three months as a mobile gacha – slapped a "single-player" label on it, and put it up for sale just to recoup their losses.  Guess what? It actually worked. Many unsuspecting players saw the shiny UE5 anime gloss and the woeful "poor studio" narrative, and opened their wallets like it's a charity drive. Then they booted it up and – surprise – it's all surface. A hollow, boring slog dressed in fancy lighting.

tldr: Hound13 **** this time. Don't fall for it.

DIVE or Die: Children of Rain is a compact roguelike that delivers a tense and atmospheric experience through its striking visuals, music, and darkness. While exploring without a map can be challenging, clear objectives, meaningful upgrades, and the knowledge gained from each run make every attempt feel rewarding. Its tightly focused design respects your time, but be prepared for plenty of heart-pounding moments.
A gripping survival-horror adventure with Lovecraftian charm and high replay value. Even though the roguelite elements are kept more in the background.

We really enjoyed Dive or Die - Children of Rain, largely because it has a clear sense of identity. It doesn't simply copy the gameplay loop of Dave the Diver and slap a Lovecraftian coat of paint on it; instead, it steers the experience into more demanding, strategic, and unsettling territory. Players who enjoy optimizing resources, making sacrifices, and learning through trial and error will find it highly compelling. Conversely, those looking for a lighthearted underwater adventure with only a dash of horror will likely clash with its mechanics and unforgiving nature. It is a title that demands commitment, patience, and a degree of tolerance for frustration, but it rewards that effort with tense sessions, memorable choices, and a progression system that becomes increasingly addictive the deeper you go. It may not be for everyone, but if it clicks with you, you’ll likely find yourself drawn into its abyss for hours on end.

DIVE or DIE - Children of Rain may not have an overly complex story or complicated gameplay routine, but it doesn't need those features as it more than makes up for it with its enthralling, haunting, underwater atmosphere and gameplay loop that will constantly have players diving again and again as they attempt to find every biome and collectible. It's a great 2D survival horror game to play, especially during a thunderstorm like I did, and for Drop Rate Studio's second game developed, it's a very impressive feat despite its few shortcomings.
Dive or Die executes underwater horror effectively, with the perfect balance between being unique and not straying too far from the roots of lovecraftian.

Anyone in the mood for a Lovecraftian version of Dave the Diver—and who doesn't care for sushi anyway—should feel right at home and give Drop Rate's game a try. Despite the comparisons, Dive or Die is highly original and delivers a remarkably addictive pull.

reviews.author: zatoor
reviews.quote: It's an interesting concept, and the gameplay is engaging. Unfortunately, the game's progression is somewhat poorly designed. Several times, I lost my main divers due to a few bad dives, which, given the strict day limit, meant that 3-4 hours of gameplay were wasted. I understand that some people might be annoyed by this gameplay design but overall, it's an interesting game.

reviews.author: Dirc
reviews.quote:
A thrilling mix of colony management and sidescrolling survival horror. The game is
clearly inspired by Darkest Dungeon, Dredge, and other popular lovecraftian indie games, and probably by Dave the Diver, though I haven't played that one myself.

The diving expeditions are short and intense, and the underwater map is very well crafted. The game makes clever use of metroidvania-style mechanics, and does a great job easing you into the game wiithout it feeling boring or tedious. The management part of the game is simple, but fun.

9/10.

ENDLESS Legend 2 is a great turn-based strategy game. It takes familiar genre ideas and enhances them in fun ways, while featuring eight factions that play differently. City expansion and development is the game’s most complex and engaging element, while tactical battles are its most familiar and, after a while, boring. Tidefalls and monsoons tweak the familiar rhythm of a 4X, and, alongside the many narrative-driven quests, keep exploration interesting in the long term. The title’s many interlocking systems can be somewhat opaque for genre newcomers, but reading explanations for keywords helps a lot. My biggest problem with the design is that there are only three victory paths to work with, and some factions don’t feel suited to them. I’ve already spent close to 80 hours with ENDLESS Legend 2, and the game has the variety to deliver fun turns for at least 80 more.
Endless Legend 2 is a magnificent example of why Amplitude is so loved by 4X fans.

Endless Legend 2 is no ordinary strategy game where you simply gather enough wood and stone, build an army, and destroy the enemy base. Here, it is truly about planning, making decisions, choosing the best path, and selecting friends and foes—all with such depth and scope that it can sometimes feel overwhelming.

Endless Legend often sells itself short. It doesn’t brag too boldly about how much is going on, and doesn’t toot its own horn as mythical events transpire all around me. These legends are strong. They need to flex even more.
Endless Legend 2 makes a strong first impression, but its gameplay fails to captivate over the long term.
A worthy sequel parsing together features from Amplitude's other strategy games.

The biggest issues with 'Endless Legend' were addressed in the second installment. You have more control over the battles, and more attention was paid to the development of your cities. Still, we miss the charm of the first game. Although 'Endless Legend 2' looks stunning, we feel that visually it lacks the appeal of its predecessor. Each faction also has its own story, which we found to be rather unconvincingly written. And while the battles are certainly better, the AI controlling your opponents often turns out to be brain-dead. Despite these criticisms, this is a standout in the genre that we can wholeheartedly recommend.

You can still feel that Amplitude has undeniable expertise when it comes to 4X games. The work put into giving each faction a different approach is successful, but unfortunately fails to break away from a shared progression that follows too rigid a set of rails. This is all the more frustrating because the tide mechanic is a fantastic idea and the real selling point of Endless Legend 2, even if it forces the game to lean a little too heavily toward expansionism. It's a perfectly decent game, but not necessarily one you can easily see yourself sinking hundreds of hours into, and for a 4X, that's still a bit of a shame.

All in all, though, this Early Access version of Endless Legend 2 is very promising. The devs know what they want to do with this game and have clearly focused on showcasing the vision, building a strong foundation they can expand upon while leaving enough room for community suggestions. [Early Access Review]

However, for more traditional 4X players, this focus on narrative is going to be a point of contention. For some, the focus on story and the way it shapes how you play will be an incredible addition to the formula that makes each new game unique. For others, the constant pop-ups to interact with the story will feel like distractions from the traditional 4X elements they came for. A potential issue I can also see with the storytelling is that the decisions you make are directly responsible for the rewards you receive. Multiple playthroughs will already see players exploring the same story over and over again, and the temptation to pick the optimal reward will discourage players from exploring other options simply for the sake of fully experiencing the narrative. [Early Access Review]

It’s not afraid to even poke a little bit of fun at itself, which is quite clear after the final battle. To be fair, some of the humor and crudeness of characters (looking at you Jazz) may wear thin on some players. For others, like me, you may find joy in the characters and their behavior. All in all, the game is quite great for playing who want a bit of visual novel, a bit of tactical RPG, and a bit of choices determine your final ending. I would have given the game a slightly higher score had it not had the bugs I encountered during the review, but I have confidence that by the time the game is in the hands of players, it will be much closer to the 9 and an enjoyable experience for all.

Ledgerbound is a delight to play if you’re the target audience. The characters are colorfully memorable, with personal stories that develop and grow believably throughout the game’s narrative. I love how well-rounded the SRPG mechanics are, as well as how the time management and relationship-building aspects are implemented throughout. It might not be for everyone, but Ledgerbound can be genuinely entertaining if, like its cast, the game’s allowed to grow on you.

Ledgerbound decides early on what it is setting out to do and as a result it does it very well. Even the technical issues of the pre-release build fail to take out the fully enjoyable nature of the game. In the end, it offers plenty of entertaining moments, aided by a fun set of characters and the excellent performances of its cast, wrapping them up alongside strong and satisfying tactical gameplay to keep players fully engaged.

While the strategic element of Ledgerbound isn’t all that captivating, the humor and dating sim elements should help it find an audience. Especially since the voice acting is so strong. The jokes and even way in which the romantic elements are handled might not be for everyone. I also wish I could actually just… save instead of relying on autosaves. But it’s a novel take on a heroic quest and rather colorful.

Ledgerbound is a bit like a misprinted form – the ink is messy and muddled in places, but you can still make out its function well enough. Repetitive, simple tactics, uneven writing and an underutilised premise meet an incredibly rich array of vocal performances and some charming character exchanges that do much of the work of bringing Ledgerbound’s diverse band of (mostly) endearing misfits to life. Ledgerbound does its job well enough to pass probation, but doesn’t deserve promotion just yet.

reviews.author: xcube24
reviews.quote: Coming at this from the perspective of a huge Fire Emblem/SRPG fan, this game has all the mechanics you are looking for. It's got the rock/paper/scissors weapons times, unit promotion choices, and map objectives to shoot for other than "keep everyone alive and kill the enemy." Playing on the hardest difficulty is fairly easy to get through for an SRPG vet but hitting all the objectives will test you in a satisfying way. I will say that the grid based battle probably isn't the main attraction here, but rather the in between battle "resterludes" where you talk to your party and try and romance as many or as few as you want. The voice acting is top notch and almost all the characters are likable in some way. There is no permadeath but there is a penalty for losing a unit in battle. The time management feature is the biggest drawback. It's a good idea but utilizing time and resources to equip and change loadouts is very frustrating. I shouldn't have to pick between having an optimal team buildout or experiencing the dialogue which, as I mentioned, is the main attraction here.

Bigger and arguably better than its predecessor, the long-awaited Tormentum II is a welcome darkly atmospheric psychological horror sequel that will have you constantly questioning yourself, even your own perception of what is real.

The duo behind Tormentum have once again showcased their artistic talent, delivering an immersive, intriguing, and visually distinctive game that truly stands out. They’ve managed to preserve what made the first game so good while building upon it and taking things even further.

Tormentum II is a masterpiece of dark surrealism that ventures into the
realm of dark fantasy, yet is rooted in existential science fiction.
Eight years of hard work by the developers have resulted in a dreamlike,
somber odyssey.

For all its frustrations, Tormentum II has given me plenty to chew on. Like one of its great creatures of the night, I’m not sated yet. I want to see more games by OhNoo Studio. That’s a big ask, I know. I promise I’m not saying I need another eight years of your lives like an ever-twisting ouroboros from one of your drawings. It’s just so hard not to want more when this Tormentum II feels like a step in a longer journey. Perhaps this is simply the type of game the developers are interested in. The puzzles need only be exactly what they are. But if OhNoo Studio is hoping to take that next step, well — I’ll be there day one.

Tormentum II is a straightforward point-and-click adventure whose greatest strength lies in its spectacular, nightmarish art inspired by H.R. Giger and Zdzisław Beksiński. Its puzzles could be more challenging and its story more cohesive, but the oppressive atmosphere, striking imagery, multiple choices and endings make this 8–9 hour descent into darkness a memorable and highly replayable journey.

Thinking back on my time in Tormentum II, I’m glad I swan-dived into its macabre world. As a point-and-click adventure, it wasn’t as taxing as I expected (occasionally a bad thing), and certainly not as bleak (mostly a good thing), but it still managed to surprise.

Gurei, from developer Lobo Sagaz Studio, is an incredibly challenging and unforgiving boss-rush game that takes pride in its gameplay simplicity while also offering complex strategy and a hefty amount of difficulty. It will properly rage-bait players, but in the nicest of ways.

Lobo Sagaz Studios made a game that knows exactly what it wants to be: a boss-rush game with immense replay value, featuring a dynamic difficulty system where your decisions determine how strong the bosses are.

Gurei is a wonderfully challenging boss rush that allows players to forge their own path. The ten bosses are all unique and feel great to fight, while the art style and music pull you into the world. The powers you get from the fights are a bit hit and miss, which can feel a bit disappointing. But not enough to ruin the fun.

Gurei is tough to recommend to a wide audience but the specific folks who can appreciate its brutal challenge and unique structure will definitely love it a lot. Throw in striking visuals and some secrets scattered about and you have one memorable action-packed game.

Gurei is a joy to play, as long as it lasts. The game’s design, focused entirely on its challenging and varied boss fights and dynamic difficulty, has a good amount of depth. Through mixing up the fight order and experimenting with its signature dynamic difficulty mode, there is a lot of fun you can have by exploring all that the game’s tough-but-fair Kami fights have to offer. However, for those who want a more story-rich experience, or which offers gameplay outside of only those boss fights, you may want to look elsewhere.

Gurei is a challenging adventure that forces you to carefully consider your route through increasingly difficult and imposing boss battles. Working out your path and creating a build that supports your run is refreshing, but the lack of support and steep skill curve may deter players who struggle with tough encounters. For those willing to embrace its demanding design, it’s a rewarding experience where victory is earned but never guaranteed. However, its rigid combat and lack of progression prevent it from reaching the heights of its inspirations.

I enjoyed this games combat, I enjoyed the side characters and I enjoyed the Kami and their personalities. As a whole package though I just can’t bring myself to recommend Gurei. The bosses never get hard enough to justify the early bosses being so easy and the game is just too short for the 20 dollar price tag. I do think there are people out there who would love this game and I can’t fault them. It was fun and engaging, the story is ok and the freedom of choosing bosses is a good idea. It just is not a game for me and that sucks because as I mentioned I love sidescrollers and I was really looking forward to this game.

For a long time, Avatar has felt like a poisoned chalice when it comes to video games, but Avatar Legends: The Fighting Game proves that it’s been a perfect fit all along. Even with it being on the smaller side, the fantastic and very Avatar combat mechanics, gorgeous style, and love for the series make it a fighter that’s going to be very hard to top.
Avatar Legends: The Fighting Game overcomes its initial intimidation to reveal a fighter that’s expressive, exhilarating, and that genuinely rewards improvement.

It's finally happened. After all these years, we finally have a good Avatar video game, and a darn good one at that. You can tell the developers have a real love for this franchise and give it way more respect than Paramount is giving it, that's for sure. Avatar Legends is a very fun fighting game that will be easy to learn for casuals and has a high enough skill ceiling that I can see the pro fighting game community going crazy for.

Avatar Legends: The Fighting Game is a title aimed at fans of the franchise and fighting games. With a fluid combat system that rewards mobility, as well as game modes that strike a balance between competitive and single-player experiences, it stands out as a robust gaming experience. Although the story is clearly just a pretext, it might be one that fans appreciate.

Avatar Legends: The Fighting Game is a beautiful, fun, and surprisingly competent fighting game for a project based on such a popular franchise. Its combat system manages to establish a unique identity, while the roster—though small—offers highly varied playstyles and a content package that exceeds expectations for a debut title.

Avatar Legends captures the fast-paced, frenetic battles of its source material and translates this into a deep, immersive fighter that requires skill and precision to unlock its full potential. Each character brims with personality, which bleeds into their moveset, making each contest feel unique. Although the roster is limited and newcomers may struggle to get to grips with the higher-level combos, it’s a rewarding fighter that captures the spirit of the series, rewarding persistence with some truly spectacular battles.
Avatar Legends: The Fighting Game is the closest the franchise has come to capturing the magic of the animated series in video game form.

Avatar Legends: The Fighting Game proves that the bending elements and fighting games were made for each other, delivering refined combat that respects both the source material and the high expectations of genre enthusiasts. However, the title stumbles on its own limitations, presenting a merely perfunctory narrative, a modest core cast, inconsistent art style, and single-player content that loses momentum too quickly. Nevertheless, there is an excellent foundation here, and it remains to be seen whether future content will allow the game to reach its true Avatar State.

Ultimately, a lackluster story mode and a lean launch roster can’t hold back what is easily one of the most mechanically refreshing 1v1 fighters I’ve played recently. Whether you're an FGC veteran looking for a gameplay-first experience or a casual Avatar fan just wanting to press some buttons and watch your favorite characters pull off incredible sequences in a gorgeously animated 2D fighter, Avatar Legends delivers where it matters most.

Avatar Legends: The Fighting Game is like a dream for both fans of the franchise and fighting games. With good graphics, a complex gameplay and fan service, the game is a good addition to the genre, but it doesn't serve as an entry point to this fighting game universe - and considering how many Avatar fans haven't mastered this genre, that's a shame.

Ratatan takes everything that was good about its spiritual predecessor and applies it to a faster, roguelike experience that really grooves.

While not perfectly polished, Ratatan does more than live up to Patapon's whimsical legacy. It takes the delightful rhythm action the PSP gem is known for, and elevates it with roguelike elements that pair with the core gameplay perfectly. The loss of Japan Studio and its excellent experimental games has been keenly felt over the last five years, but new releases like Slitterhead, Ratatan, and eventually Gen Atlas show that the heart of the company is still here and delivering the creative projects we crave.

Ratatan had some big shoes to fill, and I’m glad it didn’t just try to become the next Patapon. The shift towards a roguelike gives the familiar rhythm-based gameplay a twist, with deeper gameplay mechanics and a lot more to discover. With that being said, the game can become overly chaotic and the grinding won’t be for everyone, but building a stronger army motivated me enough to keep coming back. Ratatan isn’t Patapon 4, but it gives us a fun and innovative game without ever losing the spirit of what made the Patapon franchise work so well.

Ratatan is a welcome injection of weird into the Switch 2 roster. Hiroyuki Kotani builds on the legacy of Patapon with an addictive musical strategy title that will have “Rata” and “Un-Taka” rattling around your brain long after you walk away from your console. It will please fans of the developer's previous rhythm-action strategy, while offering something fresh and challenging for newcomers. It’s a bit light and can feel too chaotic at times, but it’s easily one of the most unique titles on Switch 2.

Ratatan is an interesting new rhythm action project that manages to rethink a now-classic unique combination within an indie-favorite format. The end result is an addictive experience that can keep players coming for more. While fans of the Patapon series are the most likely to enjoy it, its uncommon combination of elements makes it an easy recommendation for anyone with an open mind to try new things.

As an initial experiment, this Patapon revival works well, though it needs some tweaking—particularly regarding variety and controls. From a technical standpoint, it is certainly not a game worth nitpicking, especially given its price point; having played it on the Nintendo Switch 2, we encountered no performance issues and particularly enjoyed the handheld experience. The artists at Ratata Arts have done a fantastic job, and the legendary Kemmei Adachi (of Patapon and LocoRoco fame) returned to handle the music, collaborating with David Wise (*Donkey Kong Country*); the soundtrack is beyond reproach, and we appreciated how Ratatan pays homage to Patapon while establishing its own distinct identity. In short, we enjoyed Ratatan as a spiritual successor, but reaching the heights of Patapon will require an extra effort, especially concerning controls and variety.

Ratatan takes the great parts of Patapon and mixes them into a well-suited roguelike formula with colorful characters and tons of customization. However, its performance issues and lack of polish let it down on the Switch 2.

Ratatan retains the charm of Patapon, offering colorful visuals, pleasant music, and accessible rhythm-based gameplay. Unfortunately, as a roguelite, it falls short due to repetitiveness and unengaging meta-progression. Technical issues on the Switch 2 further detract from the overall experience.

NASCAR 26 from developer iRacing.com Motorsport Simulations is fun, with enough modes and detail to keep it engaging, and it seems welcoming to new racers through several modes. Graphically, it’s not the most gorgeous racing game I have seen, but it makes up for what it lacks in graphics with strong gameplay.
NASCAR 26 is a surprisingly meditative racer that captures the precision of stock car racing, even though its broader evolution is less convincing.

NASCAR 26 pulls off a difficult balancing act. It feels like a serious racing sim without alienating console players who just want to race. NASCAR 26 automates racing options and setups but allows you the leeway to micro-manage them. It is trying to satisfy casual console players and more demanding NASCAR fans at the same time. It performs well overall if you avoid going too deep into the underlying details that hardcore sim racers fuss about.

NASCAR 26 may still have a few shortcomings regarding game modes, but its sharp gameplay and polished graphics deliver a highly satisfying experience for both seasoned fans and newcomers alike. The "Peak Performance" feature is also a great help for beginners, offering an educational approach that highlights the sport's unique aspects.

Few frills and plenty of gas: that is perhaps the best way to sum up NASCAR 26. iRacing Studios focuses entirely on the driving experience, and it hardly matters if the surrounding package, despite benefiting from the prestigious official NASCAR license, is somewhat limited. We are looking at a title that focuses on the essentials when it comes to its modes (the career is really basic), but offers a very interesting and varied driving model where, however, the AI tends to make a few too many mistakes. This is particularly frustrating in races where a single contact can trigger a chain reaction capable of involving a large part of the starting grid. From a technical standpoint, the overall fluidity could certainly use some work, but the experience behind the wheel can still be enjoyed. It is a step forward compared to the previous installment, but a few more important steps are still needed to deliver the NASCAR game fans deserve.

As part of the process of consolidating the franchise's new phase under the leadership of iRacing Studios, NASCAR 26 reaffirms the principles introduced in the previous installment and implements subtle yet important refinements, particularly in the simulation mechanics and in the team and career management aspects. While not innovative, it still has room for improvement, such as the pace of progression and an audiovisual aspect that falls short of its major competitors in the genre.

It's understandable that iRacing Studios wanted to play it safe with NASCAR 25 to eliminate any possible issues with racing, but they erred too much on the side of caution. The updated Career Mode is nice, but the lack of any online championship and really anything new online is disheartening. The changes to the racing aren't as major as one would think, but it still remains solid against the AI. Just don't expect anything extremely deep. There are surface level changes here, and the dynamic lighting will help shake things up for players with excellent-looking environments at times, but there just isn't enough here to build on as a sequel. The game is still fun, but so was the previous year's.
NASCAR 26 has everything the oval-racing fan could ever want and no more. It’s better than last year’s title but is still missing something to take it to the next level in racing sims.

Budget- and family-friendly, apart from being occasionally too challenging, there's no reason not to recommend that you grab this.

Sniper Dan is the hidden object game for those who typically don't like hidden object games, with you having to shoot at objects rather than simply find them. Throw in lashings of humour and multiple ways to play, and you have a game that's fun and accessible for all.
I had so much more fun with Sniper Dan than I thought I would and I'll be thinking about its very silly scenarios for quite some time.

While others may not find enjoyment in it. I would highly recommend people who like this style of game to check it out. You will thoroughly enjoy playing. It will make you smile at some of the ridiculous jobs and solutions. I enjoyed every second of this game and I will definitely be looking out for whatever Denki does next.
A colourful, pleasingly silly game of helpful sniping, where you deploy your high-powered rifle to find hidden objects and help townsfolk with comedy calamities.

Roman Sands RE:Build is a bizarre, captivating psychological experience that transforms mundane service work into a surreal exploration of routine, survival, and identity. Its striking Y2K-inspired presentation, dark humor, memorable characters, and esoteric storytelling make it unlike almost anything else, even if its uneven second half and deliberately unconventional gameplay won’t appeal to everyone.
A frenetic tale of two realities, both alike in dysfunction, which immerses the player in servitude and struggle.

Roman Sands RE:Build is a strange game, and I mean that as a compliment. Its repetitive work can become a real obstacle, but the atmosphere, mystery, music, and unusual characters kept me invested. I recommend it if you’re looking for a psychological horror experience that leaves you with an existential crisis rather than a traditional puzzle game.

I’m glad I got to see the story through, however, with its not-so-subtle homages to the likes of Danganronpa and Evangelion. It remains one step away from its mysteries and doesn’t take them to extreme lengths. There’s a profound and alluring melancholy etched into this work, a broken and messy world that’s strange enough to foster questions, but smart enough not to provide every answer.

For the moment, though, I just want to stress that there's nothing out there like Roman Sands. Certainly, I've yet to play a two-parter that is quite so compelling and devious in its asymmetry. It's more ritual than game, at times, a sacrificial dagger wielded against both itself and against other videogames that are more at ease with their age. It is witty and expressive, doom-ridden and cathartic. It's a hideous thing, a total nightmare, absolutely no fun whatsoever. You must play it at once and tell me what you think.  [RPS Bestest Bests]

SPRAWL zero subverts the boomer shooter by trading a permanent arsenal for weapons scavenged midfight, turning each arena into a frantic scramble for survival. Its striking cyberpunk world and relentless soundtrack make that familiar formula feel new again, while its story takes the SPRAWL universe in a compelling direction. Repetitive enemy encounters and limited progression dull the momentum at times, but this is a thrilling next step for a series finding its own identity.

I went into SPRAWL zero curious about the prequel and came out wanting to play SPRAWL itself, so that already tells you something. More importantly, it reminded me why I spent so many hours with shooters like Quake, Unreal Tournament and Painkiller in the first place. I didn’t need skill trees, crafting or a dozen side systems back then; I just needed good levels, good weapons and enemies that kept me moving. SPRAWL zero gets surprisingly close to that feeling, some levels run longer than they should, and there were moments where I really wanted a better idea of how much of a mission I still had left, but the shooting stayed fun enough to keep me going. Seven hours later, I was still enjoying myself and already looking at SPRAWL in my Steam cart. Guess I know what I’m playing next.

SPRAWL moves away from its predecessor’s frenetic parkour in favor of more grounded action built around unlimited sprinting, Bullet Time, a Gravity Shield, and Gravity Gloves. Yet, the core experience remains the constant cycling of weapons: you pick them up, empty their magazines, and toss them aside, while remotely summoning new firearms or environmental objects to use against enemies. The maps are larger and more horizontally oriented, featuring plenty of checkpoints to avoid frustration. Excellent pacing, retro graphics, and a pounding soundtrack round out the package—an offering that appeals not only to fans of old-school shooters but also to anyone seeking adrenaline and instant action.

SPRAWL Zero is a very different game from its predecessor, but one that wholeheartedly embraces its mid-2000s mechanics, delivering a fun and accessible prequel that single-player FPS fans will enjoy.

SPRAWL zero turns firefights into a frantic improvisational scramble. You’ll drain, throw, and replace weapons while your Gravity-Gloves send bullets, barrels, and enemies flying. Its murky navigation, and late-game bullet sponges sometimes can spoil the flow, but once you drop into that shoot-toss-grab rhythm, this boomer shooter is a blast.

I really enjoyed SPRAWL Zero leaning heavily into beloved retro shooters from the past; it activated long-forgotten core memories from my all-night Duke Nukem days on the PlayStation or playing Doom into the early hours, and as a middle-aged gamer really appealed to me. With fast and exhilarating gameplay, it’s an incredibly fun experience.

SPRAWL zero is another example of how developer MAETH knows what makes a great shooter. The destructive chaos that comes from having to constantly pick up new guns and use the environment to our will is addictive when it works. There are more moments than I’d like where it doesn’t, and some enemies that really stop the flow of combat, but that doesn’t change how worthwhile this experience is as a fan of retro shooters.

SPRAWL zero is a love letter to 2000s first-person shooters and absolutely nails the assignment, for better and worse. The gameplay is fun, and the music is thumping. Experiencing it feels like coming home in a way I haven’t felt in a really long time, and I was rewarded throughout with callbacks and references. The story and level design suffer the most, leading to a game that trips over its own roots. That said, if you want an addictive, brain-off FPS, this is the game for you.
SPRAWL zero has wonderful gunplay and loads of seriously badass powers to master, but not everyone will appreciate the noughties charm.

Sprawl Zero presents a harmonious mix of modern touches with classic ideas of the shooters of the 2000s that manages to surprise at first, before some odd design choices suffocate the rest of the experience.

reviews.author: BusterSwordBoy
reviews.quote:
SPRAWL zero is my favorite shooter of the year, and likely now in my top 5 ever. As an underserved fan of Killzone, F.E.A.R., and bullet-time in general, I finally feel seen and satisfied. There's a stunning number of weapons to yank from fallen enemies (almost every single foe drops one!). Then you drain its stock of ammunition and chuck the gun at their comrades, downing them and giving you a fresh piece to get to work with. The varied enemy types approach fighting you differently, and their strategies, strengths, and weaknesses keep encounters fresh. Levels are designed with lots of things to climb, slide under, or take cover behind (briefly, as a lot of the environment is destructible), as well as debris and objects to sling at your enemies with your gravity glove. Groups of foes tote different weapon types, and not just pistol/SMG/shotgun/etc. Their make and style are also diverse: some are crude, misshapen pipe weapons, some are high-tech modern hardware, and some even seem to be [REDACTED] in nature. Over 40 of them in total!

The dedication to variety and freshness continues in the level design and the missions too, ranging from linear-ish killing sprees, to escaping environmental hazards while dealing with firefights, to moody rain-soaked sniper battles at night, to capturing important materials while exploring different areas of a semi-open city map in whichever order you choose. I never got tired of one style of play, because MAETH thoughtfully paced the game using the different tones and tempos of the campaign's levels. And the music, oh my god, the music. The title screen track, the BGM in Eden, and the many evolutions of the music in God's Light were standouts for me, though I never heard a track that didn't move me in some way. It really elevates the experience.

I had a feeling the gameplay would be stellar from the trailers, but what I didn't expect was for the writing to be so good, and the world to be so compelling. There's some excellent voice work too! I know the frantic gunplay is addictive, but do be sure to take a second to read those hidden lore notes scattered carefully throughout the levels; the added context pulls you even deeper into the Sprawl, and makes it even more satisfying to EXECUTE your goals as the main character, a supersoldier codenamed "**** took me about 10 hours to finish on normal difficulty, but I've since gone back and spent time with New Game+. I've played around with the many negative and positive gameplay modifiers and had a blast with those, too. This game is just such a complete and polished package, indie game or not. And it carries itself with this undercurrent of confidence; SPRAWL zero takes itself seriously but is massively fun, it wears its inspirations on its sleeve but never relies on imitating them. I'd say more but there are a few surprises in the game I wouldn't want to spoil. Just impressive all around.

I strongly recommend SPRAWL zero to anyone who enjoys first-person games, 6th gen titles (PS2, Xbox, GameCube), cyberpunk/dystopian worldbuilding, tactical shooters, reflex shooters, F.E.A.R. 1 & 2, and slow-motion bullet-time action (Max Payne series, Stranglehold). Hardcore gamers can enjoy a challenge on Formidable (Normal Difficulty) or a Herculean labor on Martyr (Hard Mode), and if you're new to the genre you can still enjoy the chaos of battle without using as much strategy or swiftness and the take in the music/world/story of SPRAWL zero on the cleverly framed Unstoppable (Easy ****'s great! A 9/10 for me. Enjoy!

reviews.author: John1_1
reviews.quote:
Ok they nailed, and I mean *nailed* the gameplay loop. It is 30 seconds of fun over and over and over. The combat is varied, empowering, and challenging at the right times. I can’t say enough about the guns and compare mechanics.

In addition the atmosphere, music, story are all engrossing, wonderfully sci-fi and dystopian. In fact, the presentation is *so* good it makes you wonder why it is relatively one note. I’d love to see the team add more moments of color and incorporate even more diverse styles.

The only negative thing is the backtracking or sheer size that several of the levels demands. They take too long or are too circuitous. Something like more distinct set pieces or more straightforward levels would’ve improved my rating. 

That said, the gameplay is SO fun it more than makes up for some of the level design. I can tell the combat, story, and overall vibe was built with intention and passion so this game is really worth your time and money.

Lootbound highly impressed me with its simple yet expressive mechanics and its loot-focused, turn-based roguelike structure. Paired with its incredible art, vivid world, and interesting characters, and you have a game that is sure to stick with you long after you’ve beaten it. Lootbound is an experience that you’ll struggle to let go… much like that legendary but under-leveled piece of gear you’re hanging on to.

Lootbound is one of the best indie games of 2026 that excels in every aspect. The combat is tactical and satisfying. The atmosphere and art direction are captivating and represent dark fantasy extremely well. The gameplay loop is rewarding, and progression is well-balanced. The only thing holding it back is its lack of story and narrative support. Every run has a sense of purpose and feels different thanks to the RPG nature. Lootbound easily stands out as one of the best roguelite and turn-based games in recent memory.

Lootbound is a great, bite-sized roguelite that’s best enjoyed in short bursts. It’s addictive, sure, but its barebones storytelling, overreliance on luck, and early-game grind can sometimes get in the way. What ultimately carries the experience is its surprisingly deep buildcrafting, which should appeal to veteran roguelite fans while giving you plenty of freedom to shape your own journey through the loot you pick, party members you recruit, and bosses you face. It knows exactly what it wants to be, giving you just enough control to feel like a Dungeon Master while leaving enough to chance to make every victory feel earned, one roll at a time.

Taken individually, Lootbound’s ideas are solid, even diverting. But developer ArtDock forgets the player in a game that tries to merge several genres without ever truly considering how those disparate concepts should interact with one another for a generic and repetitive experience.

Pro Jank Footy captures the cultural zeitgeist of Aussie Rules football with such charm you’d think it’s an Australian psyop. You can really feel the love for the sport in how well the actual game has been translated into this arcade-style version. Despite some issues with swapping from player to player, overall the gameplay is a blast, especially as it gets jankier and jankier with power-ups. It’s the perfect couch co-op game, something easy to pick up and play with some friends for a good time. It knows exactly what it wants to be, and pulls it off with so much Aussie flair.

Pro Jank Footy achieves what it sets out to do by providing an affectionate, delightfully bizarre tribute to Aussie Rules. While AI positioning and forward line density could benefit from tighter balancing, its creative power-up system, varied venues, and accessible match formats make it a fine addition to any footy fan's off-season rotation.

With that sense of cheeky humour and good fun, Pro Jank Footy is a consistent blast. It’s not the deepest game, but it certainly is one of the most funny I’ve played this year. It derives plenty of charm from its goofiness, and may earn a place in your heart for that reason.

Pro Jank Footy's simplicity is in some ways to its detriment, but the sheer slapstick spectacle of the thing, and the clear reverence for the pixelated sports games of old carry it to greatness. This isn't the sort of thing I'd play on the regular, but it is absolutely coming out at group events.

There’s nothing else like it, the story is intriguing, the voice acting fantastic, and oh my goodness the art is sublime, both in levels and in the stunningly drawn still cutscenes. The fact that this is all packed into a $25 game is remarkable, and well worth your eyes.

Ambrosia Sky Act Two is a fitting conclusion that introduces enough new twists to set it apart from the first act. There are a couple of navigational issues, but the oddly relaxing sensation of spraying down fungus combined with the many mechanics surrounding that central conceit are certainly worth experiencing. If you want to power wash some dangerous growths in a melancholy sci-fi world, I think Ambrosia Sky: Act Two will be right up your alley.

I guess that’s the problem with the episodic release format, even for one released in two halves. You release the first part, and it’s great, but then you have additional time to improve on some of the stuff that didn’t quite work for the second part, and that side of the story becomes the stronger half.
Ambrosia Sky’s second act is just more of the same—a half-decent narrative buried under a cluster of monotonous gameplay and subpar design.

A solid game aimed at young children, Paw Patrol: Dino World is a fun adventure that remains faithful to the much-loved cartoon while offering a worthwhile original story. Older kids and grown-ups might get bored of the simple missions and repetitive tasks, but for youngsters just getting to grips with playing video games, it's a great starting point.
The PAW Patrol: Dino World targets the intended audience perfectly from its frustration-free gameplay, graphics which mirror the cartoon and excellent voice acting.

PAW Patrol – Dino World makes no attempt to hide the fact that it is a game for children, delivering a solid experience with mechanics that are simple and fun for its target audience. The camera might be a bit of a headache, but nothing that hinders the ever-ready PAW Patrol on yet another mission.
PAW Patrol: Dino World is a lovely little game that makes exploring large areas as you unlock goodies for your favourite pups a real treat.

Overall, the changes made to the four stories in this Blue Reflection collection don’t compromise the central thesis of the series (even with Sun and that pesky male character): These are truly, almost painfully ethereally beautiful magical girl JRPGs with a relentlessly wholesome message behind them. I have no idea if Koei Tecmo sees a future in something this niche, but even if this collection is the grand sum of the Blue Reflection vision, it’s an enormously heartwarming 100 hours that will linger with you long after you stop playing.

A four-in-one deal of three amazing games and one poor game to drag it down. While Blue Reflection Quartet, for the most part, tells compelling stories about growing up, the unfortunate black sheep makes the uncomfortable camera angles of the other games impossible to write off as flukes. Despite its questionable fan service, it is hard not to fall in love, as Blue Reflection Quartet offers great characters and combat systems that will keep fans of the genre stuck to their Switch 2s through the rest of the summer.

Blue Reflection Quartet is absolutely worth it for the original two console games, but the adaptations of the Ray anime and Sun mobile title aren’t as strong. The two mainline releases both feel wonderful to play, look great, and still tell relevant stories. This take on Blue Reflection Sun isn’t terrible, but it lacks punch and attention to details. The Blue Reflection Ray segment is so poorly handled that it’d really be better and more entertaining to watch the anime on Crunchyroll instead.

Not all of the games that comprise BLUE REFLECTION Quartet will satisfy JRPG fans, but the tentpole entries are fun. Combat is engaging, albeit too easy, and the characters and stories are surprisingly relatable to those of us who typically don’t leave our villages to overthrow kingdoms or defeat the gods on a regular basis.

BLUE REFLECTION Quartet is at its best when it reminds you why Gust's magical girl RPGs earned such a devoted following. While the revised versions of RAY and SUN still contain compromises and some superfluous self-censorship is present, this is the most complete way to experience the Blue Reflection saga.

Blue Reflection Quartet is an attempt to bring this whole series together, across previously disparate formats. It’s not entirely successful, as you’re better off just watching the anime instead of trudging through this version of Ray’s weird recap slideshow gimmick. Sun’s impossible to play in English otherwise (or at all, really), so this is going to be your only opportunity if you’re curious. Meanwhile, this is the most efficient and effective way to play the other two games anyway, rather than individually expensive (and in the first game’s case undercooked) PC ports. I wish the Switch 2 versions weren’t locked to 30 fps, but they do look nice in 1080p. All in all, I’d say if you’re jonesing for something new and interesting in the magical girl realm that isn’t just caked in gratuity, Blue Reflection is a must. Everything else is just an odd bonus.

Blue Reflection: Quartet’s goal is noble. It’s trying to give players an all-in-one ticket to an RPG series that may well have slipped under their radars. Between the modest technical performance and half-baked adaptations of the anime and mobile game, this whole affair ends up feeling quite underwhelming. Blue Reflection and Second Light are interesting spins on the usual Gust fare, and I’d almost prefer whatever resources went into the other half of Quartet had instead been spent polishing those titles so they shone just that little bit brighter. If you’re curious about Blue Reflection and you prefer to play on Nintendo’s consoles, this will check that box well enough. I wish it did more than just that, though.

Players looking primarily for complex combat systems or sprawling open worlds may struggle with the deliberately measured pacing. Likewise, those expecting a traditional magical girl adventure filled with spectacle might be surprised by just how introspective these stories often become. For those willing to discover the series on its own terms, however, Blue Reflection offers something refreshingly different.  It’s thoughtful and sincere, and perhaps most importantly, it’s unapologetically comfortable with vulnerability, which brings me back to those Saturday mornings. When I watched Sailor Moon as a child, I didn’t understand what made it different from the cartoons surrounding it. Magical girl stories simply weren’t something I thought much about.

BLUE REFLECTION Quartet is a collection that is less than the sum of its parts, with the adaptations for Ray and Sun being extremely lackluster. Additionally, the new and improved visuals are still quite dated and also unimpressive from a performance standpoint, especially on the Switch 2. Despite its phenomenal audio design, which significantly elevates the experience and all its other elements, the collection feels more like a missed opportunity, much like its overall narrative that wasted its potential.
An absolute mixed bag, featuring 2 reasonably good and distinctive RPGs, but then 2 lesser offshoot efforts that muddy the overall picture of quality for the package.

reviews.author: Not_Batman_20
reviews.quote:
Went the censorship route to pander to a "modern audience" that didn't show up and betrayed the people that supported the series in the 1st place.

Besides that, this "collection" is incredibly lazy. The adaptation of the anime specially has 0 effort put unto it.

The additional content added to Second Light (a few extra playable characters from the gacha that have 0 interactions or story relevancy) is not even close to make up doesn't for what wasn't included from the original version or what was butchered from Blue Reflection 1.

reviews.author: Star_G19
reviews.quote:
EDIT: After clearing Blue Reflection Second Light last night.. it was truly a beautiful game, I cried to the ending and am still thinking about it..

 I honestly haven't felt this strongly about a game or it's story in years.. I am sad it is over but this game had such a wonderful story and group of girls as characters in this world. This game, Blue Reflection Second Light is how you write emotional, endearing and heartfelt stories that you care about the characters to the end! This game has so much heart to it I am really just blown away after clearing the game.

 I also love the main theme "Tie" and the soundtrack to the game is outstanding.

The game has many powerful messages about Life that just casually drop to the player during conversations amongst the girls and how they deal with the tragedy and events that conspire throughout the story.

 It is at the end, a beautiful story **** of brave girls fighting against the Apocalypse and fighting through to see things through to the very end.

Afterschool Ariette as the ending song to Blue Reflection Second Light was one of the most beautiful and amazing ending songs I have heard to a game in some time, I am truly grateful I played this game! Heartfelt and touching story with many great Life messages, a beautiful work of art. And great ensemble of girls to the characters of this wonderful story. All the thanks to the Developers Koei Tecmo Games and Gust for this experience and I am so grateful to have played it.

 I am looking forward to playing the first game now and even trying Ray and Sun afterwards. I hope the developers make a sequel to Second Light, although with how that ends, I am unsure what it would be like.. one can hope..


(earlier post before clearing the game)
I'm really loving it so far, I never played the series before so I got into Second Light first. I am really enjoying the Japanese type story and characters with the girls, music soundtrack also feels very Japanese, the story is interesting. Looking forward to learning more, only at chapter 3 and I've spent about 12 hours, been exploring alot and leveling though. Kokoro is probably my favorite character so far. Really enjoy the opening music intro too.  

Also - the combat is fun! I really like how it feels Turn based, but also real time at the same time.. it's sort of hard to explain, but one of the last Japanese style RPGs I played that wasn't made by Square-Enix, was Tales of Berseria, which although I loved the story, I didn't really care for the combat at all and could never really get into it..I just played on Auto that game. But at least for Blue Reflection Second Light I really enjoy the combat! and can understand it and what I am doing. 

Playing through more of the story, Shiho, Hinako, Kokoro, Ao are now my favorite girls in Second Light. It's a beautiful story so far, I am actually very surprised with how good the story is so far. I can't believe I missed out on this game series back in 2017 with the first and then Second light in 2021. The elements of the Ashen Apocalypse combined with a somewhat Matrix style premise hideout away from a real world in the future, it really is interesting! I hope they make a 3rd game now. (Cross fingers)

Got to Chapter 8 last night - that scene with Rena and Yuki was really heartfelt, I almost teared up a little towards the end of that scene.. The voice acting is outstanding in Japanese, even though I only know a little I can understand some things, the emotion in the Japanese VO is incredible, the writing is also very solid so far and all the chapters are intriguing. 

I am looking forward to completing the rest of the game, I feel something sad will happen at the end :(

reviews.author: Lagshard
reviews.quote: The whole wonderful blue reflection universe all in one package, i coundn’t recommend this collection more
Jotunnslayer: Hordes of Hel is a Survivor-like with a gritty Diablo-like art style and a ton of progression systems.

Jotunnslayer: Hordes of Hel is a fantastic horde arena survival game that follows the successful survivor-like formula while adding its own unique spin through its mission-based structure and rewarding hero and patron god skill systems. It’s an addictive gameplay loop that’s hard to put down, made even more compelling by the steady stream of unlocks and modifiers that extend its longevity. Sure, the framerate may have moments where it falters, but it doesn’t dampen the Hel of a great time you’ll have fighting for your freedom. Once the gods get their hooks into you, it’s incredibly difficult to put the controller down.

Jotunnslayer: Hordes of Hel doesn't revolutionize the survivor-like genre, but it builds its own identity thanks to its Nordic setting, a well-designed progression system, and gameplay that manages to stay engaging even after numerous playthroughs. Local co-op represents an added value that's far from negligible, while the excellent Nintendo Switch 2 port lets you enjoy the experience without significant compromises compared to other consoles. It's a title that stakes everything on immediacy and the constant urge to tackle just one more run, and for the most part it hits that goal perfectly.
There's a lot to do in Jotunnslayer: Hordes of Hel and the mythological aesthetic is pitch-perfect for an arcade-like survival actionfest.

Overall Jotunnslayer is a very engaging arena survival game, whilst it may not be genre defying or really adding much new, what it does offer is solid game that has enough uniqueness and quality gameplay that it does deserve a play through for anyone looking for a new Vampire Survivors style game.

With satisfying combat and meaningful progression, Jotunnslayer: Hordes of Hel captures everything that makes the roguelite genre so compelling. A shaky framerate occasionally disrupts the action, but the experience remains an easy recommendation on Nintendo Switch 2.

Jotunnslayer: Hordes of Hel is a solid entry in an ever-growing subgenre. As a relatively new fan of this style of play, I was bit by the ‘one more run’ bug early, playing during my downtime at work and trying to get through harder quests before bed. It doesn’t offer any real innovations and some performance and graphics issues keep it from being top-tier, but for those who love a good challenge or need an enjoyable ‘jump in and out’ game, this one feels like a gift from the gods.

Jotunnslayer: Hordes of Hel delivers a satisfying horde-survival experience with varied builds, rewarding progression and impressive visuals. Its objectives can become repetitive and chaotic encounters sometimes hurt visibility, but the Nintendo Switch 2 version is a solid fit for short portable sessions.

Jotunnslayer: Hordes of Hel doesn’t reinvent the genre and suffers from a degree of repetition, particularly regarding missions and map structure. However, it manages to deliver a solid, satisfying, and highly engaging gameplay loop. For fans of “Survivors-likes” and Norse mythology, it is a highly recommended purchase.

Jotunslayer: Hordes of Hel is one of the most entertaining roguelikes I've played on my Switch 2, a game with deep strategy hiding under its horde-survivor skin. The God-combo builds, the pantheon-wide meta progression, and the escalating realms had me chasing down gold across worlds and difficulty levels. It's just a shame that the Switch 2 port arrives in such a rough technical state. The framerate stumbles, the audio drops, and that Alfheim crash is a run-ending buzzkill. There's an 8, maybe higher, buried in here, and a patch or two should dig it out. But as it stands on day one, I can only score what's in front of me.

Fading Echo proves that there’s still room for original ideas in an industry obsessed with big budgets. Its brilliant visual style, an element-based combat system, and creative gameplay turn every level into a constant exercise in experimentation. Although its story and soundtrack don’t quite reach the same level of inspiration, it ultimately proves to be a charming, fresh adventure that’s very easy to recommend.
Fading Echo is an indie action-adventure brimming with bold imagination, twisting and combining simple rules to create fresh and unexpected fun.

Fading Echo makes use of elements and ideas that you've likely seen before in other games in clever ways. Even if the execution is far from perfect, it's the personality embedded in the story, its characters, and the regions you visit that form a cohesive experience that is quick to win you over with its charms.
Fading Echo utilizes a really unique style for its aesthetic, platforming and combat for a truly engaging experience.
Fading Echo is a great game with engaging combat, tricky puzzles, and a world worth exploring; it definitely deserves picking up if you want a new adventure in a far-off land.

While Fading Echo appears like yet another action platformer, it quickly sets itself apart with its element manipulation features and intense gameplay mechanics. It’s fun to play, the comic book styles cutscenes are cool, and the abstract visual design will quickly grab your attention. It also helps that the game is very creative and it continues to throw things at the wall to see what sticks. If you’re into action platformers, this is certainly right up your alley. I felt that the game manages to introduce new audiences to this genre quite well, even if the combat does feel repetitive at times. The story is easy to ignore, and you can just focus on eliminating enemies and solving puzzles. Those are the true strengths of the game, and the title certainly knows that. Overall, Fading Echo managed to scratch the 3D platformer itch, with some amazing elemental powers and lots of intense moments.

Fading Echo presents bold ideas with mixed execution, ultimately delivering a victorious adventure. Its action-RPG gameplay features creative battles and robust puzzle mechanics, which are the game's undeniable charm. The narrative is rich, and the Brazilian voice acting is impeccable. Visually, it leverages Unreal Engine 5 for stunning graphics, though this comes with high system requirements. While exploration and map design can be confusing, detracting from the experience, the engaging puzzles and compelling story outweigh these flaws. Despite some ambitious ideas not fully realized, the game offers a worthwhile 10-hour journey.

Fading Echo is exactly the kind of indie game that deserves to be discovered. Its creative combat, excellent art direction, and—above all—fantastic Brazilian voice acting manage to create a unique identity in a market crowded with similar releases.

Fading Echo is a colorful and inventive adventure built around clever elemental interactions that enhance combat, exploration, and puzzle-solving. Although repetition, and limited enemy variety prevent it from reaching its full potential, its striking art direction and distinctive mechanics make Emeteria’s debut well worth experiencing.
Fading Echoes has some issues, but it's ultimately a fun experience with badass elemental powers and a whole lot of kicking.

My only issue is that the game shows almost all its enemies and elements in the first few hours and lacks novelty in the long run, but keeping in my the game took me about 8h to complete that’s not a big deal to me

iv been playing this game near nonstop. the story is compelling, the artwork and level design is breath taking and the voice acting is best in class!

the game is a bargain and well worth buying as soon as possible

Toy Story 3: Complete Edition is a fantastic new way to experience one of the most underrated games from the 2000s. The gameplay of both the story mode and Toy Box still holds up after sixteen years, as does its unique approach to adapting the 2010 film. While the lack of any additional behind the scenes or quality-of-life features is a tad frustrating, the overall quality of the original game is more than enough to justify the price point for longtime fans and newcomers alike.

Toy Story 3: Complete Edition is a pleasant surprise that recaptures the golden age of movie-based games. Although the Story Mode is short and suffers from some unevenness in level pacing and control precision, the title truly shines in the rich Toy Box Mode, offering sandbox-style freedom packed with activities and customization options. Ultimately, the Complete Edition establishes itself as the definitive version of an absolute classic-an excellent recommendation for children and a nostalgic journey for longtime fans.
Toy Story 3 Complete Edition marks the return of an interesting platforming adventure. Although it offers hardly any new content, it’s a great opportunity to experience the game.

And Toy Story 3 Complete Edition as a remaster is a great update. While there are minor quality of life gameplay tweaks, it’s the resolution and textures get the most attention. Sadly, cut scenes remain muddy, but it’s impressive how good this already was. Toy Story 3 was great in 2010, and it’s still a ton of fun in 2026.

End of Abyss is a challenging yet rewarding adventure, at once boasting gorgeous graphics and grotesque visuals, and featuring an intricately crafted facility to explore. Each area is filled to the brim with secrets to uncover, unique enemies to defeat, and difficult bosses to conquer. Throw in a mysterious story to unravel and End of Abyss manages to stand out amongst a crowded market and deliver an experience well worth diving into.

End of Abyss is the surprise hit of year, with its forebodingly atmospheric Facility, unsettling enemy design, and well executed minimalist philosophy, it brilliantly combines its multiple genres to create a distilled and engaging survival horror experience.

End of Abyss is claustrophobic and eerie, science fiction survival horror through the eyes of Little Nightmares. Section 9 expresses its roots in new ways, incorporating intricate progression and anxious combat into the mix. By placing protagonist and player in a harsh world of dangerous paths and twisting secrets, each new door may open unto a potential flood of horrors and clutched chests.

End of Abyss is a moody and cinematic metroidvania with a tantalisingly dark sci-fi world, tactile twin-sticks combat, and a scintillating brain-teaser of a map. It’s brutally hands-off at times, but it makes the moments when you figure it all out all the more satisfying. Some bugs do taint the experience a little, but End of Abyss is a gorgeous horror-tinged must for metroidvania fans.
End of Abyss is a very interesting survival horror game with a fantastic atmosphere. It doesn't reinvent the wheel, but it is extremely well made.

End of Abyss is easily one of the better Metroidvanias to release this year. Its exceptional map design and rewarding character progression draw you in almost instantly, while the challenging monstrosities make combat fun to master. However, the game's strengths can also become a source of frustration. Its heavy reliance on Metroidvania elements, such as constantly requiring a key or specific item, combined with a complex level layout and lack of a proper fast-travel system, can leave you trekking back and forth across the map, turning progression into a major time sink. Still, either way, End of Abyss is more than worth the investment.

End of Abyss is a creepy adventure whose charm takes time to settle in. The dark atmosphere heightens the experience, making you fearful yet curious about what comes next. The difficulty is just right, and you won't run out of resources, letting you control enemy situations as you like. It's not perfect, and there are some frustrating aspects. But the negatives are far outweighed by the positives, and it's an immersive experience that will be hard to put down.

Despite the glitches, I loved snooping through the cold, industrial hallways of End of Abyss, and the bugs did surprisingly little to affect my overall opinion. I've been looking forward to End of Abyss for quite some time, and I'm pleased that it mostly lived up to those expectations.

We all know perfectly well that we’re in the middle of one of the most intense release periods in recent years. Practically everywhere you look, there’s a major game waiting for you, so the idea of jumping into something you weren’t expecting and that seemingly came out of nowhere can be quite difficult. That’s precisely where End of Abyss comes in. It’s an extremely good game in almost everything it does, but it doesn’t quite reach the heights where I’d tell you to move it to the very top of your priorities. I think that if you enjoy Tarsier’s work, you’ll absolutely love what Section 9 Interactive is bringing to the table. So, at the very least for now, this is a game you should definitely keep on your radar. And who knows? At some point, you might be able to make some room in your schedule to sit down and enjoy it.

With End of Abyss, Section 9 Interactive takes what they learnt from Little Nightmares and creates a new beast that blends their trademark unsettling atmosphere with Metroidvania exploration. The interconnected world is a thrill to explore; however, it can be difficult to determine how to reach your destination due to the lack of guidance. Vile enemies lurk in the corridors, ready to strike, requiring thoughtful combat, which increases the tension. Despite some navigational frustrations, it’s a compelling adventure that delivers a haunting experience.
