reviews.author: Sixela1978
reviews.quote:
This is a survival horror game. It doesn't really do anything original or innovative; it shamelessly "borrows" elements from other games (I won't even mention genres), like Dead Space, Signalis, Ada's scanner in RE2, Chronos, etc. But that's not inherently a problem if it implements those elements to create smooth, seamless gameplay. Does it succeed? Not at all: 

The combat is deliberately clunky to the extreme; it feels forced because, as we all know, the modern, stupid, maxim of this genre is to make aiming and movement awkward, and developers have run out of ideas to inject this nonsense. Add to that the fact that the enemies are bullet sponges and you have the perfect recipe for something we've seen countless times before, and not exactly in a good way. They never learn. The bosses are the epitome of bad design: mostly a single attack pattern, endless spamming of minions and acolytes, area-of-effect attacks with terrible hitboxes... 

The scanner mechanic simply adds an extra step to the typical interaction with doors, locks, and keys to determine if they're locked or unlocked, similar to games like Resident Evil; however, here it's not enough to just approach and interact with the door (or whatever it is) in question; instead, you have to move around aiming the scanner, at a snail's pace, scanning stuff while a progress bar fills and is finally marked on your map, constantly switching between your weapon and the damn scanner. Some developer thought this sounded fun and "freshy," creative. It ****. The scanner mechanic has some potential, such as its usefulness for finding "invisible" things, but it's poorly implemented and overshadowed by useless filler. The gameplay is tedious, boring, and irritating. 

I'm also encountering bugs like enemies clipping through walls or getting stuck in an animation, for example when you pick up a key item, while an infected suddenly appears from nowhere, without being able to cancel the animation. 

So, do I recommend this game? Do what you think is best, but never trust what they tell you in teasers or trailers.

reviews.author: Juanitp

En cuanto a los enemigos, hay cierta variedad dentro de lo que cabe, pero he echado en falta más contenido secundario, alguna misión extra o personajes interesantes con los que interactuar, al estilo de Hollow Knight, que aportasen más vida y profundidad al mundo. Las distintas zonas por las que pasamos están bien diferenciadas, pero el uso constante de una paleta de colores tan similar termina haciendo que la experiencia resulte algo monótona visualmente. Otro punto negativo es el sistema de disparos: apuntar con el mando se siente bastante incómodo y la precisión deja mucho que desear. Por último, me ha faltado música.

reviews.author: myrk

reviews.author: azinga
reviews.quote:
If you enjoy Metroidvanias, old-school games and atmospheric experiences like Little Nightmares and Reanimal, do yourself a favour and give this game a chance. ️

End of Abyss has a fantastic atmosphere, beautiful art direction and surprisingly strong level design. You have to learn the mechanics, understand enemy patterns and explore with some finesse, it’s not just about running around killing everything. That’s exactly what makes it rewarding.

For a tiny indie studio making its first game, what they’ve created is genuinely really impressive. It has its own identity, and I think that deserves to be appreciated.

It’s not flawless, and there are some bugs and rough edges, but nothing that a few updates can’t fix. What matters is the experience underneath, and that’s where this game really shines.

If this looks like your kind of game, give it a shot! You might be missing out on one of the most interesting indie games of the year.

reviews.author: kengpavel
reviews.quote: As a standalone project from former Tarsier Studios developers, it’s a solid game. It’s expansive, dark, and atmospheric, and—on top of that—mechanically interesting in terms of both gameplay and its core gameplay concept. When compared to Little Nightmares and Reanimal, this game is definitely superior—with the possible exception of Little Nightmares 2. The exploration structure is absolutely top-notch.
Expanding and improving on the original game in most conceivable ways, Minecraft Dungeons 2 is an excellent advancement in this ARPG spin-off for one of gaming's most beloved and iconic franchises.

Minecraft Dungeons II is at its best with a friend. Its item system makes experimenting with gear rewarding, while fluid, straightforward combat keeps the action moving. Late-game freezes on Xbox Series X are frustrating, but they did not spoil an enjoyable co-op adventure.

Minecraft Dungeons 2 is a brilliant sequel. It offers exactly what you want from the franchise and much more! The world is a joy to explore, and I love the new monsters and weird setting. It is fantastic with friends and great when playing alone. It captures every Minecraft vibe while remaining true to what we all love.

Minecraft Dungeons II proves that sometimes more really is better. I loved the original game, but this sequel improves its formula with deeper customization, better loot, more challenging encounters and an incredibly addictive gameplay loop. It is easy to pick up from the very first minute, yet gradually becomes deeper as you progress.

Despite a lacklustre endgame and a handful of minor issues, it’s not hard to see Minecraft Dungeons II as the game the original was meant to be. The combat is flashier, tougher and more engaging. The world is bigger and more cohesive. The character builds are more varied. Most importantly, it all just feels confident. This isn’t merely Diablo with a Minecraft skin, but a fantastic dungeon crawler with a hopefully bright future ahead.

Minecraft Dungeons II builds on its predecessor with colorful worlds, satisfying loot and accessible gameplay that still offers plenty of depth. It’s at its best in co-op, where its simple yet surprisingly addictive dungeon-crawling formula truly shines.

The only thing you need to know to buy Minecraft Dungeons II is that my cousin wanted to give it a 10. But you should also know that it’s an incredibly fun experience, featuring a professional-grade RPG system and an extraordinarily diverse combat system - so while you’re buying it for your child, younger sibling, or relative, make sure there’s a controller for you, too.

Minecraft Dungeons II takes everything that felt aimless about the original and brings it into focus. The combat is simple and the story is forgettable, but a steady drip of loot and satisfying buildcrafting make for a sticky, stay-up-too-late loop. Add clean performance and some of the most flexible co-op around, and you've got an accessible looter that works as well for Diablo vets as it does for super-excited 10-year-olds.

Minecraft Dungeons II expands its predecessor’s formula in every direction, offering a vast world, deeper loot and customization, new movement options, and more flexible co-op. The chance to explore Minecraft’s new Sift dimension further enriches the experience. Despite a few minor issues, it remains an accessible and enjoyable action RPG, ideal for newcomers and for sharing with friends and family.

Minecraft Dungeons II adds another dimension of ambition, challenge, and fun to a classic series. The game’s upgraded visuals, world navigation, and gear system gives players more flexibility and control, and the new Souls‑powered Sift dimension expands the world with fresh lore, enemies, and secrets. Though some village upgrades feel underdeveloped, the game’s customization, exploration, and co‑op options make this sequel a vibrant and engaging step forward for the Dungeons series.

reviews.author: Pokecharz11
reviews.quote: Minecraft Dungeons II takes everything that worked in the original 2020 game and expands it into a massive, interconnected experience. Replacing the rigid, mission-select central hub with a continuous, connected Overworld makes exploring the land feel far more organic and immersive.   The addition of jumping and double jumping fundamentally transforms how combat and traversal function. Airborne strikes, double-jump dodges, and multi-level arena verticality make the ground-bound, roll-only movement of the original game feel primitive by comparison.   The standout highlight is The Sift. This brand-new dimension introduces shifting environmental tides, strange new mob mechanics, and surreal landscapes that push build crafting and combat strategy to their limits. Minecraft Dungeons II isn't just a basic follow-up—it's a massive leap forward for the entire spin-off series. An easy 10 out of 10.

reviews.quote:

If you enjoy the building and crafting aspects of a survival game you will enjoy this game, if you enjoy the exploration and combat of an RPG game you will enjoy this in fact there really isn’t much to dislike. This is a game where there is always something to do, a simple trip back to your base to drop off items and you can easily find yourself spending hours tending to your garden,cooking new recipes or rearranging furniture and redesigning your house. If you enjoy either survival or multiplayer RPG games, I urge you to give the game a try.
RuneScape: Dragonwilds is a familiar yet bold twist on a classic, melding together different genres into a fun and addictive experience that seemingly has only just begun.

RuneScape: Dragonwilds intelligently takes the most iconic elements of the franchise and makes them work in an entirely new genre. It stands out amongst the survival game crowd thanks to its competency, depth, engaging systems and player freedom. Some designs can be improved, no doubt, but Dragonwilds' most exciting aspect is what it could be in the future, as the title almost explodes with limitless potential.

I had an amazing time with RuneScape: Dragonwilds, and I find it to be one of the top survival games released in the past few years. It has a wonderful building system, and spells are not a forgotten item, they are at the core of the game in many ways. The progression system is simple, yet addictive, and the co-op gameplay is one of the best in its genre. RuneScape: Dragonwilds certainly has some flaws, like building restrictions, excessive grind, repetitive combat, which can sometimes deter you from playing more. But if you get through the more challenging initial section, you will find a delightful, cozy survival experience with a beautiful story, one that you’ll want to replay at least once.
Delivers an engaging experience on AN. Jagex returns to its iconic franchise, offering a massive, beautiful, and incredibly fun survival game.

Overall, RuneScape: Dragonwilds has been a fun experience. A very beautiful atmospheric game where the way you experience it is really your choice. Jagex gives options to make it as hard or as easy as you want. You want difficulty? You got it. Want a standard play but with some exp adjustments and nothing else? You can do that. Want to negate needing runes for spells completely? You can! Super enjoyable to run around as a powerful archer.

RuneScape: Dragonwilds successfully brings the familiar world and progression of RuneScape into the survival genre. Its skill system, building mechanics and clever use of magic make exploring Ashenfall genuinely rewarding, although combat can still feel stiff and the PC version could use further optimization. A solid and surprisingly addictive survival RPG, especially when played with friends.
However you choose to play Runescape: Dragonwilds, it’s clear that Jagex is assembling another forever-game.

Despite tedious character customization menus and frustratingly vague tutorial quests, RuneScape: Dragonwilds v1.0 stands out as a breathtaking and potential-rich survival game elevated by an addicting, highly rewarding magic system. While punishing enemy aggression and a stingy stamina bar make solo play feel overwhelming, the core loop of base-building, resource gathering, and spellcasting shines brightly when shared. Overall, the game holds immense promise, though it needs a few quality-of-life tweaks and balance patches, making it an ideal title to dive into alongside friends.

RuneScape: Dragonwilds freshened my perspective on survival-crafting games with base-building and farming under dragon-dominated skies. I floundered for answers on how to progress to the next story quest without clear direction, and while I could explore in the meantime, other games in similar genres can offer the same thing with more entertainment along the way. In a genre full of compelling modern classics like Valheim, RuneScape: Dragonwilds is a difficult game to recommend.

reviews.author: NauticalTank042
reviews.quote:
As a millennial who never played RuneScape growing up, I honestly didn't know what to expect when I first played the beta last year. Needless to say I was presently surprised with the time I sank into it. Now with the 1.0 release I'm glad to say this is a great game to play with friends.

We're about 40 hours into our current world, taking things slow and only progressing the story when we are all online together, normally that could make a game feel like a slog or get boring quickly, but that's not the case. 

The lengthy progression system for skills, satisfying crafting system and honestly quite fun grind to build a massive scale base is incredibly addicting. Its easy to find yourself saying "just one more ore/logging" run only to realize another hour has gone by and you really should be getting off for the night. On top of that the combat system feels simple but varied enough to allow you to play how you want all while providing an adequate challenge. 

There's only a few real downside one of them being the quests. They can be pretty "meh" most of the time with the exception of some of the larger missions in the game. Most of them are generic fetch quests or craft this item to progress but when you find yourself fighting an acid spewing dragon atop a tower it pulls you right back in. 

The final downside is this game has some serious bugs. Like most modern titles UE5 titles I've experienced a lot of crashes, having to do some serious system tweaks to make the game stable. Another UE5 fan favorite of random frame drops making your game turn into a slideshow for a few seconds has also reared its ugly head. Base's have a tendency to get a little wonky at times leading to the collision bugging out and having your character sink halfway through the floor to eventually get ejected out the side walls and perhaps more annoying than that, the snapping system for building feels like its possessed at times, making tiles refuse to snap to the point in front of you and instead opting for the small size roof piece 10 feet away. 

I assume most of the bugs will be addressed in the future, or at least I hope they will. Either way I don't see them stopping me from continuing the adventure I have found myself on with Dragonwilds.

reviews.author: Clavevesari
reviews.quote: I am writing to formally log a severe complaint regarding the catastrophic failure of the live service infrastructure in RuneScape: Dragonwilds. Through no fault or exploit of my own, my character data was completely erased due to a critical bug tied directly to a routine, baseline feature: the appearance editor.Allowing a standard aesthetic feature to corrupt live user save data is an egregious oversight that speaks to a profound failure in Quality Assurance (QA) testing. In the software and gaming industries, total data deletion is the absolute worst-case scenario. It is a critical, tier-one failure that should have been caught long before deployment to live production servers. To ask paying customers to invest dozens of hours of grinding, effort, and commitment into your product—only to completely wipe that progress over a cosmetic button—is entirely unacceptable and unprofessional.Frankly, Jagex should have never released a game with an error this devastating. If the "Edit Appearance" feature was volatile enough to wipe player accounts, it should have never shipped with the live build in the first place. The proof of this negligence is in your most recent patch, which simply deletes the option to edit characters entirely. If the immediate solution to prevent data loss is removing the feature, then that feature should have been disabled upon release. Shipping a fundamentally broken mechanic that acts as a landmine for player data is a massive failure of developer responsibility.Furthermore, Jagex has completely failed to respond the way a studio should in a moment of absolute crisis. When a bug deletes the entire player experience, it should be an all-hands-on-deck emergency. Every single resource, engineer, and developer should be focused entirely on fixing this problem and restoring lost data, to the exclusion of all else. Instead, the response feels profoundly lazy and indifferent. Your communication has been confusing, leaving players to dig through fine print only to find out that Xbox players are being left stranded over the weekend due to certification delays, and that today's patch doesn't even contain a recovery tool for those who already lost everything.Being told to wait while my invested time is erased makes me feel completely invisible. Treating a player base as an afterthought while delaying structural fixes to core stability is a textbook definition of poor live-service management. This issue should be the absolute, singular priority of your engineering team until every piece of corrupted data is successfully restored to the affected player profiles.I expect a direct response regarding the exact timeline for my character's data restoration. I am logged into your support queue, and I expect Jagex to treat this loss with the urgency, panic, and professionalism that a catastrophic failure of this magnitude demands.

Marvel's Wolverine is a tight, focused experience that never lets up or slows down more than it absolutely has to. The action is intense and incredibly violent, the combat flows beautifully, steadily evolving into something wondrous to behold. I loved the acting and the dialogue; the pacing is excellent, and the world depicted is a brutal one. Like Spider-Man before it, Marvel's Wolverine has set a new standard for this character. Playing as Logan is unlikely to get better than this for many years.

Marvel’s Wolverine is an absolute triumph in nearly every category, doing for the character what Marvel’s Spider-Man did for Spider-Man. The story is exceptional through its deep dive into Logan’s complex character, using both allies and villains and an overarching plot to deliver the best Wolverine performance since Hugh Jackman first stepped into the role.

Marvel's Wolverine isn't the X-Men story you expect. There are familiar elements here, from tales told in other mediums, some better than others. But Insomniac Games isn't aiming to tread familiar ground, making a concerted effort with this game to tell a new story in the canon of Wolverine and the X-Men that is consistently surprising, with well-manipulated twists. And even with its points of difference, Marvel's Wolverine remains true to the canon of the iconic character, delivering a bloody and action-first narrative where the prowess and pain of James Howlett is fully on show, complete with the scale and grandeur his story deserves.

Marvel’s Wolverine is a brutal, focused and surprisingly heartfelt adventure with superb combat, excellent performances, spectacular set pieces and top-tier presentation. Its minor flaws do little to stop this from feeling like the definitive Wolverine game.

Marvel’s Wolverine… what a ride! Insomniac has successfully honoured the core of Wolverine and translated it into one of the best games of 2026. From the very first moments of the game, you are taken on a jaw-dropping and adrenaline-pumping adventure as you slice and dice your way through an army of enemies as you try to save the world from those seeking to control it. From its flawless gameplay to its realistic graphics, Marvel’s Wolverine undeniably boasts one of the best narratives of the year, which is enhanced by its stellar cast who successfully make you feel the emotions of these characters from Earth 1048. Brilliant and I can’t wait for the sequel!

Wolverine is an iconic character from Marvel comics and the most important figure in the prolific and complex “mutant universe.” He deserved a game that lived up to his stature, uncut, uncensored, and with all his wild nature unleashed. The game is a delightful tribute to our favorite mutant, but it’s a very dark tribute and not suitable for all audiences. After all, Wolverine is anything but a “friendly neighborhood.”

Marvel’s Wolverine does not reinvent the superhero action genre like other games in Sony’s portfolio. Instead, it violently refines it with flair and demonstrates how Insomniac has become fluent in beautifully brutal combat. You’ll walk away fully satiated with the presentation, even if there were some missed opportunities to take Logan’s stealth sequences and broader skillset further with the PlayStation 5’s DualSense controller.

Insomniac Games has once again delivered a very cool game with Marvel's Wolverine, offering a more story-driven and linear experience than the Spider-Man games. While the story feels somewhat stretched towards the end and the combat is fairly simple, the game performs well both graphically and gameplay-wise. If you're looking for a cool, story-driven action-adventure game that will keep you busy for around twenty hours, Marvel's Wolverine is definitely worth adding to your wishlist.

Marvel’s Wolverine is the definition of all killer, no filler. The game’s visceral and expressive combat system oozes with Logan’s trademark aggressive ferocity, and paired with deeply moving and layered character work the Wolverine has never felt sharper. Gorgeous presentation, a comic-book like structure, and fantastic writing help round out Insomniac’s best superhero outing in years, even when the story takes a stumble. Marvel’s Wolverine equally understands the heart beneath the claws, and in that balancing act it proves itself as the best there is.

Marvel's Wolverine is the best iteration of the titular clawed menace we've seen in nearly two decades. The story leans into the brutal violence and rage we've come to expect, while giving us a Logan who is more than just a harbinger of death.

reviews.author: Unsung-Paladin
reviews.quote: This game is truly a shadow of what it could have been. At the end of the day, it's fine. Playable. That's the saddest thing about the game: its absolute mediocrity. It is no better, and arguably worse, than the 2009  Xbox 260/PS3 Wolverine game, which was also remarkably brutal and gory. The gameplay is a poor man's version of the fight and block/counter style innovated and popularized by the Batman Arkham series and brings nothing new, innovative, or interesting to the table. You mash your attack, use specials when they charge up, and just block/dodge to counter when an enemy signals an attack. It doesn't get particularly more enjoyable as you progress.  The game's story is lackluster and leaves out the better known X-Men characters to use B and C list side characters in favor of focusing on Wolverine and his relationship with Jean Grey. The graphics are fine but not breathtaking and the character design leans towards the intentional uglification as pushed by Sweet Baby Inc who consulted on the game. Here's where the true tragedy begins though: development information has leaked about what this game could (and most definitely should) have been instead of what it was. It was supposed to have 3 smaller but open world areas (Canadian wilderness, Japan, and Madripoor which is fictional Singapore). It was supposed to allow exploration on your motorcycle (kind of like Days Gone). It was also supposed to have sequences which allowed you to play as Jean Grey (using psychic powers like Jesse Faden in Control) and Nightcrawler (teleportation based melee fighting). Because it was a PS5 exclusive, it was also supposed to make use of PS5 controller features like fighting based on the L2/R2 triggers to control your right and left claws. There was also the issue of Sweet Baby Inc's consulting, souring the game with politically driven ideology and intentionally ugly character design,  just like they did in Spider-Man 2; but despite their meddling, it was ultimately the matter of a convoluted and misguided development process that robbed this game of what would have made it remarkable and not just another on the rails button masher that moves clumsily from set piece to set piece.  Truly disappointing, what could have and should have been at the $305,000,000 price tag it cost to develop the game.

Roguecraft DX is a great, fun-sized title for any players who get nostalgic when they see the presentation or love the idea of fighting by simply bumping into enemies. The core mechanics are easy to pick up, the graphics are retro, and a full run rarely gets past the 30-minute mark. But it’s very easy to become bored with the repetitive nature of the gameplay, and neither the presentation nor the narrative can help with that. Roguecraft DX is a nice diversion, but it needs to add extra mechanics or at least a progression layer to make it more than a modern museum piece.

Roguecraft DX delivers an addictive, turn-based roguelike gameplay loop paired with detailed pixel art and a neat mix of DnD and Lovecraftian monsters. While its seamless exploration and combat transitions and clever class-based difficulty settings make it a great pastime, it holds back due to shallow character progression, low enemy variety, and a lack of gear customization.

Roguecraft DX packs distinct heroes and mysterious potions into brief dungeon runs filled with tactical tricks. Even its awkward diagonal movement cannot keep Mordecoom from being an entertaining place to spend a half-hour commute.
Roguecraft DX keeps things simple almost to a fault, but it's a nice game to play when you've got a spare half-hour or so.

Theropods surprised me in a lot of ways. I went into the game knowing nothing about it but finding a lovingly crafted point-and-click game that harkens back to the some of the best of the 90’s. With top notch audio design and fantastic visuals the developers manage to tell a story with lots of depth and heart without using any dialog, subtitles or wall of text. Theropods is a game that demands your full attention and doesn’t disappoint you once it has it.

The game is still very expressive, and everything that happens is told through simple but effective animations, and completely devoid of text. Not a single word other than the title of the game is visible or audible throughout the entire game, and this makes it a very accessible game, where all you need to enjoy yourself for a few hours is to keep an eye on yourself and solve some visual puzzles.

Theropods was well worth the ten-year development cycle, because, while it's not a very challenging, complex, or long point and click, it clearly is a game made with passion and is well worthy of being proud of. Its greatest achievements lie more in the animation and graphics than in its gameplay, but it's hugely enjoyable from start to finish, like picking up a light comic with a predictable but satisfying story with captivating art, one that will leave you a lovely memory and which you may want to experience again in the future.

If you need a fresh, bright presentation, an intense and touching tale of friendship and family, Theropods has all of that. It’s backed by some retro-feeling gameplay and puzzles that take some time to work out, but are all worth completing. Theropods does a lot with its short runtime, delivering a point-and-click adventure worth taking.
Theropods is a beautiful, if brief, point'n'clicker that's full of nice puzzles and scary dinosaurs.

Therapods is a fabulous new entry in the point and click genre with a style and character all of its own. Whether you’re a long-time fan or just checking in because of the dinosaurs, you’ll have a yabba-dabba-doo time – oh wait, that’s a different story of man and dinosaur co-existing.

Though never offering much challenge, Theropods is a creatively designed and beautifully realized adventure through a gorgeous fantasy world of humans, dinosaurs, and aliens that you’ll wish you had more opportunity to enjoy.

Theropods is ultimately an interesting experiment. It stands apart more than anything else because of its complete lack of dialogue, but the traditional point-and-click elements, while solid enough, don’t do much we haven’t seen before. Fans of point-and-click games who need a breath of fresh air should give it a look for its fascinating use of visual storytelling, but it won’t do much to pull in those who aren’t as engaged with the genre.

While Theropods wasn’t quite the game for me, I can see other puzzle fans enjoying it. If you like experimenting, exploring, and figuring things out without much guidance, you may have a very different experience. I enjoyed discovering its strange world, even when I struggled to figure out what it wanted from me.

A visually charming but ultimately underwhelming adventure, Theropods has a neat prehistoric setting mixed with a light sci-fi premise, as well some fine pixel art and fluid animation, but all that never delivers anything memorable. The story struggles to engross one into its world, while the simplistic or trial-and-error puzzle solving rarely provides satisfying moments of discovery. For the current asking price, there are far better point-and-clicks out there to spend three hours (max) on.

Overall, I was deeply and thoroughly impressed and entertained by Twisted Tower, which has become my new favorite game of the year. I highly recommend it to fans of BioShock, horror, or anyone looking for an incredibly unique and memorable gaming experience. The combat is fun, the level design and enemies are immaculate, and the setting is something that is certain to stick with you long after you’ve beaten the game, just like a recurring nightmare.

I don’t think anyone is going to find anything exactly new in Twisted Tower, but I think that’s the point. It’s a throwback to some of the best parts of the seventh generation first person shooters mixed with the some of the best parts of what is now called “boomer shooters” and Twisted Tower blends them well. I liked what I played in the demo and I’m glad to see that it was indeed worth waiting for (there’s also like maybe a dozen people in the credits, so this clearly was a passion project). It’s some of the most fun I’ve had in a long time and it in no way overstayed its welcome like a lot of modern games do. I mean I’m literally playing it again after finishing it, I think that’s praise in itself.

All in all, it's more than evident that Thomas Brush and his team did their homework and spent their five years of development on this game very wisely. The world of Twisted Tower is impressively vast, with so much to explore from one playthrough to the next. Its thematic and narrative depth is commendable too, though it could have pushed the envelope just a bit further on that front. With few bugs or hiccups to even think of, it's an all-around polished and genuine love letter to the dramatic narrative of BioShock, with plenty of thrilling combat to keep players busy and entertained, just as Mr. Twister would intend.

From the title screen, I knew I was going to like Twisted Tower. Drawing on a clear love of Bioshock, it tells its own twisted story in a fun and creepy way. Satisfying, brutal combat will take you on a compelling, and gory, adventure to save the damsel in distress through a well-crafted carnival of madness.
Twisted Tower is an excellent shooter that's a fun ride all the way through. You won't be disappointed once it's all over.

Thomas Brush and a small team have put together an homage to BioShock and other classic shooters. But Twisted Tower has its own set of party tricks and surprises, too. It’s one of those games where a developer’s enthusiasm for a genre leads to a perfect alignment of fresh and familiar. Twisted Tower is a must-play for fans of BioShock, classic first-person shooters, haunted carnivals, and evil amusement parks.

Twisted Tower is imperfect, short, a bit empty from time to time. It has a faulty currency balance, boring cutscenes, and overly simple puzzles. But it has soul. It has love. It has a world you want to live in, and that is what matters most. After endless 100-hour AAA open-world masterpieces, it's like a breath of fresh air (even if it smells like burnt popcorn).
Twisted Tower is the classic FPS you always wanted, with a charming horror theme park setting and some seriously ridiculous guns.

Ultimately, Twisted Tower effectively blends a theme park setting with horror, delivering memorable moments thanks to its well-crafted atmosphere, soundtrack, voice acting, and tight arena combat filled with enemies. Despite its great ideas, the game eventually becomes repetitive and inconsistent in its direction, leaning heavily into a full-on action title due to its wide array of combat and exploration elements. Regardless, it remains an extremely fun and immersive experience that will certainly appeal to players missing games in the style of Bioshock.

Twisted Tower is a quick-paced and strong old-school shooter, taking inspiration from some 'classics', and Bioshock. It doesn't overstay its welcome, keeps you progressing and has a story that may surprise you at the end. While it doesn't surpass games like Bioshock, for a tiny (mostly solo) developer, it does everything it wants to as good as it can, and well worth picking up for that reason alone.

A cozy puzzler with a hint of platforming, Rita’s charming crossword journey across generations is well worth solving.

Rita is a very clever, engaging blend of word puzzle and adventure, and if you enjoy a crossword puzzle, it's well worth your time. The platforming elements are a little scrappy, but it's not enough to ruin this unique experience.

It was a sweet story that celebrates our connection to the older members of our family, the time we spend with them and what we can learn. Despite my annoyance with some of the puzzles and occasional control issues, the end of the game made me want to pick up the phone and call everyone I know.

Rita succeeds in blending word puzzles with a difficulty that doesn’t scare people off. You can explore the world and enjoy a nice story without tearing your hair out. Some puzzles may stump you because the answer wasn’t what you were thinking, and finding every collectible can be hard. Stay for the story and appreciate the occasional challenge to find the appeal in this cute game about a family of cute chicks.

Even with Rita’s shortcomings, I’d be lying if I didn’t say that I liked it. It may only appeal to very specific tastes, but if you have those tastes – and I certainly do – it’s probably worth checking out.

Senara: The Sacrament won’t appeal to every horror fan, but those who appreciate immersive exploration and tension built through atmosphere rather than constant action will find a memorable experience. It proves that horror doesn’t always need monsters around every corner; it can be just as effective when it lets your own imagination fill in the gaps.

SENARA: The Sacrament is a tense Korean indie survival horror inspired by H.P. Lovecraft's 'Dagon'. Set aboard a realistically scanned ship, the game delivers an exceptionally scary atmosphere, impressive audio design, and an engaging story centered on faith and greed with three distinct endings. The gameplay effectively balances survival combat with sanity management in a well-optimized Unity engine build. However, immersion is held back by stiff enemy animations, overly simple AI scripts, and confusing translation errors in objective descriptions. Despite these technical flaws, it remains a consistently atmospheric.

As someone who plays horror games often, I was pleasantly surprised by SENARA: The Sacrament and what it has to offer. Not a lot of horror titles place us on a remote, stranded ship, so this was a breath of fresh air, The atmosphere was intense and interesting, and the game doesn’t shy away from offering a great amount of replay value, too, as you have a variety of choices to choose from.
It’s not perfect, though. The location itself feels repetitive quite often, and the niche appeal of the title is going to deter some people from trying it out. But if you do attempt to give it a shot, you will be rewarded with a great little story, a beautifully rendered 6000-ton ship based on a real vessel, and also an intense atmosphere. It’s not for everyone, however if you do give it a shot, it will definitely fuel your nightmares for days on end.

This horror game from independent developers holds potential beneath the surface. But did it manage to capitalize on it? Unfortunately, no. The mechanics are underutilized, and the atmosphere gradually fades away.
Dinoblade is a short and sweet experience that, while far from an innovative take on the Soulslike genre, does just enough right with its gameplay and over-the-top animations.

Dinoblade is a good example of an absurd concept being done right. Once you get past the gimmick of dinosaurs wielding blades, you'll find a Souls-like that sticks closely to the genre's core principles while introducing enough quality-of-life changes to make the experience more approachable for newcomers. The mechanics are solid, the campaign lasts just long enough, and the presentation is good enough considering the game's very small development team. Unless you absolutely hate the genre, Dinoblade is well worth picking up if you want a Souls-like that doesn't require a high double-digit investment of hours.
When it's not being bogged down by a lack of polish and uneven mechanics, Dinoblade is an exhilarating and absurd experience in the best possible way.

Dinoblade is equal parts fun and rough around the edges. There's clearly more work to be done before it can earn its place in the soulslike food chain. But its solid gameplay foundations, borrowed from its contemporaries, prove that this game can stand on its own. With an over-the-top premise centered around dinosaurs wielding greatswords, it's a game that thrives on its meme status, provided you can overlook its technical hiccups and barebones storytelling. For $20, you'll get a surprisingly serviceable soulslike that has plenty of bite and enough personality to avoid extinction in an increasingly crowded genre.

I was sold on Forever Ago from the trailer alone because I’m a sucker for these tear-jerking narrative experiences that happen to hit all the emotions. After being fully engrossed in Alfred's life, I know Third Shift has created something truly special. Forever Ago is an example of creative expression that the industry needs more of, and is definitely worth your time.

Forever Ago delivers a deeply moving narrative about aging, grief, and human connection, anchored by soulful voice performances and thoughtful presentation. Its pacing is deliberate, but as one of the most empathetic games of the year, it’s worth hitting the road for this scenic indie title.

Forever Ago is one of those games that left me feeling like I experienced something far greater than its short runtime suggests. Third Shift's debut title tells this genuinely heartfelt story about love, grief, and learning to move forward without leaving the past behind. The occasional technical hiccup is unfortunate, but it never overshadows what the game does so beautifully. Alfred's journey stuck with me long after the credits rolled, and I honestly didn't expect such a short road trip to emotionally sucker-punch me this hard. I know Forever Ago isn't perfect, but it's sincere, memorable, and easily one of the most affecting indie experiences I've played this year. Just be sure to hug your loved ones tonight and maybe call to check in on how they're doing, please.

Forever Ago is an intimate and moving narrative experience that handles complex themes like aging and loss with rare delicacy. Although its measured pace requires some patience, Third Shift’s title possesses all the warmth needed to win over anyone looking for a profound and reflective story.
Forever Ago is a beautiful tale of loss, grief and growth, and Arthur's roadtrip reminds us all that you just can't plan life.
Forever Ago takes you on an emotional journey to relive the life of a seemingly grumpy old man. It's impressive story-telling that will keep you immersed right through to the end.

Forever Ago is a celebration of life, a beautifully written road-trip on tragedy, love and healing. Despite its technical issues and lack of player agency, it's an example of how walking simulators create unique experiences.

Forever Ago is a quiet, somber yet hopeful exploration of grief, anchored by two wonderful performances in particular, that is unfortunately lacking from a gameplay perspective, but ultimately marks a solid debut for developer Third Shift.

Third Shift’s debut title, Forever Ago, is a remarkable achievement that takes a rare and courageous path in modern development by casting players as an elderly protagonist on a poignant journey through grief, redemption, and meaning, and against all odds, succeeds in crafting an experience that is as deeply reflective as it is charming and peaceful.

Forever Ago is a narrative experience that succeeds in how it handles its plot and prompts reflection on grief and the pain of loss. The gameplay could have explored the camera mechanics more, but the locations, memories, and people encountered along the journey offer moments of reflection and create a captivating experience.

As a love letter to the immersive sim genre and a whole host of games that rank among my all-time top 20, RetroSpace is an absolute joy to play. The only real shame is that it never quite manages to rise above its inspirations, despite having all the ingredients to do so. [Issue#375, p.60]

RetroSpace brings back the philosophy of classic immersive sims inside a bizarre, satirical and distinctive retro-futuristic universe. Its freedom works because weapons, stealth, Mutamods and environmental interactions remain genuine options rather than mandatory solutions. Exploration is also its most divisive element: finding your way without waypoints can be genuinely rewarding, but the minimal map and deliberately vague directions can sometimes turn discovery into frustration.

RetroSpace puts humanity’s survival in the hands of a janitor, giving its System Shock-style adventure a blue-collar twist. Its environmental interactions and weird Mutamods make it a memorable trip, even if some inconsistent stealth, vague objectives, and some shaky portable PC performance sporadically get in the way.

If you can stomach Retro Space’s cloying satire, and its stifling beholdenment to classic immersive sims, you’ll find a game with sprawling, multilayered systems which smash together in amusing and novel ways.

FC 27 rectifies many mistakes of the previous entries to the series and listens to what the community has been asking for many years. With manual gameplay at heart, skill comes to the forefront. Backed by new game modes and better overall balance, this game will be delightful for beginners and veterans alike.

EA Sports FC 27 is the edition in which the series effectively admits its recent mistakes and tries to fix them through targeted changes rather than empty promises. It is not the visual revolution some were hoping for, and anyone expecting a clear leap from the previous installment will likely be underwhelmed at first glance, but it is in how the ball moves, and in how the game demands to be played, that this season truly makes a difference.

EA Sports FC 27 offers one of the series’ most complete experiences, with more content, improvements to Career Mode, new features in Ultimate Team, and the debut of The Grounds. Attacking gameplay feels more fluid and rewarding, but heavily manual defending and inconsistencies in the AI still affect the overall balance. It is a meaningful step forward for the franchise, even if some areas still require refinement over the course of the season.

EA SPORTS FC 27 delivers exactly what one expects from a football title. It offers a rich package with a multitude of modes catering to everyone—from the casual "Sunday player" to the aspiring pro, and from those who thrive on playing with friends to those seeking deep single-player experiences. There is plenty to do, supported by a gameplay structure that minimizes CPU assistance and demands manual control; while this can be challenging—even frustrating at times—it also offers immense satisfaction. Goalkeepers are a weak point, currently representing the game's true Achilles' heel, and some refereeing decisions leave room for improvement.

EA Sports FC 27 continues to refine and improve key aspects of the game, delivering a more complete experience that captures the beauty and unpredictability of the sport. Reducing AI involvement in defense while improving attacking movement makes a huge difference, resulting in more engaging on-pitch action. The Grounds has real potential to transform the online community, creating a space where players can regularly meet and spend time with friends. While Ultimate Team still encourages additional spending, the sheer amount of content allows players to bypass much of this, although its pay-to-win nature becomes more apparent in online matches. Despite a few lingering issues, FC 27 takes meaningful strides forward both on and off the pitch, making it the strongest entry in the series to date.
EA Sports FC 27 rewards the people who put time into it. The defending and transfer overhauls carry the year, even where The Grounds hasn’t backed up its ambition with substance.

The EA FC series has constantly improved since its independence from FIFA, but FC 27 is a massive leap in quality for Career Mode players. For the first time, you can actually get a window into how clubs operate in real life, while still getting engaging match gameplay between negotiations and training plans. This may be too much paper shuffling for those who just want to play, but if you like managing a club through its ups and downs, there's no better game than FC 27.

FC 27’s The Grounds offers online devotees a long-awaited chance to link together its numerous modes and new Club types. Combined with very noticeable AI improvements in overall gameplay and presentation, this is a nice—though not massive—step up from FC 26.

EA Sports FC 2" is a solid but overly cautious step forward. The Grounds is a welcome addition and adds some much-needed variety, while the core gameplay remains enjoyable. However, limited improvements, balancing issues and technical shortcomings prevent this year’s entry from feeling like a truly meaningful evolution.

If you’re a diehard fan, then the chances are that you’ve already ordered EA Sports FC 27. However, if you’re new to the series and have been away for one or two releases, this year’s entry could be the perfect opportunity to rekindle or spark your love for the beautiful game. EA Sports FC 27 doesn’t quite score the perfect hat-trick, but with the improved gameplay, FUT and, Manager Mode, we're still bagging three goals albeit not left foot, right foot, and headed in.

reviews.author: EAisAmazing
reviews.quote:
EA SPORTS FC 27 — 2/100A 

Review by the Veterans of Butte FC

I’ve been playing football games long enough to remember when the developers seemed to understand the sport they were attempting to simulate. Through decades of FIFA releases, questionable design decisions, and increasingly dubious annual improvements, I’ve maintained a certain tolerance for EA’s particular brand of incompetence.

FC 27 has exhausted that **** simply, this is a **** game. Perhaps its most remarkable achievement is the overhaul of AI defending, a system EA somehow managed to fix by making it demonstrably worse. It’s an extraordinary accomplishment in reverse engineering: identifying a problem, dedicating resources to solving it, and producing an outcome that suggests the original problem was **** resulting gameplay has reduced attacking football to a depressingly primitive formula: lofted through balls and pace. Forget patient buildup, intelligent movement, intricate passing, or the satisfaction of dismantling a defense through genuine footballing ingenuity. The only consistently effective strategy is to launch the ball over the opposition and hope someone fast enough can chase it down. A sport celebrated for its tactical complexity has been reduced to a glorified footrace. It’s not football. It’s a 100-meter sprint with occasional interruptions.

What makes this particularly difficult to reconcile is that EA is a billion-dollar company. One might reasonably expect an organization with such extraordinary resources to employ at least a handful of developers who have actually played football. Yet the decisions underpinning FC 27 suggest a fundamental misunderstanding of the sport, its tactics, and the basic principles of human movement. 

This isn’t frustration born from a few unfortunate results. I’ve played enough iterations of this franchise to distinguish between a difficult game, a flawed game, and one that is fundamentally unpleasant to play. FC 27 belongs emphatically in the third category.

There was a time when football games rewarded anticipation, positioning, creativity, and an understanding of the sport. Increasingly, they seem determined to punish those very instincts.Perhaps the greatest indictment is that five men in their forties, who ask for nothing more than a few enjoyable hours of football together each week, have found themselves united not by their love of the game, but by their contempt for it.

After decades of loyalty, thousands of matches, and more patience than this franchise has ever deserved, my assessment is as considered as it is unequivocal:I hate this **** game.

Final Score: 2/100

The two points are awarded in recognition of the fact that, despite everything, it is still technically possible to play football with your friends. Whether doing so constitutes entertainment is another matter entirely.

lily's world XD is a short horror game that's worth the time you invest in it and the frustration you might feel from some of the puzzles. It's a game that lived in my mind even after I was finished, and I believe that its concept being grounded in reality is part of the reason for that. While you can look at Lily's situation from the outside and wonder how she got into that position, when you're inside that kind of situation, you usually don't notice until it's too late. I hope that SonderingEmily creates more indie horrors like lily's world XD in the future.

Lily's World XD weaponizes the cringeworthy nostalgia of a 2004 desktop to lower your defenses before delivering a relentless psychological horror experience. Emily Pitcher’s indie title explores the disturbing manipulation of teenage insecurities by predatory cults, brilliantly breaking the fourth wall through ARG mechanics that drag the player directly into the nightmare. However, the immersion is occasionally derailed by a frustratingly cluttered UI that refuses to let you minimize windows, dialogue choices that prematurely spoil puzzle solutions, and aggressive visual glitches that warrant a strict photosensitivity warning. Despite its mechanical shortcomings and lack of polish, it remains a claustrophobic, deeply unsettling digital descent that effectively blurs the line between investigator and prey.

Lily’s World XD is a short but powerful horror experience, packed with unique elements and an intriguing mystery surrounding the disappearance of teenager Lily. The old-school 2000s laptop interface, complete with peak teenage cringe, is a fantastic touch, while the psychological horror brings plenty of unsettling glitches and uncomfortable moments. It may lay its deeper message on a little thick at times, but if you’re looking for a thoughtful horror experience wrapped in a colourful, nostalgic package, Lily’s World XD is definitely worth a look.

Perfectly capturing the feeling of being online in the early 2000s, Lily's World XD is an intriguing desktop investigation game that shines a light on the pressures of being a teenage girl via a dark and unsettling story.

lily’s world XD is a nostalgic investigation game that recreates the 2000s with care. Its desktop format is an interesting framework for uncovering Lily’s story and the disturbing group she got involved in. Though it’s heavy-handed with its themes, they’re also raw and easy to connect with and empathise with. It’s a shame the pacing falls short, as the mystery is engaging and the story becomes increasingly compelling just as the game comes to an abrupt end. Its horror elements also feel underdeveloped, with several scary moments that unfortunately just raise more questions the game never really answers. Despite that, its nostalgic presentation and serious subject matter make it an enjoyable little experience that is still worth your time.

Too restrictive to be engaging and not subtle enough to feel believable, lily's world XD looks great and is well-intentioned but fundamentally distrusts its players regarding both story and gameplay, as if keeping parental controls on at all times.

Captain Tsubasa 2: World Fighters is a sequel done right. It builds on the original’s strong foundation, adding content and refining its ideas into an experience that looks and plays better. Tamsoft has put together one of the most unique and fun soccer games ever made, blending the real-life sport with the over-the-top anime it’s based on.

I had an incredibly fun time with CAPTAIN TSUBASA 2: WORLD FIGHTERS and it may just be my favourite team sports game ever made with its spot-on anime visuals and exciting atmosphere as well as its flashy and challenging gameplay that anyone can pick-up-and-play.

Captain Tsubasa 2: World Fighters may feature fewer game modes and a consequent drop in replay value, but significant gameplay improvements, such as the execution of special moves and control over goalkeeper actions, have made matches more fun and closer to what we see in the anime. Tsubasa has managed to lead the Japanese national team to (virtual) glory once again.

Captain Tsubasa 2: World Fighters captures the essence of the anime that captivated generations, turning it into a simulator that emphasizes narrative ties to its characters over sheer gameplay depth. The gameplay feels far more distinct and enjoyable than in the first entry, leaning into a more strategic approach despite the non-stop skirmishes. It works, it delivers emotional beats, and it taps directly into the nostalgia of discovering Tsubasa Ozora as a kid.

Captain Tsubasa II: World Fighters is a definite improvement compared to its predecessor, whether in terms of its gameplay or the overall excitement. More importantly, the game succeeded in capturing the best moments from the manga, which are filled with super exciting moments.

Captain Tsubasa 2: World Fighters offers an engaging single-player story mode covering the entire World Youth arc, making it a great entry point for newcomers and a nostalgic treat for fans. The gameplay is fast and dynamic due to simple basic moves, but mastering the Super Moves allows players to experience legendary matches. Additional features include a playable goalkeeper option for more match control, an online mode to test your skills, and a Collection mode to dive deeper into the lore. Ultimately, this game serves as a wonderful throwback that reignites a love for the franchise, despite its "FIFA-style" system.

It almost feels like, rather than comparing Captain Tsubasa 2: World Fighters to an EA FC game, you’d be better off thinking of it as Tekken played 11-a-side. The only thing I’m holding off on judging is the online mode; otherwise, it’s genuinely hard not to recommend it to anyone looking to scratch that arcade-style football itch.

Captain Tsubasa 2: World Fighters is a flashy and extreme soccer game that anyone can enjoy. Though the pacing of matches in the story mode can be a little bit bumpy, the narrative itself, in addition to the satisfying gameplay and solid visuals, makes this an accessible and highly enjoyable sports title – even if you’ve never interacted with the source material.
Captain Tsubasa 2: World Challengers is a gorgeous anime football game with a ridiculous story and tons of equally ridiculous ways to score.

Despite significant improvements to the gameplay, Captain Tsubasa 2: World Fighters ultimately delivers a much weaker package than its predecessor. The new on-field features are welcome and help make matches more dynamic, but the lack of content outside of gameplay weighs heavily on the overall experience.

reviews.author: Kryss_Everson
reviews.quote: Obviously, It was asking too much to increase the content from the first game and to polish the gameplay. This sequel has less content and is mor messy because of the light effects.

reviews.author: x6_Balan
reviews.quote:
Captain Tsubasa II: World Fighters es un juego del montón que funciona principalmente por el cariño a la saga.

Su mayor virtud está en recrear los partidos, personajes y movimientos especiales de Captain Tsubasa. Las cinemáticas de las técnicas son puro fanservice y nostalgia, y es sin duda donde mejor funciona el juego. La historia ofrece justo lo esperable: torneo de selecciones, diálogos entre compañeros y rivales y muchos momentos reconocibles para los fans.

Jugablemente, tras superar las primeras partidas y aprender los timings, se vuelve extremadamente fácil. Los retos opcionales añaden algo de dificultad, aunque algunos terminan siendo más tediosos que interesantes.

El gran problema son los tiempos de carga durante los partidos. Los numerosos eventos y escenas predefinidas obligan a pasar constantemente por cargas demasiado largas, hasta el punto de romper por completo el ritmo.

Me gusta tanto Captain Tsubasa que incluso me he sacado el platino, pero es difícil recomendarlo fuera de los fans de la saga. Entretenido y nostálgico, sí; memorable, no.

reviews.author: Nadir34
reviews.quote: Gameplay fluidissimo e grafica top. Adrenalina pura dall'inizio alla fine! È bellissimo

reviews.author: SkillPoint
reviews.quote:
Mit Captain Tsubasa 2: World Fighters liefert Bandai Namco ein unterhaltsames Sequel ab, das vor allem auf dem Platz seine Stärken ausspielt. Das actionreiche Gameplay fühlt sich erneut wunderbar nach Anime an, die Spezialfähigkeiten sorgen für spektakuläre Momente und die große Auswahl an Teams und Charakteren lässt Fans der Vorlage nur selten im Stich. Auch die unterschiedlichen Story-Routen und die Episoden-Herausforderungen bringen etwas zusätzlichen Wiederspielwert. Gleichzeitig verschenkt das Spiel aber viel Potenzial. Der eigene Charakter bleibt stumm und belanglos, die künstliche Intelligenz kann frustrieren und abseits des Story-Modus gibt es nur wenig zu tun. Vor allem der fehlende Dreamteam-Modus aus dem Vorgänger ist eine herbe Enttäuschung. Fans von Captain Tsubasa bekommen dennoch ein spaßiges Anime-Fußballspiel geboten, für einen rundum gelungenen Nachfolger hätte es aber mehr Inhalt und deutlich mehr Freiheit gebraucht.

Wertung: 74% (vollständiges Review auf skillpoint_at)

reviews.author: UltraPork
reviews.quote: This game is awesome! The animations and the shots are pretty well done. The gameplay does take some getting used to as it is different from the first game but it is a blast once you know what you are doing. The story can be a burden to get through, but it is worth it to have a wide variety of teams to play with. As someone who loved the first one, it does differ, but once you accept that, you can enjoy it for what it is, a fun, action-packed, and fast-paced soccer game!

reviews.author: Tragadeundediez
reviews.quote: Game is so different from RONC, it feels more like a fighting game rather than a soccer game.

reviews.author: ShowLorence
reviews.quote: Bandai Namco didn’t surprise me at all. It’s a mistake to expect a REAL GAME from them. You should have known better given that they made the game with UE5. The optimization is terrible. They’re asking for system requirements as if this were a next-gen AAA game. The gameplay is already way too clunky. While in RoNC you could take a shot after just two dribbles with ease, now you have to run around like a laborer. The goalkeeper controls didn’t work for me at all—let me put it that way. Maybe they’ll work for you. Just be aware of this when you play. The story is complete nonsense anyway. Don’t expect anything supernatural. The narrative is like DDLC—you’re just reading text like a fool. More than half of what they call “new shots and abilities” are actually taken from the old game. As for mods, they’ve been severely cut back. Don’t expect the freedom you had in RoNC...

reviews.author: Corsair11
reviews.quote:
The game is amazing if you are looking for a soccer game with superpowers. Excellent to play with your friends / online. The game storyline is amazing and very long. A lot of teams to choose and the CaC customization is really good.

Yes doesn't have Dream Team but those features can be updated later.

reviews.author: Joseph_11
reviews.quote: The animation is absolutely amazing, and the audio is stunning! The gameplay is quite different from Rise of New Champions, so it threw me off at first. But after playing for a while, you get used to the timing-based mechanics.

reviews.author: gold_score
reviews.quote: Captain Tsubasa 2: World Fighters is recommended only if you are a huge fan of the original anime and want to relive the nostalgia of over-the-top techniques with spectacular graphics. If you are looking for a good arcade soccer game with depth and lasting replay value, the previous title (Rise of New Champions) ironically still offers a more robust and polished experience in terms of customization and overall content.

reviews.author: KevkaDai
reviews.quote:

reviews.author: lincecum
reviews.quote: One of the best games based on a manga, faithfully capturing the spirit of the original. Highly recommended for fans of *Captain Tsubasa*.

reviews.author: Amjesus86
reviews.quote:
Captain Tsubasa World Fighters is 2 Rise of champions but on steroids:
- Better and longer story.
- Better gameplay (now all players are useful). No more broken skills for some players. All players have a specialized role in their playstyles, no more one man army and ten NPC to fill the team.
- A lot of new characters.
- New techniques.
- More stadiums.

Dream Team and a lot of features will probably be in future update based on most of the complains.

reviews.author: Sharifiardani89
reviews.quote: Captain tsubasa world fighters 2x better then rise of champions example in story,mechanic, have a teams,gameplay,stadium &....

reviews.author: HDream
reviews.quote:
Captain Tsubasa World Fighters is one step forward and three steps back compared to it's predecessor.

The game introduces a new story for Tsubasa and a custom character to explore together. The story is not bad on it's own, however compared to it's predecessor, it feels like any form of meaningful customization or decisionmaking has been removed. Rise of new Champions, it's predecessor, had 6 different middle schools one could start with, each with it's own unique plotline and gameplay mechanics. You could create a new custom character to experience each of these as well, with the goal to learn as many unique skills and moves as you could, and to interact with each character in a new way and context, which was especially aided with the game's numerous friend events that had unique dialogue depending on the route you were **** World Fighters however, there is only one story and you can only have 1 custom character. There is no reason to replay any of the offline story mode once you've beaten it for this reason, because there isn't anything else to see or obtain. Where rise of new champions had a ton of optional cutscenes in friend events, different schools you start from, skills you could get, stats you could raise and had different choices for you to try to optimize your player in ways that mattered, none of that is in World Fighters. There are only really shots and dribbles that you unlock by just going through the linear story mode, which has hampered the replayability of this mode. This linear storyline that has removed any agency from the player and their custom character also has caused the custom character to feel mostly like an afterthought. There are a lot less interactions with the CAC and other characters, as the main focus really just is the singular main story where the CAC doesn't say or do much, and there are no real choices at all.

The removal of skills and stats has also caused most characters to lose their unique identity. In Rise of New Champions, the inclusion of stats and skills had for example Carlos thrive on hogging the ball as much as possible, and Sawada was a supportive player that performed best by passing and setting up for goals. In World Fighters, the lack of this has caused all players to perform effectively the same. Defenders tackle, midfielders dribble, and forwards just try to score.

While one might expect the removal and simplification of most offline content to mean that the developers focussed more on the online content, the online mode also has glaring issues. Online play still feels rather laggy, and the removal of custom teambuilding has resulted in most online play feeling the same. There are only really 6 viable standard teams that one could use in online play, such as Japan, Canada or Germany, which means that you'll keep facing those same 6 teams over and over again. Teams like Senegal or Uruguay are not really competitively viable. The removal of customizing both players and teams causes online play to quickly feel stale as a result. 

Captain Tsubasa World Fighters is a dissappointing sequel to a series that prided itself on it's unique characters that had unique playstyles, while also giving the player agency. Much of what made the first game enjoyable has been severely simplified or removed, and the additions such as the revamp of match gameplay or new animations simply don't add enough to rectify this.

reviews.author: meta_player
reviews.quote: The gameplay has finally struck the right balance. The previous game felt like a tedious tug-of-war against the goalkeepers' stamina bars. Now, the new defensive prediction system turns every decisive shot into a tense, entertaining psychological duel. Visually, seeing the special shots rendered in such polished cel-shading creates the distinct sensation of controlling an actual anime.

reviews.author: kairst_
reviews.quote:
Nota:  (10/10)

Como fã raiz da franquia desde a época da TV Manchete, posso afirmar com toda a segurança: Captain Tsubasa 2: World Fighters é o melhor jogo de futebol arcade da história recente. O novo Chain System trouxe uma profundidade tática absurda para o meio de campo, e as defesas cinematográficas dos goleiros finalmente resolveram os problemas de balanceamento do título anterior. O modo história cobrindo o arco World Youth está impecável e me fez chorar de nostalgia. O jogo se passar no Brasil traz uma imersão fantástica para nós. Sobre a ausência de legendas em PT-BR? Sinceramente, quem é fã de verdade jogou a vida inteira em japonês no Super Nintendo e não precisa de tradução para acertar um Drive Shoot no ângulo. Jogo perfeito, dinâmico e visualmente espetacular. Nota 10 sem pensar duas vezes!
Blood Dungeon is a frantic platformer twist on that familiar Survivors formula, with fast paced action and death waiting around every corner.

Blood Dungeon is a refreshing take on the genre Vampire Survivors popularized only four years ago, and it effectively establishes its own identity both with its art style and platformer-focused mentality. It is fun to play, whereas many of these games are ultimately fun to experience passively – a build to the point where you can put the controller down and watch chaos blaze across the screen. You can’t ever put the controller down in Blood Dungeon, and that’s why it’s so easy to spend your bones (if you haven’t already purchased everything) and jump right back in for another run.

The best thing that Blood Dungeon has to offer is its unique take on the survivor-like gameplay. Bringing the experience to a 2D platformer with insane visuals and characters you’ll just chuckle and shake your head at is awesome. There is still a lot of been-there-done-that here, but the minute-to-minute gameplay is still a whole lot of fun.

Blood Dungeon is an addictive roguelike with fast-paced action and tons of charm. The crude drawings mix extremely well with the gameplay loop, which is frantic and has fantastic mechanics. Not all of the upgrades feel impactful, but it’s enough to keep me hooked and wanting to keep playing more and more.

Even though Blood Dungeon occasionally stumbles when it comes to its platforming or its hub world, it’s hard to deny just how effectively it sinks its teeth into you, convincing you to do “just one more run,” even though that’s the exact same thing you said to yourself over an hour ago. The slow drip feed of new unlocks, completed quests, and bosses to conquer is more than worth the price of admission, and I don’t see myself uninstalling this one any time soon.

I keep going back and forth with how I feel about Blood Dungeon in its entirety. It’s fun to play, has a cool aesthetic, and its emphasis on score-chasing feels distinct in this genre. But its lack of interest in expression and build-crafting really hurts that momentum, and makes playing long-term feel more and more like a chore. These games sing when you can have fun with how you put your character together each run, and when they give you space to experiment and succeed even if you play outside the dotted lines a little. Such a rigid insistence on DPS optimization puts a limit on what you’re allowed to do, and makes me wonder why the “pick three” stuff is in there in the first place. No amount of wiggly genitals and twitchy platforming can fix that.
It's a chaotic, throwaway delight, which is probably the intention. [Issue#428, p.123]
A thorough assault on the senses, Blood Dungeon’s platforming take on the bullet heaven genre is a welcome albeit ultimately shallow one.
Blood Dungeon sees a distinctive indie studio apply its design smarts to an exhausted modern genre, with surprisingly conservative but enjoyable results.

Blood Dungeon asks the player for a little more patience then I expected. Its biggest weakness is the slow speed at which runs can build towards that wonderful bullet-heaven feeling of becoming hilariously overpowered. With some genuinely great platforming, and a decent number of unlocks, it eventually delivers a decent amount of fun. I just wish it got there a little quicker.

reviews.author: PurpleMaster
reviews.quote: It's a good game, a shake up on the survivors formula. The only issue is that, after 5 hours, I haven't finished a stage yet, enemies seem to overpower me, and I bought all available upgrades.

reviews.author: BR0GAINS
reviews.quote: I’m pretty picky about what games I love, this is a game I LOVE. Very addictive, the concept is simple yet the game has a lot of depth. The controls are smooth the graphics are uniquely beautiful and the music is a subtle yet important touch. Overall I genuinely love this game, very addictive. For those who look for a comparison, think similar to Binding Of Isaac.

Midnight Moments offers little to differentiate itself from similar peers but for a change of scenery. What it does offer, however, is competent, diverting, and provides moments of quiet and peace in a world that only appears to be growing louder.

While Midnight Moments may not be for everyone, that’s exactly what makes it stand out from others. It isn’t trying to be filled with objectives or fast paced. So many times games try to add so many elements that key gameplay gets drowned out. Developers Happy Volcano on the other hand chose to stick with one element and do it well. They embrace slowing down, and focusing on a more a tranquil experience. Simply enjoying the lulling sounds of the rain and vibrant neons, being truly immersed in a cyberpunk oasis.

Midnight Moments may have won me over in a genre I normally don’t gravitate towards. I say may because I’m still playing it and working on more scenes filled with glowing streetlights, citizens chattering, and buildings where I can imagine almost anything happening inside. This is a very well-designed chill game with no pressure and a great canvas of vibing creativity.

Midnight Moments delivers on almost all its promises. The mechanics are very easy to understand, players can create a wide variety of cyberpunk-themed dioramas, and there are no time or resource pressure to create frustration. Anyone who wants to relax while creating small scenes will have fun with the title. But a few things are missing, mainly a clearer connection to the cyberpunk theme and some augmented humans to place in the dioramas. The small building area is another limitation. Midnight Moments is a solid experience created by a small team, but its core chill diorama-building concept could have been easily enhanced by the addition of a solid soundtrack and a few narrative hooks.

More assets, improved placement tools, connected wiring systems, labelled menus, and a few quality-of-life updates could transform Midnight Moments into something special. The foundation is already there. Right now, it is an enjoyable cyberpunk diorama builder that succeeds on atmosphere and offers a genuinely relaxing creative space, even if it could benefit from more depth and variety. I liked my time with it; I just wanted more of it.
A nice tool for making Cyberpunk dioramas, with an easy to use toolkit. Could do with a bit more content, though, and the fun nosedives after a build is finished.

Midnight Moments provides you with simple, straightforward tools and assets to create impressive little cyberpunk dioramas. While the tools have some slight issues and the assets could be better, the title particularly shines in using simple shapes and geometric language to create impressive scenes with unimpressive, easy-to-use shapes.

Midnight Moments is less of a traditional game and more of a creative sandbox aimed at players who enjoy designing visually striking dystopian cityscapes. It offers a solid selection of building tools, customization options, and impressive lighting effects that allow creative minds to experiment with architecture, atmosphere, and composition. However, the lack of gameplay mechanics, objectives, varied presets, and quality-of-life features such as an undo function prevents it from feeling like a fully-fledged city builder. If you’re looking for a relaxing digital canvas to create your own cyberpunk-inspired metropolis, Midnight Moments delivers a satisfying experience. Those expecting resource management, progression systems, or city simulation elements will likely find it too limited. Ultimately, it succeeds as a niche creative tool, but falls short of offering the depth and replayability many players associate with the city-building genre.

Midnight Moments joins a growing cohort of chill-em-up sandbox building experiences, stripping away all the game-y stuff and leaving you and your imagination to craft tiny cyberpunk dioramas. A strict toolset and a few quirks limit your possibilities a little, but don't prevent it being a wonderfully meditative, creative outlet.

I got four hours out of my first playthrough, but I know I’ll be going back for more, since there’s still plenty of the world left to discover — and I suspect it’ll make the ending land even harder. I’d absolutely recommend this game to anyone. The world, the characters, and the art might each seem simple on their own, but combined, they build something truly one-of-a-kind.

Helix: Descent N Ascent from developer Badass Mongoose is an addictive, gorgeous puzzle game that features some well-placed Metroidvania elements. It can be confusing and sometimes frustrating, but it’s a hoot to play overall.

Helix: Descent N Ascent is a striking monochromatic puzzle adventure driven by a brilliant "show, don't tell" philosophy. Its synergistic mechanics and creative homages reward player intuition over traditional tutorials. Despite potential pacing fatigue, the generous post-game content delivers a satisfying experience.

I’ve had a thoroughly enjoyable time playing Helix: Descent N Ascent. The dynamic art style sets it apart from other indie games, with every hand-drawn frame depicting a beautiful ancient world. The character design is equally delightful, and the abilities you use make visually exciting creations. The arcade machines were the highlight of my experience. Even when a level got particularly tricky, it never felt overly taxing. The capacity to adjust the level of difficulty, the option to skip levels, and the additional cheat codes make for an engaging video game-ception experience. Good pacing aids the game too. There is all the time in the world to navigate what you want, when, and how. You can take your time solving the puzzles, and wander around the realm as much as you like. The game gives you space to breathe, and even the arcade machines allow you to come back to levels when you’re ready for them, for the most part.

Helix: Descent N Ascent draws you in with enchanting visuals of a mysterious, alien black and white world. The seemingly simple gameplay mechanics are quickly revealing hidden depth, both in the main path and more hidden mysteries along the way. While it won’t challenge hardcore puzzle lovers, it serves as a well-rounded entry point for any curious players.
Helix: Descent N Ascent has a strong overall design, but the gameplay won’t suit everyone, which could deter some players.

Helix: Descent N Ascent is a unique puzzle game that understands exactly what makes a puzzle so fun to complete. It trusts you to be able to think critically and experiment, rather than forcefully holding your hand, assuming it’s your first day on earth. Despite some frustrations from the occasional bug, awkward design decisions and eye strain, Badass Mongoose has created an experience that respects a player’s intelligence, making each solve all the more satisfying.

Coupled with the chilly monochromatic presentation and a curiously dull drone of a score from Jim Guthrie, it makes for a puzzler that's as easy to admire as it is difficult to love. [Issue#427, p.123]
Beautiful and initially bursting with ideas, Helix Descent N Ascent quickly runs out of steam.

reviews.author: BVG2025
reviews.quote:
Helix: Descent N Ascent delivers on its promises right to the end. The demo offered a glimpse of an adventure that eschews explanation in favor of evoking a visceral experience—a promise fully realized in the complete game, driven by puzzles that constantly reinvent themselves without ever betraying their underlying logic. Here, silence is not an absence but a language in its own right, and Badass Mongoose has crafted a rare success.
