MXGP 26 feels like it came straight out of 2006, and I mean that in the most positive way possible. It’s missing a few pieces and there are some rough edges to iron out, but the foundations are all there and they work remarkably well. If your goal is to kick up some dirt and soar over jumps, Artefacts Studio’s game won’t disappoint. If you’re looking for a more detailed and feature-rich experience, however, you may run out of things to do rather quickly. The improvements over MXGP 24 are numerous and tangible; with this as a starting point, the next chapter could really shine.

MXGP 26 is one of those games that are extremely appealing for fans of the genre, and even someone who’s not into MXGP will find plenty to love here. The championship mode is the highlight, and then you also have time trials, grand prix and other modes to keep you company for a few dozen hours. Plus, there’s also a multiplayer which, when works well, is extremely fun and enjoyable.
The lack of championship mode is the game’s main downside for me, and I do wish there was more stuff to do, including sponsors or maybe track-related challenges. With that in mind, MXGP 26 doesn’t have as many technical issues as its predecessors and it’s certainly bringing the series on the right path. It seems that changing the developer was the right approach, and I hope the series will shine going forward. For now, MXGP 26 is a great step forward, and despite its shortcomings, it’s a very rewarding and immersive MXGP experience.

There is just one music track on the main menu—nothing more—which is perfect for anyone wanting to play a podcast or their favorite playlist in the background; however, those looking to immerse themselves in the adventure have to settle for the roar of the exhaust and little else.

MXGP 26 is a fine, serviceable motocross sim that checks the necessary boxes for official licensing and baseline physics, but it doesn’t push the genre forward in any meaningful way. It works well as a reliable pick-up-and-play title for handheld devices like the Steam Deck provided you don’t mind squinting at the UI but racing veterans looking for a true next-gen leap may find it a bit too playing-it-safe.

reviews.author: geekyshopping
reviews.quote: This is the MXGP game we have been waiting for for so long. The track deformation is next level. MXGP26 is a solid game.
With its charming presentation, exceptionally fun 3D combat, and rewarding unlockables and level-up systems, Kernel Hearts is a blast.

Kernel Hearts impressed me with its sense of style and its epic boss fights and narrative scope, though it gets in its own way with poorly tuned enemies and frustrating late-run platforming. If you can persevere, it’s a relatively short experience well worth playing; it just may have been better served as a narrative action-adventure than a roguelite.
Kernel Hearts is fun, visually appealing, and is best enjoyed in co-op mode. The design is great, and the story is interesting, but the gameplay loop is long and can get tedious when playing solo.

Kernel Hearts is a competent debut project that clearly showcases the creativity of the Argentine studio Whitethorn Games. The team succeeds in delivering an interesting universe, beautiful environments, and satisfying combat. However, it falls short in areas that hinder the roguelike experience—such as weak bosses, repetitive enemies, and a limited range of available moves. Even so, it is an experience I recommend, especially since most of the aforementioned issues would not be difficult to fix.

reviews.author: NinjaGamer23
reviews.quote: Very fun hack and slash game I love I wish it was on ps plus and it was on game pass recently on ps5 xbox and switch #

Another Eden Begins is another fantastic addition to the growing lineup of RPGs that were originally mobile games, yet received an offline version without any of the monetization practices from their parent mobile release. The enhancements to its visuals are stunning as someone who once played the mobile game years ago. Meanwhile, its new combat mechanics are highly addictive for those who love to optimize their battle performance. Its inconsistency of what’s voiced between language tracks is a bummer and other flaws do hold it back in unfortunate ways, but I believe how Another Eden Begins handles New Game+ is its X-factor in tipping the balance to make it an astonishing game overall.
Another Eden Begins is a compelling time travel adventure RPG which will keep you on your toes. A must-play for fans of JRPGs.

Another Eden Begins understands exactly why classic JRPGs remain so appealing. It takes a familiar formula and gives it enough personality through its time-traveling adventure, earnest characters, satisfying combat, and wealth of content to make the journey feel distinctly its own. Its rougher edges are difficult to ignore, but they never overshadow a game that consistently understands what makes a good adventure worth seeing through to the end.

Another Eden Begins has a lot going for it, with great battles, fun characters, and a strong art style. Even if the front half is a bit slower than the back, the entire experience is worth the adventure.

Another Eden Begins may look like another time-travelling JRPG, but there’s plenty of uniqueness to help the game stand out. It’s never been easier to balance a large cast of characters, and the story draws you in. There are definitely areas for improvement, but it’s minor in the grand scheme of things. Anyone who enjoys playing JRPGs will feel right at home here, and it’s even better if you love cats as well.

Admittedly, the title’s mobile origins are clearly evident, particularly in its level design. Yet, when compared directly to Another Eden, this is unequivocally the superior version. Costly gacha mechanics have been completely removed, and the story feels much more polished thanks to the addition of English voice acting and numerous content adjustments. There is also an engaging New Game Plus mode. The combat system makes a positive impression - even if it isn't overly complexb - and is excellently adapted for controller input. Ultimately, what remains is a rock-solid JRPG featuring a story with some amusing twists and charming quests, though it never quite reaches the brilliance of Chrono Trigger.

Another Eden Begins is a successful port, effectively adapting the mobile JRPG to a single-player journey, though the game experience was lukewarm. The narrative, while introducing an interesting cast, is a bit too loose and inconsistent, perhaps reflecting a live-service format that needed to attract and captivate audiences patch by patch. The turn-based combat features promising mechanics, but it doesn't challenge the player enough to employ them to the fullest. It's a good adaptation, but it can definitely get better if Another Eden Begins a new series.

Another Eden Begins sheds its gacha origins to become a warm and welcoming time-traveling JRPG. Feinne’s charm and a clever combat system make the journey worthwhile despite some easy battles and linear exploration.
The story zigzags along on a breakneck jaunt through scenes and battles other RPGs would treat as their climaxes.

Another Eden succeeds by revisiting the classic JRPG formula. The turn-based combat is enjoyable, time travel creates varied narrative scenarios, and the soundtrack effectively elevates the adventure's atmosphere. However, the game never quite shakes off its mobile identity, suffering from limited exploration, underdeveloped characters, and visuals that aren't always fluid. Ultimately, it is a pleasant but forgettable experience, hampered by the feeling that it is an adaptation unable to fully break free from its origins.

reviews.author: bthaxton1990
reviews.quote: Its a mobile gacha game turned into a console game and it is bad. Visually bad to look at and everything else is boring. One good thing is the music and that its. They should have left this game for dead.

reviews.author: SWERY_51
reviews.quote: From a Gacha F2P to a paid game, I thought I was going to play the full game. But there is a season pass (which ads 10 playable characters) that cost the same price as the game, making it way too expensive for what it offers. Also, chararcters artworks are AI generated, which could be okay for a free game, but not at this price point. The game balance is a joke, way too easy, I managed to kill some major bosses during the second turn... The only good point here is the music, that's it. Those devs are clearly not here to propose you a nice RPG experience, they are just here to steal your money. Avoid this scam even with a huge sale.

Hot Wheels Infinite Rush successfully transitions the franchise to an expansive open-world format, offering visually distinct islands that invite exploration. Despite initial pacing issues and excessive filler content, the core activities, diverse vehicle handling, and robust local multiplayer create a satisfying arcade experience that captures the signature Hot Wheels spirit.

While lacking any sort of narrative, Hot Wheels Infinite Rush is still a top-notch racing game. The open world is a fun space to explore, with collectibles and cars to find to your heart's content. It can get a little grindy, but the light-hearted and casual-focused gameplay makes up for it in spades.
Hot Wheels Infinite Rush is a feature-rich, open-world arcade racer that anyone can jump into, bringing toys to life without relying on real-world gimmicks or NFC-powered figurines.

In Hot Wheels Infinite Rush, players will experience a new open-world approach with hundreds of challenges and events to take part in, alongside four islands to explore. It features four driving styles with their own pros and cons that complement each other well. It is a visually striking and fun racing title, albeit somewhat lacking in modes. Recommended for speed fans.

Hot Wheels Infinite Rush is a fun arcade racing game. The world isn’t the most charming, but the racing is as solid as ever. There’s a ton of cool cars to unlock and secrets to find, although it won’t top Forza Horizon as the best open-world arcade racing game on PlayStation 5.

Hot Wheels Infinite Rush takes Hot Wheels Unleashed and Forza Horizon and smooshes them together, resulting in an open world arcade racer that's a huge amount of fun to play. There are some minor issues that might annoy, but if you love the idea of drifting and boosting though multiple open world locations, look no further.
Hot Wheels Infinite Rush is thoroughly enjoyable, with plenty of cars to unlock and some enjoyable challenges that make you want to explore the different islands.

With Hot Wheels Infinite Rush Milestone has successfully brought the franchise’s “toy-like” identity into an open-world setting without compromising its essence, creating four islands that differ in both aesthetics and pace, a driving model that proves enjoyable from the very first hours, and a customization system, spanning Track Builder and liveries, capable of providing entertainment well beyond the main campaign.

Hot Wheels Infinite Rush is a fun arcade racing game that really captures what makes Mattel's popular brand so special. Its accessible gameplay, imaginative tracks, and solid progression system make it easy to have a good time, although the variety of activities and some aspects of its presentation reveal its limitations.
HOT WHEELS Infinite Rush from developer Milestone S.r.l is a fun game that relies on large open-world maps with a variety of collectibles and cars to drive the experience.

reviews.author: BTTKMeta

(REVIEWED ON PS5 PRO)

To many, Hot Wheels has been a childhood memory. Whether it be ripping them out of the packs, trading them with friends or strategically placing them so they can be stepped on by your parents, these small diecast cars have made a big **** Hot Wheels: Infinite Rush, the nostalgia is there...almost. Breaking away from a traditional and grounded track based approach, Milestone have created the first ever open world Hot Wheels game. Take in the sites, sounds and **** of multiple islands to explore. Race, drift and challange other AI racers in offline mode or put your money where your mouth is online, head-to-head. Feel creative? Build a track. Sticker obsessed? Customise any car to your heart's content. The choice is your's from the very beginning.Controls are basic: Gas is R2, brake/drift is L2, square or circle will shove your car left or right, etc. Haptic feedback works surprisingly well and the engine sounds are diverse, sometimes sounding like the real car. With that being said, controlling the car when turning is very floaty but it is a toy car after all. The physics when getting air or crashing is excellent and looks genuine. During the playthrough, I caused major crashes and it made me laugh out loud!While the free roam is a nice change, it is poorly executed. You can collect one of two collectibles scattered about the islands, buy new cars and do basic challanges and races. Visually, Hot Wheels: Infinite Rush is decent, aiming for a 4K/60 on PS5 and up to 120fps on PS5 Pro. Severe grainy visuals, pop-in, artifacting, shimmering etc. hurt this game from becoming perfect. Also, depending on what you're doing, visuals can sometimes dip to 1080p or below. Honestly, a racing game like Hot Wheels shouldn't be too hard to pull off. The last two Hot Wheels: Unleashed games had impressive photo realistic visuals. In Infinite Rush, its been a massive downgrade. Motion blur can be turned off or on but having it on will cause frequent frame rate drops.While updates can surely fix the visual issues, it's still a fun and enjoyable arcade racing game suitable for any age but lacks the true "awe" from previous entries.

Crimson Moon is a great time, and when everything is considered, is a must try for those that can’t get enough roguelike action.

At the end of the day, Crimson Moon doesn’t need to reinvent the Soulslike genre to be worth your time. It knows exactly what it wants to be, a quick, loot-heavy romp you can tackle solo or with a friend, and it does that well enough to earn a spot in your rotation. The camera hiccups and a few control quirks keep it from being a home run, but for $20, it’s an easy recommendation. Sometimes a game doesn’t have to blow you away to be worth playing, and Crimson Moon proves that.

Crimson Moon from developer ProbablyMonsters is a gorgeous action RPG roguelike that is quite the uphill battle at the get-go. Still, thanks to good backend and frontend rewards, it makes the difficulty worthwhile. The controls do need some work, as do consistent updates, but in the end it’s more fun than not.

For what it is right now, Crimson Moon’s $20 price tag is entirely appropriate. I had a lot of fun with the game’s combat, which supports both solo and duo play. I can easily see developer Probably Monsters adding more levels, monsters, and gear. With a few patches to iron out the camera, Crimson Moon will be a solid choice for fans of fantasy action.
While its less-than-stellar features can be a game-breaker for some, Crimson Moon is an engaging, unique game that offers several great features.

Crimson Moon is a game I knew I’d like going in, purely as a big fan of the genres, but I was very glad to see that the game was able to mostly stand on its own as well. From the gorgeous visuals to the responsive combat, I very much enjoyed the ten hours or so it took me to hit credits, and I plan on continuing to play it for at least another five to ten more. The lack of weapon variety is the main area I’d hope to see a significant improvement on, and the game does have post-launch plans, so we’ll have to see. If you’re a fan of killing demons and the like as an angelic force of destruction, then Crimson Moon is easily worth the $19.99 USD asking price. And hell, even if you’re not, it might still be worth it just to have another fun co-op game to play with friends.

Crimson Moon serves as an exceptionally welcoming gateway into the roguelite genre, cleverly pairing Diablo-inspired angelic aesthetics with forgiving progression mechanics like purifiable gear retention and extra lives. Its flexible difficulty options and impactful loot builds ensure accessible action for newcomers while offering a satisfying loop for seasoned players. However, recurring camera glitches in narrow spaces and boss fights, coupled with uninspired enemy design and frequent PC crashes, hold back its potential. Despite these technical stumbles, its striking visual duality and beginner-friendly design make it an enjoyable entry point for genre-curious gamers.
Crimson Moon is no masterpiece in a year replete with them, but it’s a decent debut for ProbablyMonsters, nonetheless.

Crimson Moon is a decent run-based action game with interesting lore. Its combat lacks the “oomph” to make it a satisfying experience, and there are times that make the experience feel like a slog, but it can be fun if you’re looking for something to enjoy while catching up on podcasts.

There was clearly an attempt to make a good game here. While Crimson Moon’s Unreal Engine-driven environments and the great progression system try their best to carry the experience, the final result is constantly suffocated by the convoluted story, a limited weapon pool, and a lack of accessibility options. Even when the co-op action starts to click, the lethal camera system and the game’s inability to prepare you for its mechanics quickly kill the momentum.

Feed It may not last long, but it hits hard while it lasts. The visuals and sound do a lot to make it uniquely unpleasant (in a complimentary way), while the intense themes are properly portrayed throughout the fast but harsh narrative. This is a solid little horror experience for those in the mood for something upsetting and with a couple of hours to spare.

FEED IT takes something painfully complex and distills it into a surreal horror experience without losing sight of the disturbing realities. It focuses on psychological abuse, control and survival, then lets the low-fi visual atmosphere do the work. It’s quick, but branching endings and its meaningful themes make its hour-long runtime worthwhile. Short, nasty and very uneasy, but sometimes that’s exactly what horror needs to be.

FEED IT turns a simple hunger mechanic into a surprisingly unsettling battle between self-preservation and keeping a demanding monster satisfied, all inside a shifting, grimy house that never quite feels trustworthy. With its lo-fi horror visuals, disorienting architecture, and branching endings, every run feels like a piece of a larger puzzle, offering a reason to coming back for seconds.

The runtime ranges roughly between an hour and a half and two hours—a duration that is ultimately well-suited to an experience whose structure could hardly have sustained itself any longer. The deciding factor, then, remains the core premise: if you allow yourself to be drawn in by its essential nightmarish atmosphere, *Feed It* proves to be a sufficiently inspired experience.

Overall, I had a really fun time with Obakeidoro 2: Chase & Seek. The gameplay loop is perfect for quick sessions. Sure, it can get a bit repetitive after a while, but I had a blast playing it on my own with strangers online. I imagine if you could get a group of friends together on the couch, it would be a right laugh.The game delivers an equal mix of pure enjoyment and tense suspense. Coming in at a very reasonable £19.99, you really can’t complain. For all the reasons listed above, I give it a gracious 8.8 out of 10. If you like the sound of anything you’ve read here, give this one a go—I’m sure you won’t be disappointed.

Obakeidoro 2: Chase and Seek is wonderful both online and offline, although it is definitely designed with local multiplayer in mind. It is a pleasant short burst of joy that's easy to pick up and play without asking if everyone can play or if there is enough time. The charming atmosphere and attention to detail also capture a lot of the magic of playing with friends in the schoolyard!
OBAKEIDORO 2: Chase & Seek is such a fun-filled multiplayer game that'll keep you and your chums excitedly on the edge of your couch.
OBAKEIDORO 2: Chase and Seek is a fun, albeit flawed asymmetric multiplayer game that captures the spirit of kids playing hide-and-seek on Halloween.
While offering a family-friendly alternative to its horror-inspired asymmetric cousins, there’s fun to be had here, but its future feels more shaky.

Overall, my experience with Obakeidoro 2 was fine. It’s not a bad game and has some glimmer of potential; unfortunately, the overall experience wasn’t what I hoped for. Gameplay was nice and solid, and both the human and monster characters have unique abilities that can keep matches interesting. However, if you have played games like Dead by Daylight, you will quickly be underwhelmed by the lack of content. I’m sure if a child played this, they would have a much better time since it seems to be catered to a younger audience. But for me, I was fighting off both monsters and boredom when playing this game.

Montabi was a delightful surprise. When I realized I had to deal with another roguelike deckbuilder, my heart sank. Thankfully its strong game design and strategic approach to the genre kept me coming back again and again. I think that this game lays out a strong foundation to improve upon, especially in giving its titular creatures a more defined personality and broadening the tactical synergies between them. The story, music and characters aren’t anything to write home about. Yet in the end I still had a pretty great time with Montabi. Its gameplay loop feels like the right fit for a Roguelike game. While I still stand by the fact that I’m over these types of games, Montabi deserves its spot among some of the best this genre has to offer.

While of course I was hoping for a perfect experience, I’m not upset that Montabi has some minor blemishes. Because this is a very successful hybrid monster catcher, which is a rare feat, it’s also a game I’ve been utterly unable to put down for a couple of weeks now, even when I know I should be playing other games. If you’re a fan of the genre and want to try something fresh and engaging, look no further.
A melding of concepts and styles from monster trainers, deckbuilders, and tactical strategy titles packed into a new package that works well overall.

It is a game with a clever concept and charm, but too many elements—pacing, readability, controls, card ergonomics, uneven difficulty—hold it back. The fundamentals are solid, but the execution leaves *Montabi* in the "okay, but nothing more" category.

There is a lot to like about Montabi, as it does a great job of pulling the player in and hooking them into the game’s very addictive game loop. Every run feels chaotic and random, and on top of the adorable Montabi themselves, there is a lot to like in this tiny package. It’s so easy to want to push through, see what kind of boons one can acquire, and run through the three main areas over and over again, as a run to the end will take you up to thirty to forty-five minutes max per playthrough. It’s just a shame that this creature-collector roguelite has such a bare-bones story and performance issues on the Nintendo Switch that prevent it from true greatness.

Amid so many quick cash-ins that prey on nostalgia, this is a remaster done right. Dynasty Warriors 3: Complete Edition Remastered is a fantastic modernisation that completely overhauls the visuals of the original game while adding smart new features and quality of life improvements, making it just as fun and enthralling as it was a quarter of a century ago.

Dynasty Warriors 3: Complete Edition Remastered brings a PS2 legend to modern hardware with a complete technical overhaul, rock-solid frame rates, and its iconic cheesy voice acting left completely intact. While old-school map pacing and brutal archers show the game's age, optional modern dodge controls and deep co-op gameplay make it an absolute blast for nostalgia seekers.

Dynasty Warriors 3: Complete Edition Remastered is old yet new—a trip down memory lane that’s pure nostalgia from the moment the game starts. It’s a title that never tries to be anything other than what it is, staying true to the essence that made the musou genre popular worldwide.

7.5
Good
Dynasty Warriors 3: Complete Edition Remastered is a faithful revival that preserves the slower, weightier combat, campy English voice acting, repeated campaigns, and split-screen chaos that defined the original. Its Unreal Engine 5 makeover and modest gameplay additions improve the experience without sanding away its old-school identity, though dated AI, repetition, and occasional technical issues may make it a tougher sell for newer Musou fans.

Dynasty Warriors 3: Complete Edition Remastered is the first remaster of the Dynasty Warriors series from Koei Tecmo and Omega Force, and hopefully not the last. While musou games aren’t a groundbreaking genre in 2026, it’s fun to just hack and slash at cannon fodder as you try your best to complete the objective (usually to win). Though, it’s disappointing to see not many updates regarding accessibility features. Regardless, while the formula isn’t new, it’s great for those nostalgic fans and newcomers to the series.

Huge, often empty battlefields are still a chore to traverse, and mowing down hundreds of foes with the same three combos over and over again can be a big ask here in 2026. Still, with so many character stories, unlocks, and game modes to chew on, Remastered earns an easy recommendation if you're a Dynasty Warriors diehard — and I certainly wouldn't be against Koei Tecmo reviving the likes of Dynasty Warriors 4 and 5 in this style.

Dynasty Warriors 3: Complete Edition Remastered brings the 25 year old classic hack-and-slash title back to life. Fresh lighting and overhauled visuals sparkle, while modern combat elements elevate the slicing and dicing nicely. While there's plenty to cut your teeth on here, the old frustrations with stun-locking enemies, less interesting mission designs and getting crossbow mobbed irk sooner than they should. At least the dialogue is absolutely hilarious and the series' charm remains fully intact.

Dynasty Warriors 3: Complete Edition Remastered achieves its goal of breathing new life into a classic Dynasty Warriors experience, but with no changes to the gameplay, it soon begins to feel too basic and repetitive.

This remaster successfully modernizes a genre-defining classic with impressive visual updates, yet it remains anchored to twenty-five-year-old design limitations. While the simple, repetitive combat provides nostalgic satisfaction for veteran players, the experience inevitably pales in depth and mechanical complexity compared to more modern, refined entries in the series.

Dynasty Warriors 3: Complete Edition Remastered brings back a true classic in a shiny Unreal Engine 5 coat, delivering an entertaining action game packed with content and a successful visual overhaul. However, it is very much a case of quantity over quality, as the repetitive levels, nonsensical story and lack of depth become increasingly hard to ignore, especially if you don't have nostalgia on your side. As a remaster of a 2001 classic it certainly succeeds, but don't expect any kind of revolution.

reviews.author: TachibanaLuiz
reviews.quote: When they announced Dynasty Warriors 3 Remastered, I was not sure if it was a remake or a remaster. We already knew from the trailers that they kept the same voices, cutscenes, and even the mispronounced names. But actually playing it made it completely clear that it is a pure remaster and not a remake, because everything else is exactly like the PS2 classic. They just gave it beautiful modern visuals. It perfectly captures that classic **** gameplay is way more fluid. Combos are fast, the new evasion mechanic is a lifesaver, and bows are actually useful now to stun enemies or snipe when your health is low. The classic difficulty is still brutal and the peons are aggressive. It is not one overpowered guy against a thousand weaklings, you have to fight for survival. Crowd control is mandatory and the morale system actually matters. You have to kill minor officers to boost your army. The Musou Guard system that lets you use main roster characters as bodyguards is also a great addition.Completing specific stage conditions to unlock items makes map exploration really engaging. There are plenty of great items to collect, and the fire arrows were easily my personal favorite. Another huge positive is that the roster is not fully unlocked right from the start. You actually have to trigger specific battlefield parameters to reveal and unlock the secret characters one by one. That sense of progression makes the game feel much more rewarding and pushes you to try out every single character just to see how they look revamped in Unreal Engine 5. The endgame grind is also awesome with Chaos mode, which is genuinely tough, but completely worth it if you want to hunt down the fifth weapons, the unique ultimate gear for each **** revamped maps look great, especially the snow and rain effects. I loved being able to explore more, like getting up on the castle walls. The original soundtrack is still flawless. The story has not changed, it is short, hypothetical, and definitely not the place to learn Three Kingdoms history. It keeps that goofy tone veterans love, though newcomers might be confused.Missions are repetitive, but that is just the DNA of the original game. It is completely different from DW Origins in combat and design, but honestly I had more fun with this.Still, it feels a bit like a prototype for future remasters. The biggest flaw is recycling generic NPCs from DW9 instead of keeping their classic designs. It does not ruin the game, but it is a missed opportunity.Versus mode is fun, but it really needs an offline bot option for those who just want to test things out. Still, the upcoming online mode update will be huge and should boost sales.There is something that bothered me a bit, which is the loading screens. When you are about to enter the map and start a battle, there are at least two loading screens and sometimes it takes a while. I am not sure if this happens because of the device I am playing on, the Steam Deck, or if the console versions also have this problem. It is an annoying thing that wastes some of your time, but it does not really ruin the overall experience. Speaking of the Steam Deck, in terms of performance, it runs at a solid 30 FPS on medium and high settings, only dropping slightly when the screen is absolutely packed.I hope this sells incredibly well. I want them to take notes and give us Samurai Warriors 2, Dynasty Warriors 5, and Warriors Orochi Z next!

Graveyard Keeper 2 is perhaps one of the most interesting titles in its genre, delivering an incredibly unique premise, a story full of dark comedy and familiar, genre-beloved gameplay with some great quality-of-life changes. Fans of cozy life sims are bound to enjoy this cozy death sim, and all of the relaxing depravity that comes with it.

Graveyard Keeper 2 is a fantastic sequel that delivers in almost every way. It's got some serious upgrades from the original, but more than that, the overarching story is phenomenal. While some of the old-school design choices make the game a little obtuse, the game still has a lot to offer. If you're looking for a dark, cozy game to take the hours away, then Graveyard Keeper 2 is for you.

Rich with complex and layered crafting systems, Graveyard Keeper 2 can feel very overwhelming at times. But thanks to a gorgeous and charming (if grizzly) world, it's easily forgiven – and you're more likely to find yourself fully entrenched in this bizarre medieval romp.

Graveyard Keeper 2 shows that the developers listened to fan feedback, with faster movement, fast travel and voice acting making life as a Keeper much less frustrating. The humor and absurd storylines are still going strong, and I had such a blast that I’ll happily keep returning to the game after this review. However, the grind remains a central part of the gameplay, so if you enjoy messing around, experimenting and laughing at absurd situations, Graveyard Keeper 2 is right up your alley.

What really stood out to me about Graveyard Keeper 2 is how deliberately tedious it feels. Everything you do is a weirdly multi-tier process. Some of the basic things you’d expect from a farming sim or likewise sort of game take a step or two on one or more skill tree-like menus to access. Or you have to make your way to building and utilizing multiple gadgets that work together to achieve the thing you need, like a plank of wood. Everything is absurdly complex, and that seems to be the marquee feature, the defining aspect that makes Graveyard Keeper 2 itself rather than another thing like it. It isn't complex in an interesting, brain-stimulating way; it's just for every one task you want to perform, there's a gaggle of prerequisite tasks you have to go through first. I reckon there’s some kind of elevated sicko audience appeal thing happening here, for the people who look at Story of Seasons and think it’s for babies, and yearn for a labor sim game that has digital friction akin to the real damage done to your bones and muscles by manual labor in reality. Those folks are out there, certainly.

Graveyard Keeper 2 is a sequel that knows how to build on the foundations of the original, even if it doesn’t quite shake off a few quirks. The ambitious tower defence mechanics and automation features are welcome additions and help cement the game’s personality, which retains its characteristic charm and dark humour. Despite the sometimes exhausting micromanagement and a few bugs, Graveyard Keeper 2 is a fun and addictive life sim for those who enjoy watching a well-oiled machine in action.

There are some great things in Graveyard Keeper 2 that make it worth checking out. Having the undead become a real threat has a great impact on the narrative of proper burials, and I appreciate the general story beats. The voice acting is also pretty funny, and the game looks great. In terms of fundamentals, I respect it.

Graveyard Keeper II is digging its own grave with this second installment, which features new mechanics that are poorly implemented and unbalanced, and content that feels unfinished. The bear was a little too lazy this time around.

Laborious and filled with unnecessary and unoptimised grind, Graveyard Keeper 2 maintains every issue of its predecessor and magnifies them. The result is a game that occasionally threatens to settle into the rhythm necessary to pull off a sim of this kind, but insists on pushing the player out of the experience at every step.

reviews.author: pashockys
reviews.quote: An excellent game! Every mechanic has been taken to the next level compared to the first game. The early game is easily one of the best experiences in the genre. However, things became less engaging towards the end.That said, I played it at launch, and I'm sure that in a year or two, this game will be an absolute masterpiece. Even at launch, though, playing with mods was an incredible gaming experience.

reviews.author: Junkk06
reviews.quote:
Quelle surprise ! Je ne pensais pas être autant accroché à Graveyard Keeper 2, et pourtant, le jeu est extrêmement addictif. Son humour sarcastique et bien noir fonctionne toujours aussi bien, et c’est exactement le genre d’humour que j’apprécie. Le gameplay, simple mais très bien pensé, propose surtout une gestion qui sort de l’ordinaire.

Gérer son cimetière, ses corps et son église est un véritable plaisir. Partir de zéro avec une église délabrée et quelques tombes pour finir avec un cimetière gigantesque et une église dignes du Vatican est particulièrement satisfaisant. Et que dire de la possibilité de gérer sa propre armée de zombies et de les envoyer au combat ? C’est complètement absurde, mais terriblement efficace.

L’automatisation avec l’usine est également plaisante, même si c’est une mécanique devenue assez classique dans les jeux de gestion ces dernières années. L’histoire est sympathique et donne envie de continuer.

Malheureusement, Graveyard Keeper 2 souffre de gros problèmes qui viennent sérieusement entacher l’expérience. L’ergonomie dans la gestion est parfois laborieuse, notamment avec l’usine où le placement des objets demande une certaine précision. Les menus manquent également de clarté et il m’est arrivé à plusieurs reprises de me retrouver complètement perdu. Et surtout, les nombreux bugs présents dans le jeu viennent régulièrement casser le rythme.

Au final, Graveyard Keeper 2 est un bon jeu, très addictif et rempli de bonnes idées, mais il lui manque encore ce petit quelque chose pour devenir un grand jeu. Entre les problèmes d’ergonomie, les menus peu intuitifs et les bugs, l’expérience est trop souvent freinée.

reviews.author: DanDanNadNad
reviews.quote: Very grindy, lost most of it's identity compared to the first one. And even as a new game most of the mechanics aren't fun.

reviews.author: Morphaglyfics
reviews.quote:
Graveyard Keeper 2 is the sequel to a game which I liked but did not love.  There was a fair bit of tedium involved in the original that kept it from being truly great.  While the systems in this game are very similar to the original, there are some much appreciated QoL additions that make the game much more FUN to play.

I find myself progressing pretty quickly, always knowing what I want to do next, which was a problem for me in the original.  Progression wasn't always clear and I'd put the game down for months at a time.  Not here.  The progression is satisfying, similar to the original, yet again, but adding more layers to it without overcomplicating things.

The original had a great sense of humor and that remains the case with GK2, but now the game is fully voiced.  Overall, this game is not just an expanded release of the original with a new story like many claim.  It is a true sequel that improves on almost every fault that the original had.

My only gripe so far is that beginners will still be overwhelmed, but I don't necessarily consider that a fault.  It could be more accessible but I don't think it needs to be.  If you played the original and found it to be charming but frustrating at times, you should be happy with the improvements in the sequel.  It's a must-play if you enjoyed the original.  It's near perfect, in my opinion, having played through the demo and now progressed about 15 hours into 1.0.  Bravo, Lazy Bear.
With this new expansion, Blizzard redeems itself, albeit with some caveats, and makes us dream of a fourth installment once again.
A great opportunity to revisit the legendary game and enjoy some fun RPG-based quests while waiting for WoW Forever.

It's been a long wait for any new single-player RTS stories in the Warcraft universe. And while it's hard to say a drought that long was worth it, I'm not at all displeased with what we got in the end. I would have loved more RTS-style missions in Forsaken Kingdom, but the deeper RPG mechanics and a story that fits right into the Warcraft 3 era seamlessly kept me hooked to the end. Definitive Edition is now for sure my favorite graphical style of the ones available – if only it were available for the old campaigns, which I still love to replay every few years. And a new multiplayer hero has made the ladder feel dynamic and interesting again in a big, visible way. Garek… you did good, kid.

More than twenty years after The Frozen Throne, Forsaken Kingdom shows that there is still plenty of lore left to explore for another journey into Warcraft III. However, this return takes an unexpected direction, far from what we might have expected: a good Warcraft experience, but one that strays far from its RTS roots.

reviews.author: RicardoDavid
reviews.quote: Terrible campaign, which was the only reason to buy this game. I was expecting some RTS elements, but there is nothing of that here.

reviews.author: mneidoni
reviews.quote:
Following the disastruous launch of Warcraft III: Reforged, I gave Blizzard (yet) another chance, despite initially refunding the game back in 2020. The atrocious FPS drops, the removing (back then) of LAN and the new terms and conditions were bad enough, not to mention the "graphics" which were, back then, p!ss and v()mit.
Yet, I gave them another chance. Just like I did with Diablo II: Resurrected. Until they announced, of course, for the latter, the LAN removal. And the censorship. And the uglification.
Well, fast forward to 2026: Blizzcon arrives, my Linux box has W3: Reforged all well and ready, and here cometh the surprise: Yay, a new expansion for an old game we all know and loved. So, naturally, what does one do? Take out the card. pay. Play. Oh, wait. Wait. Can't play. Because, guess what, the latest patch brokes my Linux gaming. Nevermind, I said to myself, little annoyance, Blizzard will solve this, but at least a new campaign, the fun of building units and playing on the locan network via LAN mo.. oh, wait, wait: New campaign DOES NOT have building, and the LAN mode - well, it's gone. 
Game is now online for single player. Bwahahahah.
Refunded after less than an hour.
At this time, I got Diablo IV just because it was included in a HumbleBundle monthly, but I haven't even installed the damn thing, I will NOT indulge in playing the next Warcraft online-only, Diablo V or Starcraft-only-by-name-generic-lootbox-FPS-pay-for-skins.
RTS? Blizzard RTS? It's dead. Dawn of War IV is here, paying for that. ASAP. Tempest Rising? No online-only? got it, paid the Veti expansion as we speak.
Diablo? Don't know. Don't care. Bought Path of Exile II
WoW? It will be a cold day in Hell when I pay a subscription for a game.
At this point, Blizzard can rot for all I care. Starcraft Brood Ward/Starcraft 2/Old Warcraft games (and the 1.27 Warcraft 3 non reforged) are the only things from them I'm willing to touch.

reviews.author: Player10000
reviews.quote:
Release launch campaign review. The story is good and the aesthetics are nice. Unfortunately I did experience several game crashing bugs and progress lockouts. There are workarounds, but ideally players shouldn't have to be google'ing things.

Most of the characters voice acting is top tier. I dislike the Sylvanas old-person-robo-voice. Thankfully they only have a few lines to speak and are mostly a background character in this campaign.

Just like the Rexxar campaign, you do very little base building - I'm ok with this. You spend most of your time controlling hero units, exploring maps, completing quests and finding gear to make them stronger.

I like the game when you have two heroes to control. Having more makes it a bit more awkward to micromanage and gear up. I dislike that there were too many attributes on gear pieces, and many blue items seemed better than the purples I found.

You can loot consumables like health/mana potions but most are low level and it is better to just sell to vendors. Most areas have a revival altar, so you don't need to worry too much about dying which is great.

One thing I'd like so see is a breakdown of 3 main acts, so it is easier to replay certain sections. (Yes you can reload auto-saves, but it is better if they were shown on the chapter selection screen).

I couldn’t put Moonlight 2: The Endless Vault down. The dual gameplay loops are so much deeper than the first game, and that makes them even more compelling than they already were. They feed into each other masterfully, creating a cohesive whole that completely justifies the need for a sequel, while only enhancing the core of what made that experience so amazing.

It delivers a captivating evolution of the original loop through striking 3D visuals and a sophisticated inventory system that rewards spatial planning. Although the shop management lacks significant innovation, the branching expeditions and nuanced combat offer a richer experience. Despite some minor depth issues, it remains a highly addictive and polished sequel.

Moonlighter 2: The Endless Vault is appropriately a veritable trove of masterclass design choices, such that the original Moonlighter becomes a waning moon by comparison. Aside from its story, the sequel takes everything that made the first game special, stuffs it back onto the shelves, and gives nearly every part of it an upgrade. Maybe it shouldn’t have traded its ending for near-perfection in every other aspect, but it did, and we’re still left with some much-needed roguelite love for the shop layer and an overhauled combat loop that’s closer to traditional roguelite ken. I wouldn’t call that a bad deal, and I think neither would any of Will’s regulars.

Moonlighter 2 is an enjoyable game from start to finish. While it might not have the depth of dedicated games in their respective genres. It's blend of Action Roguelite and Shopkeeping kept me engaged throughout the game.

For me, Moonlighter 2: The Endless Vault replaces Moonlighter since it’s a great upgrade in literally every aspect. While it certainly has its shortcomings, I feel it’s the definitive Moonlighter experience, and the fact that it has such a great roguelike integration makes it even better. All you have to do is to avail the opportunity and play it, as it’s chock-full of content, while offering great build variety as well. Not only that, but it runs very well too, and it never crashed or had any performance problems, either.

Moonlighter 2 is an accessible roguelike with a strong sense of progression. Its mix of combat, puzzles, and shopkeeping makes for an enjoyable gameplay loop. The grind eventually becomes a bit noticeable and the loading times could be shorter. Overall, it is a visually appealing and polished improvement over its predecessor.

Moonlighter 2: The Endless Vault manages to loot everything that was great about the original and bring it into glorious cozy 3D in a huge backpack, ready to sell to the masses. The loot-and-sell loop is as addictive as ever, and anyone coming in fresh at this 1.0 release is getting a deal that will put a smile on their face. However if you were on board in Early Access, 1.0 doesn't add a whole lot to the the plinth for consideration.

Moonlighter 2: The Endless Vault feels like a meaningful evolution of the original game’s premise. Both the dungeon-crawling and shop management gameplay elements are more engaging and detailed, buoyed by a successful leap to 3D graphics. As a roguelike, it does perhaps overstay its welcome and run out of steam and new locations before long, but it’s a fun shift at Moonlighter while it lasts.

Overall, I think if you’re the kind of player who is more interested in ‘numbers go up’ than I am—for example, if you couldn’t stop playing Ball x Pit, MegaBonk, or Vampire Survivors for the progression rather than the gameplay—then this is probably right up your alley as a deeper version of the original Moonlighter. But if you’re like me, and you need the RPG elements or story as primary motivators for the dungeon diving or the mercantile gameplay, rather than simply earning gold, you might be left unsatisfied. I was left nostalgic for the 2018 original more than I thought I would be.

With no one interesting to talk to between runs, and only so much drama to be had out of the cash customers are willing to pay for your broken batteries, Moonlighter 2 eventually captures the soul-crushing ritual of clocking into a dead-end job perfectly. [Issue#429, p.120]

reviews.author: SucoDeuva
reviews.quote: If you liked the first moonlighter, go for it. But if you thought it was repetitive, this is more of the same

reviews.author: Moh4med4ziz
reviews.quote: It's a great sequel that i never expected it to be this good, maintaining the great balance between dungeon crawling and shop management in a roguelite formula, it's one of the best indie games this year.
A fun-filled adventure that strips away the stress of peril and danger, allowing you to explore the islands at your leisure. Oh, and rescue your uncle.

Lou’s Lagoon delivers a wonderfully comforting mix of lighthearted aviation, easygoing resource collection, and engaging mystery. While visual repetition among islander models kind of shrinks the world’s perceived scope, the superb flight mechanics, approachable crafting, and endearing storyline make it a journey well worth embarking on. Whether you are customizing your plane, decorating your beachside haven, or chasing clues through the clouds, it’s a charming adventure cozy game that I will happily dive back into.

As far as action-adventure games go, Lou's Lagoon is a good one to go for. It's especially ideal for those looking for a more laid-back experience, if exploring and gathering and crafting is more of your thing, rather than combat. Although combat is present, it's light and fairly easy to deal with. Flying around in the plane is a big highlight gameplay-wise, and the story is fun to go through as well. Overall, I had a really good time playing Lou's Lagoon and got really stuck into it, and I would recommend it if you're looking for something cozy but adventurous.

Lou’s Lagoon is warm, welcoming, and consistently charming, and its simple gameplay loop works well for the adventure it sets out to provide. I just wish there was a stronger reason to keep exploring and upgrading once the story had given me everything it had to offer. It may not have quite enough to turn its tropical getaway into a long-term home, but as a short, relaxing adventure, Lou’s Lagoon is still a pleasant place to visit.
It's not going to light the world on fire but Lou's Lagoon is a fun entry into the cosy genre with a compelling gather-and-build loop set in a lovely, vibrant world.

Whether it’s flying through the air in your seaplane or trekking through the tropics on foot, Lou’s Lagoon is a cozy adventure that is sometimes stunted by an awkwardly integrated crafting system. Despite some overly simplistic quest design, helping out the locals in the archipelago still makes for a decent game to romp around in for a while.

Lou's Lagoon knows what it is, offering a mostly stress-free experience for people who want to play while listening to music or a podcast. The bugs are annoying, and the item storage problem needs addressing, but those willing to overlook them will have some low-stakes fun exploring and rebuilding the islands of the Limbo archipelago. If you like Minecraft crafting with some retro 3D Nintendo platforming thrown in, this is the game for you.

Lou’s Lagoon offers a vibrant tropical getaway, and sucking up resources with the Swirler remains satisfying even after the novelty starts to fade. Unfortunately, cramped storage, sluggish crafting timers, and repetitive errands bring enough baggage to make paradise feel like work. Lagoon isn’t bad, but it should be your first destination choice.
Lou's Lagoon is a good, relaxing adventure throughout vibrant, tropical islands. However, there are bugs and odd design choices that can prevent you from fully enjoying the experience.

Lou's Lagoon does a lot of things very well, especially when it focuses on the adventure part of the game. The setting is a lot of fun to explore, the writing is more than entertaining enough that it's easy to overlook the feeling of chasing someone else's legend, and the variety in activities means there's always something different to play with. Granted, I'm expecting a lot of post-launch polish to catch bugs, and I'm ignoring the half-dozen times I had to drop to the Settings menu to click on the "I'm stuck!" button, but when Lou's Lagoon gets out of its own way it's hugely enjoyable. In a game that's half adventure-platforming and half crafting, though, having the inventory system limit such a major part of the experience just ends up being incredibly frustrating.
Box Knight is a quirky and addictive roguelike game with a silly story and fun characters. It has a great sense of humour, and it’s so satisfying to defeat enemies with a huge cardboard sword!

In terms of criticism, I can see the humour grating or falling flat after a while. Irreverence can only take you so far before becoming annoying, at least in my experience (They should have stopped after the first Deadpool). Additionally, the rooms full of spawning enemies get a little stale over time, the enemies are interesting, but when the goal is just defeat them all as fast as possible every time, you may lose interest. Finally, whilst I rarely engage in framerate discussions (30 is fine, chill guys), there are reports of drops on Steam so buyer beware. However these are fairly minor complaints, Box Knight is a excellent debut for We Made a Thing Studios (will they have to change that if they make another game?), and is a must for fans of roguelikes.

Box Knight is a fun little game, and one that you will come back to quite often. I found it to be entertaining, with a great beat’em’up gameplay and intense mechanics. Not only that, but they did a great job with the visual style, which is different from a lot of the games that you can find these days within this niche. However, this game won’t be for everyone. Combat, although fun, it’s rather basic, and there are no parries, deep combos or weapon skills you need to learn. Also, since the office setting is prevalent in the game, the room design is rather boring and it gets old fast. Despite these small mishaps, I still felt that Box Knight was a cool and engaging game. It was fun to play, and it continues to be one of those creative titles that’s worth a shot.

I ran into a few issues during my time with Box Knight, and I think it could use some tweaks here and there, but I still had a great time. Some of the issues I ran into can likely be addressed, but in my time with the game, they stood out quite a bit. Despite all that, the core gameplay is a fun romp with some fantastic humour and a unique style. It’s fun to journey through the office departments solo, but I predict playing it with a friend would be even better.

Box Knight reflects the workplace frustrations we have whenever a company gets acquired. By fighting back and showing what capitalism should provide, it’s a cathartic experience. It’s a tough game to play, and if the premise doesn’t appeal to you, you likely won’t continue playing. Give it a chance, and you might find your next best way to relieve after-work stress.

Box Knight’s office-themed setup and cartoonish visuals might make a decent first impression. But the game does little with either of these things. Shallow satire, repetitive combat, and barely noticeable roguelike upgrades will make you want to clock out before this shift ends.

Box Knight surprised me once it got going. After some slow early runs, the game opens up to become a satisfying power fantasy in which enemies that destroyed you at first become easy to defeat. The power growth is well judged to keep you grinding and I cleared everything in just over 10 hours, a length which felt perfectly judged rather than overstaying its welcome. It’s not a game that will blow you away but it could be the perfect palette cleanser between grander experiences.

Box Knight is a competent beat ‘em up roguelike, but it never evolves beyond that. Whether we’re talking about the action, the upgrades, or the abilities, it never managed to do anything interesting. While Box Knight has a good core idea for its story and world, it says so little about the office culture it tries to satirize that it never grabbed me. You could certainly jump in with a friend and play a few rounds of it, but most players will quickly find themselves longing for more.

Slayblade is a classic retro-style game that takes the idea we loved as kids and makes it a reality. It doesn't have everything figured out, and its biggest issue is that there just isn't enough game, but that's a good problem to have. If you want something simple that you can sink more than a few hours into, then Slayblade is for you. This game brought me a lot of childlike glee, and for that I'll be forever grateful.

Slayblade delivers a unique experience that'll have you smashing your way to the battle-top like a pro in no time. Simplistic roguelite runs augmented with modifiers and challenges make for a good few hours of fun.

Slayblade is a game where you battle spinning tops against each other, and your victory is determined by how you build your tops based on the number of parts you can obtain. While it can get repetitive, the different game modes add a bit of whackiness, challenge, and unpredictability to your run. Do not expect it to be a “Beyblade” clone because it is not trying to be, but the name of the game and the time of its release make comparing the two inevitable.

Slayblade delivers a charming and nostalgic experience that captures the early 2000s spinning top craze. The game shines with well-tuned arena physics and simple, fast-paced, and satisfying gameplay. Although the lack of multiplayer and repetitive roguelike events hold it back, it succeeds as a fun, casual adventure.

Slayblade was clearly built on a vision, and that vision was executed decently. However, the game left me wanting, feeling unnecessarily short, barren, and repetitive. You quickly grasp everything the game has to offer within the first 20 minutes, and it does little to keep you playing after that.

reviews.author: OG-Cerealkiller
reviews.quote: Very solid and fun. Little roguelike for $5, I found the building creative, the art, design and music were pleasant and nostalgic with a nice retro feel. Definitely worth the five bucks, it is a relatively short campaign but playing with the modifiers and different slayblade parts adds so variation, it is a roguelike but more of a mini one! I definitely enjoyed this game, I got at least 2 hours of solid fun out of it and it put a nice smile on my face, not bad for five bucks.

reviews.author: GamingCoffeePR
reviews.quote: A physics-based roguelite with customization that blends nostalgia, unpredictable combat, and solid builds, though its limited variety makes it feel repetitive all too soon.

Ultimately, Mexican Ninja is a fascinating curio. Its setting is interesting, and its humor lands in both good and bad ways. The beat-'em-up mechanics are solid and fun, even if some enemy tactics can make the game feel unfair at times. The roguelike elements give the experience some legs while also feeling like a natural fit for a genre traditionally built around games that can be completed in an hour or two. The presentation is solid, and while the lack of co-op may turn off players who expect beat-'em-ups to be multiplayer experiences, those willing to go it alone will find plenty to enjoy.

Mexican Ninja is a great beat’em’up, albeit a little on the short side. But that doesn’t matter, because the gameplay more than makes up for its shorter length. You have exceptional attention to detail, stunning visuals and intense gameplay that feels very rewarding, especially control-wise. Combat is skill-based, so it encourages you to get better and better as you play, making the experience way more interesting every time. I also liked the progression loop since every run unlocks new upgrades, combos and abilities, so make everything feel fresh. Unfortunately, the game doesn’t have co-op for now, which would be incredible and a great addition to the experience. There were also some technical issues and repetition, which is normal for this type of game. But as a whole, it felt like a great beat’em’up that doesn’t overstay its welcome. It’s intense, you can repeat the experience and make it slightly different, and the combat always feels very good.

Mexican Ninja has some readability issues in combat, but it makes up for it with fast-paced action, crass-but-clever writing, and an overall incredible setting. You won’t be disappointed by this all-around solid entry into the genre.

Mexican Ninja’s satisfying combat and art style are worth more than its low price of admission. Its standout thematic is a great start to hopefully something more from the Madbricks crew, even if some of its roguelike elements feel underdeveloped.

Mexican Ninja is a very likable Roguelike game that knows how to stand out in the right places. All in all, it's a very nice and fun experience, even if, in the final test, the combination of Mexicans and ninjas feels less high-quality and impressive than I would like it to be.

Mexican Ninja slices together Mexican and Japanese culture with the kind of crude humor most modern games won’t touch. Its roguelite brawling doesn’t share that same kind of creativity, so it eventually becomes a grind. But Nuevo Tokyo has enough personality to make this bargain-priced matinee worth catching.

Mexican Ninja is an incredibly entertaining game packed with contemporary references to geek culture and hilarious cultural mashups. Bold and irreverent, it turns its clever use of language into one of its greatest strengths. Its mechanics are somewhat limited and its visuals could use additional polish, but its humor, distinctive identity, and unapologetic personality make it a must play.

If you’ve played most of the other great games in the genre in recent years and still want more, Mexican Ninja offers a very solid experience. The more I played it, the more I was impressed by how many things are well done, even if I never entirely got past the fact that it doesn’t quite live up to the best of its competition. If I’d connected with its world, if it offered multiplayer, or if it had a few more elements that set it apart from the pack, I might have fallen in love with it, but it’s ultimately a good game worth considering.

Mexican Ninja is a pleasant little roguelite beat 'em up, with a well-functioning combat system, humour that can sometimes miss the mark, and somewhat uneven visuals. None of these issues are deal-breakers, but they do make the game seem a bit rough around the edges and unoptimised; nevertheless, it's still a game worth considering if you're a fan of the roguelite genre, especially as it's available at a good price of just over £12.

It may not be a deep roguelike that will keep you going for months, but wandering the streets of Nuevo Tokyo with a katana in hand, Latin tunes playing in the background, and a sombrero on your head was still a damn good time.

Agent 64: Spies Never Die is an impressive retro shooter with plenty of modern touches across the visuals, music, level design, and gameplay. It’ll be a great time for anyone who grew up playing late 90s shooters.
This is how homages to the past should be done – without pretense or winking, and a health dose of fun sprinkled liberally throughout.

Agent 64: Spies Never Die looks, feels, and sounds like an old game on purpose. It brings modern FPS systems to the blocky graphics of the 90s, delivering a fresh and genuinely challenging experience for both nostalgic and new players. Like all great shooters, it's easy to learn, hard to master, quick to play, and fun to play with friends. As a loving ode to the spy genre, it tells a perfectly paced and timeless spy story that anyone can enjoy. Although some old-school mechanics deliberately adapted for nostalgic effect can feel dated, those who love the FPS genre but missed the N64 era will find this retro experience charming and novel.
Agent 64: Spies Never Die is a lovely love letter to the days of old, showing that even after nearly 30 years of technological advancement, games like these can still be fun.

Agent 64: Spies Never Die is a fun shooter that goes above and beyond to act as an accurate facsimile of Nintendo 64 shooters, particularly Goldeneye. There’s even a really nice CRT filter that captures the mid-tier monitor look you may have seen often if you were around at the time. Sometimes this thing is accurate to a fault, depending on your perspective when it comes to modern conventions and “QoL” features. Sometimes it’s a little too self-indulgent when it comes to pushing mastery, when it comes to simply letting players go through the story like the adults with jobs they probably are. But that’s the picture Agent 64 is painting, and in that case the project is completed with flying colors. But coloring outside the lines a little may have been productive.

Overall, this game was a nice surprise. I expected it to be boring after 1-2 levels, making it really repetitive. Instead, I got a nice, well-layered story with some smaller twists. The level designs make this game much more enjoyable, but it’s not its only strong point. The weapon variety is another strong part. The ally system and control variety are all interesting ideas. Also making the players replay levels for additional hidden content, like the masks is a great way to earn replay value. Paradox Mode adds a nice way to change the flow of the game making it more chaotic, but enjoyable. I think this game is definitely worth playing.

Agent 64: Spies Never Die is a fun homage to a retro game, standing out as one of the few titles that captures the Nintendo 64 era. It’s enjoyable, with updated controls, a classic feel, a fun story, and interesting levels. Its generic interface, forgettable soundtrack, and forced attempt to extend the campaign with Cypher hold it back from being the perfect spiritual successor to Rare’s classics.

Agent 64: Spies Never Die doesn’t interest itself in appeasing the easy-mode player. There are simply too many bottlenecks in the experience that force you to “get good” to be accessible for the less confident shooter player. It is a shame, because the Goldeneye-isms make this a very appealing game, and the suite of options around the campaign provide the game with a lot of added depth… if you’re good enough to meet the challenge.
Despite the lack of spoken dialogue, the audio stands out thanks to dynamic, inspired music and sound effects so similar to those in GoldenEye 007 that they border on plagiarism.

Agent 64: Spies Never Die can feel a bit brief for solo players; the story mode can be completed in about 2–3 hours, with perhaps another hour or so added if you want to tackle all 14 levels across the three difficulty settings. As for the other modes, while their inclusion is certainly welcome, they are unlikely to offer more than an hour or two of entertainment to anyone who isn't genuinely nostalgic for the games that inspired this new title.

reviews.author: Pickle
reviews.quote:
I like to finish my games, and I like replaying old games as well. Goldeneye and Perfect Dark are some of the most enjoyable shooters I've played, so naturally, when this game got announced about five years ago or so, I gave the demo a try, loved my time with it, and then anticipated the full release until about two days ago when it finally came out.

The game sadly is a title riddled with strange design choices, with some being so egregious that end up ruining the entire experience for me.

Perhaps the worst aspect of the game is how poorly balanced it is. Levels are relatively long - specially when compared to early Goldeneye & Perfect Dark - yet the title retains the lack of checkpoints and few armor pickups (if any). What this means is, if you get to the last couple of minutes of a six minute level or so, and you can't find any armor, you'll probably have to redo the whole level again.

Did I mentioned enemies take away more than half your health with a single melee attack? Not taking into consideration either that on the hardest difficulty setting armor pickups are absent, so even if you were trying to get the one (literally) armor pickup that appears in the level, you're out of luck. You have to memorize the game and also hope that enemies don't appear or react in specific ways. The AI is extremely inconsistent, sometimes they follow you, sometimes they don't, sometimes they rush you, sometimes they shoot at you, sometimes they hear your shots, sometimes they don't. Sometimes they're extremely accurate, other times they're not... sometimes aim assist triggers, other times it doesn't.

Pair that up with the fact that a lot of the objectives tend to be quite annoying. Perfect Dark and Goldeneye worked because the levels were extremely short, even taking your time you could finish most levels in about three minutes or so. Failing as such, wasn't as punishing. Here is different, you get ten minute levels, by the time I'm failing a single time I'm dreading replaying through those ten minutes again from the start.

There's also the issue of the game locking the main story content behind "ciphers" you can get these ciphers by playing through harder difficulties and/or completing challenges, this last thing is a separate bonus mode that puts you in specific levels with added modifiers. Some of these challenge levels are really fun, others are clearly not tested in the least and can take you hours just trying to find ways to cheese the AI or watch guides to get through them.

Even when you do complete the challenge levels, you only get a single cipher or so. Usually you need increasingly more and more ciphers with each set of levels. So you'll eventually be forced to deal with the obnoxious and poorly balanced level of difficulty of the game in order to even see the ending. Which in turn makes me question, why even add difficulty modes in the first place dev?

People are commending it because it was made by a single person, but it's still a game that's asking for your time and money, despite being a passion project and me respecting such passion, I can't but help to point out the many issues that plague the title. They playtest the game, but they playtest it with people who have been playing Goldeneye since it came out, every single day, since it's release... how is that a good group to playtest your game? What about the rest of the players who weren't even born when the game came out.

The saddest thing though, is that the titles this game takes inspiration from don't take away your ability to finish them because you choose to play on easier settings. Nor do they implement challenge by plaguing the game with obnoxious objectives or the idea that something is better, simply because there's more of it.

I was really excited for this game, but as such, for as many times as I've tried to finish it, I've ended up binning it.

I had a great time playing Fallen Tear: The Ascension, and it’s one of those games that you will play for hours and hours without noticing. The game world is incredible, the soundtrack is great, and the platforming is solid. Its combat takes a bit of getting used to, same with the map, but once you immerse yourself into this game, it’s very hard to get out of it. Fallen Tear: The Ascension also has its highlights, like the epic boss battles, its excellent story, along with the upgrade system and great animations. It’s a game where you clearly see how much love and attention to detail was poured into it, and one that you are bound to enjoy if you like exploration or great stories.

Fallen Tear: The Ascension is one of the more genuinely ambitious Metroidvanias in a long time. It earns that ambition, despite having some flaws. The Fated Bonds system alone sets it apart from a genre that is already very saturated. It also gives progression an emotional throughline most games in this space never bother reaching for. Combat balance and an overly stingy in-game economy keep it from being an unqualified masterpiece. Neither issue, however, was enough to make me want to stop playing, and the developers have clearly been actively working to close that gap since Early Access. If you’ve got any love for Metroidvanias, JRPGs, or just games that wear their inspirations proudly while still finding their own identity, Raoah is worth the trip.
The time spent in early access has been mostly good to Fallen Tear: The Ascension.

Fallen Tear: The Ascension's ambition is commendable, as is its integration of party-based JRPG mechanics into the 2D metroidvania genre. However, the open-ended, hands-off design feels like it hinders the game's focus and balance, and leaves the overall experience feeling somewhat directionless. If you want a hardcore metroidvania platformer with some innovative mechanics, Fallen Tear: The Ascension has a lot to offer, however some remaining design issues hold it back from potential greatness.
All in all, Fallen Tear: The Ascension is an interesting exercise in fantasy worldbuilding. It’s a good time, and it’ll be a better time with a walkthrough.

Fallen Tear: The Ascension is a huge Metroidvania with plenty to explore and find, and an unusual Bond system that gives progression a different feel. The map tools are excellent for keeping track of areas that need to be revisited, including a photo system similar to Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown. Its beautiful hand-drawn animation is a strength, but inconsistent boss difficulty, including some damage sponges, frustrating 100% completion requirements, a subpar camera, and poor visibility in darker areas keep it from reaching its full potential.

Despite being visually stunning, Fallen Tear: The Ascension is hampered by its ambition to be a Metroidvania with JRPG-sized proportions. Beneath the layers of unnecessary, superficial, or tedious systems, there is certainly a good game to be found, but it takes a long time to establish a satisfying rhythm of progression—a flaw that might have been made up for had the story and characters been somewhat interesting, which is not the case here.

Even with half of the story still missing, Fallen Tear: The Ascension rarely feels like an unfinished product. The game has a sense of completeness, feeling thoughtfully designed and already offering a substantial amount of content despite how much is still to come. I have little doubt that fans of the genre will enjoy it, and even I struggled to find much to criticize during my time with the game. [Early Access Review]

The question isn't whether The Witcher 3 Remastered can still compete in 2026. The real question is which comparable game of the last ten years can go toe-to-toe with it, and that is a very short list.

The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Remastered stands as an exceptional definitive edition that goes far beyond simple resolution bumps to revitalize a legendary RPG. All the visual overhaul, newly integrated technologies, and quality-of-life enhancements add immense value to an experience that originally debuted over a decade ago. Except for modest official mod inclusions, this free update delivers an unmissable, beautifully crafted journey for newcomers and returning fans alike

This definitive remaster elevates an already legendary ARPG to modern heights, showcasing jaw-dropping path tracing, refined animations, and smarter enemy combat. Although movement still carries a slight lingering clunkiness and initial load times remain protracted, the comprehensive mechanical tweaks and bundled expansions make this return to the Continent an absolute masterpiece.

If you’re coming back to The Witcher 3 after a long break, or if you’ve never played it before, now is the perfect time to immerse yourself in this awe-inspiring world. This was my second playthrough of this title, and honestly, I enjoyed it even more than the first. If you’re looking for a new game to dive into headfirst, then you’ve come to the right place. Lose yourself in the world-building, fall in love with the characters, and soak it all in, because this is an experience to savor.
The Witcher 3 at its visual best. The remaster refines the combat, skill system, and controls, but largely leaves everything else as it was.

Without a doubt, The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt - Remastered is the best way to revisit The Witcher 3. It is beautiful, polished, still packed with timeless content, and comes as a free upgrade. The Witcher still has a story that holds up remarkably well today and a world worth exploring, and its quality has always made it better equipped than most games to withstand the passage of time.

We are talking about The Witcher 3, complete with its two excellent DLCs: Blood and Wine, which is richer in terms of content, and Hearts of Stone, which is more artistically striking. The remastering work is polished, save for a few minor hiccups—mostly involving the menus. It is truly hard to pass up, especially considering we need to get ready for Songs of the Past.

The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Remastered remains an exceptional RPG thanks to its memorable characters, outstanding side quests, and richly realized world. Its combat and movement show their age, but the writing, exploration, progression, and sheer amount of quality content make it easy to understand why Geralt’s adventure has endured for so long.
CDPR’s free upgrade offers plenty to enjoy ahead of Geralt’s final adventure, making the Continent feel at home among today’s best open worlds.

The greatest strength of The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Remastered is that it gives us an excuse to step back into the shoes of Geralt of Rivia on his journey across the Continent. Years later, it remains thrilling to wield both the steel and silver swords, and this time CD PROJEKT RED delivers an updated, smoother, and more modern combat system. The visuals have been overhauled—particularly the lighting, which has achieved a new level of realism thanks to Ray Tracing and Path Tracing. Unfortunately, however, the overall result is inconsistent, and performance takes a significant hit when these technologies are enabled. The developers have promised to release patches to address these issues soon, but for now, we have to acknowledge that the Remastered version’s performance is far from optimal. Still, the joy of riding Roach once again is priceless—and it’s a fantastic way to pass the time while waiting for Songs of the Past.
