Not since Astro Bot in 2024 have I played a game that has made so much of an impression on me, and the hours I've put into completing Big Walk with a friend have not only provided endless entertainment, but also further solidified that friendship, even if, at times, my co-op partner was left incredibly frustrated by my brainless moments or when I decided to punt a key item off a cliff, purely because I could.

I think what Big Walk does that’s so compelling is that it grabs the little part of your brain that is begging to be enriched by curiosity and interaction and massages it ever so gently with your friends as the background. That is not something that you can simply drop people into and hope happens, it is meticulously crafted and planned by expert hands.

Big Walk is completely unique and unlike anything you've played before. Between the inventive puzzles and an island begging to be explored it'll become the new group obsession for you and your friends.
A funny, exciting, and deeply rewarding multiplayer adventure that combines knockabout fun with some surprisingly big ideas.

Forged in the lineage of hiking simulators like Peak, A Short Hike and Baby Steps, Big Walk is a charming, multiplayer expedition about the simple joys of hiking with friends. While there are plenty of quaint puzzles to solve, the crux of the hike is about exploration and discovery- but without the dizzying adrenaline. You may even be inspired to embark on your own real-life hikes, too.

I’m truly excited to keep taking my Big Walks – no matter the off-putting name of the friendslop genre, this game is what you make it, and I believe each group that plays will make it their own unique kind of wonderful.

Big Walk is a triumph. It's a wonderful exercise in hanging out with your mates and getting those grey cells working at the same time, all wrapped up in a quirky and beautiful environment. It facilitates conversation, slapstick, and having a bit of a sit-down in between things.

Big Walk is a wonderful homage to friendship and the great outdoors. It reminded me that the best co-op experiences are about laughing at the journey, communicating in ways you never expected, and making memories with people you adore.

Big Walk is a big win. Evolving the social game format in a way that feels almost unrecognisable, House House has produced something that is as compelling as it is confident in achieving what it set out to achieve. With huge regard given to player freedoms, this title powerfully examines and challenges communication in a way I’ve not seen before in a game and may never see again. Grab your friends, go in blind, remove all other distractions, and experience a game world at the top of its class.

What Big Walk truly offers is a place to just be a gaggle of silly friends in a world where it seems harder and harder to spend real, quality time with the people close to you. Every step across this bizarre island built us up to its final test. The new inside jokes in the form of wacky gestures, the understanding we gained of each other’s strengths, the tailor-made language we’d developed just for this game, they all became tools to help us finally succeed. And we all found ourselves unexpectedly misty-eyed as we said our last goodbyes to the experience.

reviews.author: TheCakeIsALiar
reviews.quote:
Friendslop is a genre of game coined by players for overly co-operative multiplayer orientated experiences that capitalize and thrive on that raw untapped market of player interaction. The term slop in this context is commonly associated with a negative connotation relating to haphazardly thrown together games with little to no attention to detail for a quick buck, House House’s Big Walk, in this case, is not that.  

The new release from the creators of Untitled Goose Game is a game of the genre that capitalizes on that feeling of being alone with your friends in a vast environment and centralizes its gameplay around giving players a free rein island to explore and work together in with its various challenges and puzzles.

Big Walk is a refreshing take on the genre with its focus being on the humorous moments and fun object interactions created naturally throughout your playthrough, compared to the previously known games of the genre such as Lethal Company, REPO and Gamble with your Friends, where you are given a set objective and interactions are created as a result of such. This masterfully creates a unique charm for the game with its funny-looking clay-like characters, fantastic sound design and realistic outdoor set creating an immersion that little games come close to getting right. 

The birds chirping, the wind in your ears and the sunrise in the horizon all create a fantastic atmosphere throughout the game. The proximity chat throughout also allows a great sense of scale and distance between you, players and objects with House House capitalizing on that coherent idea of calm, realistic, atmospheric environments with the melodic, harmonious tunes, created by Aksfx, excellently complimenting the already lively soundscape. 

Throughout my experience playing Big Walk for around 11-12 hours with a small group of four friends, we had a blast, with the games fun puzzle design, intuitive map layout and teamwork puzzles that required us to think, communicate and plan for what needed to be done and where to go next creating a surprisingly intuitive gameplay loop requiring us to strategize what landmarks to go to and where to meet up.  

Furthermore, I think the map thrives on the idea of discovery with how the map was able to consistently surprise and amaze me with its size, amount of content and general layout with an easy to pick up gameplay loop and consistently fun puzzles.  

Near the end of the game though, the map does begin to become tiring with its predictable transitions and night-time crawls due to a lost flashlight, creating irritation within my group and I as a result of scrambling for objects in the pitch-black and the frustratingly annoying fact that all puzzles MUST be completed with other players, meaning that if you arrive to a puzzle early, gameplay is stunted until more people arrive.

Overall, my experience was great, other than the occasional bugs related to audio settings and inconsistent irritating moments, and it is a must-have experience for long-term friend groups due its engaging gameplay with others and captivatingly fun multiplayer mechanics. Furthermore, its low hardware requirements allow the game to be played by a wide array of users meaning that most friends can get stuck right into the fun island adventures that await. 

For a standard price of £15.99, the Big Walk is a fantastic game with a group of friends wanting to catch up and capitalizes on the charm of a cutesy walking simulator with a captivating twist. I think the game was surprisingly consistent with the level of fun you have throughout and it is a great play for a group of friends that have nothing to do for 12 hours. As a result, I will be giving Big Walk a very respectable nine out of ten for its easily understandable gameplay, fun multiplayer mechanics but slightly irritating gameplay and quality of life moments.

Another great delivery from House House. Big Walk is a game that knows what it is. While gameplay is simple in concept, the complexity is often found in garnering the attention spans of your friends/family who are busy trying to make the perfect flare gun smoke pattern combo in the middle of the gourd room. 

***Spoiler’s Zone***
Had the ending of Big Walk just been a continuation of the earlier puzzles we discovered on our journey, it would have been a good experience but not a memorable one. Unbeknownst to us, all game House House had been training us for the ending. From pointing, waving your arms, to squatting in unique poses, every group developed their own unique unspoken identity that became additionally prominent when all visual and spoken identifiers are removed. During the end, I took joy in recognizing these patterns whether it was that one friend who points way too much at things to the other friend who always runs around like a possessed kid from “Weapons”. 

In an expected yet pleasing way, the conclusion itself was way deeper than the game needed it to be. Saying goodbye to the your friends and the world yall explored together is deeply reminiscent of the relationships of your own life. In the end all that mattered was the time you had spent together in a shared space.

reviews.author: gogort
reviews.quote:
What a memorable experience. It's evident the developers were very thoughtful with every aspect of the game's design. It's a simple game in many ways, but this is clearly intentional and it's design choices only help elevate the experience. 

There are no menus, no health system, no inventory, no leveling, no quest markers, no journal. It is just you, your voice, two hands and the few items you find throughout the world. The game gives so much space to the players to make their own fun through discovery and interaction. 

With a good group of friends, you will find the game is well balanced, respects your time, and respects your ability to problem-solve on your own without holding your hand. The discoveries and "aha!" moments are worth every dollar spent. I've walked away from this game desperately searching to find another experience like it, but no other developer seems to understand how to make a digital playground to let you and friends have open-ended fun.

The only thing stopping me from giving a 10/10 is wishing there was more. We hit end credits after 15 hours, with maybe another 10 hours of content to 100% it. I wish there were more puzzle variety, more items to meddle with, more island to explore. I understand this is a small team, but a way to extend the playtime from 25 to 50+ hours would really make me bow down and say that this is a perfect game.

Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter is a fantastic conclusion to Estelle and Joshua's chapters in the Sky series. The story is fantastic, with fantastic reunions and dark moments that really stay with the player. You get to revisit and actually see the consequences of your past actions, where even smaller side characters are fun to see again. The core cast is as strong as ever, a joy to hang out with. Combat stays fun and engaging, with small tweaks that make it even better than before. Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter is a must-play for those who played its predecessor, and if you haven't, let this month's launch serve as a reminder to play 1st Chapter so you can experience 2nd Chapter properly.

Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter picks up everything 1st Chapter introduced and improves upon it. It features outstanding combat, an impeccable narrative, and a captivating cast, while cutting the slow-burn segments of the first game. It's a flawless execution and a fitting conclusion to the Bracer duo's story, while also setting the stage for what is to come in a thoroughly engaging way. This remake proves that it's entirely possible to craft a title that satisfies every single side of a JRPG fan and cements itself as one of the finest titles the genre has to offer today.

Building upon the already excellent work done in the remake of the first game, Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter is a masterclass in how to make a JRPG. Its story holds up as one of the best the genre has ever seen, even 20 years after its original release, and its completely updated gameplay further enhances the already great structure of 1st Chapter. Fans of the genre must play it.

Building on the already-great remake of the first game, Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter masterfully updates the gameplay and timeless story, adding up to what is now the Trails series’ defining entry, and one of the best RPGs of the year.

Another swing and another home run for GungHo. Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter is another stellar remake that provides plenty of quality of life improvements over the first game but also tells a fantastic story with plenty of added cutscenes and fantastic voice work. Though the majority of the games exploration and combat haven't gotten many updates, they don't really need to as the Trails games have some of the best combat in JRPG's going right now.

Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter is a masterful remake that elevates an already beloved RPG with stronger presentation, refined combat, meaningful quality-of-life improvements, and excellent character work. While its opening chapters drag and some supporting material feels underdeveloped, the experience ultimately stands as one of Falcom’s strongest Trails games and the definitive way to experience Sky SC.

Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter is the payoff 1st Chapter was building toward. The dungeons and backtracking keep it just short of perfect, but the storytelling and presentation are as good as RPGs get right now.

Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter is the excellent sequel to the first game, which serves as an introduction to everything that's to come in one of the most massive JRPG sagas—and it masterfully demonstrates how to create a remake. It's a story that gradually picks up pace, but once it does, it doesn't let you go until the very end.

Can you enjoy this remake if you’ve already played through SC? I can wholeheartedly say yes, as replaying the story again illuminated some plot points for me in ways I hadn’t expected. From a storytelling standpoint, even the remake’s 3D graphics and voice acting help present key story reveals, shedding additional light on things. Is this game worth playing if you’re a relative newcomer to the Trails series? Absolutely, especially if that newcomer has prior FC or 1st Chapter knowledge! In that regard, this game is easily the best of both worlds and a shining example of how a remake can offer something new while maintaining what made the original so special to begin with. I’m extremely grateful that I got to return to Liberl with Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter, especially knowing how the Trails series in general evolves from here!

Building on the remake expertise of the first game, Trails in the Sky the 2nd is a masterclass in modernizing a classic. With snappier pacing, deeper turn-based combat, and dynamic direction that easily overshadows modest visuals, it effortlessly hooks you for a relentless 20-plus-hour ride.

reviews.author: DrawingG
reviews.quote:
Beneath its fictional fantasy setting, Trails in the Sky weaves together themes of the trauma of war, technological revolution, and political compromise with the bonds and love between its characters, drawing on one of the JRPG genre’s greatest narrative strengths. The result is remarkably cohesive and nuanced, a kind of storytelling rarely seen even among JRPGs.
The game’s many tributes to and borrowings from *Castle in the Sky* also give it a distinctly humanist core. After a frantic pursuit through turbulent skies, the clouds part to reveal the Shining Ring, a magnificent relic of an ancient civilization. Yet it is not merely a testament to the heights of human achievement; it also embodies the coldness and oppression of absolute power. The nationwide blackout caused by its interference with orbment technology further challenges a civilization so intoxicated by technological progress that it has forgotten to question where that progress might lead. The tragedies born of the struggle to claim the power of the sealed Shining Ring echo the downfall of Laputa itself. The sky, a symbol of both romantic freedom and supreme authority, takes on a gentler, more hopeful meaning here than in *Castle in the Sky*, whose vision of the sky carries a more cautionary message. The grancel royal lineage, whose emblem is the white falcon, has always belonged to the sky. Yet, when confronted with the temptations of greed and indulgence, its ancestors made the same choice as Laputa’s people: to return to the earth and begin anew. Their descendants, in turn, have found a way to move beyond that **** the end, both stories culminate in the fall of a magnificent city. Laputa sheds the trappings of its imperial power and drifts into the heavens with its robots and animals, while the Shining Ring descends to the earth, returning to the home of its people, the very ground the Bracer Guild’s members have traversed on foot. More than its finely crafted story or vividly realized characters, it is this rich and deeply humanist core that makes Trails in the Sky such a remarkable work.

reviews.author: yszzerk
reviews.quote: A perfect reimagining of childhood memories. Despite some minor shortcomings in the voice acting and musical arrangements, the enhanced presentation, newly added in-game voice lines, and evolved combat system with greater strategic depth breathe new life into this masterpiece.While some maps are reused, revisiting familiar places and catching up with the NPCs I remember from the past, seeing how their stories have unfolded, is a joy in its own right. The Trails series has a truly unique and irreplaceable approach to worldbuilding, bringing its world to life through a vast cast of NPCs whose dialogue and circumstances continually evolve alongside the main story and side quests. It’s a level of worldbuilding that remains remarkably distinctive in the gaming landscape.Being able to relive the magic of my childhood through such a fresh and wonderful experience is a joy in itself.

The cast feels genuinely memorable, and the relationships and development throughout the story are handled incredibly well. The world-building is also on another level — even seemingly minor characters and side quests often feel like they have a **** combat has also aged extremely well, and the remake’s improvements make exploring, fighting and progressing through the game feel much smoother without taking away the identity of the **** I had one criticism, it’s that the pacing can occasionally feel slow, especially when you’re trying to track down specific objectives or complete some of the more obscure side quests. But honestly, that’s a small complaint compared with everything the game does **** fans of JRPGs, this is an absolute must-play. It has fantastic characters, excellent world-building, a great soundtrack and a story that rewards you for investing time into its world.

reviews.author: Gwyndolin
reviews.quote:
If you haven't played the 1st Chapter, please look into/play that first as this is a direct sequel taking place immediately after.

So, for those who played the 1st Chapter and was awed by it, I'd say just stop reading and jump right in and have a blast.

For those who played 1st Chapter and thought it was good but kind of slow and therefore hesitant to get into 2nd? That's valid too but I'll just say that, 1st Chapter is like the first 40% of an epic fantasy novel where it didn't even get to the climax yet. 2nd Chapter is the payoff. Does it mean it's no talking, all high-stake, all action, all the time? Not really, but kind of! 

In terms of gameplay, it should be a straight upgrade because one of the biggest complaints of 1st Chapter is the limited party members, where half the game you had control of only the two protagonists. In 2nd Chapter, other than the prologue, you are pretty much at full party size the entire game. 

There's a 10+ hour demo that carries over save data to the full game, so unless you straight up hated the 1st Chapter, it's worth checking out.

reviews.author: KikoRrr
reviews.quote:
After a 1st chapter that took its time setting up the world, 2nd Chapter finally lets loose. If you grew up with the golden age of 90s/2000s JRPGs, you’re going to love it. The story gets darker, the political stakes explode, and the antagonists (Ouroboros) are incredibly charismatic. You really get attached to Estelle, Joshua, and the entire party.
On the gameplay side, the combat system and Orbments gain a lot of depth. Personally, I’m doing a 100% run to clear all the Bracer Guild quests, and for once, it never feels like a chore: every single side quest develops the lore and NPCs in a super organic way.
Technically, while modest, the game is super clean and colorful in 4K 60fps on PS5. And a special shoutout to the soundtrack: Falcom’s music is so epic it makes you want to buy the vinyl set immediately.
In short, a masterclass that fully deserves a place as a beautiful physical edition on your shelf! An absolute must-play for fans of the genre.
Huge thanks to Falcom for this gem, and please keep bringing the series to us in French for future releases!

Despite fears and delays, Elden Ring Tarnished Edition is an excellent way to experience FromSoftware's intimidating yet flexible open world masterpiece, whether you're discovering The Lands Between for the first time or a glutton for punishment back for more.

A near-perfect port of FromSoftware’s masterpiece, Elden Ring sings on Switch 2. Minimal pop-in and occasionally stuttery enemy animations are easily overlooked when performance is otherwise so slick in handheld mode. If you want to play Elden Ring on the go, this is simply the best way to do it.
Despite minor technical flaws, Elden Ring remains a masterpiece on the Nintendo Switch 2 as well.

The memorable Elden Ring from the acclaimed FromSoftware has arrived on the Nintendo Switch 2 with a highly satisfying level of quality. This cross-gen game is one of the most captivating open-world experiences we’ve ever played, and the Switch 2 port lets you fully enjoy its charms.
A well-made port for Switch 2: Even at 30 frames and on the small screen, Elden Ring has lost none of its fascination.

In acknowledging that the Switch 2 port of Elden Ring isn’t quite up to the standard of the game playing on the PlayStation 5, this review sounds more negative than it should. The differences are a rounding error, and what is important is that this masterpiece runs perfectly well on a very portable console.
FromSoftware's epic adventure has only gotten better with time, and playing it in handheld mode on a road trip is an exquisite experience that must be seen to be believed.

This port delivers an impressively sharp and detailed rendition of FromSoftware’s masterpiece on hybrid hardware. The inclusion of the expansion and new classes provides immense value, although the performance frequently dips below its sixty-frame target. Despite small text and connectivity quirks, it remains a breathtaking, essential achievement for handheld gaming.

Elden Ring Tarnished Edition was well worth the wait on Switch 2, bringing us the base Elden Ring experience and the exceptional Shadow of the Erdtree expansion in the same package. Sure, there might be moments where performance slightly dips, but these do little to get in the way of this challenging and grand adventure. For gamers who have never experienced Elden Ring, this is a fantastic way to do so, and for returning players like myself, having this outstanding world available on a handheld is the perfect excuse to return to the Lands Between. Much like how the original Elden Ring was a defining Souls-like of the genre, Elden Ring Tarnished Edition is one of the defining ports on Switch 2, bringing a sprawling action RPG to a hybrid device. It's polished, punishing, and an essential purchase for those looking for their next challenge.

ELDEN RING Tarnished Edition arrives on Nintendo Switch 2 as a surprisingly accomplished adaptation of one of the most remarkable games of recent years. Despite the hardware’s natural limitations, it preserves the game’s scale, atmosphere and sense of exploration remarkably well, with consistent performance and visuals that are particularly impressive in handheld mode. With Shadow of the Erdtree included, this is a complete and compelling version for anyone who wants to explore the Lands Between away from the TV.

reviews.author: GrupoNPe
reviews.quote:
Elden Ring Tarnished Edition es un juego que resulta difícil de comprender al inicio, y seguramente aquellos jugadores con poca paciencia renuncien rápidamente a la aventura en su primer jefe. Sin embargo, luego de unas horas esa sensación de estar perdido comienza a transformarse en curiosidad. Y cuando finalmente derrotas a ese jefe que parecía imposible, entiendes por qué este género tiene tantos seguidores.

La adaptación a  Nintendo Switch 2 es realmente fantástica. Teniendo en cuenta lo gigantesco que es el juego, y que hayan podido hacerlo correr tan bien, debería ser un referente obligatorio a otros estudios que deseen publicar en la consola.

Si eres muy exigente con el tema del aspecto gráfico y de rendimiento de los juegos, quizá deberías jugarlo en otra consola. Aún así, el resultado general sigue siendo sobresaliente. Por otro lado, tener un mundo de esta escala funcionando en modo portátil es probablemente lo que más me ha impresionado de esta edición. Cabe añadir que en todas las horas que he estado jugando, me he topado con algunos bugs menores.

También es importante señalar que la edición física se distribuye mediante una Game-Key Card. Pero quienes estén pensando en comprarlo en formato físico deben tener en cuenta esta característica antes de adquirirlo.

Elden Ring Tarnished Edition es una aventura impresionante y una adaptación que demuestra lo bien que puede funcionar esta experiencia en modo portátil. Si nunca lo has probado y quieres conocer el género por primera vez, tendrás que armarte de paciencia, perseverancia y muchas ganas de aprender de cada derrota. Y si ya conoces las Tierras Intermedias, esta edición te ofrecerá una nueva forma de recorrerlas, llevándolas contigo y disfrutándolas donde quieras.

Wow. I just love this game. I have beaten this game four times before, so here I am on my fifth run and it still amazes me. It’s just a perfect game.
It has an awesome open world, so many builds to work on with unique weapons, and some really fun boss fights.I will admit, one bad thing is that some bosses feel like they are just reused with a different scale color but have similar fighting styles, so there is a little repetition. This game can also be brutally unfair in certain circumstances, but with a lot of preparation and learning the timing of jumping or dodge-rolling, this game can almost feel easy at times—and it’s a lot of fun!
I just love the setting, the music, and just how beautiful it all looks. Plus, I’m just obsessed with the different builds you can do in the game. I’ve even seen people do a Legend of Zelda: Link build or a Wolverine build, and it looks EPIC.I’m giving this game a perfect 10/10. It was good years ago and it’s even better now. I love the new classes added, and the new horse armors are cool too. I also thought the newly added weapons are fun to mess around with. If you haven’t played this game, give it a try. It’s hard but forgiving—just follow a guide and use summons to make it a little easier. You don’t have to do a blindfold no-hit run using the DK bongos to prove that you are awesome. Just play the game in a way that is enjoyable to you!

This masterpiece delivers a tactile and authoritative artillery simulation, blending realistic manual mechanics with a hauntingly deep narrative set in a dieselpunk Spain. While the complex initial learning curve might challenge some, its technical stability and rewarding strategic depth make it a definitive indie triumph that demands absolute precision and patience.

Iron Nest: Heavy Turret Simulator is a claustrophobic 9 to 5 where loading 12-foot explosive rounds and triangulating enemy artillery becomes second nature. It also has the best notepad in all of gaming.

IRON NEST: Heavy Turret Simulator stands out as a remarkably distinctive indie simulation game. Its tactile artillery procedures, oppressive industrial atmosphere, exceptional sound design, and demanding mission design combine to create an experience that feels both immersive and refreshingly unlike the typical military shooter. While the story is stronger as a thematic framework than as a deeply engaging character-driven narrative, the strength of its core gameplay loop makes it an easy recommendation for players who enjoy methodical simulations and hands-on mechanical interaction.

If you've ever wondered what it would be like to command a titanic war machine in Warhammer 40K or similar games, this comes quite close, even though they aren't related. With good gameplay elements, a solid introduction and calculations that aren't overly complex, you can confidently don the captain's cap and command this colossus in battle. It sounds great and offers plenty of immersion. The game won't be the longest, but you'll be left wanting more once you've fully completed the campaign and the two different modes in skirmish mode.

Iron Nest is an alternate-history simulator by artillerymen, about artillerymen, and for artillerymen. Its concept of operating a massive turret mounted on four mechanical legs, combined with realistic firing-data calculations and firing procedures, delivers all the satisfaction one could want from a simulation while stirring up a strong sense of nostalgia for anyone who has served in artillery.

Enshrouded is an exemplary entry into its genre, seamlessly combining survival crafting mechanics with ARPG exploration and progression and, in my humble opinion, delivering the best of both. While you can absolutely play the game solo, it’s even more fun with friends, scaling the adventure to your group rather than becoming too easy or outright demanding the extra hands on deck as some other survival-crafting titles do.
With its amazing game world and a building system on par with Minecraft, Enshrouded has joined the elite ranks of the survival genre. On top of that, it has plenty to offer fans of action RPGs.

Enshrouded has evolved into one of the most impressive survival games on PC. Its atmospheric open world, rewarding exploration and incredibly versatile voxel-based building system offer hundreds of hours of entertainment. The sheer freedom, variety and attention to detail make Enshrouded an outstanding survival sandbox.
Enshrouded has benefited immensely from two years in Early Access, emerging as one of the best survival crafting games in the business.
Quotation forthcoming.

Enshrouded is a good example of the evolution of modern survival games. It places the exploration and player freedom front and centre and puts survival and repetition into the background. The game understands that what many people want is to explore and shape the world and not work a second job. This makes "Enshrouded" one of the best games in the survival genres for fans of Action RPGs and even solo players, while fans of more traditional titles will still find plenty to love and dig into here.

Without reinventing the survival game formula, Enshrouded stands out as the most memorable title in the genre for us, despite fierce competition. It is beautiful, open, and rich, offering a variety of content to explore either solo or with friends. While the combat still lacks a bit of depth and the voxel-based world shows its limitations, the possibilities offered by the building—and destruction—systems more than make up for it. This makes it the perfect title for RPG fans looking to try out a different genre without feeling too far out of their element.

If you enjoyed the dev’s previous effort in Crypt Custodian, this is a no-brainer and, in my mind, an all-timer in the genre. There is always something to uncover, new creatures to befriend, and weird and excellently designed enemies to fight. I had a fantastic time from start to finish and can’t wait to revisit Well Dweller in the future.
Well Dweller is one of the most polished and captivating Metroidvanias I've played in years, and even in this packed season it's a must play.

Well Dweller is an absorbing metroidvania that thrives on smooth pacing, intuitive combat, memorable enemy design, and approachable exploration. Its straightforward mechanics and more linear structure may leave genre veterans wanting greater depth, but those same qualities help create a consistently engaging sense of flow.

Even in this crushing time of year where indies bear down like an avalanche, I couldn’t stop playing. With no time to play anything, I made time to get every achievement in the game, something I rarely ever do. And I would do it all over again if I could.

Well Dweller is, simply, a fantastic traditional metroidvania, with an incredibly well-designed world supplemented by wonderful storytelling and atmosphere in its perky and upbeat dark fairytale. Every biome in the game is downbeat, desolate or gloomy in some fashion, but the animal characters never feel beaten down by the darkness, instead having a great time despite the human world deteriorating in the background. The contrast of, for example, a merchant wishing he could live the life of a person who drinks out of a golden cup, despite the human skeleton in the background who's sitting at the table being very clearly dead, adds the touch of innocence the story needs. One of the collectibles is story pages from fairly tales, the type that end badly for all concerned, but the birds and rats and frogs are all living their best lives despite the moments of horror going on around them. Granted, it also helps that Glimmer is working his hardest to rescue everyone, and it seems highly unlikely the woodland creatures' stories would have ended anything like as happily otherwise, but a fairy tale hero's job is to wrest a happy ending from the darkest events, no matter what kind of abominations are wandering the spiked platforms of the fallen kingdom.

Like the duo's previous games, Well Dweller is a polished take on the genre that understands what makes Metroidvanias enjoyable without overcomplicating the formula. Fans of the genre should find plenty to like, and the Thompson brothers have once again delivered a strong entry in their growing catalog.

Metroidvanias have had a major impact on the indie gaming sphere and the larger AAA market for years. Plenty of approaches exist for this 2D adventure style. Well Dweller might be the best in a while, though. It's cute despite its gothic tones and hopeful even with its grim aesthetic. Especially for fans of classic exploration-centric gameplay, this might be one of 2026's best sleeper hits.

Well Dweller is a great-looking and charming metroidvania that emphasizes exploration over punishing difficulty. Its combat can become repetitive and the bosses may be too gentle for genre veterans, but Glimmer’s clever matchstick mechanics and smooth movement make getting lost withg this plucky bird surprisingly enjoyable.

This is the perfect entry point into the Metroidvania genre—a genre that has undergone a long evolution and constantly raised the bar for ambition, yet here returns to embrace its revitalized roots, deriving much of its value from elements that are all but invisible to the eye. It offers evocative atmosphere, a memorable score, a delightful movement system, and the fluidity with which veterans zip across screens—all alongside a welcoming learning curve for newcomers. Above all, there is the veneer of gentle melancholy that cloaks a universe possessing immense power in its understated minimalism. Well Dweller is a game that makes you want to play video games; an experience that, in its remarkably lean design, flows effortlessly, eliciting quiet smiles from the opening moments right through to the end credits.

This makes it a particularly appealing proposition for those who enjoy Metroidvanias but aren't necessarily looking for a combat-focused game. The story is told straightforwardly, the world is full of character, and the matchstick-related upgrades make revisiting earlier areas worthwhile. If there is a major issue, it lies in the encounters, which could have made better use of the level design's potential.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is an ambitious entry for the series, and it delivers a memorable experience that's hard to put down. Between the expansive Flame Lord campaigns, which feed into the Pale Raven campaign, there is a lot of story content to parse through. Many of the characters you meet are worth recruiting, and getting to know them over a meal is one of the better moments outside of training with them at the colosseum. What Nintendo has done with the latest Fire Emblem is nothing short of marvellous.

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is another slam-dunk for the Nintendo Switch 2. A bona fide evolution of what came before it, combining the best elements of its recent entries with spectacular results. Perhaps most impressive, is just how well paced this enormous adventure is despite its lengthy runtime.

With Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, Intelligent Systems delivers a massive epic for the Switch 2 and one of the meatiest entries in the series. The developer doesn’t shy away from going places with the story! It tries things when it comes to mechanics for the different lords’ stories and abilities.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is the most ambitious game in the series to date, and it executes that ambition with almost effortless elegance. It’s tremendously well-written, very cleverly designed, and one of the most engaging and enjoyable experiences I’ve ever had on a Nintendo console.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is an essential game for fans of Fire Emblem and SRPGs, and if you’re new to the series or genre, there’s no better place to get started. The stories of Dietrich, Theodora, Cai, and Leda are all brilliant, worthy of their own Fire Emblem game, and the fact that we get them all in one is just a bonus. It’s still early days, but I’m confident that Fortune’s Weave will be considered one of the best RPGs in the Switch 2’s library even a decade from now.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is a massively intelligent experience, with deep and rich themes, characters, and gameplay systems. In the same month that Wolverine came out, it is nice to see that one of the three big console manufacturers/publishers still respects the player’s intelligence and is out there trying to do more than endlessly iterate on the same “best practice” game-development-by-numbers slop.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave builds upon its strategic arts in ways I couldn’t have anticipated. It’s never satisfied to make me grow only as a battlefield tactician, or only in my ability to manage my time between skirmishes wisely, but both in perfect harmony. Every time I turned around, I was being given more challenges to face and more tools to master in order to overcome them. The many unique twists of each hero’s story path had me eager to see all the ways those journeys differed from each other, making the grand culmination in the final act hit so damn well. Planning out my expeditions across an imposing map became an unexpected highlight that not only hooked me, but rewarded my persistence by continuing to expand all the ways I could direct my armies as I tried to stay on top of newly emerging threats. The scope of both its formidably challenging battles and intricate management systems would be wildly ambitious for one path, let alone spread across four – yet somehow Fortune’s Weave only gets better and better each time you guide its captivating heroes into the colosseum and far beyond.

Fire Emblem Echoes: Fortune’s Weave feels like four games in one, such is the scale on show. It might too much for some, but those who fall for it will live and breathe it for a long, long time because this is about as good as it gets for tactics fans.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is a masterful tactical RPG that beautifully combines an engrossing multi-path narrative, addictive turn-based combat, and enjoyable exploration. Dungeon sections help maintain excellent pacing throughout, and the sheer scale of the world means you can easily sink hundreds of hours into this experience without seeing everything. Pair that with solid visuals, a great cast of characters, and an amazing soundtrack, and you’re looking at one of the best Nintendo Switch 2 games released thus far.

Some minor presentational blemishes and slight imbalance to the Overblaze system are about the only drawbacks present in an otherwise exceptional new entry of Fire Emblem which marries the traditional and the modern together to a level of success not reached in other recent franchise entries.

reviews.author: TycanOzor
reviews.quote:
I am creating an account for the very first time just to share my deep disappointment with this game. I have just finished it, and it has a massive problem. Fire Emblem is supposed to be a TRPG (Tactical RPG). Even though the social elements introduced in Three Houses didn't bother me that much, what they did in this game completely ruins the gameplay balance.

There are far too many boring side activities for a game sold as a tactical RPG. I spent almost as much time, if not more, dealing with the social features or fighting in a bland and flavorless RPG combat system instead of enjoying the tactical gameplay. The social aspect has been artificially stretched out by slowing down how fast support levels increase. This forces you to "farm" activities like giving gifts or sharing meals just to recruit a character, which is honestly awful.

The different parts of the game each have their strengths and weaknesses, but that is exactly where the issue lies. The developers seemed to think: "Oh, this feature is good? Let's make them do it a million times!" Sure, you can skip these activities, but if you do, say goodbye to optimization. The game introduces way more optimization options than previous installments, but forces you to do everything except TRPG gameplay to get them. Optimizing tactical phases by grinding mundane side activities is pure heresy!

As for the story, it's okay, but don't expect it to actually reach a proper conclusion. A lot of plot elements and characters are introduced but never get a real payoff. The story feels so heavily amputated that you will likely finish the game asking yourself: "Wait... why do these characters even exist and get so much screen time?"

This game is purely disappointing. It had potential, but it is not a Fire Emblem. It uses the franchise's mechanics, and very good ones at that, but dilutes them to the point of creating an awkward hybrid. If you are having fun with it, good for you. Personally, I deeply regret my purchase. From now on, Fire Emblem, if you release another nonsense like this, you will stay on the store shelf.

I know some people will love this game, but... Why do I feel like a part of the 10/10 reviews only use marketing arguments, rather than serious reviews of the game oO ??? Whether you like it or not, fine, but if you haven't played it, please don't rate it.

reviews.author: AnotherV
reviews.quote:
GAMEPLAY: The sheer amount of padding this game has is so absurd that it makes all of the minigames and sidequests in Final Fantasy VII Rebirth look tame. Way too much downtime between main quest battles with the world map and social activities if you care about any form of optimization for training and recruiting units (auto activities do not help this in the slightest). They even double down on this in the last part of the game just to stretch the time out. Forget about any kind of potential replay value with this one. Dungeon exploration and enemy encounters were done a lot better in Shadows of Valentia because at least that game still kept the tactical battles instead of Fortune's Weave's half-baked attempt at JRPG turn-based battles. Supports are very limited across the board with some units barely having any in the first place. Weapons and accessories are so unbalanced that most players will find themselves not even using some archetypes at all due the sheer amount of weight that'll slow down your units (especially axes and shields). Too many maps with gimmicks that limit player movement either via hazards or enemy reinforcement spam.

STORY: The Prologue already sets a weird tone with all of the sci-fi implications (definitely a huge departure from every other games' medieval fantasy settings). Part 1 is actually pretty decent since it goes far away from what the Prologue was trying to set up. It was pretty cool how all the Flame Lords interacted with each other in their personal struggles. Unfortunately Part 2 is where everything starts to fall off of a cliff. So much stuff that happens between Parts 1 and 2 happen offscreen, and so many plot points that are established in Part 1 just get forgotten about altogether. Part 3 feels like yet another worship fest of the avatar protagonist (Fire Emblem really needs to do away with these avatars, seriously) and another generic "friendship for the win" comeback story. Overall, it just doesn't feel finished.

MUSIC: Pretty good, honestly. There are quite a few catchy tunes (especially the Flame Lords' battle themes). Something that I've noticed though is that there are A LOT of song tracks that are copied and pasted from Three Houses. Like I get this is in the same universe as Three Houses, but dang...

VISUALS: Pretty disappointing, to be honest. The overall art style and some of the character designs are fine, but a lot of the outfit choices for the different classes do not look good. Some characters look so weird with the dedicated class outfits that I defaulted to just using the base unit outfits. Being locked to 30 FPS is sad for Nintendo at this point. Nintendo should be a lot more polished with this franchise by now.

OVERALL: I think the devs were too ambitious with this game (so much to the point that game doesn't even know what it wants to be) after seeing the amount of backlash that Engage got from the FE fanbase. Right now I think Fortune's Weave is getting the Sonic Racing Crossworlds effect in the sense that it's getting a bunch of praise from fans simply because it's not Engage much like Sonic Racing Crossworlds got hyped up for not being Mario Kart World. With more time I think more players' opinions on this game will sour. Fortune's Weave might be better than Engage (depending on who you are), but it still doesn't really feel like Fire Emblem. It's not a good game.

reviews.author: Phenderance
reviews.quote:
To give context, I liked this game enough to finish it. I played through all 4 Part 1 routes, 2 Part 2 routes (Cai and Leda), and then completed Part 3.

The elephant rider in the room is that the game has long segments of traversing the world map, exploring dungeons, menuing, wandering the hub, and picking up items for fetch quests. In prior Fire Emblem games, you'd often have prep phases between chapters but they'd usually only last as long as you wanted them to (other than Three Houses). Because recruiting characters and certain classes are hidden behind a lot of the free time activities, skipping these things will likely severely limit your potential enjoyment of the game. Free Time can last from 30min to 3 hours per section, while maps in part 1 generally are completed within 30-45min. Part 2/3 maps  are usually an hour or so each. Part 3 overworld stuff can last 1-2 hours.

Whether you will enjoy the free time activities is down to personal preference, but I didn't like them. 

The dungeon crawling they've brought back from Fire Emblem Echoes is very barebones. The dungeons are generically designed run down forts or caves that could be from any JRPG. The Clash encounters they've introduced are watered down versions of turn based battles from other JRPGs. If you've ever played something like Persona, SMT, or even Pokemon where the games are actually designed around their systems, the Clash system is so barebones that it's often not even worth manually doing. They do give you the option of skipping them... and even on hard mode, skipping them will allow you to win almost all encounters anyway, unless you were near low HP. Despite Fire Emblem historically being about strategy and tactics, the only thing to really think about is who should get the finishing blow for a bit more exp. Unfortunately, Clashes are also the best source of exp in the game so not doing them all can result in you being underleveled. Also, dungeons have smithing materials used to upgrade your weapons, so not dungeon diving will mean you have less options to play around for your units.

There are also lord-specific sidequests that require you to engage in their world map mechanic, but Cai, Leda, and Theodora all are basically variants of collecting items on the world map and menuing at towns. Dietrich has somewhat more interesting sidequests where you have him duel people. If you don't like these subquests you can choose not to do them, but promotion classes are locked behind them. If you don't do them you will miss out on classic classes like Wyvern Rider and Valkyrie, as well as completely new classes this game has introduced. Also lots of gold, renown and gear.

When you do finally get to the turn based grid focused strategy portion of the game, it is mostly pretty good. It's pretty standard Fire Emblem and honestly on the easier side, but there are some neat map designs that probably could've been cooler if the tuning was a bit tighter. Nonetheless, even if easy it's still pretty fun if you like Fire Emblem. The maps in Part 2 are designed much better and tighter, but also are generally still on the easier side if you're an experienced FE player. They might be hard if you skipped all the stuff I mentioned before though.

The game's plot is generally not too bad and fairly interesting for Fire Emblem. There are some moments that had me rolling my eyes at how tropey they were, but nothing so offensive that I hated it. But I also generally can accept a bad story if the gameplay is fun, but I didn't actually think this game's story was bad. At first. Part 1 builds up a ton of mystery and intrigue to the country of Dagda and it's leaders. You'll see a lot of cutscenes of evil villains cackling as they plot things and the game foreshadows many upcoming conflicts and plot threads. And then once you finally reach part 2 it throws a vast majority of that out the window. A central character in part 1 is off screened in the opening text crawl, a new major villain is introduced in the same text crawl, and the mysteries you never got the answers to remain unanswered. It turns that most of the answers were probably in the cut 4 routes they originally planned, so this game is also unfinished. By the time part 3 shows up, the four original lords (and sublords) also get really sidelined, feeling incredibly unimportant compared to Eshmel. Eshmel also barely even functions as a protagonist and is more of Fortuna's sock puppet.

The game just also has a thousand cuts of other issues too. Support count is generally lower to the point where you wonder why some characters even exist. They've toned down fun options like the Killing Edge. Part 3's gameplay flow is rough. Etc.

For what it's worth, I did enjoy the characters and I like FE gameplay, so I still had a good enough time. Before I hit Pt2 I liked the plot enough. But yeah, this game has a ton of flaws and didn't even release as a complete package despite it's potential length.

reviews.author: RetroGameMan
reviews.quote:
150 hours of my life down the drain. I was so looking forward to this title after being let down by Engage a few years prior, and the setting taking place in the Sothis-verse looked like a good starting point. I was prepared for this game to once again put Fire Emblem more on the map like Three Houses did at the very least. What I was NOT prepared for was this weird sci-fi themed time traveling Persona-like jumbled mess ****.

Fortune's Weave suffers from such a huge identity crisis that it just leaves me to believe that the developers were so overly ambitious that they forgot what makes a Fire Emblem game an actual Fire Emblem game. Whether it's the dumb sci-fi theming, all the forced tutorials, the crazy amount of downtime in between main quest missions with both the activities in Dagsion and the world map stuff, the dungeon exploration with the JRPG-style battles, etc. It tries way too many things at the same time that even just playing one of the Flame Lords will take hours to complete. It took me 150 hours to beat this game, and I played through Part 1 with TWO Flame Lords.

Speaking of the Flame Lords, Part 1 is easily the best part out of all three parts of this game because it focuses on the main characters (who are actually somewhat interesting) and gives the player SOMEWHAT of a feeling of a Fire Emblem game (even if it's not much). It just really **** that a lot of their development gets thrown out later on in favor of once again building up a blank slate of an Avatar protagonist because of "self-insert" reasons. Fire Emblem really needs to do away with the Avatar characters so they can focus on making actual good stories with established characters. Part 2 actually does away with the downtime fluff between main quest missions, but it is also where the game has a very noticeable difficulty spike (and it only gets worse from there). Part 3 goes back to the Dagsion + world map gimmick, but now you get to split up your party into squads. Riveting gameplay, I know... Especially for a Fire Emblem game... Yes, I know you can skip a lot of it with auto-activities and whatnot, but by doing so you are putting yourself at a huge disadvantage when it comes to resources, money, and even experience when you do that. It is OBVIOUSLY more beneficial to do the Dagsion + world map stuff.

And speaking of gameplay, the balance in this game is all kinds of wack. First of all, the battle RNG system is broken... again... I wouldn't be surprised if they just copied and pasted the same hit-rate system from Engage because holy moly the amount of times I've been hit by 30% chances is absurd. Gathering materials out on the world map is also stupid. Secondly, this game easily has the worst recruiting system of any Fire Emblem I've ever played. It's really crazy how all the characters are shuffled and locked around different levels of renown and support levels (which some characters have a very pathetic amount of conversations with their peers). Thirdly, shields and accessories add way too much weight to your characters lowering their attack speed. Most of the buffs they give are pretty negligible anyway, so you don't even need to use them. Fourthly, the weapons aren't great, and axes got completely nuked out of existence. Bring back the weapon triangle. Fifthly, whoever decided that all underworld enemies should have a permanent defense buff while getting additional buffs in miasma/hazards probably shouldn't be developing Fire Emblem games anymore. Sixthly, STOP WITH THE REINFORCEMENT SPAM!! IT WAS STUPID IN ENGAGE, AND IT'S NOT BETTER HERE!!

The game also suffers from presentation and performance issues. 30 FPS looks very jarring in a number of areas that deal with a lot of particle effects. Some of the voiceacting (especially Aurora's) was not directed properly. There also a few typos and grammar issues in the text. The story very obviously starts to fall off of a cliff after Part 1, but I've kinda already touched up on that.

I once thought that it would be really hard to pass up Engage as the black sheep of the Fire Emblem series, but Fortune's Weave somehow managed to do that for me (and judging by the increasing negative user scores coming in... I don't think I'm alone... LOL). The only positive things that I can give this game are that the music and some of the character designs are good. Other than that Fortune's Weave is the worst and most forgettable Fire Emblem game I have ever played. I am VERY concerned about the future of the series after having played it.

reviews.quote: Played on Hard/Classic (All 63 recruits survived, Divine Pulse only).Hard/Classic is definitely not a casual walk in the park. Playing as Dietrich offered a thrilling power fantasy. Clearing Act 2 rewards a glowing save-file portrait and unlocks side-story **** 3: Beyond wrapping up the plot, Act 3 introduces unique mechanics: Agartha warp gates, deeper world-building, revealing Orpheus's identity, and brilliantly designed maps like the jungle. Acts 1 & 2 essentially serve as a tutorial for Act 3's full **** 228 hours flew by. The game feels like a massive epic tightly condensed, with teases like the cloud-shrouded continent leaving great potential for DLC. The narrative alone is worth it.Unlike previous titles where SRPG combat was often the weakest link, this entry shines as a tactical masterpiece with multiple strategic solutions for every **** 90k KRW (Digital), the quality fully justifies the price. Manjachanhong (A Hundred Flowers in Full Bloom) perfectly describes this title: a seamlessly integrated "Total Growth Simulation RPG." Minor polish flaws are easily overshadowed by the obvious passion and ambition behind its development.Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light birthed the genre; Manjachanhong proves it can redefine it. reviews.author: Kira58
reviews.quote:
This game is... strange.

It has some excellent ideas, but there are also tons of things in it that I simply cannot stand.

In general, I’m very easy to please when it comes to the Fire Emblem series. Even the games I enjoyed less, like Fire Emblem Fates, were still games I appreciated quite a lot. I played through them with a smile on my face, sometimes even multiple times. I actually have a tendency to replay Fire Emblem games after finishing them.

However, this game has too many flaws in my eyes.

The long stretches of time between missions are just way too frustrating. Yes, most of it can be skipped, but if you do that, say goodbye to recruitment, say goodbye to optimization, and basically say goodbye to a huge part of what makes Fire Emblem Fire Emblem, at least in my eyes.

The game isn't completely bad. Far from it. It has some really good aspects, especially the character optimization and the sheer number of classes available. But I wish I didn't have to "work" on things I simply don't care about in order to enjoy those parts of the game.

This is the only Fire Emblem game where I barely bothered with supports. I even cheated to increase support levels because I was simply tired of doing it legitimately.

Honestly... just to get through the game faster and finally see the end, I even leveled some characters all the way to level 99 so I could finish it more quickly.

Ironically, doing that came back to bite me. I ended up having to fight a level 99 final boss, along with infinitely respawning level 98 reinforcements. They nearly made me give up on the game because my average equipped level was around 20 levels lower.

But despite all of that, I finished it.

Basically, in my eyes, this game sits right next to some genuinely excellent ideas, while also containing things that I found absolutely unbearable. That's why I give it a 5/10.

I really, really want to give it a 0 because of how frustrated and angry this game made me, but that would be letting my emotions speak. I want to try to remain at least somewhat objective.

If you're reading my review (assuming you actually are), do your own research on the game. If you dislike the same things I do, you might end up being just as disappointed as I was.

But... and this honestly hurts me to say... if you actually like the things I dislike, then this game might be a masterpiece in your eyes.

One more thing: be careful when looking at the game's reviews. There are plenty of negative reviews, and after reading quite a few of them, I can understand why people dislike the game. But there has also been positive review bombing, with entire communities deliberately pushing the rating up.

So the game is much more divisive than its overall rating might suggest.

And if you genuinely love this game despite everything... I envy you.

I wish I could have loved it too, rather than realizing that this is the one game in the series that actually weakened the love I had for the franchise.

Until now, Fire Emblem had never disappointed me to the point where I felt like I hated playing one of its games.

So... let's hope for updates together. A new difficulty, improvements, and elements that could fix some of the game's biggest problems.

And, most importantly...

Please fix all those holes in the story that made me go:

"Wait... THAT'S the ending???"

Oh, and sorry if my English is a bit rough. I'm French (everyone has their flaws!), and I used AI to translate my review.

reviews.author: Zabu
reviews.quote:
Fire emblem fortune's weave is a game made for people that don't care about Fire emblem.

Between the poverty of each map design, the units composition that are as bland as possible, the variety of weapons that have been dragged down, the tactical possibilities of each characters is still so poor.

The class variety is somehow worst than it used to be, do you think people would get lost if they have to actually pick some choices ?

The removal of the classic triangle that happened in 3 Houses with the previous issues make every fight blatantly uninteresting, the depth of the game is simply not there anymore, you used to be good Intelligent Systems, now you feel more like Dumb Systems. 
Speaking of Dumb, the award goes to the person that green lighted the single save combined with the autosave, seriously you're a genius.

The new systems are uninteresting, even in classic and hard difficulty you can simply auto battle like in a mobile game in the dungeon exploration. 
Why do you try to force a traditionnal JRPG combat with low amount of character in a tactical when you usually control way more units? 

The story being sci-fi and time travel oriented just doesn't help... Having laser turrets and guns thrown at me at the beginning felt really out of place.


The game's running as low FPS while having this visual quality is simply not acceptable.
At this point I'm questioning who thought that spending money on doing some cities visuals in 3D that look that poor and with absolutely zero interest in gameplay was thinking. Even them understood at some points that it was useless since a major part of the cities don't even have that screen.


Every time I'm done with a Main Quest, I remember why I like Fire Emblem and even though some stuff are questionnable and it still feels like a mid Fire Emblem, when I have the screen saying to me "See ya in 100 turns" my motivation to play the game simply vanishes.

In comparaison I didn't dislike as much the downtime in 3 Houses, on this one it's simply not fun for me.


All of this made clearly set for the this Fire emblem as the worst that I've played, seeing the critic reception and the direction it's going, I'm really not expecting the next titles to get better. I'll just get back to play old titles.



On the opposite I feel like some characters were really cool lore-wise and visually pleasing. The musics were still nice but I don't really have much more nice things to say about this game.

Congrats on loosing a fan for new customers I guess ¯_(ツ)_/¯

reviews.author: CrysAnna
reviews.quote:
Sadly this is no Fire Emblem anymore. I am Fire Emblem Fan since GBA times but 3H and Fortunes Weave are no good titles for me.

Fortune's Weave has like 70% socialicing and 30% battles. I rush from shop to shop to buy gifts to recruit characters im the same city just so that I can use only 5-6 during part 1 in battles which are not the main quest battle. And even there, you nearly always have guest characters. Why not use my own I spent most of the time recruiting? 

The map feels useless, the subquests + collecting materials do too and the time part also doesn't do the game any favor. Also you can miss characters (paralogues especially) when you hit a certain date which I absolutely hate. Since there is only one save, you have to restart the chapter again if you are a completist - manual saves are just overwritten regularly by automatical ones. 

The Part 1 of each character feels pretty similar except the story sometimes, but even some story battles are the same because you are teamed up with other groups - which means that in both paths you do the same battle. 

Part 2 is where the game shines more, at least in the battles. The in between is cheap, you don't have any doings anymore, just a shop (not even armory) and instead of keeping your weapons from before, you get strong standard items you need after each battle. This doesn't feel right somehow, just lazy. But it makes sense if you think about that that part is fully skippable although the story is good and the maps are too. For me, you could've just skip the in between story battles and instead only use the preparation menu.
Little spoiler here: the part 2 mainly focuses on Theodora, so if you played another flamelord, you feel kinda...useless to the story. At least I did with Leda. 

Also the Avatar feels kinda useless too. I start creating one, play the tutorial and then they vanish until Part 3. I would've loved to play my Avatar through all parts and bond with characters a bit more during battles than just answering questions as a bird.

As much as I wanna love this game, the lack of tactical focus in a tactic game series such as Fire Emblem is a big problem for me. If you wanna do Persona x Tactics that's totally fine, make a new series or subseries. I like Persona really much. But in Fire Emblem this just doesn't fit. The older ones also had some little social part but it felt rewarding. You noticed the ingame advantages during battle more and even got new characters (kids) with the parent's skills + their maps. Here on Fortune's Weave, it doesn't feel that useful.

Although this was much ranting, the game has also some good points. I liked the overall story, especially from part 2 onwards which sadly falls a bit in the background due to all of this other things you need to do. Some of the characters are pretty interesting and I absolutely love the design of the (especially female) Avatar. 

I hope that the next Fire Emblem finds back to its roots but since the broad mass prefers this (easier) Social Emblem, I guess this won't be happening.

reviews.author: GrupoNPe
reviews.quote:
Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave es una entrega tremendamente ambiciosa.

Intelligent Systems tomó la estrategia clásica de la saga y construyó alrededor de ella un RPG mucho más grande: cuatro protagonistas, exploración, gestión del tiempo, reclutamiento, mazmorras, relaciones, diferentes clases y un mundo que constantemente nos ofrece algo nuevo que hacer.

Lo mejor es que las batallas siguen siendo el corazón de la experiencia.

Eso sí, hay momentos donde la administración del mapa, las actividades secundarias y determinadas secciones compartidas entre rutas pueden sentirse repetitivas, especialmente si nuestra intención es verlo absolutamente todo. Diferentes recorridos completos han señalado precisamente esa repetición como uno de los puntos débiles de la segunda mitad.

Por eso no creo que sea un Fire Emblem para jugar con prisa. Ya que, este es de esos  juegos para adquirir, sentarse y aceptar que vamos a vivir en Dagda durante bastante tiempo.

La buena noticia es que la aventura cuenta con textos en español, así que toda la historia, menús y sistemas pueden seguirse sin esa barrera lingüística que sí encontramos en algunos de los títulos que hemos analizado anteriormente.

Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave quizá intente hacer demasiadas cosas al mismo tiempo, pero cuando sus sistemas, personajes, música y combates empiezan a encajar, es muy difícil no querer descubrir qué destino estamos tejiendo con cada decisión.

reviews.author: Bear_Form
reviews.quote:
15 hours in, I'm putting the game down. Fire Emblem is turn-based tactics with the added value of seeing your units grow and develop relationships with each other. This entry is is like what happens when you leave a systems designer unattended.
- Characters are big "quantity over quality", my first 2 recruited characters have 3 social links each, only 1 with characters in my actual squad and it's only C rank.
- MAIN CHARACTERS don't get A-rank social links with each other (Theodora & Bonaventure, a Queen and her lifelong retainer, don't even have an A rank and their B rank is INSANE to end on).
- Likely due to the cut content for the game, but there's characters without ANY social links that make no sense (Orchel is listed in Diego's likes, he says he'd die for her, and they have no support dialogue).
- There's a ton of new unnecessary systems that step on each others' toes: Overworld Map with travel time factored in, calendar & time of day mechanics that necessitate you being in town at specific times to trigger discounts or special events, weekly cooldowns on activities to progress your characters/renown that aren't tracked in any meaningful way, a huge empty town that is better to navigate with the UI fast travel - they all get in the way of the core gameplay of what Fire Emblem SHOULD be: doing tactics battles with units who develop relationships over time together.
- Dungeons are one of the most confusing additions. They are brief JRPG stints that require running around in an area doing turn-based party combat, but the systems for it do not support this type of gameplay and it's not why I play Fire Emblem games! On top of that, you unlock 3 different ways to totally skip this content (auto-battle, skip to conclusion, & overworld quick defeat).

The story seems interesting, I like a lot of the characters, but slogging through secondary gameplay to get to the core loop and having half-baked relationship arcs just killed this one for me. Feels like the direction since Fates has just really changed the direction of the series in a way that isn't for me.

Valheim is the oath of the ultimate survival crafting adventure fulfilled, with a gorgeous art style, deadly dungeons, charming homesteading mechanics, and a breathtaking scope.

After more than 300 hours, I know Valheim well. Though somehow, it can still surprise me. That is why I suspect I will keep playing it for years. Version 1.0 may mark the end of its journey into Early Access, but for me, it doesn’t feel like an ending. Valheim has given me hundreds of hours of stories and discoveries, and, after all this time, I’m still not ready to leave.
Valheim is already a paragon of the survival crafting genre, with excellent art and music highlighting a world that generates endless exciting stories from only a few simple ingredients.

Valheim is a technological masterpiece, despite its graphics. Initially frustrating, the game's procedural generation system and unique progression mechanics truly shine. It avoids typical procedural pitfalls, offering a sense of direction without repetition and encouraging exploration of both new and old biomes. Despite a small development team, Valheim delivers a rich, individualized experience where players constantly return to earlier areas for resources and new discoveries, making advancement about world exploration rather than just increasing difficulty.

There’s a whole life to be lived in Valheim, with a variety of jobs that can satisfy combatants and cozy gamers alike. My friends have flocked into a Discord call every night the past week or so, all of us with our own goals but banding together to take on a poisonous goop monster in the swamp or a half-dead goblin god dragging itself across the plains. Valheim has quietly become one of the most successful and beloved games in its genre, and it deserves every flower for how it developed during early access and now finally into its 1.0 release.

Boiling down Valheim into a single word isn’t easy, what with its multiple biomes, staggering amount of crafting recipes, deceptively complex and detailed base-building mechanics, heart-pounding combat, and all. But if I had to choose, I’d call it epic. I don’t just mean that to describe the game’s awesomeness, of which it has plenty; I also mean that in its saga-like length and the downright mythical feats players get to achieve on their way from simple survival to the halls of Valhalla itself. This is the quintessential hardcore survival experience—don’t ever let anything convince you otherwise.
Valheim is probably the most polished survival game I've ever played, with a ridiculously satisfying upgrade loop that kept me hooked.
One of the best survival games around is finally complete.

A game that hands you a goal (and a dozen better ones on the way there) and trusts you to pick whichever one you want. The Deep North just gave me a colder, more beautiful place to get distracted in, and I can’t wait to start exploring again.

reviews.author: Wedhro
reviews.quote:
Disclaimer: my vote is based on the current state of the game at release, because it's plagued by horrible map-resetting bugs that the developers are yet to iron out completely. Otherwise it would have been an 8.

So, the game is good. Or I should say, the game does some important things right and has an unique approach that makes it refreshing. While a little clunky, the fighting, survival, building and exploring is pretty good, sometimes genius, like treating food as progressively better boosts instead of the usual boring implementations, or survival being limited to cold/wet debuffs with the chance of building your base so you can fight better for longer. With an engaging loop of getting better stuff to craft better gear to beat a biome and then move to the next one, it's guaranteed to be fun for a hundred hours at least, which can easily go in the thousands if you like building.

It's rest that doesn't work. There's plenty of side activities that are not challenging nor fun to do, and even when they kind of are, the rewards range from disappointing to useless. Just an example: a NPC will ask you to recover three pieces of something. It's a long quest that requires lot of utterly uninteresting sailing true empty oceans, so you can risk your life with big baddies. Finally you move these cumbersome goods back to the NPC by boat, because they can't even be teleported, and the reward is her charging you money for a bunch of crappy items you'll never use. Multiply this x30 and you might see how a big chunk of the game consists on regretting the time wasted in futile endeavours, only to find more exercises of futility in the next biome. The risk/reward ratios is often nonsensical, so if you have limited time to play, be warned.

It's a fun game that will keep you engaged for a long time if you don't mind how useless many things are, though.

reviews.author: faijiro
reviews.quote:
What can I say? Finally version 1.0 is out and it has optimised it’s performance. I’m playing this on a 7 year old setup running GTX 1070ti on 1440p and it still runs smoothly. 

It’s the ultimate game really. The game throws you into the world and you have to build shelter and find food and other resources not just to survive but also to progress into the Deeper North. Unlike other survival games where you have to constantly manage your hunger/thirst and so one, Valheim removed all that and makes food a temporary buff rather than that constant annoyance or thing you have to think about. It makes food more rewarding as it gives you more health and stamina rather than just filling up a meter.

The enemies, well there plenty of types and if you’re not careful any of them can kill you really. You gotta learn their attack patterns and watch your stamina. I wouldn’t say it is souls-like but it has it’s vibes. You can dodge-roll and you can parry. Different enemies has different weaknesses. Some are weak to fire, some are resistant to slash damage and so on. The combat is surprisingly deep for a survival game.

And of course we have the building. If you are tired of fighting you can just chill, listen to the soundtrack which is very soothing and build. The build menu is pretty extensive, there are tons of parts and let your inner carpenter out. Just go on youtube and you can see all the amazing stuff people have build.

Lastly, the exploration. You get to go on your own odyssey. This what hooked me. You get to explore and discover new things. You can go on foot only until so far and then you have reached the limit, it is time to sail. On water you can feel the vulnerability. I have never felt this way from any game. You don’t know what lurks ahead and that is brilliant. 

Highly highly highly recommend this game.
