This is a considered, artful game and one that’s so clearly created with love. For any fan of sewing or tactile creativity, it’s a must-play experience.

I adore Dressmaker. It is easily one of my top played games of the year. It’s nostalgic, cozy and the story is so memorable. The concept is so charming and the ability to replay and try new designs as well. For some players, I can see the gameplay loop being a bit repetitive, but personally it’s comforting and adds to the appeal. Sometimes all it takes is a needle, thread and a little nostalgia to leave a stitch on your heart.

There are a few things I would change, particularly the sewing mini-game, the repeated filtering in the emporium, and the performance issues when switching away from the game. The mix of historical fashion and modern designs can also feel a little odd, although I think the freedom it gives you is worth it. Overall, though, Dressmaker gave me exactly the kind of cosy dress-up experience I wanted, with enough story and strange little characters to keep it from becoming just another decorating game.

I have no real-world skills with sewing or dressmaking, but I thoroughly enjoyed being able to let loose creatively and make some stunning dresses. The low-stress aspect (after figuring out how to fulfill all the customer-required elements) meant it was easy to just focus on the creativity and really enjoy the process. If you have an interest in dressmaking, then I highly recommend Dressmaker!

Dressmaker feels unique among other clothing creation simulations as a result of the premise, and there are a lot of customization options. The concept feels very different than other games out there. There are a few elements that feel like they need some finishing touches, especially regarding crashes and the zoom function. But after a patch or two, I think it could be a real designing gem.

Dressmaker is a delightful game that can be enjoyed in short bursts or for hours at a time. The cast of characters is unique, and their interwoven storylines make the world beyond the shop feel alive. The dressmaking gameplay is easy to understand and features many accessibility options, and the ability to mix and match many patterns, fabrics and appliqué together allows for endless creativity. While I wish there was a little more substance to the actual store side of things, I believe this is a great title for those interested in costume design, as this could be a super enjoyable way to try new things and get creative juices flowing, while also enjoying a fun story.
Dressmaker is a game that manages to make a complex craft accessible without sacrificing the joy of making clothes. The game is fundamentally very simple, but what it does, it does very well.

reviews.author: noelle02
reviews.quote: It's a lovely game. Very simple gameplay but it has a story that unlocks more creative assignments as it progresses. Goes from very basics prompts to design at the start to let you get comfortable with the game mechanics and then becomes more conceptual letting you get creative with how to interpret a client's commission.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is easily a contender for game of the year, as it blends merciless action with skill-based combat in a near-seamless way. The story and visuals complement the ridiculously sharp gameplay extremely well, and though the camera can be a little problematic on rare occasions, that shouldn’t stop you from experiencing Capcom’s latest banger.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword is a visually stunning revival that successfully brings Capcom’s classic franchise into the modern era using the RE Engine. Musashi injects a refreshing sense of personality into dark fantasy Kyoto, especially during the game’s intense and cinematic boss fights. This is definitely an action adventure game of the year contender.
As rewarding as it is difficult, Onimusha isn’t just one of the best games of the year; it’s one of the best action games ever made.

For as long as I can remember, I have wanted to be perfect for 10 seconds. Onimusha: Way of the Sword understands that desire. Each time I landed a perfectly timed Issen, pulled off a risky deflect, or landed a combo at just the right time, I felt like I had accomplished something. I had put myself to the test, and I’d succeeded. It’s a testament to Way of the Sword’s combat that I could beat it without using some of the systems designed to help you progress – not because you don’t need them, but because it leaves room for you to truly understand its action and overcome their absence through sheer determination. Even if I hadn’t intentionally made things harder for myself, though, I still would have loved spending time with Okuni, Takamura, Murasaki, Shizuka, and nearly all the denizens of this world. I still would have thought that Musashi himself is one of the coolest, most interesting protagonists in any video game, and I would have loved going on this journey with him. I still would have savored the creative fights against Ganryu and Benkei and a dozen others I won’t spoil here. My journey reflected Musashi's, and Onimusha made that possible. The best part of life is the challenge. You have to learn to love the fight.

Onimusha is a criminally underrated series, and while it was not a series I was expecting to be revived, I am delighted to see it make a comeback. And with the sheer quality that Capcom has pumped into Way of the Sword, I have no doubt that this is a game that is going to sell like hotcakes, and I'm already getting my hopes up for another new Onimusha title, In a competitive field, Onimusha: Way of the Sword is hands-down the best action-adventure title of the year so far. Its combat system is as electrifying as it is challenging to master, and it's backed up by a great story and characters, and a lovely little world to explore. Capcom can probably scarcely believe how well its 2026 is going. Here's hoping its new golden age continues for many years to come.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword isn't just an excellent series revival from a company that has seemingly mastered them, taking a proper understanding of the early entries' appeal and matching it perfectly to modern sensibilities. It's also just plainly the best action game this year, and probably for the past few years.

Onimusha is back and ready to claim the highest honors. Content,
quality, fun – the full package is right here.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword marks a triumphant return for Capcom’s samurai action series, combining spectacular visuals with deep, demanding combat built around precise parries, the classic Issen technique, and a varied arsenal of Oni weapons. Strong performances, memorable boss battles, rewarding progression, and an excellent recreation of feudal Japan make it one of Capcom’s most accomplished action games, while repetitive sub-bosses and a few minor presentation issues do little to diminish an outstanding experience.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword proves Capcom can't go wrong in 2026, offering combat that stands out with every swing of the blade and fascinating characters.

Onimusha: Way of the Sword masterfully revives the franchise with gameplay rich in mechanics and variety, full of boss battles that could make even FromSoftware fans envious. The story is like an incredible shonen anime. Musashi is a captivating and funny protagonist, accompanied by a cast of equally interesting supporting characters and antagonists who come together to create one of the best journeys Capcom has ever crafted.

The side quests are honestly pretty boring and repetitive, which makes the overall experience feel a little tedious at times. Instead of adding much to the adventure, they occasionally make the game feel like a chore and disrupt the **** difficulty is mostly well-balanced throughout the game, rewarding patience, skill, and learning enemy patterns. But the final boss is a different story. The difficulty spike feels so extreme that it comes across as unbalanced rather than challenging. I actually had to lower the difficulty for the final fight, which felt a little shameful, but honestly, the sudden jump in difficulty was just too much.Despite these shortcomings, Onimusha: Way of the Sword is still a brilliant experience. reviews.author: porsiemprejoos
reviews.quote:
De las mejores experiencias que he tenido en mucho tiempo. Desde que lo comencé noté que no parece un juego acorde a la actualidad: tiene carácter, identidad, humor, un gameplay increíble, una historia muy interesante, personajes memorables y brutalidad. 
Me transportó a esos juegos difíciles de la era de PlayStation 2 y, de nuevo, se siente como pocos.

El combate es variado y el juego no te castiga por querer hacer las cosas rápido. Si quieres que los combates terminen pronto, tendrás que poner en juego tu habilidad; de lo contrario, pondrá a prueba tu paciencia y tus reflejos, cada jefe es una experiencia única. 
Es verdad que algunos se repiten, pero en general la variedad me parece suficiente.

Soy de los que, cuando un juego los atrapa, quieren y deben conseguir el platino. En ese aspecto, el juego sufre del mismo problema que Capcom arrastra desde hace años: forzar la rejugabilidad para obtener todos los trofeos, una rejugabilidad que genuinamente no tiene.
Al terminarlo por primera vez se desbloquea una nueva dificultad, CARNAGE, con enemigos más fuertes y mayor daño recibido. El problema es que no funciona como un NG+ al estilo Souls: te resetean todas las mejoras de tu personaje (katana, armadura y guantelete). 
Como todo es más difícil, tendrás que volver a mejorar todo tu equipo si no quieres que el modo sea una tortura, y eso lo vuelve aburrido y tedioso.

Además, el juego te pide lo que se siente como tres partidas: la primera, en cualquier dificultad; la segunda, en CARNAGE; y una tercera que, aunque no implica repetir todo el juego, sí te obliga a volver a enfrentar a todos los jefes en modo CARNAGE. Se siente excesivo, como una forma artificial de alargar la duración, y más tratándose de un juego que no es precisamente corto: mi primera partida, haciendo todo, me tomó cerca de 32 horas, y la segunda, en CARNAGE, cerca de 22.

Solo en el tema de los trofeos siento que fue demasiado; en general, el juego es increíble. Si te gustan los retos, debes jugarlo. No es un Souls: tiene su propia esencia.

reviews.author: MARMIN90
reviews.quote: Onimusha: Way of the Sword è il ritorno di una serie che sembrava ormai destinata a rimanere un ricordo, e lo fa con una personalità sorprendentemente forte. Capcom riesce a riportare in vita l’anima degli Onimusha classici senza limitarsi a riproporre una formula nostalgica: il risultato è un action che guarda al passato, ma combatte con un ritmo e una spettacolarità decisamente **** punto di forza assoluto è il sistema di combattimento. Ogni scontro trasmette peso e precisione, con parate, schivate e contrattacchi che richiedono tempismo e attenzione. Le celebri Issen, marchio di fabbrica della serie, tornano a essere una componente fondamentale e regalano una soddisfazione enorme quando si riesce a eseguire un contrattacco perfetto. Affrontare più demoni contemporaneamente può trasformarsi in una danza letale fatta di posizionamento, lettura degli attacchi e decisioni prese in una frazione di secondo.Anche l'ambientazione convince parecchio. Il Giappone feudale viene rappresentato con un'estetica cupa e suggestiva, dove villaggi, castelli e paesaggi tradizionali convivono con l'orrore soprannaturale. I Geni e le creature demoniache riescono a dare al mondo di gioco quella componente dark fantasy che ha sempre distinto Onimusha, mentre la direzione artistica sfrutta ottimamente la potenza delle tecnologie moderne per rendere ogni scenario ricco di atmosfera.Particolarmente riuscita è poi la capacità di alternare esplorazione, combattimenti e momenti più narrativi senza appesantire l'esperienza. Non tutto è perfetto: in alcuni frangenti la struttura può risultare un po' più lineare di quanto ci si aspetterebbe da un action moderno e qualche elemento avrebbe meritato maggiore profondità. Anche la narrazione, pur efficace nel creare atmosfera e tensione, non raggiunge sempre gli stessi livelli di eccellenza del gameplay.Sono però difetti che non intaccano quello che rimane un ritorno in grande stile. Way of the Sword dimostra che Onimusha non appartiene soltanto alla nostalgia dei primi anni 2000: la sua formula può ancora funzionare, e può farlo alla grande se costruita intorno a un combattimento solido e appagante.Voto: 9/10Un ritorno atteso che mantiene lo spirito della serie e lo porta nel presente con grande sicurezza. Combattimenti spettacolari, atmosfera straordinaria e un sistema di parate e Issen capace di regalare momenti di puro godimento. Non è semplicemente un'operazione nostalgia: è la dimostrazione che Onimusha ha ancora molto da dire.

reviews.author: DaicoXXI
reviews.quote:
ONIMUSHA de Capcom es simplemente uno de los mejores juegos de Samuráis del género, con los Gohst de Su*kerPunch y SEKIRO de Fromsoftwere. 

La historia es TOP! Onimusha: the way of the sword es un juego de: fantasía oscura, sangrienta, gore, con héroes y su camino a convertirse en leyendas, villanos y sus malvados planes por descubrir y una traumática historia basada en la mitología y leyendas japonesas medievales mezcladas con el universo Onimusha; que es perfecto para ello; y logra conseguir, con una inconmensurable CAPCOM, meternos de lleno en el nuevo episodio de las aventuras de los ONI, que llevada con uno de los sistemas de combate con espadas basado en el estilo del lucha del japón medieval, los samuráis y sus las leyendas como la del espadachín ronin invicto Miyamoto Mushashi, más una narrativa audiovisual basada en: el cine, mangas, animes y las películas de las historias de samuráis... lleva a este ONIMUSHA a cotas altísimas y a una de las mejores experiencias "videojueguiles" del año. 

Por lo pronto lo malo que tiene el juego es sus carencias notables es respecto al diseño de niveles, mundo semi-abierto y contenido del juego sobretodo en el "endgame" que no tiene más que una "nueva partida+" con acceso a un nivel de dificultad superior, unos cuantos cosméticos a conseguir y nada más.  En cuanto a duración, pues a pesar de su diseño y aunque pases horas combatiendo el juego se hace bastante corto; Un buen mundo abierto bien diseñado y bien ejecutado le vendría de locos a una segunda parte. con obviamente una duración muchísimo mayor... si se trabajase bien podría ser hasta un The Witcher en grandeza pero... eso es una utopía. Solo con el combate, que es tan bueno, puedes quedarte horas solo enfrentándote a demonios Gemma y jefes finales. Pero a pesar de estos puntos negativos lo compensa todo con su historia y sus personajes basados en las leyendas mitológicas japonesas y algunos personajes históricos destacables que son introducidos en el universo Onimusha; como el legendario samurái Musashi Miyamoto protagonizado por un "resucitado" Toshiro Mizune; su ambientación, su buenísima banda sonora, su arte, paleta de colores, gráficos y unos combates 1 Vs 1 incluso 1 VS 2 contra jefes finales, que se podrán repetir durante la historia a modo de entrenamiento, solo dejan ganas de jugar más y más y más...

Conclusión, obra sobresaliente pero no perfecta de los nipones de CAPCOM y deja un poso de: "Cuándo saldrá el Onimusha: Way of the Sword 2? y por favor que sea pronto" además que este protagonizado por el mismo Mushashi y también por... SPOILER* pásate el juego para saberlo.

Para mí el mejor juego del año 2026 con SAROS.

reviews.author: philvin1991

The parry and dodge windows become narrower as the game **** feels frustrating to continue after a while and you feel like you want to finish it because you spend 80 dollars on it. When in the middle of combat you try to heal the heal doesn't register even if you press the buttons.This is because some other action is ongoing. It's hard to think of a better collection of games than those on Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2. Even if Metal Gear Solid 4 wasn't such a prize for players who haven't been able to revisit it for so long, the game, divorced of that context, is still excellent. While they're less headline grabbing, Peace Walker and Ghost Babel both sit alongside the very best of the franchise. An unmissable collection for Metal Gear fans.

Metal Gear Solid Master Collection Vol. 2 perfectly achieves its goal: bringing Guns of the Patriots and Peace Walker — formerly exclusive to Sony consoles — to modern platforms. The inclusion of Portuguese subtitles and a price point that aligns with the volume of content offered represent major wins for Konami with the Brazilian audience.

Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Volume 2 continues the high quality established by the first collection in the series, though slightly slimmer in the content it offers. That being said, you’ll be more than treated with a fantastic new version of Metal Gear Solid 4, and the handheld frays of the series to make for a whole tapestry that everyone can now enjoy, alongside the first volume.

Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 is a faithful preservation package that finally frees Metal Gear Solid 4 from the PS3 while giving Peace Walker and Ghost Babel another chance to shine. It does little to modernize the games beyond making them accessible, but strong ports, worthwhile extras, and the enduring quality of the originals make this an easy recommendation for longtime fans.
Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 brings with it two fantastic games, including one of PlayStation 3's best exclusives brought back to life like a shot of nanomachine suppressors to the leg.

A masterclass in game preservation, Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol 2 triumphantly rescues Hideo Kojima’s Guns of the Patriots from its PS3 hardware prison. Combined with the sprawling, essential Peace Walker and retro gems like Ghost Babel, this collection isn't just a phenomenal value; it's an essential piece of gaming history finally restored for modern players.

Metal Gear Solid Master Collection Vol.2 finally frees Metal Gear Solid 4 from PS3 prison, and being able to re-experience that brilliant-but-flawed game again is worth the price of admission alone. Packaged with the fantastic Peace Walker and overlooked spinoff Ghost Babel, this is a phenomenal collection. This time around, the games are at their absolute best too, with Vol 1’s technical issues nowhere to be seen.
Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol.2 includes two fantastic games that still hold up all these years later, along with some great content for fans that want to dive even deeper.

Rather than focusing on what Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2—and MGS4 in particular—does right or wrong, this is more about how necessary and cathartic this closure feels. Releasing the collection is practically a gesture to the fans, and if you know how to appreciate it, it’s perfect. But even judged as a modern game, completely out of context, we could still say it’s the best of all nine.

Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection – Volume 2 finally frees Guns of the Patriots from the PlayStation 3, bringing with it several very welcome visual upgrades. The bonus games are a nice touch, though they aren't exactly the most substantial part of the package. If you are a fan of the series—or want to see how the story concludes—this is a release that belongs in your collection.

Star Wars Zero Company is, simply put, the greatest tactics game in the galaxy. Creating a story worthy of the Star Wars franchise, this tactics title delivers the very best in combat the genre has to offer, wrapping it up in a cinematic delivery of the highest order.

Zero Company is a great turn-based strategy game that happens to be set in the Star Wars universe. It never feels like a corporate mandate to make a genre game with a recognizable license. Instead, it feels like a group of talented developers genuinely wanted to explore what the genre could do and had the freedom to experiment. Those ideas succeed far more often than they stumble, and the game's excellent use of the Clone Wars setting makes Zero Company one of the most entertaining turn-based strategy games I've played in a long time.

Star Wars Zero Company brilliantly merges deep XCOM-style tactical strategy with a surprisingly rich, squad-driven narrative that stands among the franchise's finest. Memorable companion dynamics, organic base management, and varied mission design deliver immense emotional and mechanical engagement throughout its campaign. Minor camera issues during turn transitions and occasional luck-based spikes slightly disrupt combat flow. Nevertheless, stunning Unreal Engine 5 visuals and refined gameplay choices make it an unmissable achievement for strategy fans and Star Wars enthusiasts alike.
STAR WARS: Zero Company is a cinematic, turn-based tactical game that doesn’t feel like a copy of XCOM but instead pulls you into this universe where your teammates are the main focus of the story.

So, is Star Wars Zero Company good? Yes. It’s great, in fact. If you like XCOM-style, turn-based tactical games, then you’ll love this, because it’s a fantastic entry into the genre. Hell, the Star Wars framing might even be enough to sell the genre to those who otherwise don’t normally engage with the turn-based tactics genre.

Star Wars: Zero Company, despite some rough edges, manages to open up the turn-based tactics genre to new players, while at the same time giving fans of the genre exactly what they crave. A cracking tactical adventure in a galaxy far, far away.

Star Wars: Zero Company is a cinematic tactics extravaganza of Star Wars storytelling and strategy. A memorable and diverse cast of dysfunctional characters at the margins of the galaxy carries you through an adventure of stellar scripted and emergent moments, a sandbox of compelling tactical decisions and an assured debut of a videogame from Bit Reactor that scratched my tactical itch with the strength of a superlaser.
Star Wars Zero Company is an incredible Star Wars game and a genuinely brilliant tactical RPG that you won't be able to put down.

Star Wars Zero Company is an incredible debut title from Bit Reactor. A tightly paced 30 hour tactics game with some of the best Star Wars storytelling in recent years. Star Wars and tactics fans alike would be remiss to not check out Zero Company.
An unmissable Star Wars epic and a well oiled, exhilarating tactical RPG all in one. An excellent entry point for people into turn-based tactics games with enough meat on its bones for veterans.

reviews.author: Maitrify
reviews.quote:
Firstly, my tactics experience reaches back to NES/SNES days, starting with Advance Wars (Famicom Wars) and the Super variants and went from there. Personally, I think the best tactics games out there are ones such as Final Fantasy Tactics, Fire Emblem, X-COM and similar titles.

This is . . . acceptable. It's not a great game. It's not BAD, it's just not great. It scratches that tactics itch but you'll be irritated with the sheer number of issues it has. Turns freezing/locking up, shots going through walls straight up, the 'exploratory' part of games feeling VERY tacked on.

Suffice it to say, I'd only get this game if you are A. A HUGE Star Wars fan and B. A HUGE tactics fan.

Even then, I'd suggest waiting til it's $30 (USD) or lower. It's just not worth $50 whatsoever.

There are problems that this game has that simply are inexcusable as they are problems that have been fixed in OTHER tactics games and should NOT appear in a game in 2026.  (i.e. Outmoded systems and limited flexibility. Drastically limited weapons (there are only 4) with no real speciality.)

Get a demo (or alternatives) if possible, as I genuinely regret spending $50 for this. I'm coming up to the point where I can't force myself to play anymore as the story is dry, the gameplay doesn't hook me (as it's not that good), the strategy/tactics aspect is minor and the characters are hard to like.

There's very little redeemability here.

reviews.author: alexpaleale
reviews.quote: Star Wars: Zero Company is a fantastic experience and an absolute treat for anyone who loves tactical gameplay and is passionate about the Clone Wars era. Coming into this as only my second tactical game after Baldur's Gate 3, I found the core gameplay and the story to be brilliant. The developers truly understand what fans love, packing the game with incredible moments that keep on giving. Highlights like seeing and playing as Anakin Skywalker, fighting alongside Captain Rex, and experiencing the gut-punch of Order 66 unfolding mid-game are unforgettable.However, the game is held back by several logistical and technical issues. There is a lot of frustrating lag during loading screens—especially when ships take off or return from missions—that freezes the screen for a few seconds and makes you feel like the game might crash. While it only fully crashed on me once, mid-combat performance can also stutter, freeze, or cause character models to clip into objects. Positioning can be finicky too, occasionally blocking you from attacking an enemy just because a character is standing too close.Additionally, it's a shame that the game abruptly ends when the campaign finishes with no option to keep playing. Other tactical games feature endless or AI-generated missions that let you keep tinkering with squad builds indefinitely, which this game desperately needs. Despite those technical hiccups and the lack of post-game content, the strong narrative and engaging gameplay make it a phenomenal ride. I highly recommend it!

reviews.author: labenelson
reviews.quote:
9.3/10

I’ve been looking forward to this game since it was announced. As an XCOM fan, I knew this game had big shoes to fill, and they absolutely delivered.

** SPOILERS BELOW **

The story starts off slow, but any prequel fan will appreciate it. It follows the timeline of Episode 3, so you can actively see the Republic fall apart as the Empire is born. Seeing it through the eyes of a mercenary family adds an interesting perspective.

The gameplay, when there are no performance issues, is top tier. You have 8 specializations to choose from that you can mix and match to your heart’s desire. Later in the game, you can unlock a second specialization, which opens things up quite a bit. Once you learn what each specialization is good at, you can combo them together to create some big-damage plays.

My only real issue with this game is the performance. There were several times where I would select a move for my turn, and my character would just sit there frozen for a minute before moving. This shouldn’t be an issue with the next patch, though.

There is also no post-game content, which is normally fine, but it would be fun to keep running missions with the squad you’ve built.

reviews.author: Robobob

One of the best Star Wars games I've played in awhile.  Love the X-Com tactical crossover.  This reminds me of the golden age of Star Wars gaming in the 90s to early 2000s where Star Wars was crossed over with popular gaming genres: Doom --> Dark Forces.  Quake --> Jedi Knight.  RPGs --> KotoR, flight simulators --> X-Wing/TIE Fighter.
The characters are all fun, unique and interesting.  You can tell the writers really love the SW universe and do it justice.  The devs do a good job of throwing new and challenging things at you through out the  story missions, though the side missions can be a little redundant and repetitive. reviews.author: S1RO
reviews.quote:
Star Wars Zero Company, 39 Cycles

A brilliant, highly strategic Star Wars spin on the XCOM formula, severely held back by abysmal optimization and mission-breaking **** a technical level, optimization is shockingly poor. Given the visual fidelity, performance shouldn't be an issue at native resolution on an RTX 3070, yet the stability is a massive drawback. The game occasionally freezes mid-mission, and inputs like the Assault class rocket launcher can suffer delays. These issues forced me to restart near-finished missions on three separate occasions.

Mechanically, it plays like a more forgiving XCOM. Standard operations (saving NPCs, planting bombs, defending zones) often recycle maps, but story and companion missions inject much-needed variety with unique twists and arenas. The game truly shines in its strict time and resource management. You simply cannot do everything. Choosing one mission over another might mean letting the enemy gain critical upgrades, and since enemy forces level up alongside you, every choice carries immense strategic weight. Managing limited intel, currency, capacitors, and infirmary beds forces you to build a deep roster rather than relying on a few elite units. Planning everything from base upgrades to character builds adds another layer of interesting depth and focus.

Narratively, the overarching plot and villains are completely forgettable, especially if you aren't a die-hard Star Wars fan. However, the companions themselves are decent. My favorite companions are the Jedi, the Mandalorian bounty hunter, and the Baroness.

Star Wars Zero Company is an accessible, highly engaging tactical game. If you love Star Wars or turn-based strategy, the gripping gameplay loop guarantees a good time, provided you have the patience to tolerate its technical flaws.

reviews.author: moby04
reviews.quote:
The game is genuinely poor.

I’m not judging the setting itself, as Star Wars isn't really my cup of tea. I liked the original trilogy, and I even enjoyed the 2000s prequel trilogy. But the further it went, the more lore holes I noticed. So, overall, the setting is just a setting to me—it neither excites me nor leaves me cold (it is what it is).

I am judging it purely on how the title holds up as a tactical game. And frankly, it's pretty bad. I mean, sure: they threw in a ton of systems, but overall it feels like spreadsheet-driven design by teams that never actually talked to each other. Most systems sound great in a pitch, but no one bothered to check how they fit together. And they don't fit together at all—practically every sensible mechanical idea is instantly crushed by another system that also sounded fine in a vacuum. They just cannibalize each other when combined.

Difficulty? Give me a break. I started straight on hard and didn't have a single issue throughout the entire game. Well, actually, I had to replay one mission because there was a turn limit to reach a specific point and I ran out of time. But in actual combat? The absolute peak of difficulty was having to send a character to the medbay about three times.

The maps themselves are simply too small for a tactical game. As a result, it’s not really a tactical game at all—it’s just a dressed-up puzzle game: you have all the information, a specific layout—now figure out how to solve it. Zero maneuvering, zero strategy, zero squad positioning. Nothing.

Equipment and base management? Suffice to say that right up until the credits rolled, I never once felt the need to buy anything from the black market, I didn't buy weapon upgrades, and any utility item or weapon mod I equipped stayed there until the very end. Just another hollow mechanic that nobody tested.

Character progression and team relationships are another issue. It’s practically impossible to lose anything. Even operators you never use get skill points (called "focus" here to fit the mystical vibe of the universe) and build relationships with each other (you just have to build them a canteen). The result? Almost zero sense of loss when choosing your squad for a mission...

I’d say that as a whole, it’s a bit of a cargo cult tactical game: the developers seemingly copied every mechanic from the biggest titles in the genre. But they had no damn clue why those mechanics were there or how they interacted with one another. They built a bamboo tower and paved a runway, but nobody bothered to ask why the damn planes stopped landing...

This genre relies on friction, dilemmas, and balancing choices. Here, all the friction has been ironed out, and in its place, they shoved bullet sponges while calling it "difficulty."

The technical state is another story. In almost every mission, the game would freeze for a few seconds—once so effectively that I had to force-quit to the system and start over. On top of that, frame rates regularly dropped into a slideshow—mostly during the pointless third-person filler segments, but it popped up in actual combat too (played on a standard PS5).

My final verdict: 4/10. Nothing special, no real challenge, poor technical performance... but still, it didn't completely turn me off, and I managed to finish it anyway.

reviews.author: TitaniumDragon
reviews.quote: Star Wars: Zero Company is an X-Com like roguelike RPG in space. You play as Hawks, the leader of Zero Company, in the dying days of the clone wars. As a private military contractor, you are hired by the Republic to deal with a strange Separatist cult called the Infinite Coil, which apparently spread themselves via some sort of disease that, when they die, powers up their **** core gameplay is relatively familiar for X-Com fans – you get a set of missions you can choose between, and between missions, you upgrade your base, hire new operatives, get better weapons, and level up your guys from the xp they gained by fighting. On the missions themselves, you get a few different kinds of mission objectives (eliminate everything, capture the target, free captives, reach the zone, etc.) and those will often change mid-mission. “Side quest” missions are mostly 1-2 activities long, all part of one battle, while story missions may have multiple separate sequential battles with brief third person over the shoulder walking between **** the other hand, it is not as familiar as it seems – xp is not gained by killing enemies, but by going on missions with allies, and helping them. This makes classes like the medic good at levelling really **** classes are where the game really differs, as it leans into the star wars theming, and the classes all have pretty significant strengths. Your six unique companions all have unique abilities, and two of them have unique classes that are easily the strongest in the ****’s also where the game difficulty dies, because if you know what you’re doing, you can build really overpowered teams that somewhat trivialize the game.This game is a weird one to rank. The core campaign is too easy even on normal mode, and even hard mode wasn’t actually that much of a challenge. This is because if you know what you are doing, you can put together teams that rapidly steamroll the enemy side, and some of the abilities you eventually get are just really overpowered. It’s also really hard for your operators to actually die, meaning that the whole “anyone can die” aspect of X-Com is absent from this **** the other hand, the game is fairly charming – the main characters all have reasonable enough character, they play off of the main character and each other reasonably well (especially your clone trooper friend and an eventual former Separatist you recruit), and the core of the plot is decent enough, with a bunch of fun “brushes with canon”, both the movies, other TV series, and even other Star Wars video games, including some allies and enemies who you may already be familiar with. And there were several jokes and puns that made me laugh out loud and share them with my **** the gripping hand, the actual core plot feels weirdly incomplete – the Coil is implied to have been created by someone who is sensitive to the force (almost certainly a Sith), and the leader of the Coil has force powers (as do some of her subordinates). There is a moment where you are in a facility which maybe has the answers to this… and you don’t get them. It feels like there was going to be something there, but it doesn’t go anywhere. Fighting the Coil also ends up being overshadowed by other events that are from canon and your little side show feels increasingly irrelevant in the face of that, and it feels like everything was supposed to tie back together, and then it never does. In the end, there’s no real sense of resolution, as you don’t find out even what was really behind the Infinite Coil, as it is implied to be much more than a mere disease, but you beat their leader and then the game just kind of **** there’s the problem that, beyond the game being not very hard, the game also ends up being a bit repetitive, as in the end, it is fairly limited mechanically and because it isn’t very hard, a lot of later game missions just end up with you plowing through them, killing all the enemies before reinforcements even show up, resulting in your victory feeling facile. I didn’t even take damage on many of the later missions, including the very last mission in the game.Well, that’s not true; I did deal a little damage to myself with one of my characters’ **** also doesn’t help that some of the game mechanics felt literally useless; improving my medbay, for instance, made no sense because I never had characters get injured outside of some very early game operative missions where they get injured not by battle, but by a RNG roll between real missions due to being put on assignments that have a risk of injury (which can later be **** in all, I think this is a good game, but I think it has a lot of things that hold it back from a full-throated hearty recommendation, and into more of a “if you like Star Wars, you will like this; if you aren’t into Star Wars, this is a fine X-Com like game but it isn’t going to blow your socks off”. It’s not perfect, but I had fun with it.

reviews.author: Sepherim
reviews.quote: Zero Company sin duda es un buen juego, en la línea de los XCOM o similares. Una de las principales diferencias es que está mucho más orientado a su narrativa e historia, con más cinemáticas, desarrollo de personajes y todo eso, lo cual por un lado añade una profundidad a lo que ocurre y lo que importa pero, a la vez, también quita cierta libertad. El combate es el centro del juego, con una profundidad estratégica bastante buena, producto de las diversas clases de personajes que puedes tener, algunos de los cuales tienen mecánicas muy específicas y propias que molan mucho. La evolución de los personajes es un poco limitada, eso sí, con sus mejoras siendo principalmente pasivas, tanto las que obtienen con px como las que se obtienen con las mejoras de la base. Hay una buena variedad de enemigos, que requieren distintas estrategias y tienen sus particularidades, así como bosses que requieren aprenderlos para luchar contra ellos eficazmente.Gráficamente el juego está muy bien, tanto en ejecución como en diseño, aunque los escenarios parecen un poco genéricos de manera que se pierde un poco lo especial de visitar planetas como Lothaal o así. El sonido está muy bien, tanto las voces (muy bien actuadas) como la música y los efectos. Eso sí, el juego tiene algunos bugs, principalmente con el overwatch, que es super importante y no siempre se activa y funciona como debería. El resultado de todo ello es un juego muy bueno que, sin duda, me dejó con ganas de más. Y es que por cómo progresa el juego, la historia y el tiempo, no hay tanta libertad para hacer las misiones random que genera el juego como me hubiera gustado, y el juego se acabó (de un modo satisfactorio) pero me dejó con ganas de que me dieran libertad post-final para seguir jugando misiones random. Pero bueno, es un muy buen juego igualmente. Un 8,5.

reviews.author: my_name_ash
reviews.quote:
I want to rate this game a 9 so badly. If you love xcom, this games for you. If you love star wars prequels and clone wars, this games for you.

The biggest issue for me is that this game lacks polish in key areas.

Overwatch, a move every character has, sometimes doesn't work or works in a weird way. This can be really frustrating in a hard battle. 

The jetpack continuously fails. Sometimes you can land in areas and sometimes you can't. It's never quite clear where you should and shouldn't be able to land and take off.

The camera continuously gets lost in the battle. It will be the enemy's turn and for some reason the camera is facing a wall and you can't see what happens. 

The big issue for me though is the saving. Sometimes the files can get corrupt on PS5. I had multiple crashes that required me to reload an old save. Sometimes the auto save would just say it failed so I would have to manually save. 

Even with these issues though, I had an incredible time on the game. I just wish it got a little bit more polish near the end of the production.

reviews.author: Blackotter
reviews.quote:
I am not generally a fan of XCOM or tactical shooters, but I wanted to give Zero Company a chance because I was intrigued with the premis of its story. And boy am I glad that I did.
Gameplay-wise, Zero Company delivers a solid experience. The mechanics are fun, feel very star-warsy, and offer a ton of fun. Team customization is especially addicting. But the real gem for me is the writing and storytelling that the team pulled off here. 
The story, the characters, and the way it all ties to the overarching star wars narrative, are just incredible. Hawks as a protagonist is a fantastic addition to the universe, and I simply adore his voice acting, humor and quick wit. I could talk about the conversations in this game for hours, and about how well-writen the character dynamics are. Simply for that fact, the game is a 10/10 for me.
On a purely technical level, UE suffers from its classic issues, as I experienced some stutter and "moments of stillness" when the AI was processing what to do next. But it is not enough to bring my rating down.
I only hope the team gets the recognition and praise they deserve for making such an amazing addition to the Star Wars universe, and for making a game that actually brings joy.

Star Wars: Zero Company is a great tactical, turn-based game. It’s highly cinematic, packed with cool moments and great surprises, and the graphics look solid overall.

reviews.author: Notizblatt
reviews.quote:
Star Wars: Zero Company hat mich in den letzten Tagen verdammt gut unterhalten, obwohl (oder gerade weil?) das Genre der Rundenstrategie für mich noch absolutes Neuland ist.
Wer nach echtem The Clone Wars-Feeling sucht, wird hier absolut fündig!

Mit einer der größten Pluspunkte vorweg: Das Spiel verzichtet komplett auf den Zwang zur nervigen EA-App. Dazu startet man mit einem komplett frei anpassbaren Hauptcharakter und auch die Trupp Mitglieder lassen sich später komplett frei gestalten, was für eine spürbare Bindung sorgt. Apropos Bindung: Das Beziehungs-Feature ist echt klasse geworden. Durch Entscheidungen, die bei den Mitgliedern gut ankommen, und erfolgreiche Teamarbeit im Gefecht stärkt man den Zusammenhalt der Truppe. Das schaltet nicht nur neue Kampffähigkeiten und Dialoge frei, sondern sorgt auch dafür, dass die Charaktere einem richtig ans Herz wachsen. Schade nur, dass es für tiefgründigere Story-Abzweigungen wie Romanzen nicht reicht. Allerdings darf man in optionalen Nebenmissionen mit den spannenderen Mitgliedern der Kompanie Null etwas tiefer abtauchen und mehr von ihren persönlichen Geschichten erleben.

Spielerisch bietet das Ganze einen verdammt runden Genre-Mix: die XCOM-artige Rundenstrategie, die dank des intuitiven Einstiegs auch für Einsteiger wie mich super funktioniert, wechselt sich flüssig mit kurzen Third-Person-Walking-Abschnitten, stimmigen Zwischensequenzen und den textbasierten Einsätzen ab. Letztere sind quasi eine Art Vorbereitung auf die Missionen oder kleine Nebenaufgaben, die man annehmen kann und dafür Belohnungen erhält. Sie sind zwar rein textuell gehalten, was etwas mehr inszenatorischen Umfang hätte vertragen können, aber die möglichen Belohnungen, Konsequenzen und moralischen Tragweiten, die sich direkt auf die Beziehung der Teammitglieder auswirken, motivieren enorm. Auch die Loot- und Upgrade-Spirale greift super: Nach nahezu jeder erfolgreichen Mission schaltet man neue Waffenmods, Ausrüstung, Talentpunkte oder schicke Klamotten frei.

Dazu zündet die Story für mich auf ganzer Linie, sie fügt sich angenehm organisch in die Clone Wars-Era ein und glänzt mit Gastauftritten von bekannten Gesichtern aus den Serien und sogar anderen EA Star Wars-Spielen. Wenn dann noch der Permadeath für Mitglieder greift, ist das auf dem Schlachtfeld an Nervenkitzel kaum zu überbieten. Die Zyklen-Mechanik zwingt einen dabei zu fiesen, strategischen Entscheidungen, einerseits eine verdammt coole Idee, andererseits blutet das Herz natürlich, wenn man wegen der harten Zeitnot nicht jeden Einsatz spielen kann.

Wo Licht ist, ist allerdings auch Schatten. Das größte Manko des ansonsten starken Pakets war ganz klar die Technik... Fehlende Animationen, teils seltsame Kamerafahrten ins Nichts oder random Wartezeiten nach dem Einsatz einer Fähigkeit reißen einen immer mal wieder kurz aus der Immersion. Gamebreaking ist davon zwar zum Glück nichts, aber es ist einfach verdammt schade, weil das Spiel mit etwas mehr Feinschliff viel runder hätte sein können.

reviews.author: KillerTeddyB3ar
reviews.quote: Star Wars Zero Company is a remarkably fun isometric turn-based strategy game developed by a chunk of the staff that worked on the XCOM titles. While it might be simple to just call this game XCOM with a Star Wars skin, I'd argue this game's action economy, story, and approach to gunfights bring quite a lot more to the table. Even if we decide to ignore the well-written story, fantastic voice acting, and the surprisingly fleshed-out cast of supporting characters, the way this game handles engagements with enemies only screams "XCOM!" in the broadest of strokes. This game revolves way more around teamwork and proper use of abilities instead of just flanking an enemy and shooting at them until they die. Almost any source of damage you deal to an enemy builds up adrenaline, which you then use to unleash incredibly strong abilities that completely turn the tide of battle. Medics can buff their allies with a heal that restores HP at the beginning of each round, Trick has a giant AOE RPG shot, a Jedi can throw their lightsaber, etc. The game is very lenient when it comes to injury and death. A character needs to be downed three times before they actually die. Getting hit once doesn't mean they instantly get injured, the game shows you the chance to hit an enemy before you even move. Flanked enemies have a 100% chance to hit, negating any frustration that comes from those missed 95% to hit shots where the player got screwed by RNG despite doing everything right. Most importantly: a single mistake doesn't mean the end of your soldier. ZCOM operates on much larger health pools compared to many similar games. Whereas games of this ilk usually treat a soldier standing out in the open as dead before they can even blink, in this game, putting a tanky soldier with boatloads of HP and armor in the middle of the battlefield to soak up some damage isn't necessarily a bad play. This means that you're not just looking at which cover to move behind, every single tile in this game is potentially a good move with the right operator and the right cast of supporting characters. A missed shot still has a high chance of destroying cover. This means that both you and the enemies are never really safe and will hence rarely stay in one place for long. This results in dynamic engagements where both sides are constantly adapting, repositioning, and targeting the enemies whose cover just disintegrated, all the while attempting to outflank each other. If you couldn't tell from my tone of writing, I really like this game and think it's a fantastic isometric turn-based strategy game. It's unfortunate that ZCOM suffers from a lack of polish. The usual UE5 frame drops and stutters are always present, the game even crashed a few times. Many times your overwatch just doesn't trigger, all the while enemies overwatch your team through walls and solid objects. I've actually missed quite a few 100% shots for some reason. This mostly occurred when I was right above an enemy, but even that wasn't consistent. These issues on their own weren't enough to ruin the experience for me, but I do believe they were present enough to keep this game out of the upper echelon of all-time great strategy games for me.

One of the best management games around, featuring gaming's best implementation of time travel.
With a fun cast of characters, lots to find, and plenty of reasons to challenge yourself with turning back time (or not), Sovereign Tower is definitely one to enjoy this year.
Sovereign Tower is a fun and deep management RPG with great writing and a strong time travel mechanic that pulls at you, for better results or for worse.

Sovereign Tower is surprising, complex, and beautiful. Its take on Arthurian myth is familiar enough to get players interested yet finds plenty of space for originality. Getting the most out of one’s Knights requires decent planning and good use of limited resources. The art is detailed, and it’s a pleasure to interact with all characters. One or two gameplay systems have a limited impact, and it’s a shame that the game doesn’t feature voice acting. But these are small issues, and any player who likes Arthurian myth or man management will find plenty to love in Sovereign Tower.

While you can always count on Wild Wits to deliver a striking, instantly recognizable art style, the studio truly excels at creating a gameplay loop that is as simple as it is addictive. It comes as no surprise, then, that you find yourself breezing through day after day as the tower's ruler, responding to your subjects' requests; this is driven by a blend of depth and simplicity that works incredibly well, all underpinned by a brilliantly executed time-travel mechanic. The writing is another standout feature, striking a masterful balance between tragedy and comedy—delivered at just the right moments and in the perfect measure. Any minor issues you might encounter do nothing to dampen the fun, making this a solid little title from the Brittany-based studio.

Sovereign Tower has a ton to offer, with systems that slowly creep into your subconscious. Even as I write this, I find myself wondering what the next round table dispatch will be and how I can equip my quirky and hilarious knights. The game lets you manage and make decisions at your own pace with a multitude of outcomes from friendships to romance, violence, to financial aid. Whatever path or paths you choose, Sovereign Tower will likely hook you with its fantasy-style hooks.

It boggles my mind how many branching nexuses I personally encountered, let alone how many there must be in total. The narrative flows like a rocky river under an autumn tree. The falling leaves strike the once smooth surface, sending ripples across its entire span before the flow is disrupted by immovable forces sweeping you into the rapids.

After the preview in January, I came away impressed, entertained and intrigued. The full game has done nothing but deepen my appreciation for the game’s fresh approach to the management and RPG genres. Soverign Knights is charming, cheeky and challenging, with lots of depth and surprises in store at nearly every turn.
Sovereign Tower puts you in control of a group of messy yet lovable knights in a management RPG that is constantly surprising in craft and care.

While it boasts an interesting and clearly functional premise, Sovereign Tower’s biggest issue is that it unmistakably runs out of steam as the campaign progresses, unable to sustain the creativity found in the opening chapters. The result is an experience that starts out addictive but ultimately reveals the limitations of a product that, while valuable, would have benefited from further refinement.

MARVEL Tōkon: Fighting Souls has been the most fun I’ve had playing a fighting game in recent years. Looking forward to seeing how they expand the roster and which new characters they will introduce in the near future.

Marvel Tōkon Fighting Souls is a super fun, very accessible and utterly gorgeous fighter with enough content to keep both the hardcore and casual fighting game player busy. As revered as the Marvel vs Capcom series is, Arc System Works have done a fantastic job in taking the Marvel Tag Fighter mantle from Capcom.

Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls is an incredible fighter that captures the high-octane, frantic fun of a superhero battle. Each character is distinct with unique abilities that add personality to every member of the roster. With a focus on assembling your team to unleash mighty combos and huge assists, this team-based battler adds a fresh spin on the genre. While there is plenty of support to aid newcomers, the number of systems in play can become overwhelming and may take time to fully understand. However, once everything clicks, the depth provides an incredibly rewarding experience that encourages experimentation and mastery.

Accessible to players of all skill levels but offering a high ceiling for pros, Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls is one of the best fighting games currently available. From its great selection of modes to its stunning presentation, this is a must-have for Marvel fans and fighting game enthusiasts alike.

With Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls, Arc System Works delivers its best work in years, creating a fighting game that will win over Marvel fans. Its gameplay strikes the perfect balance between accessibility and depth, resulting in a captivating formula that sets a new benchmark for the genre.

A new mainstay in the fighting game community has arrived. ARC SYSTEM WORKS and Marvel combine for an excellent tag-team fighter with a gorgeous art style and roster full of iconic characters in one of the better games released in the genre in recent memory.

Fresh gameplay paired with unprecedented production values make for an all-star pairing in Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls. An accessible gameplay loop paves the way for impressive depth, hopefully securing this tag fighter’s place in the FGC scene for years to come. The dodgy PC port is affecting the crossplay experience at launch, but the PS5 version is flawless and comes highly recommended – with excellent DualSense integration. Meanwhile, the offline experience isn’t quite up to the same level as genre frontrunners like Street Fighter 6, but its various comic book storylines are beautifully illustrated and excellently voiced, with writer Keiron Gillen doing a great job with the scripts. This title is a triumph on the PS5, and a reminder that Sony is capable of greenlighting compelling live service games when it puts its mind to it.

Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls is a breath of fresh air for both Marvel and the fighting game genre. Rather than recycling ideas we’ve been playing for decades, it takes a completely fresh approach that successfully blends the Marvel universe with Arc System Works’ signature brand of madness.

Marvel Tôkon: Fighting Souls is exactly the comeback Marvel fans have been waiting years for. Arc System Works once again demonstrates its mastery of the fighting genre with a game that is visually spectacular, deep in gameplay, and surprisingly accessible to new players.

Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls is an excellent tag fighter that strikes a fantastic balance between accessibility and depth. Its 4v4 system is surprisingly approachable thanks to its emphasis on assists, while a diverse roster, excellent tutorials and plenty of unlockable rewards provide plenty of incentive to keep playing. Add in gorgeous comic-book visuals, a superb soundtrack and smooth online performance, and Arc System Works has delivered one of the strongest Marvel fighting games to date.

reviews.author: SynthTier_music
reviews.quote:
Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls opens with wonderful presentation, animations, character selection, and unique mechanics. The campaign mode features four stories that have a mix of animations and still frames to drive the story for an engaging experience leading to a challenging boss fight. As a pure fighting game, it feels more like a scripted set of inputs or a button mash galore that nerfs skill. 

The auto combo system introduced in Street Fighter 6 was a small mechanic in the game, but Tokon expands on it allowing for multiple auto-combos which can lead into Ultra attacks by just landing 3 heavy attacks in a row. This substantially waters down the game in my opinion. I play this game with my 6 year old son and the moves he can pull off are incredible, but he would not be able to do those same moves in a game like Marvel vs Capcom 2. So I think it's a great game for beginners and kids, but for seasoned fighting game enthusiasts it will feel elementary. I would consider this a big budget title, and the studio holding out on these systems is Netherealm and I hope they stay true to their mechanics with the next Mortal Kombat. 

Conclusion: Beautiful game in every way, watered down fighting mechanics, kid friendly but too easy.

reviews.author: mefisto_777
reviews.quote: It was inevitable that the announcement of this title would draw comparisons to the *Marvel vs. Capcom* games of the 90s and 2000s—titles that brought us so much joy with their highly vertical gameplay. Years later, we have *Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls*, a PlayStation 5 exclusive that brings a Japanese flair to the superheroes everyone knows and **** game’s beauty lies in its animation, which perfectly captures the comic book style. Its primary gameplay experience is found in the story mode—a narrative spanning five arcs centered on defeating "The Champion," an extraterrestrial being that destroys planets. Notably, the Latin American Spanish voice cast includes the actor who voices Frieza in *Dragon Ball*; the voice acting is outstanding, with palpable enthusiasm and passion in every line. It also features extensive character banter, making it fascinating to watch group dynamics unfold.Regarding mechanics, each character fills a specific role in your team composition. You must select a main fighter (or leader), followed by a ranged character, a vertical attacker, and an assault character. While this structure is familiar from the *Marvel vs. Capcom* series, *Marvel Tōkon* demands extreme strategic thinking to align team synergy with your personal playstyle. Arc System Works has done an excellent job balancing a title with high competitive potential—suitable for tournaments like EVO—while keeping it fun and accessible for beginners through mechanics that lower the barrier to entry for those new to the **** greatest strength is undoubtedly the competitive aspect. It features international lobbies where you can train for future tournaments—events the game itself invites you to join so you can test your skills on a global stage. The entry process is seamless, requiring a specific score accumulated through online victories. Furthermore, it offers a wide variety of modes: a Battle Royale mode, classic Versus, a free-for-all brawl, and a campaign that serves as the icing on the cake thanks to its comic-book-style narrative format. It is a game that easily provides over 25 hours of content without ever becoming dull.Visually and aurally, the game is spectacular. The animations, team-up attacks, and Ultimate moves are a feast for the eyes. The soundtrack complements the action perfectly with a blend of jazz, rock, and electronic music that sweetens the combat and imbues every fight with a constant sense of epic scale.Another reason to dive into *Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls* is that it is an incredibly solid game. That said, you should keep in mind that you will encounter Arc System Works' usual habits when designing titles for mass audiences: they stick to their proven formula, avoid taking too many risks, apply their core concepts, and get the job **** conclusion, *Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls* stands out as a resounding triumph in the fighting game genre, masterfully reviving the frenetic, vertical essence of classic titles and adapting it to modern standards. It is a rock-solid offering that shines thanks to its dazzling cel-shaded visual style—which literally makes you feel like you are playing inside the pages of a living comic book—and its impeccable audio, featuring top-tier Latin American voice acting and an electrifying jazz-rock soundtrack that heightens the epic feel of every **** greatest strength lies in the flawless balance of its mechanics: the role system and accessible special move execution welcome beginners, yet the real magic lies in the deep team-building strategy, which demands a high level of tactical skill designed for top-tier international competition. Coupled with a comic-book-style campaign that serves as the icing on the cake and a generous variety of game modes, the experience easily guarantees over 25 hours of pure fun without a hint of monotony. The only thing keeping it from absolute perfection is Arc System Works' decision to play it safe, sticking to their tried-and-true formulas rather than attempting to reinvent the genre. Even so, this takes nothing away from the game's achievements: it is a spectacular, addictive, and polished title that not only honors the legacy of superhero fighting games but also stands as an undeniable contender for Fighting Game of the Year. It is a must-buy for any enthusiast, whether they are looking to compete or simply enjoy a fantastic spectacle. RATING: 8.5/10

reviews.author: HammterVille

Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls has a strong foundation, but its launch state is difficult to justify.

The gameplay and presentation show the potential of Arc System Works' 4v4 fighting system, but serious technical problems on PC (including stuttering, performance issues and reports of input delay and online problems) are particularly damaging in a fighting game where responsiveness is essential.

The requirement for an always-online connection and a PSN account on PC is also difficult to defend, especially for players in regions where PSN is unavailable. These restrictions limit access to a game that players have purchased.

Beyond this game, the industry is moving increasingly toward digital-only ownership. The decline of physical media and the growing concentration of digital distribution under companies like Sony raise legitimate concerns about competition, preservation, and consumer ownership.

reviews.author: Nocheyniebla
reviews.quote:
A Love Letter to a Truly Great Character Game
I'll be honest — I'm a pretty casual Marvel fan. I only really watch the movies at the theater, and I don't even have Disney+. So going into this game, there were quite a few characters I didn't know at all. That said, I do have memories of the older Capcom titles, so I actually started playing while thinking, "Wait, why aren't Gambit and Juggernaut in here?!"
What personally blew me away was Spidey's motion. Just watching the animation of his entire body come alive is mesmerizing, and it's proof that Arc System Works' craftsmanship is truly the best in the world. If they ever made a "Marvel Animation Cinema," I would absolutely go see it — I can't stop daydreaming about it!
To everyone at Arc System Works and PlayStation: thank you so much for creating such a wonderful game.
Honestly, I'm not really the best at fighting games. But just as the Marvel Comics-themed UI suggests, the Episode Mode — where you enjoy the story through animated comics — is absolutely fantastic. Thanks to this mode, I got to discover the charm of characters I didn't know, and I also got to enjoy their relationships with the other major characters. I've completely become a fan.
I even learned that there's a different Ghost Rider who drives a car instead of riding a motorcycle!
Marvel really should promote this game every time one of their upcoming movies — like Doctor Doom or Ghost Rider — hits theaters.
This is one of the great character games in the history of gaming. I offer my heartfelt thanks to everyone involved, and I sincerely hope that many more games made with this much love will continue to be created.

reviews.author: Welsonziron
reviews.quote:
Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls  Nota 8/10

Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls é um ótimo jogo de luta e merece uma nota 8/10. A jogabilidade é divertida, o visual é muito bonito e o elenco de personagens é excelente. Porém, alguns detalhes impedem o jogo de chegar a uma nota ainda maior.

O principal problema está na dublagem brasileira. Além de alguns personagens não terem seus nomes pronunciados da maneira como estamos acostumados no Brasil, muitas vozes simplesmente não combinam com os personagens. Venom, Wolverine e Magneto, por exemplo, ficaram abaixo do esperado. Na verdade, boa parte do elenco poderia ter recebido vozes mais adequadas.

Por outro lado, existem dublagens que ficaram excelentes, como Homem de Ferro, Capitão América e Tempestade. Spider-Man, Magia, Perigo e Deadpool também ficaram muito bons. Ou seja, existem trabalhos excelentes, mas a qualidade não é consistente em todo o elenco.

Outro ponto negativo é o modo de combo automático, que facilita demais a execução dos golpes. Seria melhor deixar o jogador escolher se quer utilizar esse recurso ou não, em vez de torná-lo tão presente na experiência.

No geral, são praticamente esses os principais problemas. Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls é um excelente jogo de luta, mas a dublagem brasileira inconsistente e o sistema de combo automático acabam tirando alguns pontos. Por isso, minha nota fica em 8/10.

reviews.author: Kooshakj80
reviews.quote: Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls is an incredible experience and one of the best fighting games I have ever played. The game is visually stunning and beautiful, and playing it on PS5 gave me the best possible experience. The story was truly amazing and engaging, making me enjoy every moment of the game. Fardust built a great setting here to tell more stories in this world, and the game pairs perfectly with recent deckbuilder Death Howl if you seek more not-quite-a-roguelite pastoral horror vibes. Focused in its vision and flamboyant on the screen, Shards of Order should land with anyone looking for smart dark fantasy storytelling that plays its cards right.

Once you get the hang of it and a feel for how it’s meant to be played… Shards Of Order is a decent bit of fun. The mechanic might take a little to get used to but it’s arguably just a variation of different RPG battles styles, essentially turn based, but where you can alter the way those turns end up by playing with time. Given the very reasonable price… I’d say it’s worth a look if you like deck building games and RPGs with a dark story.

Shard of Order proved to be an excellent addition to the deck-building genre. Unique in its concept, it leaves out the round and action-point mechanics found in almost every game of the genre, replacing them with the concept of time. Simple to grasp yet quite deep, this mechanic remains fresh even after countless battles. The game also benefits from great replayability and a nicely crafted dark-fantasy aesthetic.

Shards of Order initially takes some getting used to, especially while figuring out the party roles, sprawling skill tree and the time-based combat. Stick with it though and there’s an incredibly satisfying deckbuilding RPG waiting underneath.

While Shards of Order maintains a cohesive structural path throughout its campaign, its true strength lies in how dynamically it encourages players to step out of their comfort zones and experiment with diverse strategies for every challenge they encounter. By constantly shifting its tempo and requiring fresh tactics, the game prevents its progression from ever feeling repetitive, rewarding curiosity and creative problem-solving at nearly every turn. Although these sudden shifts in momentum can occasionally introduce friction during high-stakes combat encounters where a steady rhythm feels necessary, this intentional variation ultimately elevates the experience by giving the gameplay exceptional depth, a satisfying learning curve, and immense replay value.

I've had a blast with Shards of Order. I have qualms with some of the narrative presentation and would have loved to see more quality-of-life features in the overworld, but the deck-building and combat are top-notch, as is the art style and overall visual presentation. The  game's linear structure, which creates a purposeful, escalating experience, is also a plus, making this an easy recommendation for fans of the genre.
A gloomy fantasy RPG that clearly wears its passion on its sleeve. Its creative card-based mechanics are pretty addictive, too.

Shards of Order takes the deckbuilder formula and grafts it onto a narrative-driven RPG with no roguelite structure. Its greatest strength lies in combat: cards consume neither mana nor action points, but instead advance a shared timeline, forcing players to calculate how much room they are willing to give their enemies. The deck must be built with discipline and adapted to different encounters, objectives, and monsters. A bleak atmosphere, weighty impacts, and imposing bosses are supported by a strong art direction, although some card illustrations feel visually inconsistent with the rest. The absence of procedural runs reduces both longevity and replayability, but makes the experience more faithful to its soulslike nature.

Shards of Order turns time itself into the cost of every card, creating a tense and rewarding tactical RPG. Its shared deck system, striking dark-fantasy world and memorable battles outweigh the limited card variety, uneven pacing and occasional technical issues.

Shards of Order packs a lot into its short, approximately 10-hour experience, and it did more than enough to keep my attention throughout. Both gameplay and story were highlights in the early game. But it does feel like a bit too much story is trying to fit in too small a package by the late game, with major story beats flying by on the mad dash for the end goal...With that said, I’d do that dash again – and I will. The card battling remains consistently solid, and I’m already looking forward to playing a second time to try out different strategies and deck builds.

Monowave from Studio BBB Inc. is an incredibly creative, addictive, and fun puzzle platformer. It has amazing level and puzzle design, wrapped in a cute, simple narrative. The game ramps up the difficulty at times to offer a frustrating challenge, but nothing that goes against what the game is trying to achieve.
While not perfect, it is a beautifully creative debut full of fresh ideas and gorgeous visuals, and it is a fantastic package for any puzzle platformer fan out there.
MONOWAVE is a delightful puzzle platformer full of emotions and animals, which rewards experimentation and (thankfully) has a lovely hint system.

MONOWAVE is a small game that punches well above its modest premise. Its emotion-as-mechanic system is genuinely smart, fully explored by the time the credits roll. It is consistently rewarding to experiment with. Its hand-drawn, scratch-art visuals give it an identity few other puzzle platformers can match. The platforming beneath all of that cleverness occasionally lags behind the puzzle design. There are also some unexpected difficulty spikes, but neither issue is enough to undercut what is, overall, a thoughtful, often genuinely touching indie surprise. For anyone looking for a short, charming puzzle platformer with real heart behind its mechanics, MONOWAVE is well worth the handful of hours it asks for.

If you haven’t played S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2, ‘Cost of Hope’ marks the perfect time to jump in. Though be warned, this is a story expansion that requires you to have nearly completed the main campaign. It is seamlessly blended into the progression of the story, and it is fantastic. Genuinely scary moments abound, with the title’s trademark gunplay feeling better than ever. Consider playing in the native VO, and lose yourself in the zone.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2 returns to the Zone with The Price of Hope and, above all, an "Update 2.0" that significantly refines the experience. The DLC expands the rivalry between Duty and Freedom with new missions and two endings—preserving open-world freedom—though it suffers from narrative consequences that remain confined to the expansion itself. The update improves lighting, A-Life mechanics, fog effects, balancing, and difficulty customization, while adding new weapons, optics, and binoculars. The result is a more vibrant, solid, and complete adventure, even if some content arrived noticeably late and we will likely be stuck with certain minor enemy AI quirks forever.

STALKER 2's Cost of Hope expansion represents the next generation of a beloved franchise, but this time, it sets the stage for the most major evolution we've ever seen. It's a haunting, emotional, and twisting expansion that might not be perfect, but comes damn close.

Stalker 2 has received its first major expansion—as well as its biggest update to date—and the game is moving in a very positive direction. The foundation was solid at launch, but through successive fixes, improvements, and new content, it is increasingly becoming the game it was always meant to be.

As you wander through the Iron Forest, the care put into its reconstruction is immediately apparent—matching the level of detail found in the locations from the main adventure. The same holds true for the other areas: the aforementioned power plant and the Space Bubble. The latter is a surreal, labyrinthine setting that hosts one of the game's most intense and evocative levels, featuring staircases suspended in the void, rooms reminiscent of Piranesi’s *Imaginary Prisons*, and a generally unsettling atmosphere. This backdrop sets the stage for the plot's pivotal turning point, where Skif, the protagonist, is forced to pick a side. Regarding choices, the experience remains close to the base game: both factions have their own valid reasons and moral ambiguities. In gameplay terms, "choosing" also means following one of two branching paths, which differ in specific missions and narrative moments. In this respect, *Cost of Hope* offers genuine replayability for those who want to see absolutely everything. The themes are also classic, centering on whether or not to exploit the Zone for a greater good—even at the cost of sacrificing many lives and permanently destroying relationships that were already incredibly fragile.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2: Cost of Hope is a fantastic expansion that builds on what made the base game so compelling, even as its slow-burn pacing and punishing gameplay remain largely unchanged. Its strong narrative on two of the series’ popular factions, as well as its deeper dive into the convoluted science-fiction mythos makes it a worthwhile return to the Zone. The addition of Update 2.0 and two new explorable regions, including the iconic CNPP, gives longtime fans more than enough reason to soak in the Roentgens and smell the irradiated roses.
An almost perfect story DLC, even if I have to grit my teeth a little.

Cost of Hope works because it understands that S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2 did not simply need more land, but places, encounters and choices that make exploration meaningful again. Iron Forest, the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant and the Space Bubble succeed where the base game could sometimes feel too spread out. Duty and Freedom bring back one of the series’ defining conflicts, even if the characters remain weaker than the ideas they represent. The bestiary plays it safe, but stronger mission design and denser spaces make up for it. Update 2.0 improves the whole experience, but it should remain separate from the DLC’s value.

STALKER 2: Cost of Hope DLC is an excellent story expansion that delivers a new route for Skif to either contain/destroy or explore the Zone. The introduction to the two new major factions feels impactful, and the main characters from each of these factions are likeable. Not only does this DLC expand on the Story, but also on the Zone itself. You get to explore two new regions in the Zone, including the long-awaited CNPP. There are new weapons, new secrets, and new Artifacts to help you in this new chapter of the story.  On top of this new content, Update 2.0 makes the whole game even better with the engine rework.

The best version of S.T.A.L.K.E.R 2, whether you’re a new player or returning veteran. Update 2.0 and Cost of Hope’s DLC missions combine to deliver an impactful experience that is brutal, rewarding, and best when it lets humanity shine.

reviews.author: Amuouths
reviews.quote:
GSC didn't fix any of S2's issues related to gameplay or the amount of side content in the base game, and now they've released a DLC with even less side content than the second half of the base game. I'm not even talking about comparing it to the amount of side content in CoP or in any other major expansions from studios like CDPR.

Instead, they focused on making another CoD/Metro-like main questline, which itself is pretty good, and there's a visible increase in quality compared to the base game. But that doesn't justify the insane lack of side content, the boring exploration that rewards you with the same two medkits and one bandage 95% of the time, or the fact that the expansion doesn't add any new armor or gameplay features, CS and CoP added a whole bunch of gameplay additons compared to the previous game (weapon/armor modification, faction war, achievements that affect a world around you, new items and consumables, long side storylines, detectors for artifacts huntng, etc), CoH adds NOTHING.

The faction war it adds is also a super barebones and gutted version of the faction war from CS, a game that was released almost 20 years ago.

Instead of learning from CoP and putting less emphasis on the main quest and more on smaller stories, they decided to turn STALKER into Metro. If I wanted to play Metro, I would play Metro, not this DLC.

If they don't improve with DLC 2 and this is the future of the series, I won't support this direction with my money anymore. I'm honestly so disappointed.
