Total War: Shogun 2 – Complete Edition is an accessible and modern experience that draws new players into the struggle to unify Japan for the first time, while allowing longtime fans to rediscover this beloved game. Those approaching Creative Assembly’s title for the first time can experience that entire historical period from start to finish, from the rise of the samurai to their fall, thanks to the inclusion of the Rise of the Samurai and Fall of the Samurai expansions. Veterans, on the other hand, will find a game with restored graphics and many quality-of-life improvements to the gameplay. Total War: Shogun 2 remains a masterpiece of the strategy genre to this day, and this new Complete Edition gives us yet another excuse to fight for the shogunate.

It's a spectacular, enormous experience that strategy fans will undoubtedly be happy to play for hundreds of hours, and it should serve as the definitive introduction to the series for new fans moving forward. Is it the best Total War game of all time? Though I definitely have a soft spot for the original Rome release, it's fair to say that this is just about as good as it gets in the genre.

The new edition corrects high-resolution interface issues, modernizes controls, adds the option to adjust settings in the Divided Kingdom, and includes important current graphical features. Total War: SHOGUN 2 - Complete Edition makes it easy to return to one of the best campaigns in the series.

Total War: Shogun 2 – Complete Edition crafts a deep experience. It serves its grand strategy far better than its RTS combat, making enjoyment depend on which side of the gameplay you are mostly looking forward to.

Total War: Shogun 2 Complete Edition is something I’m absolutely thrilled to have in my life. I looked at it with rose-coloured sake glasses, and it did not disappoint. This is every bit the experience I recall from half a lifetime ago, with a new coat of ukiyo-e paint. The new visuals are absolutely stunning and bring one of the Total War franchise’s quintessential titles into modernity. I like to think I am a master of the new tactical features, but I fear that is far from the truth. This is a great “Complete Edition” for fans and newcomers alike.

I’m left feeling thoroughly satisfied with this grand new addition to a game I already loved. If you’re someone who’s been starving for Dragon’s Dogma content for a few years, then this is just about everything you were hoping for, and if you’re someone who bounced off the base game, then a lot of the more notable points of friction have been eased. Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is a tighter and more focused DLC that still manages to bring in very nearly everything about what made the base game such an incredible experience.
Dark Arisen has not only made Dragon’s Dogma 2 a must-play RPG, but it’s also one of Capcom’s best games in years.

Returning to Dragon's Dogma II is a treat in itself, but tack on a couple dozen hours of fantastic new content in a harsh but beautiful new region, and this is the best the game has ever been. Dark Arisen's unique loot cycle and challenging encounters work alongside a compelling new story to make it worth every penny.

If you love the idea of a grand fantasy adventure and experience a truly unique and immersive single-player game where you feel as if you’re actually accompanied by real players going on treacherous adventures together, with great moment-to-moment gameplay, then please, please play Dragon’s Dogma 2, then continue your adventure into Dark Arisen DLC and the cold lands of Norgan.

Dragon's Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is often Capcom's open world RPG at its absolute peak. It's one hell of a meaty expansion, delivering a surprisingly involved story, joyous exploration, and deeply compelling combat. A transformative DLC.

Whether you’re a lapsed Arisen returning to the world of Dragon’s Dogma or a curious newcomer finally taking the plunge after Capcom’s stellar track record convinced you it was worth it, Dark Arisen proves to be an absolute delight. It builds upon the excellent foundation Capcom’s been polishing for the past two years, with sharp combat and engaging exploration. It challenges you with brutal new trials, all the while making the grind less unbearable. It cements Dragon’s Dogma 2 as an unforgettable experience.

Dragon’s Dogma II: Dark Arisen does what the original expansion had accomplished and set the bar with 20 hours more. With both Dark Arisen’s original premise and the Lost Rites challenges, there is more things to do, fight, and see, within the world even before deciding to end it at the finishing fight. While some things do remain the same from its 2024 base, the effort and vastness make up for it doesn’t demand a slow crawl, but a satisfying slow pain-and-gain run. For those who could tear themselves away from Crimson Desert, this Action RPG might be for you.

The Dark Arisen expansion for Dragon’s Dogma 2 adds a ton of new content to the base game, along with much-needed quality-of-life improvements that make the overall experience the most definitive one yet. If you enjoyed the base game, Dark Arisen is a must-play.

Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is an excellent expansion that builds on the base game's strongest elements while ironing out enough of the friction its weaker parts caused upon release. It advances the foundations of its exploration and combat loop, making it feel like the definitive version of those systems and something worth diving into right away.

Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is what expansions are truly about. The wholly distinct and dangerous region of Norgan sends players to explore the treacherous cold for new threats. What will be uncovered is a rich story, phenomenal encounters, and a wealth of new content that pushes Dragon’s Dogma 2 into the territory of an unforgettable journey.

Order of the Sinking Star is a masterpiece. Its immaculate, mind-bending puzzles are perfectly designed to make you feel spectacularly stupid and then phenomenally smart. Its interconnected world, progressive revelation of layered mechanics, and post-credits continuation make it the ultimate Sokoban experience.

Order of the Sinking Star is a demanding and inventive puzzle adventure that constantly finds new ways to challenge your understanding of its rules. Its four distinct worlds, character-driven limitations, and increasingly intertwined mechanics make solving puzzles deeply satisfying, even if prolonged roadblocks can sometimes become exhausting.

Even after The Witness, Braid, and the many PuzzleScript games and Sokoban-likes that form its foundation, I'm sure I've never played anything to match. It’s not just a game of the year contender; fall in its clutches, Order of the Sinking Star might also end up the game you simply play the most, even—and most importantly—when you’re far away from the screen.

There’s no doubt that Order of the Sinking Star is one of the best puzzle games out there. The continual evolution of mechanics sprawling across a puzzle-ridden overworld is vast and exciting, and it’s so cool to see it all come from the same core concept. I like that it tells different stories within this, which leads to the bigger mystery of where we are to begin with. Sometimes it can feel a little overwhelming with every new mechanic introduced and then asked to apply, but it can also create some interesting scenarios that are enjoyable to play through.

Order of the Sinking Star is a massive, generous work full of discoveries, capable of reminding us that the best puzzle games aren't about finding a solution, but about learning to see the world in a different way.

Order of the Sinking Star is a massive and often brilliant puzzle game, built around the idea of constantly evolving rules that initially seem to have exhausted their potential. Its best moments come when different mechanics begin to interact, forcing players to rethink what they thought they had already learned. That same ambition can also weigh the experience down. With more than 1,400 puzzles, the sheer amount of content can sometimes feel excessive, while the difficulty occasionally depends more on remembering old rules than on finding an elegant solution. Even so, it remains an exceptional game for anyone looking for a demanding puzzle experience and willing to invest a considerable amount of time.

Order of the Sinking Star hands you more than a thousand handcrafted puzzles and no tutorials, and that trust makes it special. Intuitive character abilities, four distinct worlds, and a shared Overworld give every solution a sense of ownership, while undo and restart keep experimentation painless. The same philosophy backfires when progress stalls with no sign of what you missed, and the scale wears thin over long sessions. For patient problem-solvers, it is an excellent fit.

Order of the Sinking Star demands a lot from its players, but rewards them with plenty of variety through four distinct directions, each with its own mechanics, style and story. The lack of hints and increasing difficulty can be frustrating, especially for casual puzzlers, but the way the different systems come together in the Gold Rooms creates satisfying aha-moments. It is a game that trusts players to think for themselves, making it a rewarding challenge for puzzle enthusiasts.

Order of the Sinking Star is the most unique puzzle game I’ve ever encountered. Seemingly endless innovation and evolution of mechanics are just some of the key aspects of this game. While it doesn’t always hit the mark in terms of story delivery or length, it maintains its unusual gameplay throughout the many hours of gameplay. If you’re a fan of puzzles, then there’s never been a game more made for you.

Order of the Sinking Star might work better had it been a bit more curated in deploying its massive pile of puzzles, but the occasional frustration and overcomplication is an affordable price of admission to play around with so many fun ideas.

Transport Fever 3 makes building a transport empire deeply rewarding, pairing intuitive tools with engaging logistical challenges. Its charming historical campaign, highly replayable sandbox and excellent performance make it a standout transport management game. Minor interface shortcomings do little to diminish an experience that kept us happily expanding our network after 30 hours.
Transport Fever 3 offers vibrant, superbly animated game worlds where both beauty enthusiasts and logistics optimizers can let loose.

I would recommend Transport Fever 3 to anyone who enjoys city-building games. It opens the door to an entirely new world, with a huge amount of new content and systems capable of consuming thousands more hours of your time.

Transport Fever 3 is a massive game with plenty to offer and tons of fun, especially for genre fans. With a significantly improved UI and streamlined systems, new players can enter the franchise and veterans can focus on more important things than sifting through menus to assign a truck to a new fish cargo line. The simplicity of color coding and the use of radius circles really highlight these UI upgrades. And with so many industries and so much cargo to dive into, there is so much to do that it’s easy to lose track of time, which is exactly what a game like this should be.

Rethinking and centralizing operations is an integral part of Transport Fever 3: tasks initially handled by three small stations will eventually need to be routed through a single, massive terminal—a process that requires meticulous track planning as the lines increasingly crisscross one another. However, you are also free to scar the landscape with hundreds of different railway lines, turning the map into a tangled mess of spaghetti. Your game, your rules: difficulty can be adjusted via numerous options tied to every game mechanic, though I recommend veterans start on "Hard" right away to limit the abundant extra profit opportunities found in "Normal" mode. The game is available in Italian and features an excellent soundtrack.

Transport Fever 3 is a wonderful new addition to the series. With more vehicles, improved graphics, more user-friendly interface, and a modding scene that’s already impressive, I’ve had an absolute blast playing TF3 – and those measly 74 hours I’ve managed to squeeze in over the weekends and late at night are just the beginning. It’s just a shame that, although the game looks lovely, it runs a touch poorly. I really wanted to give it a 9/10, but I simply couldn’t with such severe frame rate drops on high-end hardware.

While its performance and ease of use leave something to be desired, Transport Fever 3 is a wonderfully satisfying tycoon sim that excels at creating an organic flow, with strong macro- and micromanagement systems that let you go as deep as you want and play for as long as you want. [Issue#375, p.55]

While Transport Fever 3 might feel familiar to OG fans of the series, it brings much deeper mechanics and a larger vehicle roster which makes it Urban Games’ most polished transport strategy game yet.

Transport Fever 3 offers extensive freedom in its sandbox mode, while the campaign helps players learn the game and explore its historical setting. Although the menus can initially feel overwhelming, its strong progression system keeps the experience engaging through growing towns and unlocking new vehicles and buildings. Long loading times, FPS drops, and limited graphical improvements are drawbacks, but managing transport lines remains highly engaging.

Transport Fever 3 is an absolute addicting blast to play, but this is a game where the individual has to be willing to learn and endure. The individual sense of progression and the satisfaction tied in makes up for the initial stage of the game, which is learning. It's a long learning curve and much like adding in the pinky to a guitar on Guitar Hero, you'll be opening up your thought process and streamlining more efficient logistics for the betterment of the people in the towns, and the evolution of society. Does this game have some performance issues? Yes, and hopefully they'll be taken care of soon. It feels like a game from 2000, performance issues included. The focus was on providing the devs core idea and laying just enough groundwork to get that idea and experience to players who are interested. It's also only $50 and will provide an endless amount of entertainment.

reviews.author: sumakill

An insultingly trivial economic simulation that makes bankruptcy impossible after the first hour, coupled with a cynical reliance on community modders to provide basic quality-of-life features, completely hollows out strategic management. An overpriced, technically unpolished half-step that disrespects the time and patience of simulation purists.

Their biased, disrespectful, and racist treatment of real historical figures, such as modern Turkey's founder Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, has completely destroyed my goodwill. While different studios make different games, the absolute disregard for historical respect, player community values, and basic quality control across this entire genre has become unacceptable. Between the terrible optimization, the broken cargo logic, and the sheer disrespect from major industry players, I am done. Save your money and skip this frustrating mess.

reviews.author: denixert
reviews.quote:
2/10 – Feels like a copy of the previous game

Honestly, I don’t understand why this is being presented as a new game. Transport Fever 3 feels less like a proper sequel and more like the previous game with a fresh coat of paint.

After spending time with it, I kept asking myself: “What am I actually getting here that I didn’t already have before?” The core gameplay feels almost identical, and most of the changes don’t feel meaningful enough to justify calling this a full sequel.

I expected new ideas, bigger improvements, and mechanics that would make me want to start over and build my transport network from scratch. Instead, I constantly felt like I was playing the same game again.

It’s not necessarily a terrible game on its own, but as a sequel, it feels incredibly underwhelming. If you already own the previous game, I honestly struggle to see a reason to jump to this one unless you desperately want the new features.

It feels like Transport Fever 2 wearing a different shirt.

I really wanted to like this game, but I can’t recommend it at the current price. Maybe after a lot of updates and substantial improvements, it’ll feel like a proper sequel. Right now, though, it just feels like a copy.

reviews.author: MasterofThrees
reviews.quote:
As a niche game, the best comparison is it's predecessor Transport Fever 2.  When comparing, there are areas that are better, but then in areas where it really matters it is much worse.

I am playing on a PC at 2K resolution.  As with the latest The Football Manager, the interface makes me feel that I am not the target audience.  The experience is very much consolified this time around.  It's a management game, so I like to have information that affects my management at my fingertips.  In TF2, I will often have a number of different windows pinned to monitor financials, line performance, individual trains, etc.  All while planning out my next line.  Not so in TF3.  The windows take over the screen as if designed to be viewed on a TV on the opposite side of the room.  And while I can reduce UI scale so it is similar to TF2, having certain windows open prevents you from doing anything else in the game...  And for some reason the map icons become so small they are unreadable!!

Improvements over TF2.  Well, graphics and animations for a start.  Although, that's only noticable when zoomed in.  This is a game where you will spend most of your time zoomed out planning and monitoring your transport network, and in this situation TF2 actually looks better.  They've added some more nuance to supply and demand, including happiness, although I found the happiness system to be broken particularly in the early game.

Overall I feel that while it looks prettier on the surface, this is a step backwards from TF2 in the areas that really matter.

reviews.quote: I’m requesting a refund, assuming it gets approved. I’d been waiting for this game all year and actively following the news on YouTube. I was impressed by TF2 and logged nearly 100 hours in it. However, I lost interest in continuing because I hit optimization limits; the map had grown so complex that the system couldn't handle the load anymore (and mind you, I’m running an RTX 4090).I pre-ordered it the moment it became available, and here’s the verdict:Yes, this is a stripped-down version of TF2. The previous game is leagues ahead of this "new" installment, largely thanks to mods. It’s simply unpleasant to play.From the very first minute, there’s screen stutter and lag—and that’s on my hardware. I don’t know what they were doing during the closed beta, but this is an absolute failure. 40 FPS at ground level and 120 FPS from a bird's-eye view—it’s a joke.There are plenty of bugs in the game:1. One road decided to shift a meter to the left, as if it were a separate entity.2. I couldn't get the meat supply chain working several times because the little helicopter refused to transport it to the warehouse....After playing TF2 for ten years, it’s unbearable to watch buses flip around on the X/Y axis instead of performing a proper U-turn. It’s infuriating when a vehicle is forced to drive all the way to the edge of the road instead of just turning around at the nearest intersection.Developers, do you really think that because we play from a bird's-eye view, these small details don't matter? I deal with enough Excel spreadsheets at work; why would I want to play a simulator of multicolored lines labeled as "routes"? I realize they’ll probably fix this in a couple of years and active modders will polish the game to perfection, but you’re better off playing TF2 than buying this laughingstock.Some people say the visuals have improved? My first thought when loading a map was: "Am I playing TF2 with a cartoon mod?" I’m not asking for realism—that would just unnecessarily overload the game—but the vehicles... I’ve seen better-looking cars in *SimCity* or *Cities: ****, and don't get me started on the map edges. Even in the second game, the feeling of working inside Blender really annoyed me. Why couldn't they handle the map boundaries better? Why not render an endless landscape within view and just use a semi-transparent wall as a barrier? It’s a disaster—seriously, it’s awful. Why do I need to see the layers of the earth? Why not just show the planet's core while they're at it? Am I supposed to find a dinosaur in one of those strata?So, five years of development went by—and what did they actually do? Add a subway and some little helicopters? This game is a scam; they should have just called it a TF2 DLC and pushed an update. Would I have paid for a TF2 DLC and upgrade? YES—but not at the price point of a proper AA game.Bugs: 2/10Optimization: 1/10Graphics: 3/10New mechanics: 2/10Price: 1/10Overall: 1.8/10

Control Resonant is the portrait of a bolder studio. Remedy is never scared of taking risks, and that shows through many ways in this game. Bizarre, inventive and extremely fun to play, Control Resonant will probably be running for all the prizes it can by the end of the year.

Control Resonant gambles on a new genre and it pays off. A stellar cast and some of the strongest art direction you'll find in a game this year make for a sequel that builds on the promise of the original, and delivers even more special moments. Make time for Control Resonant this year. You won't regret it.

With its incredibly fun traversal mechanics and edge-of-your-seat action gameplay, the end result is one of the most imaginative action RPGs I’ve played in years and Remedy Entertainment’s best work yet.
Control Resonant is a shining example of what a studio like this can do when given time and patience, and it's surprising and entertaining at every single turn. An astounding game.

Control is one of the best action RPGs ever made. The game combines an emotional story and rock-solid world-building with deep, satisfying combat and delightful movement. Add a breathtaking, open-ended world to the mix, and you have an absolute masterpiece that will stay with players for a long time to come.

Control Resonant proves unequivocally that Remedy understands the medium. Somehow, in crafting its most video-game-ass video game to date, it's managed to not just retain but amplify its own, peculiar and fascinating brand of storytelling. This is not only an excellent Control sequel, but a damned good character action game in its own right.
Few studios are capable of so consistently capturing that feeling of the new and awe-inspiring, and perhaps none can match Remedy's mastery of it. Resonant indeed.

Resonant is the rare sequel that dares to demand something different from the player of the original, rewiring the gun combat into crunchy melee with style. It’s perhaps more conventional than the 2019 game but executed with such flair that it’s irresistible.

Control Resonant takes the series in a different direction without losing Remedy's identity. The new melee combat is excellent and offers countless build possibilities, while the exploration of Manhattan, the secrets, and the side missions expand the universe beautifully, although enemy variety could be much better and some open-world activities are uninspired, but the overall package is excellent, making Control Resonant one of my favorite games of the year.

Control: Resonant proves that Remedy remains one of the most creative studios in the industry. Its combat, progression, and narrative strike a balance with audiovisual elements that make every setting and melody an integral part of the experience. Remedy doesn’t just build a world to explore—it creates one that invites us to pause, observe, and discover a meaning that continues to resonate long after the credits roll, proving that video games can also be art.

reviews.author: Thiebault
reviews.quote:
After 70+ hours across nine days of thorough exploration, side content, mechanics, and research (including reviews and streams), Control Resonant stands as an exceptional achievement by Remedy. The studio continues its tradition of timeless, meticulously crafted classics that reward patient play rather than day-one rushes. The world is highly compelling: exploration feels purposeful, loot placement is thoughtfully designed (rarely forced or out of place), and the desire to see what lies around the next corner persists throughout.

The game evokes the best of Cyberpunk 2077, Batman Arkham, Witcher 3 (world discovery), and Portal 2 (puzzles and “aha” moments). Combat is deeply satisfying once systems click, becoming almost dance like after 20–25 hours and never grows tedious, for me at least. Movement upgrades should be prioritized early; they transform the initially slower pace and unlock the game’s full enjoyment. The preferred build (Strike + Crush + Ignite + Push combinations with artifacts) delivers strong power fantasy and variety; other combinations also refresh combat effectively. Pushing enemies off ledges is particularly enjoyable.

Atmosphere is the standout strength; stronger even than pure lore or plot, though the story remains distinctive and engaging. Side quests match or exceed the main narrative in quality and interest, offering excellent breaks via puzzles and meaningful rewards. Skipping them significantly reduces the experience. Completing them and upgrading the full arsenal elevates the game from solid to outstanding; players who rush or neglect this often report lower enjoyment, slower progression and tougher early fights.

Most criticism appears unfounded or stems from external factors: limited time, incomplete upgrades, sequence breaking, unclear map navigation (intentionally incomplete for story reasons), hardware limitations, or mismatched expectations. Remedy has already eased early difficulty. Genuine flaws are minor; few non-game breaking bugs, one notable map-related frustration (all fixed now), and the lack of quick weapon swapping mid-combat (game needs this!). The map’s ambiguity encourages exploration but can frustrate players hunting specific loot.

Dylan’s growing power feels tangible and rewarding. The game supports varied playstyles and difficulty scaling through player choices. Humor lands well, and Zoe’s character (voiced excellently by Frankie Kevich, also funny btw) adds warmth and a compelling growth arc. Many players, including a notable number of women, have become strong fans.

For anyone drawn to Remedy’s worlds (Remedyverse) and willing to invest time in exploration and side content, Resonant delivers a near flawless 9.5–10/10 experience. It is a masterclass in design that should enjoy a long sales tail, inspire future titles and expand the fanbase. Objectively solid 8–9/10 for any reasonable players who engage with its systems; a full 10/10 for those who fully immerse themselves. Huge credit to the entire Remedy team for an outstanding, memorable game.

reviews.author: Poouuyya
reviews.quote: I’m currently playing Control: Resonance, and despite having experienced only around 30% of the game, I simply couldn’t wait until I finished it to write this review. I genuinely couldn’t keep this to myself any longer.I can say this without hesitation: I am experiencing one of the best, strangest, most unique, and most indescribable games I have ever played in my life.First of all, I have to give Remedy a standing ovation for having the courage to make something like this. In an era where so many games feel increasingly safe, repetitive, and built from the same familiar formula, Remedy decided to take risks. They created something genuinely different. Something ambitious, weird, unpredictable, and unmistakably their own. And honestly, I have enormous respect for them for having the courage to do it.Then I reached the area beneath the ****.After finishing that section, I genuinely couldn’t stop myself from coming here and writing this review. The game design is absolutely incredible. I have been gaming for more than three decades, and I can honestly say that what I have experienced so far belongs among the most impressive game design I have ever seen. There are moments where you just have to stop and think, “How did they even come up with this?”Huge applause to the director, the designers, and everyone involved in creating this experience. The level design, the atmosphere, the music, the quests, the graphics, the action, the difficulty, and the way the upgrades and progression work — everything has come together in a way that I find incredibly impressive. The combat in particular is incredibly satisfying, and I love how the game gives you room to improve your character and experiment with different upgrades as you progress.I think there is something important to understand about this game: you have to appreciate the worlds that Remedy **** you love the strange, surreal, mysterious worlds created by Remedy and Sam Lake — the worlds of Control and Alan Wake, the obsession with parallel worlds, other dimensions, altered realities, time, and all those wonderfully bizarre concepts — then I genuinely believe you are going to absolutely love this game.Because I am.This is the first time in my life that I have felt compelled to review a game before even finishing it. I have never done this before. I normally don’t care about review scores, and I certainly don’t let other people’s scores determine whether I enjoy a game.What makes it even more impressive is that, despite being a newly released game, I have experienced virtually no technical problems so far. No frustrating performance issues, no major frame-rate problems, nothing that has taken me out of the experience. Everything has been running beautifully for me.I absolutely love this game.I love what Remedy is trying to do. I love how strange it is. I love its design, its atmosphere, its music, its quests, its world, and most importantly, its creative **** you are a fan of Remedy, Sam Lake, Alan Wake, Control, surreal storytelling, parallel worlds, alternate dimensions, mysterious realities, and games that are willing to take genuine creative risks — I strongly recommend experiencing this game for **** you already love that world, you are going to absolutely love what Remedy has created here.I know I do.I haven’t even finished the game yet, and I already feel comfortable saying this Resonance is my Game of the Year.

reviews.author: MikeToTheT
reviews.quote:
Control Resonant is one of those games in which the story keeps you eerily engaged. I find myself refusing to put down the controller because I am excited to find out what is coming around the bend. The game's narrative borrows from the likes of Inception, Exorcist and The Matrix fusing into a strange, adrenaline-fueled experience.

If you played the first Control, the theme is the same. You are facing off with The Hiss, an interdimensional antagonist. Although, there are other entities at play here as you soon find out. The story picks up right where it left off, but this time you are playing as Dylan, Jesse's brother.

The combat is satisfying, especially after a few hours of play time. As Dylan becomes familiar with his paradimensional tools you find the sweet spot with combos and upgrades that allow you to tear through the enemies. Some of these encounters include enemies that are hit sponges and so you really want to tweak your playstyle to accommodate.

Overall the title is immensely satisfying in gameplay and narrative. I will say that Dylan can be a little limp wristed at times and could be a bit tougher as a character, but to each his own. I have had hours of fun with this game. The physics are unique and the creativity is next to none. I wholeheartedly recommend this adventure, especially if you like to be immersed. It's trippy, it's engaging, it's not afraid to go places. It's Remedy.

The Diablo IV: Age of Hatred Collection is an exceptional package and a technically impressive port that has sunk its claws into me. The ever-escalating campaign across three stories, the open-world design, and the sublime endgame all come together to create a fantastic experience on the Switch 2. I was so impressed by just how well Diablo IV fits the Switch 2… The game is built around short bursts of combat, constant progression and the ever-present temptation of just one more dungeon for that one piece of loot. It feels almost tailor-made for a portable system, making the online requirement all the more frustrating. For longtime Diablo fans, this is a substantial package that brings together years of content into one enormous adventure. For newcomers, it offers an incredibly deep action RPG with enough content to potentially keep you playing for hundreds of hours. After spending so much time in Sanctuary, I can safely say that Hell has found a surprisingly comfortable home on Switch 2.

Diablo IV: Age of Hatred Collection brings the complete Diablo IV experience to Switch 2, including the base game and both expansions. It is a substantial package with plenty of content for newcomers, while cross-progression makes it easy to continue playing across different platforms. The Switch 2 version runs well and offers a choice between 30fps Quality and 40fps Performance modes, though the lack of 60fps and always-online requirement are notable drawbacks. Overall, it is a solid way to experience the current version of Diablo IV on a handheld.
Diablo 4: Age of Hatred Collection on Switch 2 is solid value for people who have never experienced it elsewhere.

Diablo 4 arrives on the Nintendo Switch 2 as yet another superb port—both technically and visually—but it fails to reach its full potential by requiring a constant online connection, which is baffling for a console with a portable mode. And, despite having been available on other consoles for three years, it’s launching at a high price, with no option to purchase just the base game.

So, which gamers would I recommend the Nintendo Switch 2 to? It is a fantastic package if you are someone who moves between countries or cities and wants to keep gaming wherever you go. It is ideal for those who enjoy playing while lounging at home, or for players who want to continue their adventures on the Switch 2 because a spouse or child has taken over the TV or computer. However, it is not the right fit for gamers who want to head outdoors to play when bored, or who want to clear a couple of dungeons on the bus or complete a "Helltide" event while waiting in line. Unless you have a portable modem and a generous data plan—or are in a foreign country with seamless Wi-Fi access—getting the most out of the portable experience can be difficult. You can make your final decision based on this.

The requirement to remain constantly connected to the internet limits one of the key strengths of a hybrid console. For those willing to live with that requirement, this is an excellent adaptation of one of the genre's true benchmarks.

Diablo IV: Age of Hatred Collection is one of the best ways to enjoy Blizzard's title for handheld gaming enthusiasts. Beyond the additional content, it brings nearly all its strengths intact, from its gameplay and story to its soundtrack. Sacrifices were obviously made, but that doesn't make it a lesser version.

Diablo IV: Age of Hatred Collection is a successful port, especially in handheld mode, where graphical compromises matter far less and the experience remains thoroughly enjoyable. The package is incredibly rich thanks to the inclusion of both expansions, though occasional performance dips and the mandatory internet connection slightly limit its portability.

Diablo IV: Age of Hatred Collection is an enjoyable and addictive RPG experience that feels like a good fit for the hybrid platform. Some minor missteps aside, the moody art style, addictive loot system, enormous amount of content, and near-infinite replayability make this one an easy recommendation to anyone looking for a good ‘time sink’ for their library. The debate will always wear on about where this one belongs in the overall series hierarchy, but it’s tough to argue that this isn’t one of the best modern examples of an ARPG. Online-only is something to consider, but Diablo IV offers some of the best bang for your buck on the system.

Diablo IV: Age of Hatred Collection is a huge pile of hack-and-slash RPG fun, whether you go it alone or venture forth in a group. With the base game and two meaty expansions’ worth of Sanctuary to explore, this game will keep you busy for dozens of hours. If you really fall into the deep end of keeping up with the seasonal content, you could easily get hundreds of hours out of it. This port makes some sensible compromises to offer a rather playable experience in both docked and handheld play. It’s just a shame that you’ll have to spend all of those in the vicinity of an internet connection. That online requirement is a real buzzkill, and it takes away one of the main reasons a person might want to play it on this console. Still great, just with some caveats to consider.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is one of the most impressive games I’ve played this generation. The sprawling world and multifaceted story are wonders to behold, while the combat walks the perfect line between complexity and accessibility. Though there is a little bit of open-world jank to contend with, you’d be missing out by choosing not to play this game, as it may already be the best release in an extremely competitive September.

Rebel Wolves may have built the game on familiar open-world RPG foundations, but The Blood of Dawnwalker ultimately establishes an identity entirely its own. Its ambitious storytelling, rewarding combat and excellent vampire mechanics make it a genuine Game of the Year contender, and an absolute must-play for RPG fans.

Ultimately, I loved exploring the world Rebel Wolves has built with The Blood of Dawn Walker. While Coen and his companions often feel a bit too young and beautiful for the gritty story they inhabit, Vale Sangora feels rich within the limits of its mountain range. The directional combat was a lovely change from simple three-button combos and a pleasure to master, while the time resource management mechanic helped me maintain focus without feeling overly pressured. If you have ever enjoyed Skyrim, The Witcher, or a Red Dead game, I suspect there is a lot here you will love. My family will soon be complaining that I’m busy saving Coen’s family too often as I run through multiple playthroughs over the coming weeks.

Simply exploring the world counts as a free action for those who just want to see what’s around and discover what they can find, while finding secrets and transforming your Coen as a result is an engaging blast. The scenario writing and character work deliver on all the expectations from The Witcher 3, with plenty of morally tricky propositions for the player to uncover and crack. It’s the sort of game that you want to revisit as soon as you set it down. Strong graphics, great storytelling, and solid gameplay all come together to deliver one of the best games of the year. If you like games like The Witcher 3 or Elden Ring, Blood of the Dawnwalker is a must-play experience. Even if you don’t like those games, the strength of the execution in Rebel Wolves’ first game is worth checking out and admiring.

Supported by sharp combat, deep day-night synergy, a fantastic score, and a lived-in world, the game delivers on its ambitious promises. Minor hiccups like stiff facial animations or initial calendar anxiety do nothing to diminish what Rebel Wolves has achieved here. The Blood of Dawnwalker isn't just an outstanding RPG; it is a landmark statement in game design that proves restraint, atmosphere, and meaningful player agency beat mindless scale every single time. An absolute, brilliantly executed dark fantasy masterpiece.

Most Western RPGs have been overshadowed this year by an incredible run of JRPGs, both those already released and several more looming on the horizon in the coming months. Against that backdrop, The Blood of Dawnwalker might genuinely be one of the best games 2026 has to offer. It has it all and then some, constantly surprising with consummate professionalism and polish.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is a game that lays its ambitions bare at the beginning, and one-by-one pays off all those ambitions in remarkable ways. It’s a game that grips you early on, and sinks its teeth into you more with every passing hour.

The Blood of Dawnwalker understands something that most open-world RPGs seem to forget. You cannot experience everything. Time is always moving forward, and how you spend it is important. Having to make those sacrifices initially frustrated me because I wanted to see everything the game had to offer, but eventually it became the reason I enjoyed the journey so much. It also makes The Blood of Dawnwalker highly replayable, because there will always be things you left behind to discover on another playthrough. And with that, I am off to play it all again.

The Blood of Dawnwalker does almost everything right that you'd expect from an action role-playing game. Exceptional gameplay, a story full of twists and turns, and an immersive gaming experience make Rebel Wolves' debut a contender for Game of the Year.
The Blood of Dawnwalker is a fantastic RPG worthy of diving and sinking your fangs into again and again.

reviews.author: Unsung-Paladin
reviews.quote:
WITCHER 3 + FAR CRY (3,4,5,6) = BLOOD OF THE DAWNWALKER
.
 This was made by a contingent of the group who made the outstanding Witcher 3. The game is in many ways a spiritual successor.
.
I make the Far Cry comparison because the game's main villain abducts your family and is saving them for a blood feast at the end of the month. You have 30 days and nights to power yourself up and empower the resistance against the vampires to storm the castle and save them. The main evil vampire has 3 lieutenants who control 3 regions of the map (à la Far Cry). You do missions to undermine their control, and in return they take punitive actions to make your resistance more difficult, like additional enemy patrols and such.
The whole 30 days thing is interesting because the game is not on an actual timer (thankfully), but when you take specific actions (undergoing a quest or leveling up specific abilities), the timer will progress. 
.
Gameplay wise it's solid. During the day, you are limited to swordsmanship and witchcraft (the spellcasting ability), while at night you can do those 2 plus you have vampire abilities. I have seen arguments that the controls are different from Witcher 3. People are complaining about the combat, but the biggest difference between this and Witcher 3 is a directional block mechanic. The enemy shows if they're going to attack up, down, left, or right. You can do a general block regardless of direction, but that uses up some stamina, while blocking in the correct direction does not.
.
The game is fun, not amazing, but enjoyable and definitely worth playing for Witcher 3 fans who are waiting for Witcher 4 (and hoping it doesn't get ruined by CD PROJECT RED's new staff with Sweet Baby Inc/DEI affiliations and a penchant for injecting modern leftist socio-politics into games).

reviews.author: FanOfFanservice
reviews.quote: Would be a 10 but like a 9.5 or something but couple janky things here or there, good update should make those fleshed out or something for the next game. Story The dark fantasy is so good with the mixture of religious content and fantasy to their core but on its head within a mirror. The way Vrakhir depicted predation and a sense of wanting taking someone’s life force or energy. Coen with his character development and his family being taken, then with how good the writing style is makes it really relate in some older medieval sense. The lore encompasses many themes I have known or read about in some form in my own life like: religion, Christianity in its actual entirety (loaded statement too), occult, mythology, history, legends, and then mix in how the idea of pride or selfishness can make those things palatable in another way on what some might call evil intentions, and you take the vampire/Vrakhir that take Christian ideas, especially something simple as “the blood of Jesus” but change “the blood of Brencis” and you have a literal version of god doing similar miracles but with different ideologies or forms of community they express. The way choices mattered was insanely well done and I loved how options were able to be both good/bad right/wrong as more separate categories rather than equivalent categories. I also appreciate Coen and how he was written, it was cool to feel like I was truly learning through this world in some way. They utilized how dark fantasy can take things we see as grotesque or inhuman and think, hmm maybe that’s a right thing to do though even though it feels bad? (Such as inviting Vrakhir in) Combat Really cool, I always felt like I was Aragorn in LOTR fighting in battles. The counter system was fluid and really rewarding because it was designed in this dynamic environment too with multiple enemies. Sword/claw were cool to switch between, I played a lot of claws when I could or it did bleeding damage, but loved the way counters felt for both. The blood magic/vrakhir-powers were pretty cool and liked how one seems more good and the other seems more bad/evil even though both are sacrilegious. All the powers magic were nice and seemed pretty unique but familiar. Sound/musicI really loved the score and all the sound effects and design choices. The menus, reading books/scrolls in game, and when reading the magic abilities/stats would jump scare was super creepy and set the mood well. Overall One of the bloodiest games out there, one of the best evil aesthetics I’ve seen let alone the religious aspects of everything. I really enjoyed how the story **** me in and with headphones make this super captivating and engrossing. The time mechanic was really what made this game way better, I honestly can’t say how much I loved the feeling it gave to the overall experience. This is going on my favorite games list.

reviews.author: Elfyth
reviews.quote: Great atmosphere and some excellent ideas, ruined for me by opaque quest design. A perfectly reasonable dialogue choice can silently lock you out of an entire major character/ally questline with no meaningful warning, potentially discovered many hours later. I play large RPGs once and explore them properly; a game shouldn't require save-scumming or multiple playthroughs just to avoid invisible traps.

The directional combat was cool for all of 10 minutes before it was just annoying. Combat as a whole is also extremely monotonous and I fought the same 3-4 enemy types for all 10 hours that I played. I also thought the time mechanic would be something cool and new but tying skill tree upgrades to it was another mechanism that didnt seem very well thought out in my opinion. Speaking of the skill tree, it didn't seem to add any truly worthwhile upgrades to combat and I had about 8-10 points to spend when I stopped playing, but didnt really care to invest them because "10% more damage" or similiar upgrades dont really make a meaningful impact in combat that is already slow and boring, especially when you consider that they cost a skill point and time. The time mechanic itself also seemed unusually implemented at times. Like taking 3 hours to destroy like 8 buckets of leeches makes no sense. The UI is clunky at best and having to switch between multiple sub-menus while fighting to use abilities was annoying. Being a vampire at night literally adds almost nothing meaningful to the gameplay itself and solely aids with the story which is boring and generic. The Ubisoft towers from 2009 make an appearance which is the only reason shadow step exists. The shadow step mechanic was just as clunky as the UI and I mostly used it on flat ground to traverse faster. There was one positive aspect in my opinion, though. The choices you make during npc quests were very well thought out in my opinion. In the side content I did, there didnt seem to be clear cut right or wrong decisions, which I love in video games. The moral ambiguity of these side quests forces the player to really think about how they should carry out certain acts and I thought this aspect of the game was outstanding. All in all, I dont think this game is worth 70 dollars at all, which pains me to say because most AAA studios just push out corporatized slop and attempt to monetize every aspect of gaming. I really respect that these devs tried to do something different and I know a ton of people seem to love this game, but for me, it just didnt do enough to keep me interested in playing it and fell flat on the goals it was trying to accomplish.

reviews.author: yugkn
reviews.quote:
I was very hyped for this game from the first trailer. I really enjoyed the first 10 hours; the story was impressive, the prologue had consequences, and the fight mechanics were fun and challenging to play. But after the first 15 hours, I got tired. The world is very empty, it is not worthy and rewarding to explore. You won't find any useful material, only junk that will fill your inventory. There are no beautiful landscapes; the marsh looks exactly like the forest, and there is no diversity in the scenery. Also there are only 5-6 enemy types that get stronger with you; you will fight wolves for like 15 mins at the end of the game, when you're supposed to be OP and a fearsome half-vampire. NGL the wolves and bears were more challenging than any boss fights. The game lacks enemy and boss types; very disappointing. 

The music is a lesser Witcher rip-off; at some point, I was waiting for the le le le le le part to start playing. I was expecting some kind of Balkan music for this game, because it is set in Romania and the Carpathian area, but the developers decided that they want to be a vampiric Witcher copy, so for me, another big L. 

Also, the whole UI is exactly like in the 2015 witcher. The investigation part too. Even the selected dialogue option is yellow like in the withcer 3. Are we for real? They literally used the same formula for their game, but with an emptier world, bad mechanics, and full of bugs.  

And this game costs 70 bucks, like other AAA games. If this game cost 50 dollars, I would look over these critiques, but in 2026 it is expected to have these things in a AAA game.

The characters were good, the choice-consequence mechanics were good, and I wanted to replay it multiple times, but I won't. I just can't fight my way through these boring, repetitive monsters. The fight is fun for like 10 hours, but it gets frustrating after some time because of enemy level scaling. Very, very bad game design decision.

I recommend trying it out, but for me, it's a big missed opportunity. Hopefully, the developers will read the critiques, and they will learn from them and make a better game in the future.

reviews.author: Mean_KoreaNZ
reviews.quote: I found this game incredibly frustrating, slow, and boring. What annoyed me the most was the dialogue-skipping mechanic: you have to hold the 'O' button for about a second to skip, but if the timing is off, that hold period might overlap with the end of the current line. Consequently, the moment you press the button, it skips the *next* line as well, causing you to skip two segments of dialogue at once. I simply cannot understand why they designed it this way; it is extremely inconvenient. There were other issues, too—I really wished there was an on-screen mini-map, and the minor bugs were irritating. Ultimately, I found the game itself unengaging, and with all these inconveniences, I have no desire to keep playing. I’m not sure how it feels for people who buy a single game and play it for a long time, but for a casual gamer like me—someone who buys one or two games a week, enjoys the story much like a movie, and then immediately moves on to the next title—this is truly the worst game imaginable.

reviews.author: Kurama_Hakusho

I also have some issues with some of the other parts of the general gameplay loop, like the secondary missions/activities feeling a bit uninspired and repetitive and the day/night cicles not having nearly enough impact as they should. Also the open world could feel a little empty at times. On the technical side, the game is unfortunately full of bugs and graphic issues, which will hopefully be fixed on later patches. As much as I wanted to love this game, it pains me to say that overall it's really mid and only worth playing if you loved The Witcher, but I wouldn't recommend it for full price

reviews.author: Kwstis_Sidi
reviews.quote:
Rebel Wolves’ debut RPG, successfully sinks its fangs into the dark fantasy genre, delivering a beautifully bleak experience. 
The Atmosphere: The 14th-century Carpathian setting is an absolute triumph of gothic grotesque design. The world oozes a thick, shared sense of dread, flawlessly blending the horrors of the Black Plague with brutal vampire tyranny.
The Storytelling: Anchored by a unique 30-day time constraint, the choice-based narrative forces agonizing, morally grey decisions. The game avoids basic "good vs. evil" tropes, ensuring every choice heavily impacts the valley and its characters.
The Gameplay: The duality of playing a mortal spell-sword by day and a blood-thirsty predator by night keeps exploration constantly engaging. The directional swordplay feels weighted and intentional.
The Downside: The combat loop is occasionally dragged down by a frustratingly erratic camera. During fast-paced fights—especially when shadow-dashing or managing multiple aggressive enemies—the lock-on struggles to keep up, leading to disorienting angles that can disrupt your flow.
Verdict: Despite the finicky camera and a few technical rough edges, The Blood of Dawnwalker is a compelling, high-stakes triumph. It is a must-play for any dark fantasy RPG fan.

reviews.author: xaosyn
reviews.quote:
I have played this game from beginning to end, seen multiple endings, and I'm still working toward a platinum. I am not a person who generally "gives up" on games. 

I love a good open world action RPG. If you liked Witcher, you'll probably like this, but overall, I felt like I'd played this game a dozen times before, and it didn't really stand out from the pack for me.

For most of the game, I found combat repetitive, clunky, and I felt underpowered.  This feeling didn't really go away until I was close to the end of the game, because it took the investment of many, many skill points before I felt like the systems started to gel together. The game pretty much requires you to get good at the directional block system, but the UI for blocking is difficult to keep track of during combat when you and the enemies are constantly moving and the camera is swinging all over the place. Every hit you take feels like a punishment, because for most of the game, healing is a pain in the ass. I felt extremely underpowered especially during the daytime (which the developers have said is intentional), but this made me avoid combat as much as possible during the day. It wasn't until I unlocked several crafting, gathering, and passive health regen perks that I actually felt like I was keeping up with the game's demands.

The speed of combat also feels off to me. It felt like too many things happening at once, too many different UIs to keep track of, between directional blocking, directional counterattacking, the healing and ability UIs being on the same toggle menu, trying to keep track of which menu I was on while being swarmed by enemies and trying to block them, counterattack, heal or fire off an ability, etc. etc. This cycle repeated through my 50ish hours with the game.

The choice to link witchcraft abilites to health loss is interesting narratively, but coupled with a combat-heavy game, it makes health management integral and frustrating, given my criticism of the healing systems.

Exploration felt dull. It was all video game chores in a copy-pasted game world, and we've all done this a dozen times before. If you've explored one cave or killed one pack of bandits, you've explored or killed them all.

There are some graphical issues, mainly textures popping in and out during cutscenes. Nothing buggy, but definitely rough around the edges.

The one thing I didn't really mind was the day/night time management system. I thought it was the one innovative thing Rebel Wolves did, and it did force me to think about what to spend my time on.

I think what I was missing most was a deeper dive into what it feels like to be a vampire, outside of combat.  There are a few vampire-focused games to compare to: Skyrim, Vampyr, Vampire The Masquerade: Bloodlines 1 & 2. There is an interesting world and lore here, I just wanted to spend more time stalking the dark streets of Svartrau, shadowstepping across rooftops to track a victim, navigating vampire politics. I wanted more consequence in my choices.  I never really felt I was making an impact on the world. All quests essentially lead to the same two endings: either you deal with Brencis, or kill him. Everything else is just spice.

I wonder: if the game had been more focused on being a vampire in Svartrau specifically, a more linear story, fewer chores, more focus on the interwoven stories of side characters leading you to various endings, would have been more successful? Something like Mass Effect, Dishonored?

Combolands takes a genre mashup that could easily have felt gimmicky and turns it into something genuinely compelling. It features tight gameplay, combo-driven runs with real strategic depth, a huge amount of build variety to explore, and performance that punches well above its modest development team size. Its biggest weakness is a difficulty curve that flattens out a bit too gently for players craving a real late-game challenge, but that’s a minor complaint against a game this replayable and this cheap. For fans of city builders, roguelites, or anyone who’s ever gotten lost chasing one more combo in Balatro, Combolands is an easy recommendation.

Combolands is an excellent experience that fully pulls off everything it sets out to accomplish. It’s smart, challenging strategy that pushes players to experiment with various mechanics while stacking as many bonuses as possible, and then watching the numbers get bigger. I was kept up far too late at night because of how engaged I was, and I can only say that this is a fantastic first outing for Crux Games, and I look forward to seeing what they make next.

The limitation of Combolands becomes apparent in the long run, when the quantity of available elements no longer translates into a corresponding variety of situations. The minimalist graphics turn each island into a small-scale model; the overall look is pleasing and cohesive, even if the game’s personality is somewhat understated. Buildings are easily recognizable in the early stages, whereas more crowded cities tend to become harder to read. However, the interface effectively organizes a considerable amount of information. The lack of Italian language support is a drawback, given the constant need to read descriptions, combinations, and keywords.

Combolands has a solid foundation, turning an unusual idea into an engaging experience at its best, with an intuitive mix of building, positioning, strategy, and combos that still rewards players who take the time to master its deeper interactions. The variety of guilds, items, builds, progression, and difficulty levels provides plenty of reasons to keep playing, while the satisfying evolution from an almost empty island into a small machine of chained effects is particularly compelling. However, slow structure unlocks, limited map variety, and some unclear mechanics keep the game from reaching the full potential of its premise. Even so, I enjoyed Combolands considerably, and with more polish and variety, it could turn a very good idea into something truly impressive.

I’m not sure what business decisions led to this version being greenlit and produced, though there is more new Steins;Gate in the pipeline so perhaps this was to be the vehicle to remind fans why they loved the game and find some new fans in the process. Whatever the reason, Re:Boot is the definitive edition of a true giant of the visual novel genre. As long as you can get along with the tweaked art direction, I doubt you’re going to have any complaints with Re:Boot.

Steins;Gate is quite simply one of the most important visual novels ever made, and Steins;Gate Re:Boot is the perfect way to play it. Unlike games such as The Adventures of Elliot, each of its endings provides a uniquely satisfying conclusion to the tale, and you will want to seek each of them out before you finish. I suggest you fire up the PhoneWave (name subject to change) and send a message telling your past self to pick the game up. Then you will truly be living in the best timeline.

Steins;Gate remains my favourite VN and one of my favourite time travel stories. For fans of that particular sub-genre of fiction, Re:Boot is an essential play and the new features add to the experience for both newcomers and long-time fans alike.

Steins;Gate RE:BOOT doesn't replace the original, nor does it try to erase what came before. Instead, it stands as a respectful modernization of one of the greatest VNs ever made, redefining its presentation, smoothing out the pacing, and offering enough meaningful new content to justify another trip through its tangled web of both old and new Worldlines. Whether you're stepping into the Future Gadget Lab for the very first time or returning after years watching just the anime, this remake captures everything that made Steins;Gate unforgettable. It's not a perfect remake, but it's easily now the definitive way to experience one of gaming's finest science-fiction stories.

STEINS;GATE RE:BOOT is the perfect way to dive into the universe of Science Adventure’s second installment. The new edition’s animated models are well handled, and the story continues to be just as powerful as it has always been. For people who haven’t already tried out any of the previous versions or have just watched the anime, it’s a fantastic reason to dig deeper into the alternative possibilities of Okabe Rintaro’s journey.

This is, to my tastes, the best version of Steins;Gate - but I don't necessarily see that being the universal opinion. If you've never read or experienced the story, I have no qualms suggesting you start here; I just can't help but wish this wasn't effectively the only option on the market for so many players.

STEINS;GATE RE:BOOT is a slow-burn experience that rewards patience with a compelling blend of science fiction, drama, and suspense. Its thoughtful approach to time travel, modernized presentation, and Phone Trigger system give the story extra depth, while the new scenario and multiple endings offer plenty for fans to discover. It may take its time to get going, but ultimately delivers one of the strongest and most memorable time-travel stories gaming has to offer.

STEINS;GATE RE:BOOT is a game that rewards your patience with some incredible storytelling. The character work is top-notch, and the updated visuals, streamlined story beats, and excellent performances make this easy to recommend to anyone looking for a new story to dive into.

Whether you're a veteran fan or a newcomer to the franchise, STEINS;GATE RE:BOOT is a great choice. With a completely revamped production compared to the original version, this remake delivers beautiful visuals and competent sound work. The story, full of interesting events and characters, is the highlight, admirably balancing Japanese pop culture and technological terms. A great recommendation for fans of anime or visual novels in general.

STEINS;GATE's place in the medium hardly needs explaining. It has long since established itself as one of the most successful visual novels ever made. With STEINS;GATE RE:BOOT completely remaking the original using modern technology, there was little reason to expect much in the way of new content. All it really needed to do was preserve as much of the original experience as possible. Fortunately, STEINS;GATE RE:BOOT does a pretty good job of that, at least more so than STEINS;GATE ELITE.

Over Requiemz is a refreshingly creative take on The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, giving the story a fresh spin by adding some memorable romance to a beloved classic. I greatly enjoyed my time playing this VN and appreciated that it actually avoids attempting to pigeonhole players into playing in certain ways simply to see a “true” ending. Over Requiemz is one portal fantasy I certainly wouldn’t mind getting lost in again.

OVER REQUIEMZ delivers a compellingly dark spin on The Wizard of Oz, using its Fact and Dark Routes to explore damaged characters, psychological breakdowns, and relationships pushed to disturbing extremes. Its broader mysteries and restrained romance do not always land as strongly, but excellent character writing, polished presentation, and believable corruption arcs give this otome game a memorable identity.
All in all, OVER REQUIEMZ is a very solid otome game that made me eager to see more of its tormented main cast. Here’s hoping there’s a second game.

Over Requiemz is a darker otome game that lets you roleplay as the heroine rather than selecting what you think the virtual men want to hear. It’s filled with some satisfying moments as well as packed with heartbreaking and darker turns. I really appreciated some of the narrative choices and found its freeform approach worked well. As long as you know you are getting into a more mature game with dangerous situations, you should have a good time.

Feed the Scorchpot is an intricate experience that delivers an engaging and addictive core loop. The sequence of dice rolling, harvest gathering, adding as much flavor as possible, and then spending resources to deliver an even better result is more complex than it first appears. Accept that relatively quick failure for the first few runs is the price of learning what and how to do. The game also, wisely, gives players the option to simply unlock everything. The art style is simply great, compensating for the relatively limited narrative elements. Feed the Scorchpot is one of the most innovative Balatro-inspired titles and has a ton of small mechanical and artistic touches that make it stand out.
Feed the Scorchpot combines several types of games and genres into a very addictive package. Careful, as you may lose many hours to this one!

Feed the Scorchpot takes a quickly saturating genre mashup and still finds a genuinely compelling identity within it. This is backed by its charming presentation, satisfying core loop, and combinatorial depth. A steep initial learning curve and some frustration around harsh RNG swings are worth going in aware of, but neither stops this from being one of the stronger entries in the current wave of Balatro-inspired hybrids. For fans of Catan, Balatro, or anyone drawn to games about breaking systems in creative ways, Feed the Scorchpot earns its recommendation easily.

Feed the Scorchpot delivers an addictive board-game roguelike experience, balancing strategic planning with the chaotic nature of dice rolls. While the satisfying synergies and charming aesthetic encourage repeated play sessions, the late-game balance suffers from RNG dependencies and unclear feedback, occasionally dampening the otherwise engaging challenge of managing the dragon's hunger.

CULTIC successfully emulates the horror-adjacent boomer shooter greats while carving out its own, compelling niche with terrific and unnerving atmosphere. Great level design, weapons, set pieces and visual flourishes make this something of a must-play.

Cultic goes far beyond a simple homage to the retro style of first-person shooter games, and proves itself right in creating an experience that is undeniably full of good inspirations, but is also unique and different from what the current (or past) market offers. Even with some inconsistencies in the art style and narrative pacing, it doesn't settle for being "just" a great boomer shooter, and is certainly a safe bet for anyone who appreciates an excellent mix of action, cosmic horror, and a healthy dose of gore violence.

Cultic at once feels it’s much too similar to Blood: Refreshed Supply, and yet, it does enough differently to earn an easy recommendation. With a focus on much more deliberate atmospherics and thoughtful level design, not to mention an array of genuinely satisfying weaponry, Cultic is absolutely deserving of your hard-earned cash.

Honoring classic FPS tropes while incorporating modern elements, CULTIC is a fantastic choice for fans of intense gunplay. Its high-quality audiovisual presentation creates a palpable sense of tension that complements the gameplay, pitting the player against both dangerous humans and monsters. A wide array of resources is at the player's disposal, including various weapons, items, and movement mechanics to navigate the levels. Despite some minor issues, it is an excellent pick for fans of engaging and entertaining shooters.

Cultic from developer Jasozz Games is a fun game that is a tip-of-the-hat to old-school first-person shooters from the early 90s, while also sporting some modern gameplay amenities to make it feel familiar to most gamers who love the genre.

CULTIC is a true love letter to classic shooters: fierce, bloody, and insanely fun, it captures the spirit of the great '90s FPS games while adding a crushing horror atmosphere and razor-sharp gameplay that keeps you glued to the screen from start to finish.

Despite its undeniable merits, bear in mind that CULTIC pulls no punches: it begins in a classic, almost electrifying fashion, only to become increasingly sprawling and diffuse. Its core remains the same, but this split personality is something to seriously consider—especially given the shift in pacing and the resulting frustration caused by the more crowded sections.

reviews.author: balie
reviews.quote: Cultic is genuinely one of the best boomer shooters ever created. It has an incredibly interesting setting with awesome gunplay and excellent retro, pixelated visuals. The gameplay is fast and action packed with huge levels and plenty of enemies to blast in challenging, chaotic scenarios. But then there are slower moments, dripping with thick, spooky atmosphere... OMG THE ATMOSPHERE... it's truly remarkable what they manage to achieve with the retro aesthetic. Moments of full-on horror where you are walking around the dark and there are spooky sounds and creepy visuals, and something at the end of a long, dark hallway staring at you or stalking and jumping out at you. Just completely unexpected but pleasantly suprised by the horror elements of this game. An absolute must-play, masterpiece boomer shooter.

Echo Weaver is a thrilling metroidbrainia that turns knowledge into progression, combining a tightly designed time loop with expressive platforming, rewarding exploration, and an engrossing mystery. Its abilities continually recontextualize the world and encourage experimentation, making repeat playthroughs especially compelling. A few minor progression quirks and the strict loop timer may not work for everyone, but Moonlight Kids delivers an inventive and deeply satisfying take on the metroidvania formula.

Echo Weaver is a very compelling concept for a Metroidvania, and presents some truly great gameplay ideas that I don’t think I’ve seen before. It’s a melding of various mechanics and while some of the resulting design choices make the game stumble just short of reaching excellence, the overall experience is one I can still see echoing in my brain for a long time to come.

Echo Weaver successfully blends story and time-manipulation gameplay into a "metroidBRAINia" experience—one where progress stems from the gradual acquisition of knowledge, mechanics, and abilities that were available all along, even if the player didn't realize it. Exploration via time loops is dynamic, and new discoveries are logged in an accessible, instructive way; however, the sheer number of shortcuts, techniques, and connections can eventually become mind-boggling, complicating the flow of this beautiful 2D platformer. The world itself is a massive puzzle, making the game recommended for those who enjoy unraveling the intricacies of its inner workings.

Echo Weaver’s unique approach to the Metroid structure is admirable, unique, and well executed. The sense of discovery is fantastic, and though I realistically probably won’t immediately play the game again, the idea that I could start with knowledge of basically all of the abilities to rip through the game at high speed is an enticing one. Developer Moonlight Kids puts a lot of trust in the player to figure out how it all works, and the reward is palpable. That trust leads to some frustrated, aimless wandering, and the platforming challenges occasionally venture into feeling unfair, but by the end you will feel like a genius. That’s a good feeling to leave a game with.

Echo Weaver is a bold take on the Metroidvania formula: a tightly constructed adventure that wholeheartedly commits to familiar science fiction elements and, in the process, makes them its own. Endlessly creative, sometimes frustrating, but always ingenious, it will worm its way into your brain and won’t let you go until you’re satisfied you’ve done everything it will let you. My advice is to play it today, with a few hours set aside for the first of several sessions that you’ll likely spend before you see and do everything. You’ll probably want them.
